metadata.title: Free nilspaces, double-coset nilspaces, and Gowers norms

extraction_notes.note: Numbered displays that the text calls 'the conclusion', 'the main claim' and 'the following fact' were retyped from equation to claim; EP21 (H'_k = Gamma_k), described as 'the following description', stayed an equation.
Remark A.7 is the argument deriving Lemma 3.5 from Theorem A.6, so it was retyped as a proof of LP13; Remark 3.4 only introduces the term 'filtered degree' and was retyped as a definition.

Theorem 1.20 and Theorem 7.16 state the same U^3 inverse theorem (attributed to Jamneshan-Tao, Thm 1.10, re-proved here); kept as one external node with the Section 7.4 copy in also_stated_at, proved by PP78.
Definitions 3.1, 7.5 and 7.12 repeat Definitions 1.2, 1.9 and 1.10 and are recorded in also_stated_at; Theorem 7.14 is kept separate from Theorem 1.12 because it omits the cocompactness clause.
The 'observation' inside the proof of Theorem 4.1 (lower-degree extensions of free nilspaces split) is cited later in that proof, so it is a Level-1 claim with its own steps rather than a step.
Many numbered displays are tikz commutative diagrams rather than formulas; they are kept as equation nodes with the diagram code as statement.
Defined-term warnings left unresolved on purpose: $G_\bullet$ is used throughout for arbitrary filtrations (not the DP50 convention) and 'equivalent' mostly occurs in its ordinary sense.
The paper outline (Section 1.5), proof roadmaps (e.g. before Proposition 8.4) and motivating discussion paragraphs were not extracted as nodes.

nodes.name: Jamneshan-Tao conjecture
nodes.statement: Moreover, these specific nilspaces are relevant to an interesting recent conjecture of Jamneshan and Tao concerning the inverse theorem \cite[Conjecture 1.11]{J&T}. Indeed, this conjecture posits that in the case of finite abelian groups, the underlying object generating the correlating harmonics in the inverse theorem can always be taken to be a (not necessarily connected) nilmanifold.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: For finite abelian groups, correlating harmonics in the inverse theorem can be taken from (not necessarily connected) nilmanifolds.

nodes.name: Nilcharacter
nodes.statement:
The homomorphism $\phi$ is then replaced by a nilspace morphism\footnote{Note that the quotient notation here takes the wider meaning of quotienting by the \emph{action} of $\Gamma$ ($\Gamma$ is not necessarily a subgroup of $\mathbb{Z}^r\times\mathbb{R}^s$).} $\varphi:\mathrm{Z}\rightarrow (\mathbb{Z}^r\times\mathbb{R}^s)/\Gamma$, and the map $e$ by a Lipschitz function $F:(\mathbb{Z}^r\times\mathbb{R}^s)/\Gamma\rightarrow \mathbb{C}$, thus obtaining what we call a \emph{nilcharacter} on $\mathrm{Z}$:
\[
\chi:\mathrm{Z} \xrightarrow{\quad\varphi\quad} (\mathbb{Z}^r\times\mathbb{R}^s)/\Gamma \xrightarrow{\quad F\quad} \mathbb{C}. 
\]
nodes.section: 1.1 \textsc{cfr} nilspaces as quotients of $\mathbb{Z}^r\times \mathbb{R}^s$ by higher-order lattice actions
nodes.statement_short: A nilcharacter on $\mathrm{Z}$ is a nilspace morphism into $(\mathbb{Z}^r\times\mathbb{R}^s)/\Gamma$ composed with a Lipschitz function to $\mathbb{C}$.

nodes.name: Heisenberg group as a quotient of a free nilspace
nodes.statement: A basic non-abelian example is provided by the Heisenberg group. This group has appeared already in many works in higher-order Fourier analysis since \cite{GT08}; recall that it is the group of $3\times 3$ upper unitriangular real matrices $\mathcal{H}= \begin{psmallmatrix} 1 & \mathbb{R} & \mathbb{R}\\[0.1em]0 & 1 & \mathbb{R}\\[0.1em] 0 & 0 & 1 \end{psmallmatrix}\vspace{0.05cm}$. A special case of what we prove in this paper is that, as a nilspace, the Heisenberg group is isomorphic to a nilspace expressible in terms of structures which are among the most basic ones in nilspace theory, and which play a key role in this paper, namely the nilspaces $\mathcal{D}_k(\mathbb{R})$. (Given any abelian group $\mathrm{Z}$ and $k\in\mathbb{N}$, we denote by $\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z})$ the $k$-step nilspace associated with the filtered group $(\mathrm{Z},\mathrm{Z}_\bullet)$, where the filtration $\mathrm{Z}_\bullet=(\mathrm{Z}_i)_{i\geq 0}$ consists of $\mathrm{Z}_i=\mathrm{Z}$ for $i\leq k$ and $\mathrm{Z}_i=\{\mathrm{id}\}$ otherwise; see \cite[\S 2.2.4]{Cand:Notes1}.) Indeed, the group nilspace consisting of $\mathcal{H}$ equipped with the Host-Kra cubes (relative to the lower-central series) is isomorphic to the product nilspace $F=\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{R}^2)\times \mathcal{D}_2(\mathbb{R})$ (in this special case, this can be checked directly, an isomorphism being $\varphi:(x,y,z)\in F \mapsto \begin{psmallmatrix} 1 & x & z\\[0.1em]0 & 1 & y\\[0.1em] 0 & 0 & 1 \end{psmallmatrix}\in \mathcal{H}\vspace{0.05cm}$). The Heisenberg nilmanifold is the quotient space $\mathcal{H}/\Gamma$ where $\Gamma$ is the \emph{discrete} Heisenberg group $\begin{psmallmatrix} 1 & \mathbb{Z} & \mathbb{Z}\\[0.1em]0 & 1 & \mathbb{Z}\\[0.1em] 0 & 0 & 1 \end{psmallmatrix}\vspace{0.05cm}$. Using this isomorphism, it is easily seen that $\mathcal{H}/\Gamma$ is isomorphic (as a nilspace) to the quotient of $F$ by the action of the group generated by the following transformations on $F$, which are specific examples of \emph{nilspace translations} (see \cite[\S 3.2.4]{Cand:Notes1}): $\alpha(x,y,z)=(x+1,y,z)$ and $\beta(x,y,z)=(x,y+1,z+x)$. Indeed, these two translations correspond (via the isomorphism $\varphi$) to the right multiplications in $\mathcal{H}$ by the elements $\begin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0\\[0.1em]0 & 1 & 0\\[0.1em] 0 & 0 & 1 \end{psmallmatrix}$ and $\begin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0\\[0.1em] 0 & 1 & 1\\[0.1em] 0 & 0 & 1 \end{psmallmatrix}$ respectively, and these elements generate $\Gamma$.
nodes.section: 1.1 \textsc{cfr} nilspaces as quotients of $\mathbb{Z}^r\times \mathbb{R}^s$ by higher-order lattice actions
nodes.statement_short: The Heisenberg nilmanifold $\mathcal{H}/\Gamma$ is the quotient of $\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{R}^2)\times\mathcal{D}_2(\mathbb{R})$ by two explicit translations.

nodes.name: Nilspace $\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z})$
nodes.statement: (Given any abelian group $\mathrm{Z}$ and $k\in\mathbb{N}$, we denote by $\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z})$ the $k$-step nilspace associated with the filtered group $(\mathrm{Z},\mathrm{Z}_\bullet)$, where the filtration $\mathrm{Z}_\bullet=(\mathrm{Z}_i)_{i\geq 0}$ consists of $\mathrm{Z}_i=\mathrm{Z}$ for $i\leq k$ and $\mathrm{Z}_i=\{\mathrm{id}\}$ otherwise; see \cite[\S 2.2.4]{Cand:Notes1}.)
nodes.section: 1.1 \textsc{cfr} nilspaces as quotients of $\mathbb{Z}^r\times \mathbb{R}^s$ by higher-order lattice actions
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z})$ is the $k$-step group nilspace of $\mathrm{Z}$ with filtration $\mathrm{Z}_i=\mathrm{Z}$ for $i\le k$, trivial after.

nodes.name: Free nilspace
nodes.statement: A \emph{free nilspace} is a direct product (in the nilspace category) of finitely many components of the form $\mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{R})$ and $\mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{Z})$ where $i\in \mathbb{N}$. We say that a free nilspace is \emph{discrete} if it is a direct product of components of the form $\mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{Z})$, and that it is \emph{continuous} if it is a direct product of components of the form $\mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{R})$.
nodes.section: 1.1 \textsc{cfr} nilspaces as quotients of $\mathbb{Z}^r\times \mathbb{R}^s$ by higher-order lattice actions
differentia: finitely many components of the form $\mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{R})$ and $\mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{Z})$
also_stated_at: A \emph{free nilspace} is a direct product (in the nilspace category) of finitely many components of the form $\mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{Z})$ and $\mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{R})$ where $i\in \mathbb{N}$. We say that a free nilspace is \emph{discrete} if it is a direct product of components of the form $\mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{Z})$, and is \emph{continuous} if it is a direct product of components of the form $\mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{R})$.

nodes.name: Translation group of $\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{R})\times \mathcal{D}_2(\mathbb{Z})\times \mathcal{D}_3(\mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{Z})$
nodes.statement: Let $F=\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{R})\times \mathcal{D}_2(\mathbb{Z})\times \mathcal{D}_3(\mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{Z})$. Then the translation group $\Theta(F)$ consists of functions of the form \[ (x,y,z,t)\mapsto \left(x+a_1,\; y+a_2,\; z+a_3+a_4x+a_5\binom{x}{2}+a_6y,\; t+a_7+a_8y\right) \] where $a_1,a_3,a_4,a_5,a_6\in \mathbb{R}$ and $a_2,a_7,a_8\in \mathbb{Z}$. Informally speaking, the variable $x\in \mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{R})$ is \emph{continuous} and thus it will only appear in higher-order \emph{continuous} components. Moreover, it is \emph{of step 1}, so in the $\mathcal{D}_3(\mathbb{R})$ component (say) it can appear as a polynomial of degree only at most 2, in order to satisfy the general rule given in Theorem \ref{thm:decrip-trans-group}, according to which the ``step" of the variable (here the step of $x$ is 1) times the degree of its involving polynomial should be less than the step of the coordinate in which this polynomial appears (namely here the step of $\mathcal{D}_3(\mathbb{R})$, which is 3). Similarly, $y$ is of \emph{step 2} and thus (by the same rule) it can only appear in $\mathcal{D}_3(\mathbb{R})$ or $\mathcal{D}_3(\mathbb{Z})$ as a polynomial of degree at most $1$; similarly for $t$.
nodes.section: 1.1 \textsc{cfr} nilspaces as quotients of $\mathbb{Z}^r\times \mathbb{R}^s$ by higher-order lattice actions
nodes.statement_short: Explicit polynomial form of the translations of a 3-step free nilspace, illustrating the step-times-degree rule.

nodes.name: Fiber-transitive group of translations
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be a $k$-step free nilspace and let $\Gamma$ be a subgroup of the translation group $\Theta(F)$. We say that $\Gamma$ is a \emph{fiber-transitive group on} $F$ if the following holds: for all $x,y\in F$, if there exists $\gamma\in \Gamma$ and $i\in[k]$ such that $\gamma(x)=y$ and $\pi_i(x)=\pi_i(y)$, then there exists $\gamma'\in \Gamma\cap \Theta_{i+1}(F)$ such that $\gamma'(x)=y$.
nodes.section: 1.1 \textsc{cfr} nilspaces as quotients of $\mathbb{Z}^r\times \mathbb{R}^s$ by higher-order lattice actions
nodes.statement_short: $\Gamma\le\Theta(F)$ is fiber-transitive if whenever $\gamma(x)=y$ with $\pi_i(x)=\pi_i(y)$, some $\gamma'\in\Gamma\cap\Theta_{i+1}(F)$ also maps $x$ to $y$.

nodes.name: Canonical projection $\pi_j$ on a free nilspace
nodes.statement: Specifically, if $F$ is a free nilspace $\prod_{i=1}^k \mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{Z}^{a_i}\times \mathbb{R}^{b_i})$, the projection $\pi_j$ is defined as the map that just deletes the coordinates with index $i > j$, namely $\pi_j:F=\prod_{i=1}^k \mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{Z}^{a_i}\times \mathbb{R}^{b_i})\rightarrow F_j=\prod_{i=1}^j \mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{Z}^{a_i}\times \mathbb{R}^{b_i})$.
nodes.section: 1.1 \textsc{cfr} nilspaces as quotients of $\mathbb{Z}^r\times \mathbb{R}^s$ by higher-order lattice actions

nodes.name: Induced homomorphism $\eta_j$
nodes.statement: Similarly, note that a translation $\alpha\in \Theta(F)$ can be seen as a translation in $F_j$ just by forgetting about its action on the higher-order components. Thus the projection $\pi_j$ induces a map $\eta_j:\Theta(F)\rightarrow \Theta(F_j)$, which is in fact a group homomorphism.
nodes.section: 1.1 \textsc{cfr} nilspaces as quotients of $\mathbb{Z}^r\times \mathbb{R}^s$ by higher-order lattice actions
nodes.statement_short: Forgetting higher coordinates gives a group homomorphism $\eta_j:\Theta(F)\to\Theta(F_j)$.

nodes.name: Top translation group of a free nilspace
nodes.statement: Finally, recall (using for example  \cite[Lemma 3.2.37]{Cand:Notes1}) that for every $k$-step free nilspace $F$ we have $\Theta_k(F)\cong \mathbb{Z}^{a_k}\times \mathbb{R}^{b_k}$.
nodes.section: 1.1 \textsc{cfr} nilspaces as quotients of $\mathbb{Z}^r\times \mathbb{R}^s$ by higher-order lattice actions
conclusions: Finally, recall (using for example  \cite[Lemma 3.2.37]{Cand:Notes1}) that for every $k$-step free nilspace $F$ we have $\Theta_k(F)\cong \mathbb{Z}^{a_k}\times \mathbb{R}^{b_k}$.

nodes.name: Fiber-discrete and fiber-cocompact actions on free nilspaces
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be a free nilspace and let $\Gamma$ be a fiber-transitive group on $F$. We say that $\Gamma$ is \emph{fiber-discrete} if for every $j\in[k]$, the group $\eta_j(\Gamma)\cap \Theta_j(F_j)$ is a discrete subgroup of $\Theta_j(F_j)\cong \mathbb{Z}^{a_j}\times \mathbb{R}^{b_j}$. We say that $\Gamma$ is \emph{fiber-cocompact} if for every $j\in[k]$, the group $\eta_j(\Gamma)\cap \Theta_j(F_j)$ is cocompact in $\Theta_j(F_j)$.
nodes.section: 1.1 \textsc{cfr} nilspaces as quotients of $\mathbb{Z}^r\times \mathbb{R}^s$ by higher-order lattice actions
nodes.statement_short: A fiber-transitive $\Gamma$ is fiber-discrete (fiber-cocompact) if each $\eta_j(\Gamma)\cap\Theta_j(F_j)$ is discrete (cocompact) in $\Theta_j(F_j)$.
nodes.label: def:FDCA

nodes.name: Fiber-discrete implies discrete; fiber-cocompact does not imply cocompact
nodes.statement: Note that given a fiber-transitive group $\Gamma$, if it is \emph{fiber}-discrete then it is a discrete subgroup of $\Theta(F)$ in the usual sense; see Lemma \ref{lem:closedconseq}. However, note that $\Gamma$ being fiber-cocompact does \emph{not} imply that $\Gamma$ is a cocompact subgroup of $\Theta(F)$; see Example \ref{ex:fiber-co-comp-not-co-comp}. On the other hand $\Gamma$ being fiber-cocompact does imply that the topological space $F/\Gamma$ is compact; this is clear in Example \ref{ex:fiber-co-comp-not-co-comp}, and in general it follows from Lemma \ref{lem:cong-equi} and Corollary \ref{cor:quo-cfr-nil}.
nodes.section: 1.1 \textsc{cfr} nilspaces as quotients of $\mathbb{Z}^r\times \mathbb{R}^s$ by higher-order lattice actions
nodes.statement_short: Fiber-discreteness implies discreteness in $\Theta(F)$; fiber-cocompactness gives compact $F/\Gamma$ but not cocompactness.

nodes.name: Higher-order lattice action
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be a $k$-step free nilspace on $\mathbb{Z}^r\times \mathbb{R}^s$ (i.e.\ $F=\prod_{i=1}^k \mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{Z}^{a_i}\times \mathbb{R}^{b_i})$ where $\sum_i a_i=r$ and $\sum_i b_i=s$). A \emph{$k$-th order lattice action} on $F$ (or on $\mathbb{Z}^r\times \mathbb{R}^s$) is an action by a subgroup $\Gamma$ of the translation group $\Theta(F)$ such that $\Gamma$ is fiber-transitive and fiber-discrete. We say that this action is \emph{cocompact} if $\Gamma$ is also fiber-cocompact.
nodes.section: 1.1 \textsc{cfr} nilspaces as quotients of $\mathbb{Z}^r\times \mathbb{R}^s$ by higher-order lattice actions
nodes.statement_short: A $k$-th order lattice action on a free nilspace is an action by a fiber-transitive, fiber-discrete subgroup of $\Theta(F)$; cocompact if also fiber-cocompact.

nodes.name: Representation of CFR nilspaces as quotients of free nilspaces by higher-order lattice actions
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step compact finite-rank nilspace. Then there exists a $k$-step free nilspace $F$, and a $k$-th order lattice action on $F$ by some group $\Gamma\subset \Theta(F)$, such that $\mathrm{X}\cong F/\Gamma$.
nodes.section: 1.1 \textsc{cfr} nilspaces as quotients of $\mathbb{Z}^r\times \mathbb{R}^s$ by higher-order lattice actions
assumptions: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step compact finite-rank nilspace.
conclusions: Then there exists a $k$-step free nilspace $F$, and a $k$-th order lattice action on $F$ by some group $\Gamma\subset \Theta(F)$, such that $\mathrm{X}\cong F/\Gamma$.
nodes.statement_short: Every $k$-step CFR nilspace is $F/\Gamma$ for a $k$-step free nilspace $F$ and a $k$-th order lattice action $\Gamma$.
nodes.label: thm:gpcongrep-intro

nodes.name: Groupable nilpair
nodes.statement: Let $(G,G_\bullet)$ be a filtered group of degree $k$ and let $K,\Gamma$ be subgroups of $G$. We say that $(K,\Gamma)$ is a \emph{groupable nilpair} in $(G,G_\bullet)$ if any of the following equivalent properties is satisfied: \begin{enumerate} \item For every $x\in G$ and every $i\ge 0$ we have $(Kx\Gamma)\cap(G_ix\Gamma)=(K\cap G_i)x\Gamma$. \item For every $x\in G$ and every $i\ge 0$ we have $(Kx\Gamma)\cap(KxG_i)=Kx(\Gamma\cap G_i)$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 1.2 \textsc{cfr} nilspaces as double-coset spaces
nodes.statement_short: $(K,\Gamma)$ is a groupable nilpair if $(Kx\Gamma)\cap(G_ix\Gamma)=(K\cap G_i)x\Gamma$ for all $x,i$ (equivalently the symmetric condition).
also_stated_at: Let $(G,G_\bullet)$ be a filtered nilpotent group of degree $k$ and let $K,\Gamma$ be subgroups of $G$. We say that $(K,\Gamma)$ is a \emph{groupable nilpair} in $(G,G_\bullet)$ if any of the conditions in Lemma \ref{lem:sym-nil-pair} hold. We then denote the associated double-coset nilspace as $K\backslash G/\Gamma$.

nodes.name: Closed right-discrete and fiberwise cocompact nilpairs
nodes.statement: Let $(G,G_\bullet)$ be a degree-$k$ filtered Lie group such that for each $i\in[k]$ the subgroup $G_i$ is closed in $G$. Let $(K,\Gamma)$ be a groupable nilpair in $(G,G_\bullet)$. For each $i\in [k]$ let $K_i=K\cap G_i$, $\Gamma_i=\Gamma\cap G_i$. We say the nilpair $(K,\Gamma)$ is \emph{closed right-discrete} if for every $i\in[k]$ the group $(KG_{i+1})/G_{i+1}$ is a closed subgroup of $G/G_{i+1}$ and $K_i \Gamma_i G_{i+1} /(K_iG_{i+1})$ is a discrete subgroup of $G_i/(K_iG_{i+1})$. We say the nilpair $(K,\Gamma)$ is \emph{fiberwise cocompact} if for every $i\in[k]$, the group $K_i\Gamma_iG_{i+1}/(K_iG_{i+1})$ is a cocompact subgroup of $G_i/(K_iG_{i+1})$.
nodes.section: 1.2 \textsc{cfr} nilspaces as double-coset spaces
nodes.statement_short: Topological conditions on a groupable nilpair in a filtered Lie group: closedness of $KG_{i+1}/G_{i+1}$ and discreteness/cocompactness of $K_i\Gamma_iG_{i+1}/(K_iG_{i+1})$.
also_stated_at: Let $(G,G_\bullet)$ be a degree-$k$ filtered Lie group such that for each $i\in[k]$ the subgroup $G_i$ is closed in $G$. Let $(K,\Gamma)$ be a groupable nilpair in $G$. For each $i\in [k]$ let $K_i=K\cap G_i$, $\Gamma_i=\Gamma\cap G_i$. We say the nilpair $(K,\Gamma)$ is \emph{closed right-discrete} if for every $i\in[k]$ the group $(KG_{i+1})/G_{i+1}$ is a closed subgroup of $G/G_{i+1}$ and $K_i \Gamma_i G_{i+1} /(K_iG_{i+1})$ is a discrete subgroup of $G_i/(K_iG_{i+1})$. We say the nilpair $(K,\Gamma)$ is \emph{fiberwise cocompact} if for every $i\in[k]$, the group $K_i\Gamma_iG_{i+1}/(K_iG_{i+1})$ is a cocompact subgroup of $G_i/(K_iG_{i+1})$.
nodes.label: def:CRDCnilpair

nodes.name: Sufficient conditions for a double-coset nilspace to be CFR
nodes.statement: Let $(G,G_\bullet)$ be a degree-$k$ filtered Lie group such that for each $i\in [k]$ the subgroup $G_i$ is closed in $G$. Let $(K,\Gamma)$ be a groupable nilpair in $(G,G_\bullet)$ that is closed right-discrete and cocompact. Then the double-coset nilspace $\mathrm{X}=K\backslash G/\Gamma$ is a $k$-step \textsc{cfr} nilspace. Moreover, for each $i\in [k]$ the $i$-th structure group of $\mathrm{X}$ is $G_i/(\Gamma_i K_i G_{i+1})$.
nodes.section: 1.2 \textsc{cfr} nilspaces as double-coset spaces
assumptions: Let $(G,G_\bullet)$ be a degree-$k$ filtered Lie group such that for each $i\in [k]$ the subgroup $G_i$ is closed in $G$.
Let $(K,\Gamma)$ be a groupable nilpair in $(G,G_\bullet)$ that is closed right-discrete and cocompact.
conclusions: Then the double-coset nilspace $\mathrm{X}=K\backslash G/\Gamma$ is a $k$-step \textsc{cfr} nilspace.
Moreover, for each $i\in [k]$ the $i$-th structure group of $\mathrm{X}$ is $G_i/(\Gamma_i K_i G_{i+1})$.
nodes.statement_short: A closed right-discrete cocompact groupable nilpair in a filtered Lie group gives a $k$-step CFR double-coset nilspace with structure groups $G_i/(\Gamma_iK_iG_{i+1})$.
nodes.label: thm:suffDC

nodes.name: CFR nilspaces are double-coset nilspaces
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step compact finite-rank nilspace. Then there exists a degree-$k$ filtered Lie group $(G,G_\bullet)$, and closed subgroups $K,\Gamma$ of $G$ forming a groupable nilpair $(K,\Gamma)$ in $(G,G_\bullet)$ that is closed right-discrete and cocompact, such that $\mathrm{X}\cong K\backslash G/\Gamma$.
nodes.section: 1.2 \textsc{cfr} nilspaces as double-coset spaces
assumptions: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step compact finite-rank nilspace.
conclusions: Then there exists a degree-$k$ filtered Lie group $(G,G_\bullet)$, and closed subgroups $K,\Gamma$ of $G$ forming a groupable nilpair $(K,\Gamma)$ in $(G,G_\bullet)$ that is closed right-discrete and cocompact, such that $\mathrm{X}\cong K\backslash G/\Gamma$.
nodes.statement_short: Every $k$-step CFR nilspace is isomorphic to $K\backslash G/\Gamma$ for a closed right-discrete cocompact groupable nilpair in a filtered Lie group.
nodes.label: thm:cfr=double-coset-intro

nodes.name: Compact nilspaces are inverse limits of CFR nilspaces
nodes.statement: It is known that every $k$-step compact nilspace is an inverse limit of $k$-step \textsc{cfr} nilspaces \cite[Theorem 2.7.3]{Cand:Notes2}.
nodes.section: 1.3 Compact nilspaces as quotients of pro-free nilspaces and as double-coset spaces
conclusions: It is known that every $k$-step compact nilspace is an inverse limit of $k$-step \textsc{cfr} nilspaces \cite[Theorem 2.7.3]{Cand:Notes2}.

nodes.name: Graded pro-free nilspace
nodes.statement: Let $d\in \mathbb{N}\cup\{\omega\}$. For every $i< d$ let $F_i$ be a free nilspace. We call the product nilspace $F:=\prod_{i<d} F_i$ a \emph{pro-free} nilspace, and together with the sequence $(F_i)_{i< d}$ we call it a \emph{graded pro-free nilspace}. We say $F$ is \emph{$k$-step} if each $F_i$ is $k$-step.
nodes.section: 1.3 Compact nilspaces as quotients of pro-free nilspaces and as double-coset spaces
nodes.statement_short: A product of countably many free nilspaces, with its sequence of factors, is a graded pro-free nilspace.
nodes.label: def:free-graded-nilspace

nodes.name: Compact nilspaces as quotients of graded pro-free nilspaces
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step compact nilspace. There exists a $k$-step graded pro-free nilspace $F$, and a fiber-transitive subgroup $\Gamma$ of the corresponding graded translation group on $F$, such that $\mathrm{X}$ is isomorphic as a compact nilspace to $F/\Gamma$ \textup{(}with the quotient topology\textup{)}.
nodes.section: 1.3 Compact nilspaces as quotients of pro-free nilspaces and as double-coset spaces
assumptions: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step compact nilspace.
conclusions: There exists a $k$-step graded pro-free nilspace $F$, and a fiber-transitive subgroup $\Gamma$ of the corresponding graded translation group on $F$, such that $\mathrm{X}$ is isomorphic as a compact nilspace to $F/\Gamma$ \textup{(}with the quotient topology\textup{)}.
nodes.statement_short: Every $k$-step compact nilspace is $F/\Gamma$ for a graded pro-free nilspace $F$ and a fiber-transitive subgroup of its graded translation group.
nodes.label: thm:cpct-as-quo-of-free-inf

nodes.name: Compact nilspaces are double-coset nilspaces
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step compact nilspace. There exists a $k$-step pro-free nilspace $F$, a pro-Lie subgroup $G$ of $\Theta(F)$, and a fiber-transitive group $\Gamma\subset G$ such that, letting $K:=\mathrm{Stab}_G(x_0)=\{\alpha\in G:\alpha(x_0)=x_0\}$ for some $x_0\in \mathrm{X}$, we have that $\mathrm{X}$ is isomorphic as a compact nilspace to $K\backslash G/\Gamma$.
nodes.section: 1.3 Compact nilspaces as quotients of pro-free nilspaces and as double-coset spaces
assumptions: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step compact nilspace.
conclusions: There exists a $k$-step pro-free nilspace $F$, a pro-Lie subgroup $G$ of $\Theta(F)$, and a fiber-transitive group $\Gamma\subset G$ such that, letting $K:=\mathrm{Stab}_G(x_0)=\{\alpha\in G:\alpha(x_0)=x_0\}$ for some $x_0\in \mathrm{X}$, we have that $\mathrm{X}$ is isomorphic as a compact nilspace to $K\backslash G/\Gamma$.
nodes.statement_short: Every $k$-step compact nilspace is isomorphic to $K\backslash G/\Gamma$ with $G$ a pro-Lie group of translations of a pro-free nilspace.
nodes.label: thm:cpct-nil-as-dou-coset

nodes.name: Natural surjective homomorphism $\varphi:\mathbb{Z}^n\rightarrow \mathrm{Z}$
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{Z}$ be a finite abelian group. Then there is a natural surjective homomorphism $\varphi:\mathbb{Z}^n\rightarrow \mathrm{Z}$; namely, letting $\mathrm{Z}=\prod_{j=1}^n\mathbb{Z}/k_j\mathbb{Z}$ be the invariant factor decomposition (where $k_j$ divides $k_{j+1}$ for all $j<n$), we let $\varphi:\mathbb{Z}^n\rightarrow \mathrm{Z}$ be the homomorphism that takes the quotient by $k_j\mathbb{Z}$ in the $j$-th component of $\mathbb{Z}^n$.
nodes.section: 1.4 Main applications
nodes.statement_short: Via the invariant factor decomposition, a finite abelian group $\mathrm{Z}$ is the quotient of $\mathbb{Z}^n$ by a natural surjective homomorphism.

nodes.name: Lifting morphisms through fibrations
nodes.statement: Suppose now that $\mathrm{X},\mathrm{Y}$ are compact nilspaces and that we have a morphism $m:\mathrm{Z}\rightarrow \mathrm{X}$ and a fibration $\psi:\mathrm{Y} \rightarrow \mathrm{X}$. Then the map $g:=m\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\varphi:\mathbb{Z}^n\rightarrow \mathrm{X}$ is a morphism in $\hom(\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{Z}^n),\mathrm{X})$, and it can then be lifted to $\mathrm{Y}$, in the sense that there exists $g'\in \hom(\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{Z}^n),\mathrm{Y})$ such that $\psi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} g' = g$ (see \cite[Corollary A.7]{CGSS-p-hom}).
nodes.section: 1.4 Main applications
assumptions: Suppose now that $\mathrm{X},\mathrm{Y}$ are compact nilspaces and that we have a morphism $m:\mathrm{Z}\rightarrow \mathrm{X}$ and a fibration $\psi:\mathrm{Y} \rightarrow \mathrm{X}$.
conclusions: Then the map $g:=m\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\varphi:\mathbb{Z}^n\rightarrow \mathrm{X}$ is a morphism in $\hom(\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{Z}^n),\mathrm{X})$, and it can then be lifted to $\mathrm{Y}$, in the sense that there exists $g'\in \hom(\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{Z}^n),\mathrm{Y})$ such that $\psi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} g' = g$ (see \cite[Corollary A.7]{CGSS-p-hom}).
nodes.statement_short: A morphism $\mathbb{Z}^n\to\mathrm{X}$ lifts through any fibration $\mathrm{Y}\to\mathrm{X}$ of compact nilspaces.

nodes.name: Family of double-coset nilspaces / higher-order lattice actions; metrization
nodes.statement: A \emph{family of double-coset nilspaces} is an array $\mathcal{N}=((G,K,\Gamma)_{k,i})_{k,i\in\mathbb{N}}$ where for each $k,i$ the triple $ (G,K,\Gamma)_{k,i}$ consists of a degree-$k$ filtered Lie group $(G,G_\bullet)$ and subgroups $K,\Gamma$ of $G$ forming a closed right-discrete and cocompact groupable nilpair. Similarly, a \emph{family of higher-order lattice actions} is an array $\mathcal{M}=((F,\Gamma)_{k,i})_{k,i\in\mathbb{N}}$ where for each $k,i$ the pair $ (F,\Gamma)_{k,i}$ consists of a free $k$-step nilspace $F$ and a subgroup $\Gamma$ of $\Theta(F)$ with a $k$-th order lattice action on $F$. A \emph{metrization} of $\mathcal{N}$ (resp.\ $\mathcal{M}$) is a sequence $D=(d_{k,i})_{k,i\in\mathbb{N}}$ where for each $k,i$ we have that $d_{k,i}$ is a compatible metric on the double-coset space $K\backslash G /\Gamma$ corresponding to the triple $(G,K,\Gamma)_{k,i}$ (resp.\ on the quotient space $F/\Gamma$ corresponding to the pair $(F,\Gamma)_{k,i})$.
nodes.section: 1.4 Main applications
nodes.statement_short: Indexed arrays of double-coset nilpairs or lattice actions, with compatible metrics on the quotient spaces.

nodes.name: Inverse theorem with double-coset nilspaces
nodes.statement: There exists a family of double-coset nilspaces $\mathcal{N}$, such that for any metrization $D$ of $\mathcal{N}$ the following holds. For any $\epsilon>0$ and $k\in\mathbb{N}$, there exists $M_{k,\epsilon}>0$ such that for any finite abelian group $\mathrm{Z}$ and any 1-bounded function $f:\mathrm{Z}\rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ with $\|f\|_{U^{k+1}(\mathrm{Z})}\ge \epsilon$, for some $i\leq M_{k,\epsilon}$ the triple $(G,K,\Gamma)_{k,i}$ in $\mathcal{N}$ satisfies the following: \setlength{\leftmargini}{0.7cm} \begin{enumerate} \item there is a polynomial map $g\in \hom(\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{Z}^n),G_\bullet)$ such that, letting $\pi_{K,\Gamma}:G\rightarrow K\backslash G/\Gamma$ be the quotient map and $\varphi:\mathbb{Z}^n\rightarrow\mathrm{Z}$ be the natural surjective homomorphism, there exists a morphism $m:\mathcal{D}_1(\mathrm{Z})\rightarrow K\backslash G/\Gamma$ with $\pi_{K,\Gamma}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} g = m\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \varphi$, \item there is a continuous function $F:K\backslash G/\Gamma\rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ with Lipschitz norm $O_{k,\epsilon}(1)$, \end{enumerate} and letting $D\subset \mathbb{Z}^n$ be any fundamental domain of $\mathbb{Z}^n/\ker(\varphi)$, we have \[ \left|\mathbb{E}_{x\in D} f(x) \overline{F\left(K g(x) \Gamma\right)}\right|\gg_{k,\epsilon} 1. \]
nodes.section: 1.4 Main applications
nodes.statement_short: Functions with large $U^{k+1}$ norm on a finite abelian group correlate with $F(Kg(x)\Gamma)$ for a polynomial map $g$ into a double-coset nilspace from a fixed family.
nodes.label: thm:inv-double-coset-intro

nodes.name: Additional structure of $G$, $K$, $\Gamma$ in the inverse theorem
nodes.statement: Our proof gives additional information on the Lie group $G$ and subgroups $K,\Gamma$ in the above result. Indeed we obtain that $G$ can be taken to be the translation group of a free $k$-step nilspace $F$ (which is proved to be a Lie group), that $K$ is the stabilizer in $G$ of a point in $F$, and that $\Gamma$ is a discrete subgroup of $G$ such that the pair $(K,\Gamma)$ satisfies Definition \ref{def:CRDCnilpair}. The polynomial map $g$ can also be described in more detail via Taylor expansion \cite[Lemma B.9]{GTZ}.
nodes.section: 1.4 Main applications
nodes.statement_short: $G$ is the translation group of a free nilspace, $K$ a point stabilizer and $\Gamma$ discrete, forming a closed right-discrete nilpair.

nodes.name: Inverse theorem with higher-order lattice actions
nodes.statement: There exists a family of higher-order lattice actions $\mathcal{M}$, such that for any metrization $D$ of $\mathcal{M}$ the following holds. For any $\epsilon>0$ and $k\in\mathbb{N}$, there exists $N_{k,\epsilon}>0$ such that for any finite abelian group $\mathrm{Z}$ and any 1-bounded function $f:\mathrm{Z}\rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ with $\|f\|_{U^{k+1}(\mathrm{Z})}\ge \epsilon$, for some $i\leq N_{k,\epsilon}$ the pair $(F,\Gamma)_{i,k}$ in $\mathcal{M}$ satisfies the following: \setlength{\leftmargini}{0.7cm} \begin{enumerate} \item there is a polynomial map $g:\mathbb{Z}^n\rightarrow F$ such that, letting $\pi_{\Gamma}:F\rightarrow F/\Gamma$ be the quotient fibration and $\varphi:\mathbb{Z}^n\rightarrow\mathrm{Z}$ be the natural surjective homomorphism, there exists a morphism $m:\mathcal{D}_1(\mathrm{Z})\rightarrow F/\Gamma$ with $\pi_{\Gamma}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} g = m\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \varphi$, \item there is a continuous function $\phi:F/\Gamma\rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ with Lipschitz norm $O_{k,\epsilon}(1)$, \end{enumerate} and letting $D\subset \mathbb{Z}^n$ be any fundamental domain of $\mathbb{Z}^n/\ker(\varphi)$, we have \[ \left|\mathbb{E}_{x\in D} f(x) \overline{\phi(\pi_\Gamma(g(x)))}\right|\gg_{k,\epsilon} 1. \]
nodes.section: 1.4 Main applications
nodes.statement_short: Functions with large $U^{k+1}$ norm on a finite abelian group correlate with $\phi(\pi_\Gamma(g(x)))$ for a polynomial map $g$ into a free nilspace modulo a lattice action.
nodes.label: thm:inv-high-ord-latti-intro

nodes.name: Inverse theorem for the $U^3$-norm on finite abelian groups
nodes.statement: Let $\epsilon>0$, let $\mathrm{Z}$ be a finite abelian group, and let $f:\mathrm{Z}\rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ be a 1-bounded function with $\|f\|_{U^{3}(\mathrm{Z})}\ge \epsilon$. Then there exists a 2-step connected filtered nilmanifold $G/\Gamma$ drawn from some finite collection $\mathcal{N}_\epsilon$ (where each such nilmanifold is endowed with an arbitrary compatible metric), a continuous function $F:G/\Gamma\rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ of Lipschitz norm $O_\epsilon(1)$, and a nilspace morphism $g:\mathcal{D}_1(\mathrm{Z})\rightarrow G/\Gamma$, such that $|\mathbb{E}_{x\in \mathrm{Z}} f(x) \overline{F(g(x))}|\gg_{\epsilon} 1$.
nodes.section: 1.4 Main applications
assumptions: Let $\epsilon>0$, let $\mathrm{Z}$ be a finite abelian group, and let $f:\mathrm{Z}\rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ be a 1-bounded function with $\|f\|_{U^{3}(\mathrm{Z})}\ge \epsilon$.
conclusions: Then there exists a 2-step connected filtered nilmanifold $G/\Gamma$ drawn from some finite collection $\mathcal{N}_\epsilon$ (where each such nilmanifold is endowed with an arbitrary compatible metric), a continuous function $F:G/\Gamma\rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ of Lipschitz norm $O_\epsilon(1)$, and a nilspace morphism $g:\mathcal{D}_1(\mathrm{Z})\rightarrow G/\Gamma$, such that $|\mathbb{E}_{x\in \mathrm{Z}} f(x) \overline{F(g(x))}|\gg_{\epsilon} 1$.
nodes.statement_short: A 1-bounded function with $\|f\|_{U^3}\ge\epsilon$ on a finite abelian group correlates with a nilsequence on a 2-step connected nilmanifold from a finite family.
also_stated_at: Let $\epsilon>0$, let $\mathrm{Z}$ be a finite abelian group. Let $f:\mathrm{Z}\rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ be a 1-bounded function with $\|f\|_{U^{3}(\mathrm{Z})}\ge \epsilon$. Then there exists a degree-2 connected nilmanifold $G/\Gamma$ drawn from some finite collection $\mathcal{N}_\epsilon$ of such manifolds (where each such nilmanifold is endowed with an arbitrary compatible metric), a $O_\epsilon(1)$-Lipschitz function $F:G/\Gamma\rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ and a nilspace morphism $\phi:\mathcal{D}_1(\mathrm{Z})\rightarrow G/\Gamma$, such that $|\mathbb{E}_{x\in \mathrm{Z}} f(x) \overline{F(\phi(x))}|\gg_{\epsilon} 1$.

nodes.name: Compact nilspace
nodes.statement: Let us start by recalling that a \emph{compact nilspace} is a nilspace $\mathrm{X}$ equipped with a compact topology such that for every $n\ge 0$ the cube set $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$ is a closed subset of the product (compact) space $\mathrm{X}^{\db{n}}$.
nodes.section: 2 Locally-compact Hausdorff nilspaces
differentia: equipped with a compact topology such that for every $n\ge 0$ the cube set $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$ is a closed subset of the product (compact) space $\mathrm{X}^{\db{n}}$

nodes.name: LCH nilspace
nodes.statement: We say that a nilspace $\mathrm{X}$ is an \textsc{lch}\emph{ nilspace} if $\mathrm{X}$ is a locally-compact Haursdorff second-countable topological space such that the following property holds for every integer $n\geq 0$: \begin{enumerate} \item The cube set $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$ is closed in the product topology on $\mathrm{X}^{\db{n}}$. \item The coordinate projection $p^{\db{n}}:\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})\rightarrow \mathrm{Cor}^n(\mathrm{X})$ is an open map. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 2 Locally-compact Hausdorff nilspaces
nodes.statement_short: A nilspace with a locally compact Hausdorff second-countable topology whose cube sets are closed and whose corner projections are open maps.
nodes.label: def:top-nil-open-maps-version

nodes.name: Corner-completion function $\mathcal{K}$
nodes.statement: For a $k$-step nilspace $\mathrm{X}$, since completion of $k+1$ corners is unique, there is a well-defined function $\mathcal{K}:\mathrm{Cor}^{k+1}(\mathrm{X})\rightarrow \mathrm{X}$ that maps any given corner to the point in $\mathrm{X}$ that completes this corner\footnote{We will denote this completion map by $\mathcal{K}_{k+1}$ when there are many completion functions for different dimensions in the same argument.}.
nodes.section: 2 Locally-compact Hausdorff nilspaces

nodes.name: Continuity of the completion function on LCH nilspaces
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step \textsc{lch} nilspace. Then the completion function $\mathcal{K}:\mathrm{Cor}^{k+1}(\mathrm{X})\rightarrow\mathrm{X}$ is continuous.
nodes.section: 2 Locally-compact Hausdorff nilspaces
assumptions: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step \textsc{lch} nilspace.
conclusions: Then the completion function $\mathcal{K}:\mathrm{Cor}^{k+1}(\mathrm{X})\rightarrow\mathrm{X}$ is continuous.
nodes.label: lem:cont-if-open

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.2
nodes.statement: The map $p^{\db{k+1}}:\mathrm{C}^{k+1}(\mathrm{X})\rightarrow \mathrm{Cor}^{k+1}(\mathrm{X})$ is open and bijective by assumption. Hence its inverse $(p^{\db{k+1}})^{-1}$ is continuous. Composing this inverse with the projection to the coordinate indexed by $1^{k+1}$, we obtain precisely the map $\mathcal{K}$, which is therefore continuous.
nodes.section: 2 Locally-compact Hausdorff nilspaces
nodes.statement_short: The corner projection is an open bijection, so its inverse is continuous; compose with a coordinate projection.

nodes.name: Inverse of the corner projection is continuous

nodes.statement_short: The open bijective corner projection has continuous inverse.

nodes.name: Completion is a composition of continuous maps

nodes.name: A 1-step nilspace with closed cubes that is not a topological group
nodes.statement: On the abelian group $(\mathbb{Z},+)$ let us define the topology $\tau$ generated by all the sets $\{n\}$ for $n\in \mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}$ and the sets $\{0,3^m,3^{m+1},\ldots\}$ for $m\in \mathbb{N}$. It can be checked that this topology is \textsc{lch}. Hence, in particular this is a metric space. We claim that $(\mathbb{Z},\tau)$ satisfies that for all $n\ge 0$, the set $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{Z}))$ is closed in $\mathbb{Z}^{\db{n}}$, but $(\mathbb{Z},\tau,+)$ is not a topological group. In order to prove that the cube sets are closed, note that it suffices to prove that $\mathrm{C}^2(\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{Z}))$ is closed (since every higher-dimensional cube set is an intersection of preimages of 2-dimensional cube sets by continuous coordinate-projection maps). Let $((x_n,y_n,z_n,t_n))_n$ be a sequence in $\mathrm{C}^2(\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{Z}))$ (that is, satisfying $x_n+y_n=z_n+t_n$ for each $n$) and converging to some limit $(x,y,z,t)$. We want to prove that $x+y=z+t$. Note that in this topology there are two types of convergent sequences. If $b\in \mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}$, then $b_n\rightarrow b$ means that $b_n=b$ for $n$ sufficiently large. If $b=0$, then $b_n\rightarrow b$ means that either $b_n=0$ for $n$ large enough, or there exists a subsequence $(b_{n_m})_m$ such that $b_{n_m}=3^{\iota(m)}$ for some strictly increasing function $\iota:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow \mathbb{N}$. Thus, if $(b_n)$ converges then either $b_n$ is eventually constant or we can restrict to a subsequence such that $b_{n_m}=3^{\iota(m)}$ for an increasing $\iota$. Coming back to the convergent sequence $(x_n,y_n,z_n,t_n)$, we have the following exhaustive cases. In the first case, all four component sequences are eventually constant, and we then have the desired closure. In a second case, only one of the sequences has a strictly increasing subsequence, and then (relabeling the subsequence), we have $x_n=3^{\iota(n)}$, and $y_n,z_n,t_n$ are eventually constant. We would then have $3^{\iota(n)}$ equal to the constant $z+t-y$, which is impossible for $n$ large enough. In the third case, two of the component sequences in the tuple $(x_n,y_n,z_n,t_n)$ have a strictly increasing subsequence. Then note that the only subcase here that is not obviously impossible is when these two components are on different sides of the equation $x_n+y_n = z_n+t_n$. Suppose that these components are $x_n$ and $z_n$. Passing to a subsequence if necessary, we may assume that $x_n=3^{\iota_1(n)}$. If, on this subsequence, the component $z_n$ becomes eventually constant (zero), then we are back into the previous case, yielding a contradiction. Otherwise we can pass to a further subsequence in which $x_n=3^{\iota_1(n)}$ and $z_n=3^{\iota_2(n)}$. Then, as $y_n$ and $t_n$ are eventually constant, for $n$ large enough they are equal to $y$ and $t$ respectively. But now, if we write the equation $3^{\iota_1(n)}+y=3^{\iota_2(n)}+t$ in base 3, it follows that as $\iota_1$ and $\iota_2$ are strictly increasing, the equation can hold for all such large enough $n$ only if $y=t$ and $\iota_1(n)=\iota_2(n)$. Thus, the limit of $(x_n,y_n,z_n,t_n)$ is $(0,y,0,y)$, which is in $\mathrm{C}^2(\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{Z}))$. The case when three of the component sequences have infinite increasing subsequences (and the fourth one is eventually constant) is treated similarly, considering subcases, in each of which either one obtains a contradiction or a conclusion confirming the desired closure. The case when all four sequences have a strictly increasing subsequence leads to the limit $(0,0,0,0)$, which is in $\mathrm{C}^2(\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{Z}))$ as required. Finally, note that $(\mathbb{Z},\tau,+)$ is not a topological group, because the sequence $(3^n,3^n)$ converges to $(0,0)$ but $3^n+3^n=2\cdot3^n$ diverges as $n\rightarrow\infty$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.4
nodes.statement: Fix any $x\in \mathrm{X}$ and let $(y_n)$ be any sequence of points $y_n\sim_i x$ converging to some $y\in \mathrm{X}$. We just need to show that $y\sim_i x$. This follows by definition of $\sim_i$ and the cube-set closure assumptions; indeed there is an $(i+1)$-cube $\mathrm{c}_n$ equal to $x$ everywhere except at one vertex where it equals $y_n$, and the convergence of $y_n$ to $y$ implies that $\mathrm{c}_n$ converges to a map $g$ that equals $x$ everywhere except at one vertex where it equals $y$. By the closure of $\mathrm{C}^{i+1}(\mathrm{X})$ we deduce that $g$ is a cube, which implies that $y\sim_i x$ as required. To see that the graph of $\sim_i$ is a closed subset of $\mathrm{X}\times \mathrm{X}$, the argument is similar: suppose that $(x_n,y_n)$ is a convergent sequence in this graph, that is we have $x_n\sim_i y_n$ for all $n$ and there is $(x,y)\in \mathrm{X}\times\mathrm{X}$ such that $(x_n,y_n)\rightarrow (x,y)$ in $\mathrm{X}\times \mathrm{X}$. Now $x_n\sim_i y_n$ means there is an $(i+1)$-cube $\mathrm{c}_n$ equal to $x_n$ at all vertices except at $1^{i+1}$ where it equals $y_n$. The convergence $(x_n,y_n)\rightarrow (x,y)$ implies that $(\mathrm{c}_n)$ converges in $\mathrm{X}^{\db{i+1}}$ to a map $g$ equal to $x$ at every vertex except at $1^{i+1}$ where it equals $y$. By closure of $\mathrm{C}^{i+1}(\mathrm{X})$ we have that $g\in \mathrm{C}^{i+1}(\mathrm{X})$, so $(x,y)$ is in the graph of $\sim_i$ as required.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.5
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lem:closure}, each fiber $F$ of $\pi_{k-1}$ is a closed subset of $\mathrm{X}$. It is straightforwardly seen that then the subspace topology on $F$ is also locally-compact second-countable Hausdorff. Fix any such fiber $F$ on $\mathrm{X}$, i.e. an equivalence class of $\sim_{k-1}$. Recall from \cite[Corollary 3.2.16]{Cand:Notes1} that we can regard $F$ as an abelian group by fixing an arbitrary $e\in F$. The group operation can be defined as follows: for any $x,y\in F$, let $\mathrm{c}'=\mathrm{c}'_{x,y}\in\mathrm{Cor}^{k+1}(\mathrm{X})$ be the corner such that $\mathrm{c}'(1,0,1^{k-1})=x$, $\mathrm{c}'(0,1^k)=y$ and $\mathrm{c}'(v)=e$ otherwise. Letting $\mathcal{K}:\mathrm{Cor}^{k+1}(\mathrm{X})\rightarrow \mathrm{X}$ denote the (continuous) completion function, we define $x+y:=\mathcal{K}(\mathrm{c}_{x,y})$. For $k=2$ we can represent this for instance as follows: $(x,y)\mapsto \smallcorner{e}{e}{e}{e}{e}{x}{y}\mapsto \mathcal{K}(\mathrm{c}_{x,y})$. Letting $\iota:F\times F\rightarrow \mathrm{Cor}^{k+1}(\mathrm{X})$, $(x,y)\mapsto \mathrm{c}_{x,y}$, we have that $x+y:=\mathcal{K}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\iota (x,y)$. By \cite[Lemma 3.2.7]{Cand:Notes1} we have $x+y\in F$. Since both $\iota$ and $\mathcal{K}$ are continuous, the addition operation on $F$ is also continuous. A similar argument shows that inversion is also a continuous operation (see \cite[Proposition 2.4.1]{Cand:Notes1}). We have thus shown that on any particular fiber $F$ of $\pi_{k-1}$, the structure and topology of $\mathrm{X}$ induces a structure of \textsc{lch} abelian group on $F$. Next, we prove that every two such fibers are homeomorphic. To see this, let $F,F'$ be any two fibers of $\pi_{k-1}$ and fix any points $e\in F,e'\in F'$, which we shall use as identity elements in the respective groups. For any $x\in F$, define $\mathrm{c}_x\in\mathrm{Cor}^{k+1}(\mathrm{X})$ by $\mathrm{c}_x(1^k,0)=x$, $\mathrm{c}_x(v,0)=e$ for $v\in \db{k}$ and $\mathrm{c}_x(v,1)=e'$ for $v\in \db{k}\setminus\{1^k\}$. We then define the map $\theta:F\rightarrow F'$, $\theta(x):=\mathcal{K}(\mathrm{c}_x)$. For $k=2$, again we can visualize this as follows: $x\mapsto \mathrm{c}_x:=\smallcorner{e}{e}{e}{x}{e'}{e'}{e'}\mapsto \mathcal{K}(\mathrm{c}_x)$. By the continuity assumptions for the corner-completion function, this map $\theta$ is continuous. As its inverse is defined exactly the same way, we have that $\theta$ is an isomorphism of topological groups between $F$ and $F'$. Let $\mathrm{Z}_k$ denote the resulting topological group. Since $\mathrm{Z}_k$ is homeomorphic to each fiber $F$, its topology is \textsc{lch}. The action of $\mathrm{Z}_k$ on each fiber is continuous. However, we need to establish continuity of the action of $\mathrm{Z}_k$ globally on $\mathrm{X}$, that is, we need to show that the map $\mathrm{X}\times \mathrm{Z}_k\rightarrow \mathrm{X}$, $(x,z)\mapsto x+z$ is continuous. This follows from the fact that this map is a composition of the following form (illustrated for $k=2$; for $k>2$ it is similar): $(x,z)\mapsto \mathrm{c}_{x,z }:=\smallcorner{e}{e}{e}{e+z}{x}{x}{x}\mapsto \mathcal{K}(\mathrm{c}_{x,z})$. Again, continuity of completion and the addition function on $F$ implies that $\mathcal{K}(\mathrm{c}_{x,z})$ is continuous as well.
nodes.section: 2 Locally-compact Hausdorff nilspaces
nodes.statement_short: Define the group law on a fiber via corner completion and check continuity; fibers are homeomorphic via completion, and the global action is a composition of continuous maps.

nodes.name: Fibers are closed and LCH
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lem:closure}, each fiber $F$ of $\pi_{k-1}$ is a closed subset of $\mathrm{X}$. It is straightforwardly seen that then the subspace topology on $F$ is also locally-compact second-countable Hausdorff.
nodes.section: 2 Locally-compact Hausdorff nilspaces
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 2.4 gives closed fibers with LCH subspace topology.

nodes.name: Group law on a fiber
nodes.statement:
Fix any such fiber $F$ on $\mathrm{X}$, i.e. an equivalence class of $\sim_{k-1}$. Recall from \cite[Corollary 3.2.16]{Cand:Notes1} that we can regard $F$ as an abelian group by fixing an arbitrary $e\in F$. The group operation can be defined as follows: for any $x,y\in F$, let $\mathrm{c}'=\mathrm{c}'_{x,y}\in\mathrm{Cor}^{k+1}(\mathrm{X})$ be the corner such that $\mathrm{c}'(1,0,1^{k-1})=x$, $\mathrm{c}'(0,1^k)=y$ and $\mathrm{c}'(v)=e$ otherwise. Letting $\mathcal{K}:\mathrm{Cor}^{k+1}(\mathrm{X})\rightarrow \mathrm{X}$ denote the (continuous) completion function, we define $x+y:=\mathcal{K}(\mathrm{c}_{x,y})$. For $k=2$ we can represent this for instance as follows:
$(x,y)\mapsto
\smallcorner{e}{e}{e}{e}{e}{x}{y}\mapsto \mathcal{K}(\mathrm{c}_{x,y})$.
nodes.section: 2 Locally-compact Hausdorff nilspaces
nodes.statement_short: Define addition on a fiber via corner completion.

nodes.name: Continuity of the group operations
nodes.statement:
Letting $\iota:F\times F\rightarrow \mathrm{Cor}^{k+1}(\mathrm{X})$,  $(x,y)\mapsto \mathrm{c}_{x,y}$, we have that $x+y:=\mathcal{K}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\iota (x,y)$. By \cite[Lemma 3.2.7]{Cand:Notes1} we have $x+y\in F$. Since both $\iota$ and $\mathcal{K}$ are continuous,  the addition operation on $F$ is also continuous. A similar argument shows that inversion is also a continuous operation (see \cite[Proposition 2.4.1]{Cand:Notes1}).

We have thus shown that on any particular fiber $F$ of $\pi_{k-1}$, the structure and topology of $\mathrm{X}$ induces a structure of \textsc{lch} abelian group on $F$.
nodes.section: 2 Locally-compact Hausdorff nilspaces
nodes.statement_short: Addition and inversion are continuous as compositions with $\mathcal{K}$.

nodes.name: Fibers are isomorphic topological groups
nodes.statement:
Next, we prove that every two such fibers are homeomorphic. To see this, let  $F,F'$ be any two fibers of $\pi_{k-1}$ and fix any points $e\in F,e'\in F'$, which we shall use as identity elements in the respective groups. For any $x\in F$, define $\mathrm{c}_x\in\mathrm{Cor}^{k+1}(\mathrm{X})$ by $\mathrm{c}_x(1^k,0)=x$, $\mathrm{c}_x(v,0)=e$ for $v\in \db{k}$ and $\mathrm{c}_x(v,1)=e'$ for $v\in \db{k}\setminus\{1^k\}$. We then define the map $\theta:F\rightarrow F'$, $\theta(x):=\mathcal{K}(\mathrm{c}_x)$. For $k=2$, again we can visualize this as follows:
$x\mapsto \mathrm{c}_x:=\smallcorner{e}{e}{e}{x}{e'}{e'}{e'}\mapsto \mathcal{K}(\mathrm{c}_x)$.

By the continuity assumptions for the corner-completion function, this map $\theta$ is continuous. As its inverse is defined exactly the same way, we have that $\theta$ is an isomorphism of topological groups between $F$ and $F'$.
nodes.section: 2 Locally-compact Hausdorff nilspaces
nodes.statement_short: Show any two fibers are homeomorphic via a completion map.

nodes.name: The map $\theta$ between fibers
nodes.statement:
To see this, let  $F,F'$ be any two fibers of $\pi_{k-1}$ and fix any points $e\in F,e'\in F'$, which we shall use as identity elements in the respective groups. For any $x\in F$, define $\mathrm{c}_x\in\mathrm{Cor}^{k+1}(\mathrm{X})$ by $\mathrm{c}_x(1^k,0)=x$, $\mathrm{c}_x(v,0)=e$ for $v\in \db{k}$ and $\mathrm{c}_x(v,1)=e'$ for $v\in \db{k}\setminus\{1^k\}$. We then define the map $\theta:F\rightarrow F'$, $\theta(x):=\mathcal{K}(\mathrm{c}_x)$. For $k=2$, again we can visualize this as follows:
$x\mapsto \mathrm{c}_x:=\smallcorner{e}{e}{e}{x}{e'}{e'}{e'}\mapsto \mathcal{K}(\mathrm{c}_x)$.

nodes.name: $\theta$ is a topological isomorphism
nodes.statement: By the continuity assumptions for the corner-completion function, this map $\theta$ is continuous. As its inverse is defined exactly the same way, we have that $\theta$ is an isomorphism of topological groups between $F$ and $F'$.
nodes.section: 2 Locally-compact Hausdorff nilspaces
nodes.statement_short: Continuity of completion and symmetric inverse.

nodes.name: $\mathrm{Z}_k$ is LCH
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{Z}_k$ denote the resulting topological group. Since $\mathrm{Z}_k$ is homeomorphic to each fiber $F$, its topology is \textsc{lch}.
nodes.section: 2 Locally-compact Hausdorff nilspaces

nodes.name: The action is globally continuous
nodes.statement:
The action of $\mathrm{Z}_k$ on each fiber is continuous. However, we need to establish continuity of the action of $\mathrm{Z}_k$ globally on $\mathrm{X}$, that is, we need to show that the map $\mathrm{X}\times \mathrm{Z}_k\rightarrow \mathrm{X}$, $(x,z)\mapsto x+z$ is continuous. This follows from the fact that this map is a composition of the following form (illustrated for $k=2$; for $k>2$ it is similar): $(x,z)\mapsto \mathrm{c}_{x,z }:=\smallcorner{e}{e}{e}{e+z}{x}{x}{x}\mapsto \mathcal{K}(\mathrm{c}_{x,z})$.
Again, continuity of completion and the addition function on $F$ implies that $\mathcal{K}(\mathrm{c}_{x,z})$ is continuous as well.
nodes.section: 2 Locally-compact Hausdorff nilspaces
nodes.statement_short: The action map is a composition with the completion function.

nodes.name: Openness of $\pi_{k-1}$ and LCH quotient topology on $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step nilspace endowed with an \textsc{lch} topology such that for every $n\ge 0$ the cube set $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})\subset \mathrm{X}^{\db{n}}$ is closed and the completion of $(k+1)$-corners is continuous. Then the canonical quotient map $\pi_{k-1}:\mathrm{X}\rightarrow\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ is an open map and $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ equipped with the quotient topology is an \textsc{lch} space.\footnote{Note this claim is just about the quotient topology on $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$, we are not claiming yet that $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ is an \textsc{lch} nilspace.}
nodes.section: 2 Locally-compact Hausdorff nilspaces
assumptions: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step nilspace endowed with an \textsc{lch} topology such that for every $n\ge 0$ the cube set $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})\subset \mathrm{X}^{\db{n}}$ is closed and the completion of $(k+1)$-corners is continuous.
conclusions: Then the canonical quotient map $\pi_{k-1}:\mathrm{X}\rightarrow\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ is an open map and $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ equipped with the quotient topology is an \textsc{lch} space.\footnote{Note this claim is just about the quotient topology on $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$, we are not claiming yet that $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ is an \textsc{lch} nilspace.}
nodes.label: cor:quotient-top-k-1-factor

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 2.6
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{prop:k-th-group-action} the saturation of any open set in $\mathrm{X}$ by the action of $\mathrm{Z}_k$ is also an open set, and this implies that $\pi_{k-1}$ is an open map (in other words, the relation $\sim_{k-1}$ is an open relation, in the sense of \cite[p.\ 52, Definition 2]{BourbakiGT1}). By Lemma \ref{lem:closure} the graph of $\sim_{k-1}$ is closed in $\mathrm{X}\times\mathrm{X}$. Hence $\pi_{k-1}(\mathrm{X})=\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ is Hausdorff, by \cite[p.\ 79, Proposition 8]{BourbakiGT1}. By \cite[p.\ 107, Proposition 10]{BourbakiGT1}, it follows that $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ is locally compact. Finally, since the continuous surjective open image of a second-countable space is second-countable, so is $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$.
nodes.section: 2 Locally-compact Hausdorff nilspaces
nodes.statement_short: Saturations by $\mathrm{Z}_k$ of open sets are open; closed graph gives Hausdorff; Bourbaki gives local compactness.

nodes.name: $\pi_{k-1}$ is open
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{prop:k-th-group-action} the saturation of any open set in $\mathrm{X}$ by the action of $\mathrm{Z}_k$ is also an open set, and this implies that $\pi_{k-1}$ is an open map (in other words, the relation  $\sim_{k-1}$ is an open relation, in the sense of \cite[p.\ 52, Definition 2]{BourbakiGT1}).
nodes.section: 2 Locally-compact Hausdorff nilspaces
nodes.statement_short: Saturation by the continuous $\mathrm{Z}_k$-action keeps sets open.

nodes.name: Quotient is Hausdorff
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lem:closure} the graph of $\sim_{k-1}$ is closed in $\mathrm{X}\times\mathrm{X}$. Hence $\pi_{k-1}(\mathrm{X})=\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ is Hausdorff, by \cite[p.\ 79, Proposition 8]{BourbakiGT1}.
nodes.section: 2 Locally-compact Hausdorff nilspaces

nodes.name: Quotient is locally compact and second-countable
nodes.statement:
By \cite[p.\ 107, Proposition 10]{BourbakiGT1}, it follows that $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ is locally compact.
Finally, since the continuous surjective open image of a second-countable space is second-countable, so is $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$.
nodes.section: 2 Locally-compact Hausdorff nilspaces

nodes.name: Compact sets in $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ lift to compact sets
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step nilspace satisfying the hypothesis of Corollary \ref{cor:quotient-top-k-1-factor}. Then for every compact set $K'\subset \mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ there exists a compact $K\subset \mathrm{X}$ such that $\pi_{k-1}(K)=K'$.
nodes.section: 2 Locally-compact Hausdorff nilspaces
assumptions: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step nilspace satisfying the hypothesis of Corollary \ref{cor:quotient-top-k-1-factor}.
conclusions: Then for every compact set $K'\subset \mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ there exists a compact $K\subset \mathrm{X}$ such that $\pi_{k-1}(K)=K'$.
nodes.label: cor:cpct-sets-are-im-of-cpct-sets

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 2.7
nodes.statement: This follows from \cite[p.\ 107, Proposition 10]{BourbakiGT1}.
nodes.section: 2 Locally-compact Hausdorff nilspaces

nodes.name: Closedness of cube sets on $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step nilspace endowed with an \textsc{lch} topology such that for every $n\ge 0$ the cube set $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})\subset \mathrm{X}^{\db{n}}$ is closed and the completion function on $(k+1)$-corners is continuous. Then $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$ is a closed subset of $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}^{\db{n}}$ in the product topology.
nodes.section: 2 Locally-compact Hausdorff nilspaces
assumptions: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step nilspace endowed with an \textsc{lch} topology such that for every $n\ge 0$ the cube set $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})\subset \mathrm{X}^{\db{n}}$ is closed and the completion function on $(k+1)$-corners is continuous.
conclusions: Then $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$ is a closed subset of $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}^{\db{n}}$ in the product topology.
nodes.label: lem:closure-cube-in-k-1-factor

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.8
nodes.statement: Since $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ is a $(k-1)$-step nilspace, we have that if $\mathrm{C}^k(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$ is closed, then arguing as in the proof of \cite[Lemma 2.1.1]{Cand:Notes2} we deduce that so is $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$ for every $n>k$. Thus it suffices to show that $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$ is closed for every $n\leq k$. But for such $n$, any lift of any $n$-cube on $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ under $\pi_{k-1}^{\db{n}}$ is an $n$-cube on $\mathrm{X}$ (recall \cite[Remark 3.2.12]{Cand:Notes1}), so ${\pi_{k-1}^{\db{n}}}^{-1}(\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})) = \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$. Since $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$ is closed, we deduce that $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$ is closed in the quotient topology on $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}^{\db{n}}$ induced by $\pi_{k-1}^{\db{n}}$. But this quotient topology is homeomorphic to the $\db{n}$-power of the quotient topology on $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ induced by $\pi_{k-1}$ (by \cite[p.\ 55, Corollary]{BourbakiGT1}, so we conclude that $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$ is indeed closed in the product topology on $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}^{\db{n}}$.

nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $n\le k$; there cube sets are saturated preimages, so closed in the quotient topology, which equals the product topology.

nodes.name: Reduce to $n\le k$
nodes.statement: Since $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ is a $(k-1)$-step nilspace, we have that if $\mathrm{C}^k(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$ is closed, then arguing as in the proof of \cite[Lemma 2.1.1]{Cand:Notes2} we deduce that so is $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$ for every $n>k$. Thus it suffices to show that $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$ is closed for every $n\leq k$.

nodes.statement_short: Higher cube sets are closed once $\mathrm{C}^k$ is.

nodes.name: Cubes on $\mathrm{X}$ are full preimages
nodes.statement: But for such $n$, any lift of any $n$-cube on $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ under $\pi_{k-1}^{\db{n}}$ is an $n$-cube on $\mathrm{X}$ (recall \cite[Remark 3.2.12]{Cand:Notes1}), so ${\pi_{k-1}^{\db{n}}}^{-1}(\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})) = \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$.

nodes.statement: Since $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$ is closed, we deduce that $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$ is closed in the quotient topology on $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}^{\db{n}}$ induced by $\pi_{k-1}^{\db{n}}$. But this quotient topology is homeomorphic to the $\db{n}$-power of the quotient topology on $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ induced by $\pi_{k-1}$ (by \cite[p.\ 55, Corollary]{BourbakiGT1}, so we conclude that $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$ is indeed closed in the product topology on $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}^{\db{n}}$.

nodes.statement_short: Quotient topology on the power equals the product topology.

nodes.name: Canonical factors of LCH nilspaces are LCH nilspaces
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be an \textsc{lch} $k$-step nilspace. Then $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$, equipped with the cube sets $(\pi_{k-1}^{\db{n}}(\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})))_{n\ge 0}$, is a $(k-1)$-step \textsc{lch} nilspace with respect to the quotient topology.

assumptions: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be an \textsc{lch} $k$-step nilspace.
conclusions: Then $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$, equipped with the cube sets $(\pi_{k-1}^{\db{n}}(\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})))_{n\ge 0}$, is a $(k-1)$-step \textsc{lch} nilspace with respect to the quotient topology.
nodes.label: thm:factor-of-lch-nil

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.9
nodes.statement: Note that the algebraic part of this result follows from \cite[Lemma 3.2.10]{Cand:Notes1}. Combining Corollary \ref{cor:quotient-top-k-1-factor} and Lemma \ref{lem:closure-cube-in-k-1-factor} we have that the topology on $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ is also \textsc{lch}, and part $(i)$ of Definition \ref{def:top-nil-open-maps-version} follows. Hence, we just have to prove part $(ii)$, i.e., that the projection maps $p_{k-1}^{\db{n}}:\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})\rightarrow \mathrm{Cor}^{n}(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$ are open. First let us assume that $n\le k$. In this case, the sets $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$ are closed and saturated with respect to $\pi_{k-1}^{\db{n}}$. That is, $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$ is closed and $(\pi_{k-1}^{\db{n}})^{-1}(\pi_{k-1}^{\db{n}}(\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})))=\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$. By \cite[Theorem 22.1]{Mu} the restricted map $\pi_{k-1}^{\db{n}}|_{\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})}:\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})\rightarrow \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$ is a quotient map. Similarly, the restriction $\pi_{k-1}^{\db{n}\setminus\{1^n\}}|_{\mathrm{Cor}^n(\mathrm{X})}:\mathrm{Cor}^n(\mathrm{X})\rightarrow \mathrm{Cor}^n(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$ is a quotient map. Given any open set $U\subset \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$, we claim that $p_{k-1}^{\db{n}}(U)\subset \mathrm{Cor}^n(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$ is open. By definition of the quotient topology, $p_{k-1}^{\db{n}}(U)$ is open if and only if $(\pi_{k-1}^{\db{n}\setminus\{1^n\}}|_{\mathrm{Cor}^n(\mathrm{X})})^{-1}(p_{k-1}^{\db{n}}(U))$ is. But this set is precisely $p^{\db{n}}((\pi_{k-1}^{\db{n}}|_{\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})})^{-1}(U))$ where $p^{\db{n}}:\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})\rightarrow\mathrm{Cor}^n(\mathrm{X})$. As $\pi_{k-1}^{\db{n}}|_{\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})}:\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})\rightarrow\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$ is continuous, we have that $(\pi_{k-1}^{\db{n}}|_{\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})})^{-1}(U)$ is open, and then the openness of $p^{\db{n}}$ gives us the desired conclusion. In particular, if $n=k$ we get the result that the completion function $\mathcal{K}:\mathrm{Cor}^k(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})\rightarrow \mathrm{C}^k(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$ is continuous (as it is the inverse of the open map $p_{k-1}^{\db{k}}:\mathrm{C}^k(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})\rightarrow \mathrm{Cor}^k(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$). For $n>k$ note that we have a bijection $\mathrm{Cor}^n(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})\rightarrow \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$, which is also continuous (as it just consists in applying $\mathcal{K}$ on some upper face of $\db{n}$). But by definition, the inverse of this function is $p_{k-1}^{\db{n}}:\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})\rightarrow \mathrm{Cor}^n(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$. Hence $p_{k-1}^{\db{n}}$ is open and the result follows.

nodes.name: Characterization of LCH nilspaces via continuity of completion
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step nilspace endowed with an \textsc{lch} topology. Then $\mathrm{X}$ is an \textsc{lch} nilspace if and only if the following conditions are satisfied: \begin{enumerate} \item For every $n\ge 0$, the cube set $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$ is a closed subset of $\mathrm{X}^{\db{n}}$. \item For every $n\in[k]$, the corner completion function $\mathcal{K}_{n+1}:\mathrm{Cor}^{n+1}(\mathrm{X}_n)\rightarrow \mathrm{X}_n$ is continuous, where the canonical factor $\mathrm{X}_n$ is endowed with the quotient topology. \end{enumerate}

Then $\mathrm{X}$ is an \textsc{lch} nilspace if and only if the following conditions are satisfied:
\begin{enumerate}

    \item For every $n\in[k]$, the corner completion function $\mathcal{K}_{n+1}:\mathrm{Cor}^{n+1}(\mathrm{X}_n)\rightarrow \mathrm{X}_n$ is continuous, where the canonical factor $\mathrm{X}_n$ is endowed with the quotient topology.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.10
nodes.statement: For the forward implication, note that $(i)$ follows from Definition \ref{def:top-nil-open-maps-version}, and $(ii)$ follows from Lemma \ref{lem:cont-if-open} applied to each factor of $\mathrm{X}$, using Theorem \ref{thm:factor-of-lch-nil} to pass to lower-step factors. To prove the converse, first note that we can apply Proposition \ref{prop:k-th-group-action}. Hence, the structure group $\mathrm{Z}_k$ is an \textsc{lch} topological group that acts on $\mathrm{X}$ continuously. By Corollary \ref{cor:quotient-top-k-1-factor}, we get that for every $n\in[k]$ the projection map $\pi_n:\mathrm{X}\rightarrow\mathrm{X}_n$ is an open quotient map. First, note that for $m>k$ the openness of $p^{\db{m}}:\mathrm{C}^m(\mathrm{X})\rightarrow \mathrm{Cor}^m(\mathrm{X})$ is trivial as its inverse can be recovered using $\mathcal{K}_{k+1}$ (which is continuous by hypothesis). For $m\le k$, note that it is enough to prove that $p^{\db{m}}(\mathrm{C}^m(\mathrm{X})\cap \prod_{v\in\db{m}} A_v)$ is open for open sets $A_v\subset \mathrm{X}$, $v\in \db{m}$. Moreover, we can restrict our attention to sets where $A_v=\mathrm{X}$ for all $v\not=1^m$, since we have \[ p^{\db{m}}\big(\mathrm{C}^m(\mathrm{X})\cap \prod_{v\in\db{m}} A_v\big)=\big(\prod_{v\in\db{m}\setminus\{1^m\}} A_v\big)\cap p^{\db{m}}\big(\mathrm{C}^m(\mathrm{X})\cap [\mathrm{X}^{\db{m}\setminus\{1^m\}}\times A_{1^m}]\big). \] But for those sets we know how to compute such images. Let \setlength{\leftmargini}{0.4cm} \begin{itemize} \item $\pi_{m-1}:\mathrm{X}\rightarrow\mathrm{X}_{m-1}$ be the quotient map, which is also open. \item $\pi_{m-1}^{\db{m}\setminus\{1^m\}}:\mathrm{Cor}^m(\mathrm{X})\rightarrow\mathrm{Cor}^m(\mathrm{X}_{m-1})$ be the coordinate-wise application of $\pi_{m-1}$ (which is continuous). \item $\mathcal{K}_m:\mathrm{Cor}^m(\mathrm{X}_{m-1})\rightarrow \mathrm{X}_{m-1}$ the completion function (which is continuous by hypothesis). \end{itemize} Then $p^{\db{m}}(\mathrm{C}^m(\mathrm{X})\cap [\mathrm{X}^{\db{m}\setminus\{1^m\}}\times A_{1^m}]) =(\pi_{m-1}^{\db{m}\setminus\{1^m\}})^{-1}(\mathcal{K}_{m}^{-1}(\pi_{m-1}(A_{1^m})))$, which is open, and the result follows.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.12
nodes.statement: For any simplicial set $S\subset \db{n}$, let us say that $v\in S$ is \emph{maximal} if there is no $w\in S$ with $w\not=v$ such that $w\sbr{j}\ge v\sbr{j}$ for all $j\in[n]$. We claim that the projection map $p':\hom(S,\mathrm{X})\rightarrow\hom({S\setminus\{v\}},\mathrm{X})$ is open. It suffices to check this for open sets of the form $\prod_{w\in S} U_w\cap \hom(S,\mathrm{X})$ where $U_w\subset \mathrm{X}$ are open for all $w\in S$. Letting $|v|:=\sum_{j=1}^n v\sbr{j}$, and defining the sets $V_{w'}:=\mathrm{X}$ if $w'\not=1^{|v|}$ and $V_{1^{|v|}}=U_v$, we claim that \[ p'(\prod_{w\in S} U_w\cap \hom(S,\mathrm{X}))= \prod_{w\in S\setminus\{v\}} U_w\cap \hom({S\setminus\{v\}},\mathrm{X}) \cap r^{-1}\big(p^{\db{|v|}}(\prod_{w'\in \db{|v|}} V_{w'}\cap \mathrm{C}^{|v|}(\mathrm{X}))\big) \] where $r$ is the map $\hom({S\setminus\{v\}},\mathrm{X})\rightarrow \mathrm{Cor}^{|v|}(\mathrm{X})$ that projects to the coordinates $w\in S$ such that $w\sbr{j}\le v\sbr{j}$ for all $j\in[n]$, relabeling these coordinates to the set $\db{|v|}$. Clearly $r$ is continuous, and as $p^{\db{|v|}}$ is open by hypothesis the result follows. Then, for any simplicial $S\subset \db{n}$ we can find a sequence $v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_t\in \db{n}$ such that $S=\db{n}\setminus\{v_1,\ldots,v_t\}$, and for every $\ell=0,\ldots,t$ we have that $\db{n}\setminus\{v_1,\ldots,v_\ell\}$ is simplicial and $v_{\ell+1}$ is maximal in $\db{n}\setminus\{v_1,\ldots,v_\ell\}$. We can then write $p^S:\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})\rightarrow\hom(S,\mathrm{X})$ as a composition of $t$ open maps $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})\rightarrow \hom(\db{n}\setminus\{v_1\},\mathrm{X})\rightarrow \hom(\db{n}\setminus\{v_1,v_2\},\mathrm{X})\rightarrow \cdots \rightarrow\hom(S,\mathrm{X})$ which is open in particular.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.13
nodes.statement: It suffices to prove the result for $i=k-1$, and then apply this case $i-1$ times. For $i=k-1$ there are two cases. Let us deal with $n\le k$ first. Note that it is enough to prove the result for open sets of the form $\prod_{v\in\db{n}} U_v\cap \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$ where $U_v\subset \mathrm{X}$ are open. We claim that in this case \[ \pi_{k-1}^{\db{n}}(\prod_{v\in\db{n}} U_v\cap \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}))=\prod_{v\in\db{n}} \pi_{k-1}(U_v)\cap \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}_{k-1}). \] If this is true then the result will follow for $n\le k$, $\pi_{k-1}$ is an open map. In order to prove that, note that clearly the LHS is contained in the RHS. For the other inclusion, let $\pi_{k-1}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}$ be such that $(\pi_{k-1}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c})(v)\in \pi(U_v)$ for all $v\in \db{n}$. For each $v\in \db{n}$ there exists $d(v)\in U_v$ such that $(\pi_{k-1}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c})(v)=(\pi_{k-1}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} d)(v)$. By \cite[Corollary 3.2.8]{Cand:Notes1} we have that in particular $d\in \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$ and the result follows in this case. For $n>k$, note that we can write the map $\pi_{k-1}^{\db{n}}$ as the composition of the following maps: \[ \begin{tikzpicture} \matrix (m) [matrix of math nodes,row sep=3em,column sep=4em,minimum width=2em] {\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}) & \hom({\db{n}_{\le k}},\mathrm{X}) & \hom({\db{n}_{\le k}},\mathrm{X}_{k-1}) & \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}_{k-1}) \\}; \path[-stealth] (m-1-1) edge node [above] {$p_{\db{n}_{\le k}}$} (m-1-2) (m-1-2) edge node [above] {$\pi_{k-1}^{\db{n}_{\le k}}$} (m-1-3) (m-1-3) edge node [above] {$\mathcal{K}'$} (m-1-4); \end{tikzpicture} \] Here $p_{\db{n}_{\le k}}$ is defined as in Lemma \ref{lem:simplicial-proy}, $\db{n}_{\le k}:=\{v\in\db{n}:\sum_{j=1}^n v\sbr{j}\le k\}$, $\pi_{k-1}^{\db{n}_{\le k}}$ is the coordinate-wise application of $\pi_{k-1}$ and $\mathcal{K}'$ is the composition of several applications of the completion function $\mathcal{K}:\mathrm{Cor}^k(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})\rightarrow\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ in order to complete an element of $\hom({\db{n}_{\le k}},\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$. By Lemma \ref{lem:simplicial-proy} we have that $p_{\db{n}_{\le k}}$ is open. By an argument very similar to the one in the previous paragraph we have that $\pi_{k-1}^{\db{n}_{\le k}}$ is open as well, and $\mathcal{K}'$ is open as its inverse is continuous (because it is just a projection to some coordinates).

nodes.name: Fiber product of nilspaces
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{X}, \mathrm{X}'$ and $\mathrm{Y}$ be nilspaces and let $\varphi:\mathrm{X}\rightarrow\mathrm{Y}$ and $\varphi':\mathrm{X}'\rightarrow\mathrm{Y}$ be fibrations. We define the \emph{fiber product} of $\mathrm{X}$ and $\mathrm{X}'$ as the nilspace consisting of the set $\mathrm{X}\times_{\mathrm{Y}}\mathrm{X}':=\{(x,x')\in \mathrm{X}\times\mathrm{X}': \varphi(x)=\varphi'(x')\}$ endowed with the cubes $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X} \times_{\mathrm{Y}} \mathrm{X}'):=\{(\mathrm{c},\mathrm{c}')\in \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})\times \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}'):\varphi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}=\varphi'\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}'\}$.
nodes.section: 2 Locally-compact Hausdorff nilspaces
nodes.statement_short: Pairs of points (and of cubes) with equal images under the two fibrations to $\mathrm{Y}$.
nodes.label: def:fib-prod

nodes.name: Fiber products are nilspaces
nodes.statement: It is proved in \cite[Lemma 4.2]{CGSS} that such fiber products are indeed nilspaces.
nodes.section: 2 Locally-compact Hausdorff nilspaces
conclusions: It is proved in \cite[Lemma 4.2]{CGSS} that such fiber products are indeed nilspaces.

nodes.name: Notation for fiber products
nodes.statement: Note that in this definition we have not assumed anything about the topology on $\mathrm{X},\mathrm{X}'$ or $\mathrm{Y}'$. We will do so in the following lemmas. Note also that in the expression $\mathrm{X}\times_{\mathrm{Y}}\mathrm{X}'$ there is no reference to $\varphi$ or $\varphi'$. These maps will be clear from the context.
nodes.section: 2 Locally-compact Hausdorff nilspaces

nodes.name: Cartan principal bundle
nodes.statement: Let $B$ be a $G$-principal bundle. Let the action of $G$ over $B$ be given by $(g,b)\in G\times B\mapsto gb\in B$. We say that the bundle is a \emph{Cartan principal bundle} if given the map $T:B\times G\rightarrow B\times B$ defined by $(b,g)\mapsto(b,gb)$ there exists a continuous map\footnote{Here the image ${\rm im}(T)$ is understood to have the subspace topology.} $R:{\rm im}(T)\rightarrow B\times G$ such that $R\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} T=\mathrm{id}_{B\times G}$.
nodes.section: 2 Locally-compact Hausdorff nilspaces
nodes.label: def:Cartan

nodes.name: Cartan criterion for abelian principal bundles
nodes.statement: Thus, if the action of $G$ on $B$ is given by $(g,b)\mapsto g+b$, the principal $G$-bundle $B$ is Cartan if and only if the \emph{difference map}, i.e.\ the map $\{(b,b')\in B\times B:\exists g\in G \text{ s.t. }g+b=b'\}\rightarrow G$, $(b,b')\mapsto b'-b$, is continuous.
nodes.section: 2 Locally-compact Hausdorff nilspaces
conclusions: Thus, if the action of $G$ on $B$ is given by $(g,b)\mapsto g+b$, the principal $G$-bundle $B$ is Cartan if and only if the \emph{difference map}, i.e.\ the map $\{(b,b')\in B\times B:\exists g\in G \text{ s.t. }g+b=b'\}\rightarrow G$, $(b,b')\mapsto b'-b$, is continuous.
nodes.statement_short: For abelian $G$, a principal $G$-bundle is Cartan iff the difference map is continuous.

nodes.name: Structure-group bundles of LCH nilspaces are Cartan
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step \textsc{lch} nilspace. For each $i\in[k]$, let $\mathrm{Z}_i$ be the $i$-th structure group of $\mathrm{X}$. Then for every $i\in[k]$, the $\mathrm{Z}_i$-principal bundle $\mathrm{X}_i$ is a Cartan principal bundle.
nodes.section: 2 Locally-compact Hausdorff nilspaces
assumptions: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step \textsc{lch} nilspace.
For each $i\in[k]$, let $\mathrm{Z}_i$ be the $i$-th structure group of $\mathrm{X}$.
conclusions: Then for every $i\in[k]$, the $\mathrm{Z}_i$-principal bundle $\mathrm{X}_i$ is a Cartan principal bundle.
nodes.label: lem:diff-cont

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.17
nodes.statement: By induction on $k$ it suffices to prove this for $i=k$. Recall that $\mathrm{Z}_k$ can be identified with any fixed equivalence class (or fiber) in $\mathrm{X}$ for the relation $\sim_k$, in which we have fixed a particular element $e\in F$ to be the identity for addition. Then, given $x,y\in \mathrm{X}\times_{\mathrm{X}_{k-1}}\mathrm{X}$, let $\mathrm{c}_{x,y}\in\mathrm{Cor}^{k+1}(\mathrm{X})$ be the corner defined by $\mathrm{c}_{x,y}(v,0):=y$ for $v\in \db{k}\setminus\{1^k\}$, $\mathrm{c}_{x,y}(1^k,0):=x$ and $\mathrm{c}_{x,y}(v,1)=e$ for $v\in\db{k}\setminus\{1^k\}$. The difference $x-y$ can be then expressed as $\mathcal{K}(\mathrm{c}_{x,y})$ where $\mathcal{K}:\mathrm{Cor}^{k+1}(\mathrm{X})\rightarrow\mathrm{X}$ is the unique-completion function. As an example, for $k=2$ this composition can be viewed as follows: $(x,y)\mapsto \mathrm{c}_{x,y}:=\smallcorner{y}{y}{y}{x}{e}{e}{e}\mapsto \mathcal{K}(\mathrm{c}_{x,y})$. As the map $(x,y)\mapsto \mathrm{c}_{x,y}$ is continuous, so is $\mathcal{K}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}_{x,y}$ and the result follows.

nodes.statement_short: Express the difference map as corner completion of a continuously varying corner.

nodes.name: Difference via completion

nodes.name: Difference is continuous

nodes.name: Fiber products of LCH nilspaces are LCH nilspaces
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{X},\mathrm{X}'$ and $\mathrm{Y}$ be $k$-step \textsc{lch} nilspaces, and let $\varphi:\mathrm{X}\rightarrow\mathrm{Y}$, $\varphi':\mathrm{X}'\rightarrow\mathrm{Y}$ be (continuous) fibrations. Then the corresponding fiber product $\mathrm{X} \times_{\mathrm{Y}} \mathrm{X}'$ (recall Definition \ref{def:fib-prod}) is also an \textsc{lch} nilspace. Moreover, if $\mathrm{Z}_i(\mathrm{X}),\mathrm{Z}_i(\mathrm{X}')$ and $\mathrm{Z}_i(\mathrm{Y})$ are the $i$th structure groups of $\mathrm{X},\mathrm{X}'$ and $\mathrm{Y}$ respectively, then the $i$th structure group of $\mathrm{X} \times_{\mathrm{Y}} \mathrm{X}'$ is $G_i:=\{(z,z')\in \mathrm{Z}_i(\mathrm{X})\times\mathrm{Z}_i(\mathrm{X}'): \phi_i(z)=\phi'_i(z')\}$ where $\phi_i:\mathrm{Z}_i(\mathrm{X})\rightarrow\mathrm{Z}_i(\mathrm{Y})$ and $\phi'_i:\mathrm{Z}_i(\mathrm{X}')\rightarrow\mathrm{Z}_i(\mathrm{Y})$ are the structure homomorphisms of $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$ respectively.
