conclusions: Then the corresponding fiber product $\mathrm{X} \times_{\mathrm{Y}} \mathrm{X}'$ (recall Definition \ref{def:fib-prod}) is also an \textsc{lch} nilspace.

Moreover, if $\mathrm{Z}_i(\mathrm{X}),\mathrm{Z}_i(\mathrm{X}')$ and $\mathrm{Z}_i(\mathrm{Y})$ are the $i$th structure groups of $\mathrm{X},\mathrm{X}'$ and $\mathrm{Y}$ respectively, then the $i$th structure group of $\mathrm{X} \times_{\mathrm{Y}} \mathrm{X}'$ is $G_i:=\{(z,z')\in \mathrm{Z}_i(\mathrm{X})\times\mathrm{Z}_i(\mathrm{X}'): \phi_i(z)=\phi'_i(z')\}$ where $\phi_i:\mathrm{Z}_i(\mathrm{X})\rightarrow\mathrm{Z}_i(\mathrm{Y})$ and $\phi'_i:\mathrm{Z}_i(\mathrm{X}')\rightarrow\mathrm{Z}_i(\mathrm{Y})$ are the structure homomorphisms of $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$ respectively.
nodes.label: lem:fib-prod-top-nil

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.18
nodes.statement: By \cite[Lemma 4.2]{CGSS} we know that this fiber product is a $k$-step nilspace (algebraically speaking). Hence, we just have to check that the conditions of Definition \ref{def:top-nil-open-maps-version} are satisfied. From the continuity of $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$ it is easy to check that the topology on $\mathrm{X} \times_{\mathrm{Y}} \mathrm{X}'$ is also \textsc{lch}. Indeed, this set is a closed subset of $\mathrm{X}\times\mathrm{X}'$, as it is the preimage of the diagonal of $\mathrm{Y}\times \mathrm{Y}$ under the map $(x,x')\mapsto(\varphi(x),\varphi'(x'))$. Similarly, for each $n\geq 0$ the cube set $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X} \times_{\mathrm{Y}} \mathrm{X}')$ is closed, since it is $\big[\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}\times\mathrm{X}')\big]\cap (\mathrm{X} \times_{\mathrm{Y}} \mathrm{X}')^{\db{n}}$, which is a closed subset of $(\mathrm{X}\times\mathrm{X}')^{\db{n}}$, so in particular it is a closed subset of $(\mathrm{X} \times_{\mathrm{Y}} \mathrm{X}')^{\db{n}}$. Instead of proving the second part of Definition \ref{def:top-nil-open-maps-version} we use Lemma \ref{lem:eq-def-lch-nil} and just check that $\mathrm{X} \times_{\mathrm{Y}} \mathrm{X}'$ satisfies property $(ii)$ in this lemma. By \cite[Proposition A.20]{CGSS-p-hom}, for each $i\in [k]$ the $i$-step characteristic factor of this nilspace is $\mathrm{X}_i\times_{\mathrm{Y}_i}\mathrm{X}'_i$. Also, by the proof of \cite[Proposition A.20]{CGSS-p-hom}, the $i$-th structure group of $\mathrm{X} \times_{\mathrm{Y}} \mathrm{X}'$ is $G_i:=\{(z,z')\in \mathrm{Z}_i(\mathrm{X})\times\mathrm{Z}_i(\mathrm{X}'): \phi_i(z)=\phi'_i(z')\}$ where $\phi_i:\mathrm{Z}_i(\mathrm{X})\rightarrow\mathrm{Z}_i(\mathrm{Y})$ and $\phi'_i:\mathrm{Z}_i(\mathrm{X}')\rightarrow\mathrm{Z}_i(\mathrm{Y})$ are the structure homomorphisms of $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$ respectively (see \cite[Definition 3.3.1]{Cand:Notes1}). To see that part $(ii)$ of Lemma \ref{lem:eq-def-lch-nil} holds for $i=k$, note that the completion function on $\mathrm{Cor}^{k+1}(\mathrm{X} \times_{\mathrm{Y}} \mathrm{X}')$ is continuous, as it is just the coordinate-wise application of the $(k+1)$-completion functions on $\mathrm{X}$ and $\mathrm{X}'$. For $i< k$, we already have a purely algebraic nilspace isomorphism $(\mathrm{X} \times_{\mathrm{Y}} \mathrm{X}')_i \rightarrow \mathrm{X}_i \times_{\mathrm{Y}_i} \mathrm{X}_i'$. If we show that this is also a homeomorphism then we will be done, as we can then repeat the preceding argument to obtain the continuity of the completion function. To obtain the homeomorphism property it suffices to show that the quotient topology on $(\mathrm{X} \times_{\mathrm{Y}} \mathrm{X}')_i$ is equal to the subspace topology on $\mathrm{X}_i \times_{\mathrm{Y}_i} \mathrm{X}_i'$ induced by the product topology on $\mathrm{X}_i\times\mathrm{X}_i$. Note that it suffices to show this for $i=k-1$, as the rest of the cases follow by induction on $k$. Hence, let us consider the following diagram: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned}[c] \begin{tikzpicture} \matrix (m) [matrix of math nodes,row sep=2em,column sep=4em,minimum width=2em] {\mathrm{X} \times_{\mathrm{Y}} \mathrm{X}' & \\ (\mathrm{X} \times_{\mathrm{Y}} \mathrm{X}')_{k-1} & \mathrm{X}_{k-1} \times_{\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}} \mathrm{X}_{k-1}', \\}; \path[-stealth] (m-1-1) edge node [above] {$T$} (m-2-2) (m-1-1) edge node [right] {$\pi$} (m-2-1) (m-2-1) edge node [above] {$\iota$} (m-2-2); \end{tikzpicture} \end{aligned} \end{equation} \vspace{-0.3cm} \noindent where $T(x,x'):=(\pi_{k-1}(x),\pi_{k-1}(x'))$, $\pi$ is the quotient map for the relation $\sim_k$ (see \cite[Definition 3.2.3]{Cand:Notes1}) and $\iota(\pi(x,x'))=(\pi_{k-1}(x),\pi_{k-1}(x'))$. Recall that by \cite[Proposition A.21]{CGSS-p-hom}, $\iota$ is a well-defined bijective morphism. We want to prove that it is a homeomorphism. We already know that the relation $\sim_k$ on $\mathrm{X} \times_{\mathrm{Y}} \mathrm{X}'$ comes from the continuous action of the group $G_{k}$. Also, using the closure of $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X} \times_{\mathrm{Y}} \mathrm{X}')$ it follows that the set $\{((x_0,x_0'),(x_1,x_1'))\in (\mathrm{X} \times_{\mathrm{Y}} \mathrm{X}')^2: (x_0,x_0')\sim_k(x_1,x_1')\}$ is closed. Hence we can apply Lemma \ref{lem:quo-by-cont-gr-act} to conclude that the topology on $(\mathrm{X} \times_{\mathrm{Y}} \mathrm{X}')_{k-1}$ is \textsc{lch} and, in particular, it is metrizable. Let us now check that $\iota$ is continuous. Indeed, if $U\subset \mathrm{X}_{k-1} \times_{\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}} \mathrm{X}_{k-1}'$ is open, then since $\iota^{-1}(U)=\pi(T^{-1}(U))$, the continuity of $T$ and the openness of $\pi$ imply that $\iota^{-1}(U)$ is open as required. To prove that $\iota^{-1}$ is continuous, it suffices to prove that if $(\pi_{k-1}(x_n),\pi_{k-1}(x_n'))$ converges to $(\pi_{k-1}(x),\pi_{k-1}(x'))$ in $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}\times_{\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}}\mathrm{X}_{k-1}'$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$ then $\pi(x_n,x_n')\rightarrow \pi(x,x')$ as $n\rightarrow \infty$. By Lemma \ref{lem:conv-quot}, it suffices to prove that there exists a sequence $(g_n\in G_{k})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ such that $(x_n,x_n')+g_n\rightarrow (x,x')$, which we do in the remainder of this proof. Note that, without loss of generality, we can assume that $\varphi(x_n)=\varphi'(x_n')$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$ (so far we only know that $\varphi_{k-1}(\pi_{k-1}(x_n))=\varphi'_{k-1}(\pi_{k-1}(x_n'))$) and similarly that $\varphi(x)=\varphi'(x')$. Indeed, if this is not the case, say if $\varphi(x)\not=\varphi'(x')$, then since $(\pi_{k-1}(x),\pi_{k-1}(x'))$ is in $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}\times_{\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}}\mathrm{X}_{k-1}'$, we have $\pi_{k-1}(\varphi(x))=\varphi_{k-1}(\pi_{k-1}(x)) = \varphi'_{k-1}(\pi_{k-1}(x'))=\pi_{k-1}(\varphi'(x'))$. In particular, there exists $s\in \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})$ such that $\varphi(x)=\varphi'(x')+s$. Using the surjectivity of $\phi'_k$ we can find some $r\in \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X}')$ such that $\phi'_k(r)=s$, whence $\varphi(x)=\varphi'(x'+r)$. With similarly chosen $r_n$ for each $n$, we obtain the claimed additional assumption for $(x_n,x_n'+r_n)$ and $(x,x'+r)$ (and note that $\pi(x_n,x_n'+r_n)=\pi(x_n,x_n')$ and similarly for $(x,x'+r)$, by the invariance of $\pi_{k-1}$ under the action of $\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X}')$). By Lemma \ref{lem:conv-quot} in $\mathrm{X}$, there is a sequence $(z_n)_n$ in $\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})$ such that $x_n+z_n\rightarrow x$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$ in $\mathrm{X}$. For every $n\in \mathbb{N}$, by the surjectivity of $\phi_k'$ there is $z_n'\in \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X}')$ such that $(z_n,z_n')\in G_k$. Note that $\varphi(x+z_n)\rightarrow\varphi(x)$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$ and that $\varphi(x_n+z_n)=\varphi'(x_n'+z_n')$ for all $n\in \mathbb{N}$. Next, by Lemma \ref{lem:conv-quot} applied in $\mathrm{X}'$, for every $n\in \mathbb{N}$ there exists $z_n''\in \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X}')$ such that $x_n'+z_n'+z_n''\rightarrow x'$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$. We claim that $\phi'_k(z_n'')\rightarrow 0$ as $n\rightarrow \infty$. Indeed $\varphi'(x_n'+z_n'+z_n'')\rightarrow \varphi'(x')=\varphi(x)$ and also $\varphi'(x_n'+z_n'+z_n'')=\varphi'(x_n'+z_n')+\phi_k'(z_n'')=\varphi(x_n+z_n)+\phi_k'(z_n'')$. As $\varphi(x_n+z_n)\rightarrow \varphi(x)$ we get that $\phi'_k(z_n'')\rightarrow 0$ (here we are using Lemma \ref{lem:diff-cont}). Again by Lemma \ref{lem:conv-quot} we get that there exists $z_n^*\in \ker(\phi'_k)$ such that $z_n''-z_n^*\rightarrow 0$ in $\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X}')$. We claim now that the sequence $(g_n:=(z_n,z_n'+z_n^*)\in G_k)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ works, i.e., that $(x_n,x'_n)+g_n\rightarrow (x,x')$. Indeed $x_n'+z_n'+z_n^*=(x_n'+z_n'+z_n'')+(z_n^*-z_n'')$, where the first summand converges to $x'$ and the second to $0$.

Using the surjectivity of $\phi'_k$ we can find some $r\in \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X}')$ such that $\phi'_k(r)=s$, whence  $\varphi(x)=\varphi'(x'+r)$. nodes.section: 2 Locally-compact Hausdorff nilspaces

nodes.name: Construct the sequence $g_n$
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lem:conv-quot} in $\mathrm{X}$, there is a sequence $(z_n)_n$ in $\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})$ such that $x_n+z_n\rightarrow x$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$ in $\mathrm{X}$. For every $n\in \mathbb{N}$, by the surjectivity of $\phi_k'$ there is $z_n'\in \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X}')$ such that $(z_n,z_n')\in G_k$. Note that  $\varphi(x+z_n)\rightarrow\varphi(x)$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$ and that $\varphi(x_n+z_n)=\varphi'(x_n'+z_n')$ for all $n\in \mathbb{N}$. Next, by Lemma \ref{lem:conv-quot} applied in $\mathrm{X}'$, for every $n\in \mathbb{N}$ there exists $z_n''\in \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X}')$ such that $x_n'+z_n'+z_n''\rightarrow x'$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$. We claim that $\phi'_k(z_n'')\rightarrow 0$ as $n\rightarrow \infty$. Indeed $\varphi'(x_n'+z_n'+z_n'')\rightarrow \varphi'(x')=\varphi(x)$ and also $\varphi'(x_n'+z_n'+z_n'')=\varphi'(x_n'+z_n')+\phi_k'(z_n'')=\varphi(x_n+z_n)+\phi_k'(z_n'')$. As $\varphi(x_n+z_n)\rightarrow \varphi(x)$ we get that $\phi'_k(z_n'')\rightarrow 0$ (here we are using Lemma \ref{lem:diff-cont}). Again by Lemma \ref{lem:conv-quot} we get that there exists $z_n^*\in \ker(\phi'_k)$ such that $z_n''-z_n^*\rightarrow 0$ in $\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X}')$. We claim now that the sequence $(g_n:=(z_n,z_n'+z_n^*)\in G_k)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ works, i.e., that $(x_n,x'_n)+g_n\rightarrow (x,x')$. Indeed  $x_n'+z_n'+z_n^*=(x_n'+z_n'+z_n'')+(z_n^*-z_n'')$, where the first summand converges to $x'$ and the second to $0$.
nodes.section: 2 Locally-compact Hausdorff nilspaces
nodes.statement_short: Combine convergent lifts in $\mathrm{X}$ and $\mathrm{X}'$ and correct by kernel elements.

nodes.name: Lifts in $\mathrm{X}$ and $\mathrm{X}'$
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lem:conv-quot} in $\mathrm{X}$, there is a sequence $(z_n)_n$ in $\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})$ such that $x_n+z_n\rightarrow x$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$ in $\mathrm{X}$. For every $n\in \mathbb{N}$, by the surjectivity of $\phi_k'$ there is $z_n'\in \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X}')$ such that $(z_n,z_n')\in G_k$. Note that  $\varphi(x+z_n)\rightarrow\varphi(x)$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$ and that $\varphi(x_n+z_n)=\varphi'(x_n'+z_n')$ for all $n\in \mathbb{N}$. Next, by Lemma \ref{lem:conv-quot} applied in $\mathrm{X}'$, for every $n\in \mathbb{N}$ there exists $z_n''\in \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X}')$ such that $x_n'+z_n'+z_n''\rightarrow x'$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$.
nodes.section: 2 Locally-compact Hausdorff nilspaces
nodes.statement_short: Use Lemma conv-quot in both spaces.

nodes.name: $\phi_k'(z_n'')\to 0$

Indeed $\varphi'(x_n'+z_n'+z_n'')\rightarrow \varphi'(x')=\varphi(x)$ and also $\varphi'(x_n'+z_n'+z_n'')=\varphi'(x_n'+z_n')+\phi_k'(z_n'')=\varphi(x_n+z_n)+\phi_k'(z_n'')$. As $\varphi(x_n+z_n)\rightarrow \varphi(x)$ we get that $\phi'_k(z_n'')\rightarrow 0$ (here we are using Lemma \ref{lem:diff-cont}).
nodes.section: 2 Locally-compact Hausdorff nilspaces

nodes.name: Two expressions for $\varphi'(x_n'+z_n'+z_n'')$
nodes.statement: Indeed $\varphi'(x_n'+z_n'+z_n'')\rightarrow \varphi'(x')=\varphi(x)$ and also $\varphi'(x_n'+z_n'+z_n'')=\varphi'(x_n'+z_n')+\phi_k'(z_n'')=\varphi(x_n+z_n)+\phi_k'(z_n'')$.
nodes.section: 2 Locally-compact Hausdorff nilspaces

nodes.name: Conclude the limit
nodes.statement: As $\varphi(x_n+z_n)\rightarrow \varphi(x)$ we get that $\phi'_k(z_n'')\rightarrow 0$ (here we are using Lemma \ref{lem:diff-cont}).

nodes.name: Kernel approximants
nodes.statement: Again by Lemma \ref{lem:conv-quot} we get that there exists $z_n^*\in \ker(\phi'_k)$ such that $z_n''-z_n^*\rightarrow 0$ in $\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X}')$.
nodes.section: 2 Locally-compact Hausdorff nilspaces

nodes.name: The sequence $g_n$ works
nodes.statement: We claim now that the sequence $(g_n:=(z_n,z_n'+z_n^*)\in G_k)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ works, i.e., that $(x_n,x'_n)+g_n\rightarrow (x,x')$. Indeed  $x_n'+z_n'+z_n^*=(x_n'+z_n'+z_n'')+(z_n^*-z_n'')$, where the first summand converges to $x'$ and the second to $0$.

nodes.name: Lie-fibered nilspace
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step \textsc{lch} nilspace. We say that $\mathrm{X}$ is a \emph{locally-compact and finite-rank} nilspace, or \emph{Lie-fibered nilspace}, if all its structure groups are compactly generated (abelian) Lie groups.
nodes.section: 2 Locally-compact Hausdorff nilspaces
differentia: all its structure groups are compactly generated (abelian) Lie groups
nodes.label: def:lcfr-nil

nodes.name: Local triviality of the factor bundle of a Lie-fibered nilspace
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a Lie-fibered $k$-step nilspace. Then there is a covering of $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ by open sets $U$ with the property that for each $U$ there is a homeomorphism $\phi_U:\pi_{k-1}^{-1}(U)\rightarrow U\times \mathrm{Z}_k$ which is $\mathrm{Z}_k$-equivariant.
nodes.section: 2 Locally-compact Hausdorff nilspaces
assumptions: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a Lie-fibered $k$-step nilspace.
conclusions: Then there is a covering of $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ by open sets $U$ with the property that for each $U$ there is a homeomorphism $\phi_U:\pi_{k-1}^{-1}(U)\rightarrow U\times \mathrm{Z}_k$ which is $\mathrm{Z}_k$-equivariant.
also_stated_at: For any such nilspace $\mathrm{X}$, the factor projection $\pi_{k-1}:\mathrm{X}\rightarrow\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ is locally trivial as a bundle projection.
nodes.label: thm:local-triviality-bundle

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.20
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{prop:k-th-group-action} and Lemma \ref{lem:diff-cont}, the nilspace $\mathrm{X}$ is a Cartan principal $\mathrm{Z}_k$-bundle, and therefore by \cite[Theorem in \S 4]{P61}) this bundle is locally trivial.
nodes.section: 2 Locally-compact Hausdorff nilspaces
nodes.statement_short: The nilspace is a Cartan principal $\mathrm{Z}_k$-bundle, so Palais' theorem gives local triviality.

nodes.name: Open mapping theorem for topological groups
nodes.statement: A well-known version of the open mapping theorem for topological groups states that if $G$ and $H$ are \textsc{lch} topological groups, with $G$ being $\sigma$-compact, and $\varphi:G\rightarrow H$ is a continuous surjective homomorphism, then $\varphi$ is an open map \cite[p.\ 669]{H&M-Cpct}.
nodes.section: 2.1 The open mapping theorem for Lie-fibered nilspaces
conclusions: A well-known version of the open mapping theorem for topological groups states that if $G$ and $H$ are \textsc{lch} topological groups, with $G$ being $\sigma$-compact, and $\varphi:G\rightarrow H$ is a continuous surjective homomorphism, then $\varphi$ is an open map \cite[p.\ 669]{H&M-Cpct}.

nodes.name: Open mapping theorem for Lie-fibered nilspaces
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{X}$,$\mathrm{Y}$ be Lie-fibered $k$-step nilspaces, and let $\varphi:\mathrm{X}\rightarrow\mathrm{Y}$ be a continuous fibration. Then $\varphi$ is an open map.
nodes.section: 2.1 The open mapping theorem for Lie-fibered nilspaces
assumptions: Let $\mathrm{X}$,$\mathrm{Y}$ be Lie-fibered $k$-step nilspaces, and let $\varphi:\mathrm{X}\rightarrow\mathrm{Y}$ be a continuous fibration.
conclusions: Then $\varphi$ is an open map.
nodes.label: thm:open-mapping-thm

nodes.name: Continuous translations of Lie-fibered nilspaces are homeomorphisms
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a Lie-fibered $k$-step nilspace, and let $\alpha$ be a continuous translation on $\mathrm{X}$. Then $\alpha$ is a homeomorphism. In particular $\alpha^{-1}$ is continuous and the set of continuous translations on $\mathrm{X}$ is a group under composition.
nodes.section: 2.1 The open mapping theorem for Lie-fibered nilspaces
assumptions: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a Lie-fibered $k$-step nilspace, and let $\alpha$ be a continuous translation on $\mathrm{X}$.
conclusions: Then $\alpha$ is a homeomorphism.
In particular $\alpha^{-1}$ is continuous and the set of continuous translations on $\mathrm{X}$ is a group under composition.
nodes.label: cor:inv-cont-lcfr

nodes.name: Notation $\Theta(\mathrm{X})$ for continuous translations
nodes.statement: Hence, for a Lie-fibered nilspace $\mathrm{X}$, the notation $\Theta(\mathrm{X})$ will always refer to the group of \emph{continuous} translations on $\mathrm{X}$.
nodes.section: 2.1 The open mapping theorem for Lie-fibered nilspaces

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 2.22
nodes.statement: Any translation on $\mathrm{X}$ is a fibration. Hence, by Theorem \ref{thm:open-mapping-thm} a continuous translation is an open map, so its inverse is continuous.
nodes.section: 2.1 The open mapping theorem for Lie-fibered nilspaces
nodes.statement_short: Translations are fibrations, so Theorem 2.21 makes them open.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.21
nodes.statement: We argue by induction on $k$. The case $k=1$ holds by the open mapping theorem for topological groups. For $k>1$, we shall use that the bundle map $\pi:\mathrm{X}\rightarrow\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ is locally trivial, which is given by Theorem \ref{thm:local-triviality-bundle}. That is, we shall use that there exists a covering of $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ by open sets $\{U_i\}_{i\in I}$ such for each $i$ there is a map $\pi_{k-1}^{-1}(U_i)\rightarrow U_i \times\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})$ that is a homeomorphism which is also $\mathrm{Z}_k$-equivariant. Fix any $x\in\mathrm{X}$. We now show that for small enough neighborhoods of $x$, their images under $\varphi$ are open. Let $V\subset \mathrm{Y}_{k-1}$ be any open neighborhood of $\pi_{k-1}(\varphi(x))$ such that there is a $\mathrm{Z}_k$-equivariant homeomorphism $\tau:V\times \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})\rightarrow \pi_{k-1}^{-1}(V)$. Note that we can express $\tau$ as $(\pi_{k-1}(y),z')\mapsto s'(\pi_{k-1}(y))+z'$ for some continuous map $s':V\rightarrow \pi_{k-1}^{-1}(V)$. The set $\varphi^{-1}(\pi_{k-1}^{-1}(V))$ is an open neighborhood of $x$. Thus $\pi_{k-1}(\varphi^{-1}(\pi^{-1}(V)))$ is an open neighborhood of $\pi_{k-1}(x)$ (recall that $\pi_{k-1}$ is an open map by Corollary \ref{cor:quotient-top-k-1-factor}). Let $U^*$ be an open neighborhood of $\pi_{k-1}(x)$ such that there is an equivariant homeomorphism $U^*\times \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})\rightarrow \pi_{k-1}^{-1}(U^*)$, $(\pi_{k-1}(x),z)\mapsto s(\pi_{k-1}(x))+z$. Take $U:=U^*\cap \pi_{k-1}(\varphi^{-1}(\pi^{-1}(V)))$ and note that the same homemorphism works replacing $U^*$ with $U$. Identifying $\pi_{k-1}^{-1}(U)$ with $U\times \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})$, we can then define the base of neighborhoods of $x$ consisting of sets of the form $A\times H\subset U\times \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})$, where $A\subset U$ and $H\subset \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})$ are open. The image of any such neighbourhodd $A\times H$ under $\varphi$ is \[ \varphi(A\times H)=\tau^{-1}\Big(\,\{(\varphi_{k-1}(u),\phi_k(z)+(\varphi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} s-s'\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \varphi_{k-1})(a)): (a,z)\in A\times H\}\Big), \] where $\phi_k:\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})\rightarrow\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})$ is the $k$-th structure homomorphism of $\varphi$ and $\varphi_{k-1}:\mathrm{X}_{k-1}\rightarrow\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}$ is the morphism between the $k-1$ factors of $\mathrm{X}$ and $\mathrm{Y}$ (note that $\phi_k$ is continuous and surjective since $\varphi$ is a fibration). To see that this image is open, it suffices to prove the claim that the composition $U\times \mathrm{Z}_k\rightarrow U\times \mathrm{Z}_k'\rightarrow V\times \mathrm{Z}_k'$, $(u,z)\mapsto (u,\phi_k(z))\mapsto (\varphi_{k-1}(u),\phi_k(z)+(\varphi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} s-s'\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \varphi_{k-1})(u))$ is open. Since the first of these maps is clearly open, we focus on showing that the second map, namely $T:U\times \mathrm{Z}_k'\rightarrow V\times \mathrm{Z}_k'$, $(u,z')\mapsto (\varphi_{k-1}(u),z'+(\varphi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} s-s'\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \varphi_{k-1})(u))$, is open. Let $I:U\times Z_k'\rightarrow U\times Z_k'$, $(u,z')\mapsto (u,z'-(\varphi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} s-s'\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \varphi_{k-1})(u))$. Since $I$ is clearly a homeomorphism, it suffices to show that $T\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} I$ is open. But $T\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} I(u,z')=(\varphi_{k-1}(u),z')$, which is clearly open. This proves our claim. By induction $\varphi_{k-1}(A)$ is open and by the open mapping theorem for topological groups so is $\phi_k(H)$. It follows that $\varphi(A\times H)$ is open as required We have thus proved that images under $\varphi$ of the above basic open neighbourhoods are open, so the openness of $\varphi$ follows by taking unions.

nodes.name: Open mapping theorem for fibrations onto Lie-fibered nilspaces
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step \textsc{lch} nilspace, and let $\mathrm{Y}$ be a $k$-step Lie-fibered nilspace. Then any continuous fibration $\varphi:\mathrm{X}\rightarrow\mathrm{Y}$ is an open map.

assumptions: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step \textsc{lch} nilspace, and let $\mathrm{Y}$ be a $k$-step Lie-fibered nilspace.
conclusions: Then any continuous fibration $\varphi:\mathrm{X}\rightarrow\mathrm{Y}$ is an open map.

nodes.name: Quotient of an LCH nilspace by a closed subgroup of the last structure group
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step, \textsc{lch} nilspace and $\mathrm{Z}$ a closed subgroup of its last structure group. Then $\mathrm{X}/\mathrm{Z}$ with the cubes $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}/\mathrm{Z}):=\{\pi_{\mathrm{Z}}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}: \mathrm{c}\in \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}) \}$ is an \textsc{lch} nilspace.\footnote{Here as usual $\mathrm{X}/\mathrm{Z}$ is understood as the quotient of $\mathrm{X}$ modulo the action of $\mathrm{X}$ with the quotient topology and $\pi_{\mathrm{Z}}$ is the quotient map.} Moreover, $(\mathrm{X}/\mathrm{Z})_{k-1}\cong \mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ and the $k$-th structure group of $\mathrm{X}/\mathrm{Z}$ is isomorphic to $\mathrm{Z}_k/\mathrm{Z}$ as topological groups where $\mathrm{Z}_k$ is the $k$-th structure group of $\mathrm{X}$.

assumptions: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step, \textsc{lch} nilspace and $\mathrm{Z}$ a closed subgroup of its last structure group.
conclusions: Then $\mathrm{X}/\mathrm{Z}$ with the cubes $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}/\mathrm{Z}):=\{\pi_{\mathrm{Z}}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}: \mathrm{c}\in \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}) \}$ is an \textsc{lch} nilspace.\footnote{Here as usual $\mathrm{X}/\mathrm{Z}$ is understood as the quotient of $\mathrm{X}$ modulo the action of $\mathrm{X}$ with the quotient topology and $\pi_{\mathrm{Z}}$ is the quotient map.}

Moreover, $(\mathrm{X}/\mathrm{Z})_{k-1}\cong \mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ and the $k$-th structure group of $\mathrm{X}/\mathrm{Z}$ is isomorphic to $\mathrm{Z}_k/\mathrm{Z}$ as topological groups where $\mathrm{Z}_k$ is the $k$-th structure group of $\mathrm{X}$.
nodes.label: prop:quot-last-str-gr

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.24
nodes.statement: The algebraic part of the proof follows from \cite[Proposition A.19]{CGSS-p-hom}, so here we just prove the topological part. We need to prove first that the topology of $\mathrm{X}/\mathrm{Z}$ is \textsc{lch} and later we will use Lemma \ref{lem:eq-def-lch-nil} to prove that it is indeed an \textsc{lch} nilspace. Let $\pi_{k-1}:\mathrm{X}\rightarrow \mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ be the usual quotient map in $\mathrm{X}$. First we prove that the set $C=\{(x,x')\in \mathrm{X}^2: x=gx' \text{ for some } g\in \mathrm{Z}\}$ is closed. Since $\mathrm{X}$ is a Cartan bundle over $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$, on the closed set $C'=\{(x,x')\in\mathrm{X}^2:\pi_{k-1}(x)=\pi_{k-1}(x')\}$ we know that the difference function $C'\rightarrow \mathrm{Z}_k$, $(x,x')\mapsto x-x'$ is well-defined and continuous; since $C$ is the preimage under this function of the closed set $\mathrm{Z}$, it is indeed closed. By Lemma \ref{lem:quo-by-cont-gr-act} the topology on $\mathrm{X}/\mathrm{Z}$ is \textsc{lch}. Next, we want to see that $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}/\mathrm{Z})$ is closed for all $n\in \mathbb{N}$. As the map $\pi_{\mathrm{Z}}:\mathrm{X}\rightarrow \mathrm{X}/\mathrm{Z}$ is open and continuous, the map $\mathrm{X}^{\db{n}}\rightarrow (\mathrm{X}/\mathrm{Z})^{\db{n}}$ is a quotient map. Hence, it suffices to check that $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})+\mathrm{Z}^{\db{n}}$ is a closed subset of $\mathrm{X}^{\db{n}}$. For $n\le k$ the result is trivial and the case $n>k+1$ follows from the case $n=k+1$, so let us just prove this latter case. Let $\mathrm{c}_n+d_n\in \mathrm{C}^{k+1}(\mathrm{X})+\mathrm{Z}^{\db{k+1}}$ be a convergent sequence. Let $r_n':=(\mathrm{c}_n+d_n)|_{\db{k+1}\setminus{1^{k+1}}}\in \mathrm{Cor}^{k+1}(\mathrm{X})$. This is clearly convergent so let us define $r_n\in \mathrm{C}^{k+1}(\mathrm{X})$ its unique completion for all $n\in \mathbb{N}$ and note that then $r_n\in \mathrm{C}^{k+1}(\mathrm{X})$ is a convergent sequence. It follows that $\mathrm{c}_n-r_n\in \mathrm{C}^{k+1}(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}_k))$ and $(\mathrm{c}_n-r_n)(v) \in \mathrm{Z}$ for all $v\not=1^{k+1}$. Thus, applying the $\sigma_{k+1}$ operator (see \cite[Definition 2.2.22]{Cand:Notes1}) we get that $\sigma_{k+1}(\mathrm{c}_n-r_n)=0$ (by \cite[Proposition 2.2.28 $(iii)$]{Cand:Notes1}) so in particular $(\mathrm{c}_n-r_n)(1^{k+1})\in \mathrm{Z}$ as well. Thus, if we let $e_n:=\mathrm{c}_n-r_n$ we have that $\mathrm{c}_n+d_n = r_n+(e_n+d_n)$. As both $\mathrm{c}_n+d_n$ and $r_n$ are convergent sequences so is $e_n+d_n\in \mathrm{Z}^{\db{k+1}}$. Using that $\mathrm{C}^{k+1}(\mathrm{X})$ and $\mathrm{Z}^{\db{k+1}}$ are closed we have that $\mathrm{c}_n+d_n$ converges to a limit in $\mathrm{C}^{k+1}(\mathrm{X})+\mathrm{Z}^{\db{k+1}}$. Lemma \ref{lem:eq-def-lch-nil} $(i)$ follows. Next, let us prove first that the completion function $\mathrm{Cor}^{k+1}(\mathrm{X}/\mathrm{Z})\rightarrow \mathrm{X}/\mathrm{Z}$ is continuous. If $\pi_{\mathrm{Z}}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}_n\in \mathrm{Cor}^{k+1}(\mathrm{X}/\mathrm{Z})$ is convergent, by Lemma \ref{lem:conv-quot} applied for each $v\in \db{k+1}\setminus\{1^{k+1}\}$, we can assume that $\mathrm{c}_n\in \mathrm{X}^{\db{k+1}\setminus\{1^{k+1}\}}$ is a convergent sequence as well. And moreover, note that if $\pi:\mathrm{X}/\mathrm{Z}\rightarrow \mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ is the map such that $\pi_{k-1}=\pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\pi_{\mathrm{Z}}$, by \cite[Proposition A.19 $(iii)$]{CGSS-p-hom} we have that $\pi$ is a morphism. If we let $F\subset \db{k+1}\setminus\{1^{k+1}\}$ be any $k$-dimensional face containing $0^{k+1}$, $\pi_{k-1}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} (\mathrm{c}_n|_F) = \pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \pi_{\mathrm{Z}}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} (\mathrm{c}_n|_F)$. But $\pi_{\mathrm{Z}}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} (\mathrm{c}_n|_F)\in \mathrm{C}^k(\mathrm{X}/\mathrm{Z})$ so in particular, $\pi_{k-1}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} (\mathrm{c}_n|_F)\in \mathrm{C}^k(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$. Thus by \cite[Remark 3.2.12]{Cand:Notes1} we conclude that $\mathrm{c}_n\in \mathrm{Cor}^{k+1}(\mathrm{X})$. Hence, the continuity of completion of $(k+1)$-corners for $\mathrm{X}/\mathrm{Z}$ follows from that for $\mathrm{X}$. By \cite[Proposition A.19 $(iii)$]{CGSS-p-hom} we have a nilspace isomorphism $(\mathrm{X}/\mathrm{Z})_{k-1}\rightarrow \mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ (purely algebraically). We want to prove that this map is also a homeomorphism. Let $\pi'_{k-1}:\mathrm{X}/\mathrm{Z}\rightarrow (\mathrm{X}/\mathrm{Z})_{k-1}$ be the quotient map to the $(k-1)$-step factor of $\mathrm{X}/\mathrm{Z}$. We want to prove that the map $\pi'_{k-1}(\pi_{\mathrm{Z}}(x)) \mapsto \pi_{k-1}(x)$ is a homeomorphism (we already know that it is an algebraic nilspace isomorphism). By Corollary \ref{cor:quotient-top-k-1-factor} we have that $\pi'_{k-1}$ is open and continuous. As both $\pi_{k-1}$ and $\pi_{\mathrm{Z}}$ are also open and continuous, it follows that the previous map is a homeomorphism. Hence, $(ii)$ of Lemma \ref{lem:eq-def-lch-nil} for $n$-corners, $n\le k$, follows from the fact that $\mathrm{X}$ is an \textsc{lch} nilspace. The $k$-th structure group of $\mathrm{X}/\mathrm{Z}$ is isomorphic to $\mathrm{Z}_k/\mathrm{Z}$. To prove this, recall that by \cite[Corollary 3.2.16]{Cand:Notes1} the $k$-th structure group of $\mathrm{X}/\mathrm{Z}$ is isomorphic (as a degree-$k$ abelian group) to any fiber of the factor map $\pi_{k-1}$ on $\mathrm{X}/\mathrm{Z}$. Moreover, on this fiber we consider the subspace topology. By \cite[Proposition A.20]{CGSS-p-hom} we know that algebraically the $k$-th structure group of $\mathrm{X}/\mathrm{Z}$ is isomorphic to $\mathrm{Z}_k/\mathrm{Z}$. To see that the isomorphism is also topological, fix any $\pi_{k-1}$-fiber $\pi_{\mathrm{Z}}(e)+\mathrm{Z}_k/\mathrm{Z}$ of $\mathrm{X}/\mathrm{Z}$. Note that $\pi_{\mathrm{Z}}|_{e+\mathrm{Z}_k}: e+\mathrm{Z}_k\rightarrow \pi_{\mathrm{Z}}(e)+\mathrm{Z}_k/\mathrm{Z}$ is a continuous map (being the restriction of a continuous map). Moreover, it is also a homomorphism of groups when we identify $e+\mathrm{Z}_k$ with $\mathrm{Z}_k$ and $\pi_{\mathrm{Z}}(e)+\mathrm{Z}_k/\mathrm{Z}$ with the $k$-th structure group of $\mathrm{X}/\mathrm{Z}$. By the open mapping theorem for Polish groups this map is open and thus the $k$-th structre group of $\mathrm{X}/\mathrm{Z}$ is topologically isomorphic to $\mathrm{Z}_k$ modulo the kernel of $\pi_{\mathrm{Z}}|_{e+\mathrm{Z}_k}$, which is precisely $\mathrm{Z}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.23
nodes.statement: Let $\phi_k:\mathrm{Z}_k\rightarrow\mathrm{Z}_k'$ be the last structure morphism of $\varphi$ (where $\mathrm{Z}_k$ and $\mathrm{Z}_k'$ are the $k$-th structure groups of $\mathrm{X}$ and $\mathrm{Y}$ respectively). By \cite[Proposition A.19]{CGSS-p-hom} and Proposition \ref{prop:quot-last-str-gr} we have that $\mathrm{X}/\ker(\phi_k)$ is a $k$-step \textsc{lch} nilspace. The canonical factor map $\pi_{\ker(\phi_k)}:\mathrm{X}\rightarrow\mathrm{X}/\ker(\phi_k)$ is continuous and open, and $\varphi$ factors through a continuous fibration $\varphi':\mathrm{X}/\ker(\phi_k)\rightarrow\mathrm{Y}$, $x+\ker(\phi_k)\mapsto \varphi(x)$, i.e., $\varphi = \varphi'\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \pi_{\ker(\phi_k)}$. Note that since $\phi_k$ is a continuous surjective homomorphism, by Lemma \ref{lem:quot-polish-gr-lie-gr} we have that $\mathrm{Z}_k/\ker(\phi_k)\cong \mathrm{Z}_k'$ is a Lie group. By \cite[Theorem 2.3.3]{P61}, $\mathrm{X}/\ker(\phi_k)$ is a locally-trivial abelian bundle over $(\mathrm{X}/\ker(\phi_k))_{k-1}\cong \mathrm{X}_{k-1}$. By induction on $k$ we can suppose that $\varphi'_{k-1}$ is open. We can then argue as in the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:open-mapping-thm}, using the local triviality, to deduce that $\varphi'$ is open. Since $\pi_{\ker(\phi_k)}$ is also open, we deduce that $\varphi$ is open.

nodes.statement_short: Factor through the quotient by the kernel of the last structure morphism, which is Lie-fibered-like and locally trivial, then argue as in Theorem 2.21 by induction.

nodes.name: Quotient by the kernel
nodes.statement: Let $\phi_k:\mathrm{Z}_k\rightarrow\mathrm{Z}_k'$ be the last structure morphism of $\varphi$ (where $\mathrm{Z}_k$ and $\mathrm{Z}_k'$ are the $k$-th structure groups of $\mathrm{X}$ and $\mathrm{Y}$ respectively). The canonical factor map $\pi_{\ker(\phi_k)}:\mathrm{X}\rightarrow\mathrm{X}/\ker(\phi_k)$ is continuous and open, and $\varphi$ factors through a continuous fibration $\varphi':\mathrm{X}/\ker(\phi_k)\rightarrow\mathrm{Y}$, $x+\ker(\phi_k)\mapsto \varphi(x)$, i.e., $\varphi = \varphi'\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \pi_{\ker(\phi_k)}$.

nodes.statement_short: Quotient group is Lie; Palais gives local triviality.

nodes.name: Continuous abelian bundle
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{B}$ be an abelian bundle with base $S$, structure group $\mathrm{Z}$ and projection $\pi$. We say that $\mathrm{B}$ is \emph{continuous} if the following conditions hold: \begin{enumerate} \item $\mathrm{B}$ and $S$ are topological spaces. \item $\mathrm{Z}$ is an abelian topological group. \item The action $\alpha:\mathrm{Z}\times \mathrm{B}\rightarrow \mathrm{B}$ is continuous. \item A set $U\subset S$ is open if and only if $\pi^{-1}(U)$ is open in $\mathrm{B}$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 2.2 Topological aspects of nilspace extensions
nodes.label: def:CtsAbBund

nodes.name: LCH abelian $\mathrm{Z}$-bundle
nodes.statement: We say that $\mathrm{B}$ is an \emph{\textsc{lch} abelian $\mathrm{Z}$-bundle} if it is a continuous abelian bundle and in addition the topologies on $\mathrm{B}$, $S$, $\mathrm{Z}$ are all locally-compact, second-countable Hausdorff.
nodes.section: 2.2 Topological aspects of nilspace extensions

nodes.name: Cartan continuous $\mathrm{Z}$-bundle
nodes.statement: We also say that $\mathrm{B}$ is a \emph{Cartan continuous $\mathrm{Z}$-bundle} if, in addition to $\mathrm{B}$ being a continuous $\mathrm{Z}$-bundle, it is also a Cartan principal $\mathrm{Z}$-bundle (i.e.\ the difference map is continuous: see Definition \ref{def:Cartan}).
nodes.section: 2.2 Topological aspects of nilspace extensions

nodes.name: Irrational rotation bundle that is not Cartan
nodes.statement: Note that there are examples of continuous abelian bundles that are not Cartan. Take for example $\mathrm{B}=\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ and consider the action of $\mathbb{Z}$ on $\mathrm{B}$ defined as $(x\mod 1,n)\mapsto x+n\alpha \mod 1$ for some irrational $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$. If we let $S:=\mathrm{B}/\mathbb{Z}$ with the quotient topology we have that this is a continuous abelian bundle. However, it can be checked not to be Cartan.
nodes.section: 2.2 Topological aspects of nilspace extensions
nodes.statement_short: $\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ with an irrational rotation action of $\mathbb{Z}$ is a continuous abelian bundle that is not Cartan.

nodes.name: Algebraic extension of nilspaces
nodes.statement: In what follows, when we say that a nilspace is an \emph{algebraic} extension of another nilspace, we mean that it is an extension in the purely algebraic sense of \cite[\S 3.3.3]{Cand:Notes1} (before any topological aspects are added).
nodes.section: 2.2 Topological aspects of nilspace extensions

nodes.name: Continuous extension of LCH nilspaces
nodes.statement: Let $k,t\ge 0$ be integers. Let $\mathrm{X}$, $\mathrm{Y}$ be $k$-step \textsc{lch} nilspaces such that $\mathrm{Y}$ is an algebraic nilspace extension of $\mathrm{X}$ of degree $t$, by some \textsc{lch} abelian group $\mathrm{Z}$, with associated projection $p:\mathrm{Y}\rightarrow\mathrm{X}$. We say that $\mathrm{Y}$ (or $p:\mathrm{Y}\rightarrow \mathrm{X}$) is a \emph{continuous extension} of $\mathrm{X}$ if $\mathrm{Y}$ is additionally an \textsc{lch} abelian $\mathrm{Z}$-bundle with base $\mathrm{X}$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Topological aspects of nilspace extensions
nodes.label: def:ext-lch-nil

nodes.name: Equivalent formulation of continuous extensions
nodes.statement: Equivalently $\mathrm{Y}$ is a continuous $\mathrm{Z}$-extension of $\mathrm{X}$ if the action of $\mathrm{Z}$ on $\mathrm{Y}$ is continuous and $p$ is a continuous open map. Note that, in this case, the topology on $\mathrm{X}$ is equal to the quotient of the topology on $\mathrm{Y}$ under the action of $\mathrm{Z}$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Topological aspects of nilspace extensions
nodes.label: rem:topquot

nodes.name: Extensions of Lie groups are Lie
nodes.statement: Recall that if $0\rightarrow H\rightarrow G\rightarrow F\rightarrow 0$ is a proper short exact sequence of \textsc{lch} groups  where $H$ and $F$ are Lie, then so is $G$ (see \cite[Thm.\ 2.6]{Mosk}, \cite[Lem.\ A.3]{HK-non-conv}).
nodes.section: 2.2 Topological aspects of nilspace extensions
assumptions: $0\rightarrow H\rightarrow G\rightarrow F\rightarrow 0$ is a proper short exact sequence of \textsc{lch} groups  where $H$ and $F$ are Lie
conclusions: then so is $G$

nodes.name: Extensions of Lie-fibered nilspaces by Lie groups are Lie-fibered
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{X}$, $\mathrm{Y}$ be \textsc{lch} $k$-step nilspaces, and suppose that $\mathrm{Y}$ is a degree-$k$ algebraic nilspace extension of $\mathrm{X}$ by an abelian \textsc{lch} group $\mathrm{Z}$. Let $p:\mathrm{Y}\rightarrow \mathrm{X}$ be the associated fibration. If $p$ is continuous, $\mathrm{X}$ is Lie-fibered, and $\mathrm{Z}$ is a Lie group, then $\mathrm{Y}$ is also Lie-fibered. Moreover $\mathrm{Y}$ is then a continuous extension of $\mathrm{X}$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Topological aspects of nilspace extensions
assumptions: Let $\mathrm{X}$, $\mathrm{Y}$ be \textsc{lch} $k$-step nilspaces, and suppose that $\mathrm{Y}$ is a degree-$k$ algebraic nilspace extension of $\mathrm{X}$ by an abelian \textsc{lch} group $\mathrm{Z}$.
Let $p:\mathrm{Y}\rightarrow \mathrm{X}$ be the associated fibration.
If $p$ is continuous, $\mathrm{X}$ is Lie-fibered, and $\mathrm{Z}$ is a Lie group

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.28
nodes.statement:
Recall that $p$ is indeed a fibration (\cite[Proposition A.18]{CGSS-p-hom}), and note that $p_{k-1}:\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}ightarrow \mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ is then a continuous fibration as well. Moreover $p_{k-1}$ is bijective. Indeed, for any elements $\pi_{k-1}(x),\pi_{k-1}(x')\in\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}$ such that $p_{k-1}(\pi_{k-1}(x))=p_{k-1}(\pi_{k-1}(x'))$, we have $\pi_{k-1}(p(x))=\pi_{k-1}(p(x'))$ and thus there exists a cube $\mathrm{c}\in \mathrm{C}^k(\mathrm{X})$ such that $\mathrm{c}(v)=p(x)$ for all $v
ot=1^k$ and $\mathrm{c}(1^k)=p(x')$. Let $\mathrm{c}':\db{k}ightarrow\mathrm{Y}$ be the map with $\mathrm{c}'(v)=x$ for all $v
ot=1^k$ and $\mathrm{c}'(1^k)=x'$. Since $\mathrm{c}'$ restricted to $\db{k}\setminus\{1^k\}$ is a corner and $p$ is a fibration with $p\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}'|_{\db{k}\setminus\{1^k\}}=\mathrm{c}|_{\db{k}\setminus\{1^k\}}$, there exists $z\in \mathrm{Z}$ such that the map $\mathrm{c}'+1_{\{1^k\}}z$ is in $\mathrm{C}^k(\mathrm{Y})$. But note that $\mathrm{Z}^{\db{k}} = \mathrm{C}^k(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}))$, so $1_{\{1^k\}}z\in \mathrm{C}^k(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}))$, and therefore $\mathrm{c}'\in \mathrm{C}^k(\mathrm{Y})$. Hence $\pi_{k-1}(x)=\pi_{k-1}(x')$. By Theorem ef{thm:open-mapping-general} the map $p_{k-1}$ is open, and therefore $p_{k-1}$ is an isomorphism of 	extsc{lch} nilspaces. Hence every structure group of $\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}$ is a Lie group. It therefore remains only to prove that the last structure group $\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})$ is also a Lie group. Recall from Proposition ef{prop:k-th-group-action} that $\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})$ is isomorphic to any fixed fiber $F$ of $\pi_{k-1,\mathrm{Y}}$ where we fix some (any) element $e\in F$ to be the identity. Similarly, in $\mathrm{X}$ we fix the fiber $F':=p(F)$ and fix $p(e)$ as the zero element of $\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})$. The free action of $\mathrm{Z}$ on $F$ induces an inclusion of $\mathrm{Z}$ into $\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})$. The homormorphism $\phi_k:\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})ightarrow\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})$ can then be identified with $p|_F:Fightarrow F'$. First we claim that the kernel of this homomorphism $p|_F$ is precisely $e+\mathrm{Z}\subset F$. To see this, let $x\in F$ be any element such that $p(x)=p(e)$. By hypothesis on $p$, this means that if $\mathrm{c}\in F^{\db{k+1}}$ is the map $\mathrm{c}(v)=e$ for all $v
ot=1^{k+1}$ and $\mathrm{c}(1^{k+1})=x$, there exists $d\in \mathrm{Z}^{\db{k+1}}$ such that $\mathrm{c}+d\in \mathrm{C}^{k+1}(\mathrm{Y})$. Note that we are not assuming that either $\mathrm{c}$ or $d$ are cubes for any nilspace, only that the sum $\mathrm{c}+d$ is. Then, by definition of the cubes in $\mathrm{C}^{k+1}(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}))$ in terms of the single Gray-code linear equation, we can find a cube $d'\in \mathrm{C}^{k+1}(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}))$ such that $d'(v)=-d(v)$ for all $v
ot=1^{k+1}$. Hence $c+d+d'\in \mathrm{C}^{k+1}(\mathrm{Y})$. Note that all values of this cube are $e$ except perhaps the value at $1^{k+1}$. By uniqueness of completion, this value must also be $e$. Hence $x+z=e$ for some $z\in \mathrm{Z}$, which proves our claim. Next, note that using the definition of addition in the fiber $F$ we have that the action of $\mathrm{Z}$ is also well defined and continuous. Furthermore, as mentioned above this free action induces an inclusion of $\mathrm{Z}$ in $\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})$, and $e+\mathrm{Z}$ is closed because it is precisely $p^{-1}(\{p(e)\})$. Thus we have a short exact sequence $0ightarrow \mathrm{Z} ightarrow \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y}) ightarrow \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})ightarrow 0$ where all groups are 	extsc{lch} and $\mathrm{Z},\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})$ are Lie. By \cite[Theorem 2.6]{Mosk} $\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})$ is Lie. Finally, by Theorem ef{thm:open-mapping-thm} the map $p$ is open, so $\mathrm{Y}$ is a continuous extension of $\mathrm{X}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 2.29
nodes.statement: If $t\ge k$ then we can directly apply Proposition \ref{prop:ext-lie-is-lie-1} with $k=t$ (since $\mathrm{X},\mathrm{Y}$ are in particular $t$-step nilspaces). For $t<k$, note that by \cite[Proposition A.18]{CGSS-p-hom} the nilspace $\mathrm{Y}$ is algebraically isomorphic to the fiber-product $\mathrm{Y}_t\times_{\mathrm{X}_t}\mathrm{X}$, with projection maps $p_t:\mathrm{Y}_t\rightarrow\mathrm{X}_t$ and $\pi_t:\mathrm{X}\rightarrow\mathrm{X}_t$. Note that the algebraic isomorphism is the map $\varphi(y)=(\pi_t(y),p(x))$, so here this is also a continuous map. Note that $p_t$ is also continuous, thus implying that $p_t$ is continuous as well because $p_t\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \pi_{t,\mathrm{Y}} = \pi_{t,\mathrm{X}} \circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} p$. As $p$ is continuous and both $\pi_{t,\mathrm{Y}}$ and $\pi_{t,\mathrm{X}}$ are open and continuous we conclude that $p_t$ is continuous. By Proposition \ref{prop:ext-lie-is-lie-1} we get that $\mathrm{Y}_t$ is Lie-fibered as well, and $p_t$ is a continuous extension of $\mathrm{X}_t$. By Lemma \ref{lem:fib-prod-top-nil} we know that $\mathrm{Y}_t\times_{\mathrm{X}_t}\mathrm{X}$ is an \textsc{lch} nilspace. Hence, in order to prove that it is Lie-fibered, it suffices to prove that its structure groups are Lie groups. The structure groups of $\mathrm{Y}_t\times_{\mathrm{X}_t}\mathrm{X}$ are easy to compute. Using the formula given in Lemma \ref{lem:fib-prod-top-nil} we deduce that for $i\le t$, the $i$-th structure group of $\mathrm{Y}_t\times_{\mathrm{X}_t}\mathrm{X}$ is $\mathrm{Z}_i(\mathrm{Y}_t)$, which is Lie. For $i>t$ the $i$-th structure group of $\mathrm{Y}_t\times_{\mathrm{X}_t}\mathrm{X}$ is $\mathrm{Z}_i(\mathrm{X})$ (which is Lie by assumption). Hence $\mathrm{Y}_t\times_{\mathrm{X}_t}\mathrm{X}$ is Lie-fibered. Then, Theorem \ref{thm:open-mapping-general} implies that the isomorphism $\varphi$ is also a homeomorphism. Hence $\mathrm{Y}$ is Lie-fibered. The last sentence in the corollary follows from Theorem \ref{thm:open-mapping-thm}.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.31
nodes.statement: That $\mathcal{T}$ is \emph{algebraically} a $\mathrm{Z}_k$-bundle over $\mathcal{T}_{k-1}$ follows from the fact, recalled above, that $\mathcal{T}$ is a $k$-step nilspace with $(k-1)$-step factor $\mathcal{T}_{k-1}$ (see e.g.\ \cite[Lemma 3.3.35]{Cand:Notes1}). In particular, it follows from \cite[Proposition 3.3.36]{Cand:Notes1} that the $k$-th structure group of $\mathcal{T}$ is $\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})$ (acting diagonally as recalled above). We check that $\mathcal{T}$ is also an \textsc{lch} \emph{continuous} $\mathrm{Z}_k$-bundle. First note that the topology on $\mathcal{T}$ is \textsc{lch} because the product topology on $\mathrm{X}\times \mathrm{X}$ is \textsc{lch} and $\mathcal{T}$ is a closed subset (being the preimage, under the continuous map $(\alpha\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \pi_{k-1,\mathrm{X}}) \times \pi_{k-1,\mathrm{X}}$, of the diagonal in $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}\times\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$, which is closed by the Hausdorff property of $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$). Now we check that the properties defining a continuous bundle (\cite[Definition 2.1.6]{Cand:Notes2}) hold. Property $(i)$ is clear: $\mathcal{T}$ has the above-described \textsc{lch} topology and $\mathcal{T}_{k-1}$ is given the quotient topology under the $\mathrm{Z}_k$-action. Property $(ii)$ holds in that $\mathrm{Z}_k$ comes naturally with an \textsc{lch} topology, i.e.\ the one given from $\mathrm{X}$. To see property $(iii)$, note that the continuity of the diagonal $\mathrm{Z}_k$-action follows from the continuity of the action of $\mathrm{Z}_k$ on $\mathrm{X}$ (looking at convergent sequences in $\mathcal{T}\times \mathrm{Z}_k$, for example). Property $(iv)$ holds since we equip $\mathcal{T}_{k-1}$ with the quotient topology. Finally, the fact that the quotient topology on $\mathcal{T}_{k-1}$ is \textsc{lch} follows from Lemma \ref{lem:quo-by-cont-gr-act}, provided that the set $C=\{(x,x')\in\mathcal{T}\times\mathcal{T}: \exists\,z\in \mathrm{Z}_k\textrm{ such that }x=x'+z\}$ is a closed subset of $\mathcal{T}\times\mathcal{T}$. To see this closure, suppose that a sequence $(x_n,x'_n)=((x_{0,n},x_{1,n}),(x_{0,n}',x_{1,n}'))$ in $C$ converges in $\mathcal{T}\times \mathcal{T}$ to some $((x_0,x_1),(x_0',x_1'))\in (\mathrm{X}\times\mathrm{X})^2$. Then $x_{0,n}\rightarrow x_0$, $x_{1,n}\rightarrow x_1$, $x_{0,n}'\rightarrow x_0'$, $x_{1,n}'\rightarrow x_1'$ in $\mathrm{X}$ (using the product topology). By the definition of $C$, for each $n$ there is $z_n\in \mathrm{Z}_k$ such that $x_{0,n}'=x_{0,n}+z_n$ and $x_{1,n}'=x_{1,n}+z_n$ for all $n$. Then, since $\mathrm{X}$ is an \textsc{lch} nilspace, by Lemma \ref{lem:closure} the graph of $\sim_{k-1}$ on $\mathrm{X}$ is closed, so there exist $z_0,z_1\in \mathrm{Z}_k$ such that $x_0'=x_0+z_0$ and $x_1'=x_1+z_1$. By continuity of the difference map (Lemma \ref{lem:diff-cont}) we have $z_n=x_{0,n}'-x_{0,n}\rightarrow x_0'-x_0=z_0$, and similarly $z_n\rightarrow z_1$, so $z_0=z_1$ and we are done.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.32
nodes.statement: The algebraic part of this result is given by \cite[Proposition 3.3.39]{Cand:Notes1}. To avoid confusion, let us denote the projection $\mathrm{X}\rightarrow \mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ by $\pi_{k-1,\mathrm{X}}$, and the bundle projection $\mathcal{T}\rightarrow \mathcal{T}_{k-1}$ by $\pi_{k-1,\mathcal{T}}$. By Lemma \ref{lem:transbnd-ctsbnd} we know that $\mathcal{T}$ is an \textsc{lch} continuous $\mathrm{Z}_k$-bundle over $\mathcal{T}_{k-1}$. Recall that the (purely algebraic) translation $\beta$ on $\mathrm{X}$ lifting $\alpha$, given by \cite[Proposition 3.3.39]{Cand:Notes1}, is defined by $\beta(x)=m(\pi_{k-1,\mathrm{X}}(x))\, (x)$, where $m(\pi_{k-1,\mathrm{X}}(x))$ is a \emph{local translation} from $\pi_{k-1,\mathrm{X}}^{-1}\pi_{k-1,\mathrm{X}}(x)$ to $\pi_{k-1,\mathrm{X}}^{-1}\alpha (\pi_{k-1,\mathrm{X}}(x))$ \cite[Definition 3.2.26]{Cand:Notes1} which is applied to $x$. We now prove the continuity of the map $\beta$. Let $(x_n)_n$ be a convergent sequence in $\mathrm{X}$ with limit $x$. Fix any sequence $((x_0^{(n)},x_1^{(n)}))_n$ in $\mathcal{T}$ such that $m(\pi_{k-1,\mathrm{X}}(x_n))=\pi_{k-1,\mathcal{T}}(x_0^{(n)},x_1^{(n)})$ for every $n$, and similarly fix $(x_0',x_1')\in \mathcal{T}$ such that $m(\pi_{k-1,\mathrm{X}}(x))=\pi_{k-1,\mathcal{T}}(x_0',x_1')$. The continuity of $m$ then implies that $\pi_{k-1,\mathcal{T}}(x_0^{(n)},x_1^{(n)})\rightarrow \pi_{k-1,\mathcal{T}}(x_0',x_1')$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$. By Lemma \ref{lem:conv-quot}, there is a sequence $(z_n)_n$ in $\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})$ such that $(x_0^{(n)}+z_n,x_1^{(n)}+z_n)\rightarrow (x_0',x_1')$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$. Now, for any pair of points $x_0,x_1\in \mathrm{X}$ and any $x\sim_{k-1} x_0$, let $\mathrm{c}'_{(x_0,x_1),x}$ denote the $(k+1)$-corner on $\mathrm{X}$ defined by $\mathrm{c}'_{(x_0,x_1),x}(v,0)=x_0$ for $v\neq 1^k$, $\mathrm{c}'_{(x_0,x_1),x}(1^k,0)=x$, and $\mathrm{c}'_{(x_0,x_1),x}(v,1)=x_1$ for $v\neq 1^k$. For $k=2$ the corner $\mathrm{c}'_{(x_0,x_1),x}$ is $ \smallcorner{x_0}{x_0}{x_0}{x}{x_1}{x_1}{x_1}.\\ $ By definition of $\beta$ and of local translations, for each $x\in \mathrm{X}$ we have $\beta(x)=\mathcal{K}_{k+1}(\mathrm{c}'_{(x_{0,x},x_{1,x}),x})$, where $(x_{0,x},x_{1,x})$ is any element of $\mathcal{T}$ with $\pi_{k-1,\mathcal{T}}(x_{0,x},x_{1,x})=m(\pi_{k-1,\mathrm{X}}(x))$ (in particular $x_{0,x}\sim_{k-1} x$). Now the continuity of $\mathcal{K}_{k+1}$ implies the following convergence, confirming the continuity of $\beta$:\quad $\beta(x_n)=\mathcal{K}_{k+1}(\mathrm{c}'_{(x_0^{(n)}+z_n,x_1^{(n)}+z_n),x_n})\rightarrow \mathcal{K}_{k+1}(\mathrm{c}'_{(x_0',x_1'),x})=\beta(x)$.

nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step \textsc{lch} nilspace. Let $\mathrm{Y}$ be a degree-$k$ algebraic nilspace extension of $\mathrm{X}$ by an abelian group $\mathrm{Z}$, with corresponding fibration $q:\mathrm{Y}\rightarrow\mathrm{X}$. Suppose that $\mathrm{Y},\mathrm{Z}$ are equipped with \textsc{lch} topologies making $\mathrm{Y}$ a Cartan continuous $\mathrm{Z}$-bundle over $\mathrm{X}$. Suppose also that the following hold: \setlength{\leftmargini}{0.8cm} \begin{enumerate} \item For every $n\geq 0$ the cube set $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{Y})$ is a closed subset of $\mathrm{Y}^{\db{n}}$. \item The completion function $\mathcal{K}:\mathrm{Cor}^{k+1}(\mathrm{Y})\rightarrow \mathrm{Y}$ is continuous. \end{enumerate} Then $\mathrm{Y}$ is an \textsc{lch} nilspace.
nodes.section: 2.2 Topological aspects of nilspace extensions
assumptions: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step \textsc{lch} nilspace.
Let $\mathrm{Y}$ be a degree-$k$ algebraic nilspace extension of $\mathrm{X}$ by an abelian group $\mathrm{Z}$, with corresponding fibration $q:\mathrm{Y}\rightarrow\mathrm{X}$.
Suppose that $\mathrm{Y},\mathrm{Z}$ are equipped with \textsc{lch} topologies making $\mathrm{Y}$ a Cartan continuous $\mathrm{Z}$-bundle over $\mathrm{X}$.
conclusions: Then $\mathrm{Y}$ is an \textsc{lch} nilspace.
nodes.label: lem:top-degree-k-k-ext

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.35
nodes.statement: Most of the conditions in Definition \ref{def:top-nil-open-maps-version} are already satisfied. Indeed, the only missing one is that for each $n\le k$ the map $p^{\db{n}}:\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{Y})\rightarrow\mathrm{Cor}^n(\mathrm{Y})$ is open (for $n >k$ this property already follows from $(ii)$). By Remark \ref{rem:topquot}, the topology on $\mathrm{X}$ is precisely the quotient of the topology on $\mathrm{Y}$ under the action of $\mathrm{Z}$. In particular, the map $q^{\db{n}}:\mathrm{Y}^{\db{n}}\rightarrow \mathrm{X}^{\db{n}}$ is also a quotient open map. Note that for $n\leq k$ the set $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{Y})\subset \mathrm{Y}^{\db{n}}$ is saturated with respect to the action of $\mathrm{Z}^{\db{n}}$ on $\mathrm{Y}^{\db{n}}$. Thus, the restriction $q^{\db{n}}|_{\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{Y})}:\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{Y})\rightarrow \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$ is also open. Now we want to prove that $p^{\db{n}}_{\mathrm{Y}}:\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{Y})\rightarrow \mathrm{Cor}^n(\mathrm{Y})$ is open for $n\le k$. It suffices to prove that for every open $U\subset \mathrm{Y}$ the set $p_{\mathrm{Y}}^{\db{n}}(E_U)$ is open where $E_U:=\left(U\times \prod_{v\in\db{n}\setminus\{1^n\}} \mathrm{Y}\right)\cap\mathrm{C}^{n}(\mathrm{Y})$. By definition of cubes in an extension we have $p_{\mathrm{Y}}^{\db{n}}(E_U) = (q^{\db{n}\setminus\{1^n\}})^{-1}(p^{\db{n}}_{\mathrm{X}}(q^{\db{n}}(E_U)))$, where $p^{\db{n}}_{\mathrm{X}}:\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})\rightarrow \mathrm{Cor}^n(\mathrm{X})$ is the usual projection on $\mathrm{X}$. Since $\mathrm{X}$ is an \textsc{lch} nilspace, $p^{\db{n}}_{\mathrm{Y}}$ is open. The result follows.
nodes.section: 2.2 Topological aspects of nilspace extensions
nodes.statement_short: Only openness of corner projections for $n\le k$ remains; obtain it from the open quotient map to $\mathrm{X}$.

nodes.name: Remaining condition
nodes.statement: Most of the conditions in Definition \ref{def:top-nil-open-maps-version} are already satisfied. Indeed, the only missing one is that for each $n\le k$ the map $p^{\db{n}}:\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{Y})\rightarrow\mathrm{Cor}^n(\mathrm{Y})$ is open (for $n >k$ this property already follows from $(ii)$).

nodes.name: Open quotient on cubes
nodes.statement: By Remark \ref{rem:topquot}, the topology on $\mathrm{X}$ is precisely the quotient of the topology on $\mathrm{Y}$ under the action of $\mathrm{Z}$. In particular, the map $q^{\db{n}}:\mathrm{Y}^{\db{n}}\rightarrow \mathrm{X}^{\db{n}}$ is also a quotient open map. Note that for $n\leq k$ the set $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{Y})\subset \mathrm{Y}^{\db{n}}$ is saturated with respect to the action of $\mathrm{Z}^{\db{n}}$ on $\mathrm{Y}^{\db{n}}$. Thus, the restriction $q^{\db{n}}|_{\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{Y})}:\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{Y})\rightarrow \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$ is also open.

nodes.statement_short: Remark 2.27 gives an open quotient map on cube sets.

nodes.name: Openness of corner projections
nodes.statement: Now we want to prove that $p^{\db{n}}_{\mathrm{Y}}:\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{Y})\rightarrow \mathrm{Cor}^n(\mathrm{Y})$ is open for $n\le k$. It suffices to prove that for every open $U\subset \mathrm{Y}$ the set $p_{\mathrm{Y}}^{\db{n}}(E_U)$ is open where $E_U:=\left(U\times \prod_{v\in\db{n}\setminus\{1^n\}} \mathrm{Y}\right)\cap\mathrm{C}^{n}(\mathrm{Y})$. By definition of cubes in an extension we have $p_{\mathrm{Y}}^{\db{n}}(E_U) = (q^{\db{n}\setminus\{1^n\}})^{-1}(p^{\db{n}}_{\mathrm{X}}(q^{\db{n}}(E_U)))$, where $p^{\db{n}}_{\mathrm{X}}:\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})\rightarrow \mathrm{Cor}^n(\mathrm{X})$ is the usual projection on $\mathrm{X}$. Since $\mathrm{X}$ is an \textsc{lch} nilspace, $p^{\db{n}}_{\mathrm{Y}}$ is open. The result follows.

nodes.statement_short: Express images as preimages of open sets in $\mathrm{X}$.

nodes.name: Fiber-completion continuity
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{Y}$ be a nilspace endowed with an \textsc{lch} topology and let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step \textsc{lch} nilspace. Suppose that $\mathrm{Y}$ is a degree-$t$ algebraic nilspace extension of $\mathrm{X}$ by an abelian group $\mathrm{Z}$. Let $\Delta_{q:\mathrm{Y}\rightarrow\mathrm{X}}:= \{(\mathrm{c}',\mathrm{c})\in \mathrm{Cor}^{t+1}(\mathrm{Y})\times \mathrm{C}^{t+1}(\mathrm{X}):q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}'(v)=\mathrm{c}(v)\text{ for all } v\not=1^{t+1}\}$. Let $\mathcal{K}_{(q)}:\Delta_{q:\mathrm{Y}\rightarrow\mathrm{X}}\rightarrow \mathrm{Y}$ be the function that maps each $(\mathrm{c}',\mathrm{c})\in \Delta_{q:\mathrm{Y}\rightarrow\mathrm{X}}$ to the unique element $y\in\mathrm{Y}$ which completes the corner $\mathrm{c}'$ and satisfies $q(y)=\mathrm{c}(1^{t+1})$. We say that the extension is \emph{fiber-completion continuous} if $\mathcal{K}_{(q)}$ is continuous (endowing $\mathrm{Cor}^{t+1}(\mathrm{Y})$ with the subspace topology induced by the product topology on $\mathrm{Y}^{\db{t+1}\setminus\{1^{t+1}\}}$).
nodes.section: 2.2 Topological aspects of nilspace extensions
nodes.label: def:fib-comp-cont

nodes.name: Top-degree extensions are fiber-completion continuous
nodes.statement: Note that if $t=k$ and the completion on $\mathrm{Cor}^{k+1}(\mathrm{Y})$ is continuous, then the extension is  automatically fiber-continuous.
nodes.section: 2.2 Topological aspects of nilspace extensions
conclusions: Note that if $t=k$ and the completion on $\mathrm{Cor}^{k+1}(\mathrm{Y})$ is continuous, then the extension is  automatically fiber-continuous.

nodes.name: LCH criterion for extensions of LCH nilspaces
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step \textsc{lch} nilspace. Let $\mathrm{Y}$ be a degree-$t$ algebraic nilspace extension of $\mathrm{X}$ by an abelian group $\mathrm{Z}$, with corresponding fibration $q:\mathrm{Y}\rightarrow\mathrm{X}$. Suppose that $\mathrm{Y}$, $\mathrm{Z}$ are equipped with \textsc{lch} topologies making $\mathrm{Y}$ a Cartan continuous $\mathrm{Z}$-bundle over $\mathrm{X}$. Suppose also that the following hold: \begin{enumerate} \item For every $n\geq 0$ the cube set $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{Y})$ is a closed subset of $\mathrm{Y}^{\db{n}}$. \item The completion function $\mathcal{K}:\mathrm{Cor}^{k+1}(\mathrm{Y})\rightarrow \mathrm{Y}$ is continuous. \item The extension is fiber-completion continuous. \end{enumerate} Then $\mathrm{Y}$ is an \textsc{lch} nilspace.

assumptions: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step \textsc{lch} nilspace.
Let $\mathrm{Y}$ be a degree-$t$ algebraic nilspace extension of $\mathrm{X}$ by an abelian group $\mathrm{Z}$, with corresponding fibration $q:\mathrm{Y}\rightarrow\mathrm{X}$.
Suppose that $\mathrm{Y}$, $\mathrm{Z}$ are equipped with \textsc{lch} topologies making $\mathrm{Y}$ a Cartan continuous $\mathrm{Z}$-bundle over $\mathrm{X}$.

Suppose also that the following hold:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item For every $n\geq 0$ the cube set $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{Y})$ is a closed subset of $\mathrm{Y}^{\db{n}}$.
    \item The completion function $\mathcal{K}:\mathrm{Cor}^{k+1}(\mathrm{Y})\rightarrow \mathrm{Y}$ is continuous.
    \item The extension is fiber-completion continuous.
conclusions: Then $\mathrm{Y}$ is an \textsc{lch} nilspace.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.37
nodes.statement:
We argue by induction on $k$ (with $t$ fixed). For $k=1$ the result follows by Lemma ef{lem:top-degree-k-k-ext}. For $k>1$, we prove that $\mathrm{Y}$ is an 	extsc{lch} nilspace by proving that the conditions of Lemma ef{lem:eq-def-lch-nil} are satisfied. Note that by $(i)$ the cube sets are closed, so we just need to prove that the completion functions are continuous. For $n>k$ this follows from $(ii)$. It then suffices to prove that $\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}$ is a degree-$t$ extension of $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ that satisfies all the assumptions in the theorem. Indeed, if we prove this, then by induction the completion functions on the factors of $\mathrm{Y}$ will also be continuous, as required in Lemma ef{lem:eq-def-lch-nil}-$(ii)$. By Lemma ef{lem:top-degree-k-k-ext} we can assume that $t<k$. Recall that by \cite[Proposition A.19]{CGSS-p-hom} the following diagram commutes:  egin{equation}  egin{aligned}[c]  egin{tikzpicture} \matrix (m) [matrix of math nodes,row sep=3em,column sep=4em,minimum width=2em] {\mathrm{Y} & \mathrm{X} \ \mathrm{Y}_{k-1} & \mathrm{X}_{k-1}, \}; \path[-stealth] (m-1-1) edge node [above] {$q$} (m-1-2) (m-1-1) edge node [right] {$\pi$} (m-2-1) (m-1-2) edge node [right] {$\pi$} (m-2-2) (m-2-1) edge node [above] {$q_{k-1}$} (m-2-2); \end{tikzpicture} \end{aligned} \end{equation} \vspace{-0.3cm} 
oindent where $q_{k-1}$ defines a degree-$t$ extension of $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$. (We just write $\pi$ instead of $\pi_{k-1}$ to avoid overloading the notation; the space where $\pi$ is defined will be clear from the context.) Let us then prove that $\mathrm{Y}_{k-1},\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ satisfy all the assumptions in the theorem. Firstly, $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ with the quotient topology is an 	extsc{lch} nilspace, by Theorem ef{thm:factor-of-lch-nil} applied to $\mathrm{X}$. Let us now analyze some properties of objects and maps in \eqref{diag:factor-of-ext-1}. The map $\pi:\mathrm{X}ightarrow\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ is open and continuous by Corollary ef{cor:quotient-top-k-1-factor}. By Corollary ef{cor:quotient-top-k-1-factor} applied to $\mathrm{Y}$, the topology on $\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}$ is also 	extsc{lch}. By Proposition ef{prop:k-th-group-action} the $k$-th structure group $\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})$ is an 	extsc{lch} topological group acting continuously on $\mathrm{Y}$. The group $\mathrm{Z}$ is an 	extsc{lch} group by assumption. We claim that the action of $\mathrm{Z}$ on $\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}$ is continuous. This action is defined by the formula $\pi(y)+z:=\pi(y+z)$ (see \cite[Proposition A.19]{CGSS-p-hom}). To see that it is continuous, fix any sequences $(y_n)$ in $\mathrm{Y}$ and $(z_n)$ in $\mathrm{Z}$ such that $\pi(y_n)ightarrow \pi(y)$ and $z_nightarrow z$. By Lemma ef{lem:conv-quot} there exists a sequence $g_n\in \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})$ such that $y_n+g_nightarrow y$. The continuity of the action of $\mathrm{Z}$ on $\mathrm{Y}$ implies that $(y_n+g_n)+z_nightarrow y+z$. As $\pi$ is continuous, we know that $\pi((y_n+g_n)+z_n)ightarrow \pi(y+z)=:\pi(y)+z$. We leave it as an exercise for the reader (using the uniqueness of completion on $\mathrm{Cor}^{k+1}(\mathrm{Y})$) to see that $(y_n+g_n)+z_n=(y_n+z_n)+g_n$. Then $\pi((y_n+g_n)+z_n)=\pi(y_n+z_n)=\pi(y_n)+z_n$, and the claimed continuity follows. This shows that Definition ef{def:CtsAbBund}-$(iii)$ holds. Next, note that since $q:\mathrm{Y}ightarrow\mathrm{X}$, $\pi:\mathrm{X}ightarrow \mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ and $\pi:\mathrm{Y}ightarrow\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}$ are open and continuous, we have that $q_{k-1}$ is open and continuous as well, by the commutativity of the diagram \eqref{diag:factor-of-ext-1}. This shows that Definition ef{def:CtsAbBund}-$(iv)$ holds. So far, we have proved that $q_{k-1}:\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}ightarrow\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ is a continuous $\mathrm{Z}$-bundle. We now prove that this bundle is also Cartan (i.e.\ the difference map is continuous). Suppose that $(\pi(y_n),\pi(y_n'))ightarrow (\pi(y),\pi(y'))$ for some $(\pi(y_n),\pi(y_n'))$ and $ (\pi(y),\pi(y'))\in \mathrm{Y}_{k-1}	imes_{\mathrm{X}_{k-1}}\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}$. By Lemma ef{lem:conv-quot} there are sequences $(g_n),(g_n')$ in $\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})$ such that $y_n+g_nightarrow y$ and $y_n'+g_n'ightarrow y'$ in $\mathrm{Y}$. Hence, without loss of generality $y_nightarrow y$ and $y'_nightarrow y'$ as $nightarrow\infty$. As $q_{k-1}(\pi(y_n))= q_{k-1}(\pi(y'_n))$, there exists $z_n\in \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})$ such that $q(y_n)+z_n=q(y_n')$. As $\mathrm{X}$ is an 	extsc{lch} nilspace, and $q$ is continuous, $z_nightarrow q(y)-q(y')=z\in \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})$ as $nightarrow\infty$. We leave it as an exercise for the reader to check that with the given assumptions (i.e.\ that $t<k$) the $k$-th structure homomorphism of $q$, $\phi_k:\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})ightarrow \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})$, is an (algebraic) group isomorphism (this follows from \cite[Definition 3.3.13]{Cand:Notes1} using the definition of cubes in an extension). To prove that $\phi_k$ is continuous, let $z_n'\in \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})$ such that $z_n'ightarrow z'$ as $nightarrow \infty$. Fix any $y_0\in \mathrm{Y}$. Then by definition $\phi_k(z_n')=q(y_0+z_n')-q(y_0)$. Since $\mathrm{Y}$ is Cartan, this is the composition of two continuous maps. Thus the limit is $q(y_0+z')-q(y_0)=\phi_k(z')$ as required. Hence, we have that $y_n+\phi_k^{-1}(z_n)ightarrow y+\phi_k^{-1}(z)$ and $y_n'ightarrow y'$. As $(y_n+\phi_k^{-1}(z_n),y_n')\in \mathrm{Y}	imes_{\mathrm{X}}\mathrm{Y}$, by continuity of the difference map in $\mathrm{Y}$ we have $(y_n+\phi_k^{-1}(z_n))-y_n'ightarrow (y+\phi_k^{-1}(z))-y'$. ootnote{Note that in this last equation the ``$+$'' signs denote addition of an element of $\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})$ and the ``$-$'' signs denote difference of two points that give an element in the extension group $\mathrm{Z}$.} This confirms that the difference map $\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}	imes_{\mathrm{X}_{k-1}}\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}$ is continuous. It remains to check that $\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}$ satisfies properties $(i)$, $(ii)$, $(iii)$ in the theorem. Property $(i)$ follows from Lemma ef{lem:closure-cube-in-k-1-factor} applied to $\mathrm{Y}$. Let us now prove $(ii)$, i.e.\ that completion on $\mathrm{Cor}^k(\mathrm{Y}_{k-1})$ is continuous. Let $\pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}_n'ightarrow \pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}'$ be a convergent sequence in $\mathrm{Cor}^k(\mathrm{Y}_{k-1})$ (for some $\mathrm{c}_n',\mathrm{c}'\in \mathrm{Cor}^k(\mathrm{Y})$). We want to prove that their completions also converge. By Lemma ef{lem:conv-quot} there exists $d_n\in \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})^{\db{k}\setminus\{1^k\}}$ such that $\mathrm{c}_n'+d_nightarrow \mathrm{c}'$ in $\mathrm{Cor}^k(\mathrm{Y})$. By continuity of $q$, we have $q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} (\mathrm{c}_n'+d_n)ightarrow q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}'$ in $\mathrm{Cor}^k(\mathrm{X})$. Now we argue by a diagonalization, as follows. Let $\mathrm{c}\in \mathrm{C}^k(\mathrm{Y})$ be such that $p^{\db{k}}(q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c})=q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}'$ where $p^{\db{k}}:\mathrm{C}^k(\mathrm{X})ightarrow \mathrm{Cor}^k(\mathrm{X})$. For every $m\in \mathbb{N}$, let $B_{1/m}(q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c})\subset \mathrm{C}^k(\mathrm{X})$ be the open ball of radius $1/m$ and center $q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}$. As $p^{\db{k}}$ is an open map, the sets $p^{\db{k}}(B_{1/m}(q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}))$ are open subsets of $\mathrm{Cor}^k(\mathrm{X})$ that contain $q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}'$. As $q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} (\mathrm{c}_n'+d_n)ightarrow q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}'$, there exists $N_m\ge 0$ such that if $n\ge N_m$ then $q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} (\mathrm{c}_n'+d_n)\in p^{\db{k}}(B_{1/m}(q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}))$. Without loss of generality we can suppose that the sequence $N_m$ is increasing. Now let $	au(n):=\sup\{m:n\ge N_m\}$. Then for each $n$ let $\mathrm{c}_n\in \mathrm{C}^k(\mathrm{Y})$ be any cube such that $p^{\db{k}}(q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}_n)=q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}(\mathrm{c}_n'+d_n)$ and $q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}_n\in B_{1/	au(n)}(q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c})$. In particular $q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}_nightarrow q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}$ in $\mathrm{C}^k(\mathrm{X})$ as $nightarrow\infty$ (this is why we chose $N_m$ to be increasing, so that $	au(n)ightarrow\infty$ as $nightarrow\infty$). This is the point where fiber-completion continuity becomes useful. Indeed, by property $(iii)$ for $q:\mathrm{Y}ightarrow \mathrm{X}$, we can complete continuously the pair $(\mathrm{c}_n'+d_n,q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}_n)\in \mathrm{Cor}^k(\mathrm{Y})	imes \mathrm{C}^k(\mathrm{X})$, that is, we can apply $\mathcal{K}_{(q)}$ to obtain a cube $\mathrm{c}_n+f_n$ for some $f_n\in \mathrm{C}^k(\mathcal{D}_t(\mathrm{Z}))$ in such a way that $(\mathrm{c}_n+f_n)(v)=(\mathrm{c}_n'+d_n)(v)$ for all $v
ot=1^k$. Note that for this step to work it is crucial that $t<k$, as we are precisely applying the fiber-completion function to faces of dimension $t+1$ inside $\db{k}$. The process is as follows: first, for every $n\ge 1$ choose an element $f_n\in\mathrm{C}^k(\mathcal{D}_t(\mathrm{Z}))$ such that $(\mathrm{c}_n+f_n)(v) =(\mathrm{c}_n'+d_n)(v)$ for $v\in \db{k}_{\le t}$. But then, by uniqueness of fiber-completion $\mathrm{c}_n+f_n$ automatically equals $\mathrm{c}_n'+d_n$ for all $v
ot=1^k$. Then, the continuity of the fiber-completion implies that $(\mathrm{c}_n+f_n)(1^k)$ converges to the unique completion of $(\mathrm{c}',q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c})$. Finally, letting $\mathcal{K}_k:\mathrm{Cor}^k(\mathrm{Y}_{k-1})ightarrow \mathrm{Y}_{k-1}$ be the unique completion function, note that $\mathcal{K}_k(\pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}_n')=\mathcal{K}_k(\pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} (\mathrm{c}_n'+d_n))=\mathcal{K}_k(\pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} (\mathrm{c}_n+f_n)|_{\db{k}\setminus\{1^k\}}) = \pi((\mathrm{c}_n+f_n)(1^k))$, which converges by the continuity of the fiber-completion function. The limit of $(\mathrm{c}_n+f_n)(1^k)$ is precisely $\mathcal{K}_{(q)}(\mathrm{c}',q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c})$ (recall Definition ef{def:fib-comp-cont}). Hence $\mathcal{K}_k(\pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}_n')ightarrow \pi(\mathcal{K}_{(q)}(\mathrm{c}',q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}))$. Since $\pi(\mathcal{K}_{(q)}(\mathrm{c}',q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c})) = \mathcal{K}_k(\pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}')$, this confirms the desired continuity property $(ii)$. Finally, let us prove that $(iii)$ holds. Let $(\pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}_n',\pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}_n)\in \Delta_{q_{k-1}:\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}ightarrow\mathrm{X}_{k-1}}$ be a sequence converging to some limit $(\pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}',\pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c})\in \Delta_{q_{k-1}:\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}ightarrow\mathrm{X}_{k-1}}$. We want to prove that the completions of the corners $\pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}_n'$ converge as well. By Lemma ef{lem:conv-quot} there exists $d_n\in\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})^{\db{t+1}\setminus\{1^{t+1}\}}=\mathrm{Cor}^{t+1}(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})))$ such that $\mathrm{c}_n'+d_nightarrow \mathrm{c}'$ in $\mathrm{Cor}^{t+1}(\mathrm{Y})$. Then, clearly $q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} (\mathrm{c}_n'+d_n)$ is a lift of $\pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}_n|_{\db{t+1}\setminus\{1^{t+1}\}}$. Applying again Lemma ef{lem:conv-quot}, this time to $\mathrm{c}_n(1^{t+1})$, we get a sequence of elements $z_n\in \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})$ such that $\mathrm{c}_n(1^{t+1})+z_nightarrow \mathrm{c}(1^{t+1})$. Now for each $n$ let $\mathrm{c}^*_n: v\mapsto  egin{cases} q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}(\mathrm{c}_n'+d_n)(v) & 	ext{ if }v
ot=1^{t+1}\ \mathrm{c}_n(1^{t+1})+z_n & 	ext{otherwise} \end{cases}$. By \cite[Remark 3.2.12]{Cand:Notes1} (using that $t<k$) we have $\mathrm{c}^*_n\in \mathrm{C}^{t+1}(\mathrm{X})$ for every $n$. Furthermore, these cubes converge to some limit $\mathrm{c}^*\in \mathrm{C}^{t+1}(\mathrm{X})$ such that $\pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}^*=\pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}$. Indeed, for $v
ot=1^{t+1}$ we have $\mathrm{c}^*_n(v)=q(\mathrm{c}_n'+d_n)(v)$ which converges because $(\mathrm{c}_n'+d_n)(v)$ converges and $q$ is continuous, and $\mathrm{c}^*_n(1^{t+1})=\mathrm{c}_n(1^{t+1})+z_n$, which converges by assumption (the resulting $\mathrm{c}^*$ is a cube again by \cite[Remark 3.2.12]{Cand:Notes1}). Thus, we can apply the fiber-completion continuity to the sequence $(\mathrm{c}_n'+d_n,\mathrm{c}_n^*)$. The limit of the completions is the completion of their limit, i.e.\ $(\mathrm{c}',\mathrm{c}^*)\in \Delta_{q:\mathrm{Y}ightarrow\mathrm{X}}$. Letting $\mathcal{K}_{(q_{k-1})}$ be the completion function in $\Delta_{q_{k-1}:\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}ightarrow\mathrm{X}_{k-1}}$, note that $\mathcal{K}_{(q_{k-1})}(\pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}_n',\pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}_n) = \pi(\mathcal{K}_{(q)}(\mathrm{c}_n'+d_n,\mathrm{c}_n^*))$, and the latter, by continuity of $\pi$ and $\mathcal{K}_{(q)}$, converges to $\pi(\mathcal{K}_{(q)}(\mathrm{c}',\mathrm{c}^*))$. Arguing as in the previous sentence, we have $\pi(\mathcal{K}_{(q)}(\mathrm{c}',\mathrm{c}^*)) = \mathcal{K}_{(q_{k-1})}(\pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}',\pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}^*) = \mathcal{K}_{(q_{k-1})}(\pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}',\pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c})$, and $(iii)$ follows.
nodes.section: 2.2 Topological aspects of nilspace extensions
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $k$: show the factor extension $\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}\to\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ satisfies all hypotheses (continuous Cartan bundle, closed cubes, continuous completion, fiber-completion continuity). Completion continuity uses a diagonal choice of cubes and fiber-completion continuity.

nodes.name: Base case $k=1$
nodes.statement: We argue by induction on $k$ (with $t$ fixed). For $k=1$ the result follows by Lemma \ref{lem:top-degree-k-k-ext}.
nodes.section: 2.2 Topological aspects of nilspace extensions

nodes.name: Reduce to the factor extension
nodes.statement: For $k>1$, we prove that $\mathrm{Y}$ is an \textsc{lch} nilspace by proving that the conditions of Lemma \ref{lem:eq-def-lch-nil} are satisfied. Note that by $(i)$ the cube sets are closed, so we just need to prove that the completion functions are continuous. For $n>k$ this follows from $(ii)$. It then suffices to prove that $\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}$ is a degree-$t$ extension of $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ that satisfies all the assumptions in the theorem. Indeed, if we prove this, then by induction the completion functions on the factors of $\mathrm{Y}$ will also be continuous, as required in Lemma \ref{lem:eq-def-lch-nil}-$(ii)$. By Lemma \ref{lem:top-degree-k-k-ext} we can assume that $t<k$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Topological aspects of nilspace extensions
nodes.statement_short: Suffices that $\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}\to\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ satisfies the hypotheses; WLOG $t<k$.

nodes.name: Factor diagram
nodes.section: 2.2 Topological aspects of nilspace extensions
nodes.statement_short: Recall the commutative diagram of factors.

nodes.name: Commutative diagram of an extension and its $(k-1)$-factors
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned}[c] \begin{tikzpicture} \matrix (m) [matrix of math nodes,row sep=3em,column sep=4em,minimum width=2em] {\mathrm{Y} & \mathrm{X} \\ \mathrm{Y}_{k-1} & \mathrm{X}_{k-1}, \\}; \path[-stealth] (m-1-1) edge node [above] {$q$} (m-1-2) (m-1-1) edge node [right] {$\pi$} (m-2-1) (m-1-2) edge node [right] {$\pi$} (m-2-2) (m-2-1) edge node [above] {$q_{k-1}$} (m-2-2); \end{tikzpicture} \end{aligned}
nodes.section: 2.2 Topological aspects of nilspace extensions
nodes.label: diag:factor-of-ext-1

nodes.name: $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ is LCH
nodes.statement:
Let us then prove that $\mathrm{Y}_{k-1},\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ satisfy all the  assumptions in the theorem.

Firstly, $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ with the quotient topology is an \textsc{lch} nilspace, by Theorem \ref{thm:factor-of-lch-nil} applied to $\mathrm{X}$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Topological aspects of nilspace extensions

nodes.name: Topological properties of the diagram
nodes.statement: Let us now analyze some properties of objects and maps in \eqref{diag:factor-of-ext-1}. The map $\pi:\mathrm{X}\rightarrow\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ is open and continuous by Corollary \ref{cor:quotient-top-k-1-factor}. By Corollary \ref{cor:quotient-top-k-1-factor} applied to $\mathrm{Y}$,  the topology on $\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}$ is also \textsc{lch}. By Proposition \ref{prop:k-th-group-action} the $k$-th structure group $\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})$ is an \textsc{lch} topological group acting continuously on $\mathrm{Y}$. The group $\mathrm{Z}$ is an \textsc{lch} group by assumption.
nodes.section: 2.2 Topological aspects of nilspace extensions

nodes.name: Action of $\mathrm{Z}$ on $\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}$ is continuous
nodes.statement: We claim that the action of $\mathrm{Z}$ on $\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}$ is continuous. This action is defined by the formula $\pi(y)+z:=\pi(y+z)$ (see \cite[Proposition A.19]{CGSS-p-hom}). To see that it is continuous, fix any sequences $(y_n)$ in $\mathrm{Y}$ and $(z_n)$ in $\mathrm{Z}$ such that $\pi(y_n)\rightarrow \pi(y)$ and $z_n\rightarrow z$. By Lemma \ref{lem:conv-quot} there exists a sequence $g_n\in \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})$ such that $y_n+g_n\rightarrow y$. The continuity of the action of $\mathrm{Z}$ on $\mathrm{Y}$ implies  that $(y_n+g_n)+z_n\rightarrow y+z$. As $\pi$ is continuous, we know that $\pi((y_n+g_n)+z_n)\rightarrow \pi(y+z)=:\pi(y)+z$. We leave it as an exercise for the reader (using the uniqueness of completion on $\mathrm{Cor}^{k+1}(\mathrm{Y})$) to see that $(y_n+g_n)+z_n=(y_n+z_n)+g_n$.  Then $\pi((y_n+g_n)+z_n)=\pi(y_n+z_n)=\pi(y_n)+z_n$, and the claimed continuity follows. This shows that Definition \ref{def:CtsAbBund}-$(iii)$ holds.
nodes.section: 2.2 Topological aspects of nilspace extensions
nodes.statement_short: Lift convergent sequences and commute actions.

nodes.name: Lift sequences
nodes.statement: This action is defined by the formula $\pi(y)+z:=\pi(y+z)$ (see \cite[Proposition A.19]{CGSS-p-hom}). To see that it is continuous, fix any sequences $(y_n)$ in $\mathrm{Y}$ and $(z_n)$ in $\mathrm{Z}$ such that $\pi(y_n)\rightarrow \pi(y)$ and $z_n\rightarrow z$. By Lemma \ref{lem:conv-quot} there exists a sequence $g_n\in \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})$ such that $y_n+g_n\rightarrow y$.

nodes.name: Continuity upstairs
nodes.statement: The continuity of the action of $\mathrm{Z}$ on $\mathrm{Y}$ implies  that $(y_n+g_n)+z_n\rightarrow y+z$. As $\pi$ is continuous, we know that $\pi((y_n+g_n)+z_n)\rightarrow \pi(y+z)=:\pi(y)+z$.

nodes.name: Commuting actions
nodes.statement: We leave it as an exercise for the reader (using the uniqueness of completion on $\mathrm{Cor}^{k+1}(\mathrm{Y})$) to see that $(y_n+g_n)+z_n=(y_n+z_n)+g_n$.  Then $\pi((y_n+g_n)+z_n)=\pi(y_n+z_n)=\pi(y_n)+z_n$, and the claimed continuity follows. This shows that Definition \ref{def:CtsAbBund}-$(iii)$ holds.
nodes.section: 2.2 Topological aspects of nilspace extensions

nodes.name: $q_{k-1}$ is open and continuous
nodes.statement: Next, note that since $q:\mathrm{Y}\rightarrow\mathrm{X}$, $\pi:\mathrm{X}\rightarrow \mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ and $\pi:\mathrm{Y}\rightarrow\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}$ are open and continuous, we have that $q_{k-1}$ is open and continuous as well, by the commutativity of the diagram \eqref{diag:factor-of-ext-1}. This shows that Definition \ref{def:CtsAbBund}-$(iv)$ holds.
nodes.section: 2.2 Topological aspects of nilspace extensions

nodes.name: Cartan property of the factor bundle
nodes.statement:
So far, we have proved that $q_{k-1}:\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}\rightarrow\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ is a continuous $\mathrm{Z}$-bundle. We now prove that this bundle is also Cartan (i.e.\ the difference map is continuous). Suppose that $(\pi(y_n),\pi(y_n'))\rightarrow (\pi(y),\pi(y'))$ for some $(\pi(y_n),\pi(y_n'))$ and $ (\pi(y),\pi(y'))\in \mathrm{Y}_{k-1}\times_{\mathrm{X}_{k-1}}\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}$. By Lemma \ref{lem:conv-quot} there are sequences $(g_n),(g_n')$ in $\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})$ such that $y_n+g_n\rightarrow y$ and $y_n'+g_n'\rightarrow y'$ in $\mathrm{Y}$. Hence, without loss of generality $y_n\rightarrow y$ and $y'_n\rightarrow y'$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$. As $q_{k-1}(\pi(y_n))= q_{k-1}(\pi(y'_n))$, there exists $z_n\in \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})$ such that $q(y_n)+z_n=q(y_n')$. As $\mathrm{X}$ is an \textsc{lch} nilspace, and $q$ is continuous, $z_n\rightarrow q(y)-q(y')=z\in \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$. We leave it as an exercise for the reader to check that with the given assumptions (i.e.\ that $t<k$) the $k$-th structure homomorphism of $q$, $\phi_k:\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})\rightarrow \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})$, is an (algebraic) group isomorphism (this follows from \cite[Definition 3.3.13]{Cand:Notes1} using the definition of cubes in an extension). To prove that $\phi_k$ is continuous, let $z_n'\in \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})$ such that $z_n'\rightarrow z'$ as $n\rightarrow \infty$. Fix any $y_0\in \mathrm{Y}$. Then by definition $\phi_k(z_n')=q(y_0+z_n')-q(y_0)$. Since $\mathrm{Y}$ is Cartan, this is the composition of two continuous maps. Thus the limit is $q(y_0+z')-q(y_0)=\phi_k(z')$ as required. 
Hence, we have that $y_n+\phi_k^{-1}(z_n)\rightarrow y+\phi_k^{-1}(z)$ and $y_n'\rightarrow y'$. As $(y_n+\phi_k^{-1}(z_n),y_n')\in \mathrm{Y}\times_{\mathrm{X}}\mathrm{Y}$, by continuity of the difference map in $\mathrm{Y}$ we have $(y_n+\phi_k^{-1}(z_n))-y_n'\rightarrow (y+\phi_k^{-1}(z))-y'$.\footnote{Note that in this last equation the ``$+$'' signs denote addition of an element of $\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})$ and the ``$-$'' signs denote difference of two points that give an element in the extension group $\mathrm{Z}$.} This confirms  that the difference map $\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}\times_{\mathrm{X}_{k-1}}\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}$ is continuous.
nodes.section: 2.2 Topological aspects of nilspace extensions
nodes.statement_short: Continuity of the difference map via lifts and continuity of $\phi_k^{-1}$.

nodes.name: Lift convergent pairs

Hence, without loss of generality $y_n\rightarrow y$ and $y'_n\rightarrow y'$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$.
