nodes.name: Difference map is continuous
nodes.statement: Hence, we have that $y_n+\phi_k^{-1}(z_n)\rightarrow y+\phi_k^{-1}(z)$ and $y_n'\rightarrow y'$. As $(y_n+\phi_k^{-1}(z_n),y_n')\in \mathrm{Y}\times_{\mathrm{X}}\mathrm{Y}$, by continuity of the difference map in $\mathrm{Y}$ we have $(y_n+\phi_k^{-1}(z_n))-y_n'\rightarrow (y+\phi_k^{-1}(z))-y'$.\footnote{Note that in this last equation the ``$+$'' signs denote addition of an element of $\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})$ and the ``$-$'' signs denote difference of two points that give an element in the extension group $\mathrm{Z}$.} This confirms  that the difference map $\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}\times_{\mathrm{X}_{k-1}}\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}$ is continuous.
nodes.section: 2.2 Topological aspects of nilspace extensions

nodes.name: Property (i)
nodes.statement:
It remains to check that $\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}$ satisfies properties $(i)$, $(ii)$, $(iii)$ in the theorem.

Property $(i)$ follows from Lemma \ref{lem:closure-cube-in-k-1-factor} applied to $\mathrm{Y}$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Topological aspects of nilspace extensions

nodes.name: Property (ii): completion on $\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}$ is continuous
nodes.statement: Let us now prove $(ii)$, i.e.\ that completion on $\mathrm{Cor}^k(\mathrm{Y}_{k-1})$ is continuous. Let $\pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}_n'\rightarrow \pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}'$ be a convergent sequence in $\mathrm{Cor}^k(\mathrm{Y}_{k-1})$ (for some $\mathrm{c}_n',\mathrm{c}'\in \mathrm{Cor}^k(\mathrm{Y})$). We want to prove that their completions also converge. By Lemma \ref{lem:conv-quot} there exists $d_n\in \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})^{\db{k}\setminus\{1^k\}}$ such that $\mathrm{c}_n'+d_n\rightarrow \mathrm{c}'$ in $\mathrm{Cor}^k(\mathrm{Y})$. By continuity of $q$, we have $q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} (\mathrm{c}_n'+d_n)\rightarrow q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}'$ in $\mathrm{Cor}^k(\mathrm{X})$. Now we argue by a diagonalization, as follows. Let $\mathrm{c}\in \mathrm{C}^k(\mathrm{Y})$ be such that $p^{\db{k}}(q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c})=q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}'$ where $p^{\db{k}}:\mathrm{C}^k(\mathrm{X})\rightarrow \mathrm{Cor}^k(\mathrm{X})$. For every $m\in \mathbb{N}$, let $B_{1/m}(q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c})\subset \mathrm{C}^k(\mathrm{X})$ be the open ball of radius $1/m$ and center $q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}$. As $p^{\db{k}}$ is an open map, the sets $p^{\db{k}}(B_{1/m}(q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}))$ are open subsets of $\mathrm{Cor}^k(\mathrm{X})$ that contain $q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}'$. As $q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} (\mathrm{c}_n'+d_n)\rightarrow q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}'$, there exists $N_m\ge 0$ such that if $n\ge N_m$ then $q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} (\mathrm{c}_n'+d_n)\in p^{\db{k}}(B_{1/m}(q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}))$. Without loss of generality we can suppose that the sequence $N_m$ is increasing. Now let $\tau(n):=\sup\{m:n\ge N_m\}$. Then for each $n$ let $\mathrm{c}_n\in \mathrm{C}^k(\mathrm{Y})$ be any cube such that $p^{\db{k}}(q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}_n)=q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}(\mathrm{c}_n'+d_n)$ and $q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}_n\in B_{1/\tau(n)}(q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c})$. In particular $q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}_n\rightarrow q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}$ in $\mathrm{C}^k(\mathrm{X})$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$ (this is why we chose $N_m$ to be increasing, so that $\tau(n)\rightarrow\infty$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$). This is the point where fiber-completion continuity becomes useful. Indeed, by property $(iii)$ for $q:\mathrm{Y}\rightarrow \mathrm{X}$, we can complete continuously the pair $(\mathrm{c}_n'+d_n,q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}_n)\in \mathrm{Cor}^k(\mathrm{Y})\times \mathrm{C}^k(\mathrm{X})$, that is, we can apply $\mathcal{K}_{(q)}$ to obtain a cube $\mathrm{c}_n+f_n$ for some $f_n\in \mathrm{C}^k(\mathcal{D}_t(\mathrm{Z}))$ in such a way that $(\mathrm{c}_n+f_n)(v)=(\mathrm{c}_n'+d_n)(v)$ for all $v\not=1^k$. Note that for this step to work it is crucial that $t<k$, as we are precisely applying the fiber-completion function to faces of dimension $t+1$ inside $\db{k}$. The process is as follows: first, for every $n\ge 1$ choose an element $f_n\in\mathrm{C}^k(\mathcal{D}_t(\mathrm{Z}))$ such that $(\mathrm{c}_n+f_n)(v) =(\mathrm{c}_n'+d_n)(v)$ for $v\in \db{k}_{\le t}$. But then, by uniqueness of fiber-completion $\mathrm{c}_n+f_n$ automatically equals $\mathrm{c}_n'+d_n$ for all $v\not=1^k$. Then, the continuity of the fiber-completion implies that $(\mathrm{c}_n+f_n)(1^k)$ converges to the unique completion of $(\mathrm{c}',q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c})$. Finally, letting $\mathcal{K}_k:\mathrm{Cor}^k(\mathrm{Y}_{k-1})\rightarrow \mathrm{Y}_{k-1}$ be the unique completion function, note that $\mathcal{K}_k(\pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}_n')=\mathcal{K}_k(\pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} (\mathrm{c}_n'+d_n))=\mathcal{K}_k(\pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} (\mathrm{c}_n+f_n)|_{\db{k}\setminus\{1^k\}}) = \pi((\mathrm{c}_n+f_n)(1^k))$, which converges by the continuity of the fiber-completion function. The limit of $(\mathrm{c}_n+f_n)(1^k)$ is precisely $\mathcal{K}_{(q)}(\mathrm{c}',q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c})$ (recall Definition \ref{def:fib-comp-cont}). Hence $\mathcal{K}_k(\pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}_n')\rightarrow \pi(\mathcal{K}_{(q)}(\mathrm{c}',q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}))$. Since $\pi(\mathcal{K}_{(q)}(\mathrm{c}',q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c})) = \mathcal{K}_k(\pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}')$, this confirms the desired continuity property $(ii)$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Topological aspects of nilspace extensions
nodes.statement_short: Diagonal choice of cubes plus fiber-completion continuity.

nodes.name: Lift convergent corners
nodes.statement: Let us now prove $(ii)$, i.e.\ that completion on $\mathrm{Cor}^k(\mathrm{Y}_{k-1})$ is continuous. nodes.statement: This is the point where fiber-completion continuity becomes useful. nodes.name: Conclude convergence of completions
nodes.statement: Finally, letting $\mathcal{K}_k:\mathrm{Cor}^k(\mathrm{Y}_{k-1})\rightarrow \mathrm{Y}_{k-1}$ be the unique completion function, note that $\mathcal{K}_k(\pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}_n')=\mathcal{K}_k(\pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} (\mathrm{c}_n'+d_n))=\mathcal{K}_k(\pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} (\mathrm{c}_n+f_n)|_{\db{k}\setminus\{1^k\}}) = \pi((\mathrm{c}_n+f_n)(1^k))$, which converges by the continuity of the fiber-completion function. nodes.name: Property (iii)
nodes.section: 2.2 Topological aspects of nilspace extensions
nodes.statement_short: Build convergent lifted pairs and apply fiber-completion continuity on $\mathrm{Y}$.

nodes.name: Lift the corners and cubes
nodes.statement: Finally, let us prove that $(iii)$ holds. Let $(\pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}_n',\pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}_n)\in \Delta_{q_{k-1}:\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}\rightarrow\mathrm{X}_{k-1}}$ be a sequence converging to some limit $(\pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}',\pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c})\in \Delta_{q_{k-1}:\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}\rightarrow\mathrm{X}_{k-1}}$. We want to prove that the completions of the corners $\pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}_n'$ converge as well. By Lemma \ref{lem:conv-quot} there exists $d_n\in\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})^{\db{t+1}\setminus\{1^{t+1}\}}=\mathrm{Cor}^{t+1}(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})))$ such that $\mathrm{c}_n'+d_n\rightarrow \mathrm{c}'$ in $\mathrm{Cor}^{t+1}(\mathrm{Y})$. Then, clearly $q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} (\mathrm{c}_n'+d_n)$ is a lift of $\pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}_n|_{\db{t+1}\setminus\{1^{t+1}\}}$. Applying again Lemma \ref{lem:conv-quot}, this time to $\mathrm{c}_n(1^{t+1})$, we get a sequence of elements $z_n\in \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})$ such that $\mathrm{c}_n(1^{t+1})+z_n\rightarrow \mathrm{c}(1^{t+1})$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Topological aspects of nilspace extensions

nodes.name: Modified cubes $\mathrm{c}^*_n$
nodes.section: 2.2 Topological aspects of nilspace extensions

nodes.name: Limit of completions
nodes.statement: Thus, we can apply the fiber-completion continuity to the sequence $(\mathrm{c}_n'+d_n,\mathrm{c}_n^*)$. The limit of the completions is the completion of their limit, i.e.\ $(\mathrm{c}',\mathrm{c}^*)\in \Delta_{q:\mathrm{Y}\rightarrow\mathrm{X}}$. Letting  $\mathcal{K}_{(q_{k-1})}$ be the completion function in $\Delta_{q_{k-1}:\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}\rightarrow\mathrm{X}_{k-1}}$, note that  $\mathcal{K}_{(q_{k-1})}(\pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}_n',\pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}_n) = \pi(\mathcal{K}_{(q)}(\mathrm{c}_n'+d_n,\mathrm{c}_n^*))$, and the latter, by continuity of $\pi$ and $\mathcal{K}_{(q)}$, converges to $\pi(\mathcal{K}_{(q)}(\mathrm{c}',\mathrm{c}^*))$. Arguing as in the previous sentence, we have $\pi(\mathcal{K}_{(q)}(\mathrm{c}',\mathrm{c}^*)) = \mathcal{K}_{(q_{k-1})}(\pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}',\pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}^*) = \mathcal{K}_{(q_{k-1})}(\pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}',\pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c})$, and $(iii)$ follows.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.33
nodes.statement: The proof of the algebraic part of the statement follows similarly to \cite[\S 3.3.4]{Cand:Notes1}. Note that the action of $\mathrm{Z}_k$ on $\mathcal{T}$ is $((x_0,x_1),z)\mapsto (x_0,x_1+z)$. The projection $q:\mathcal{T}\rightarrow \mathrm{X}$ is $(x_0,x_1)\mapsto x_0$. We prove that the conditions in Theorem \ref{thm:ext-lch-nil} hold for $\mathrm{X}$, $\mathrm{Y}=\mathcal{T}$. By assumption $\mathrm{X}$ is an \textsc{lch} nilspace. We first claim that $\mathcal{T}$ is a Cartan continuous $\mathrm{Z}_k$-bundle over $\mathrm{X}$. We are endowing $\mathcal{T}$ with the subspace topology induced by the product topology on $\mathrm{X}\times \mathrm{X}$, and in the latter topology the set $\mathcal{T}$ is easily seen to be closed. Hence (as noted previously, e.g.\ in the proof of Proposition \ref{prop:k-th-group-action}) the subspace topology on $\mathcal{T}$ is also \textsc{lch}. The group $\mathrm{Z}_k$ comes naturally equipped with a structure of \textsc{lch} topological group, being the $k$-th structure group of $\mathrm{X}$. The continuity of the action of $\mathrm{Z}_k$ on $\mathcal{T}$ follows from that of the action of $\mathrm{Z}_k$ on $\mathrm{X}$ (considering convergent sequences). Similarly the difference continuity (Cartan property) follows from that of $\mathrm{X}$. The map $q:\mathcal{T}\rightarrow \mathrm{X}$ is clearly continuous. To prove that it is open, note that if $(U\times V)\cap \mathcal{T}$ is an open set of $\mathcal{T}$, then $q((U\times V)\cap \mathcal{T})=U\cap \pi^{-1}(\alpha^{-1}(\pi(V)))$ which is open as well. We have thus confirmed our claim at the start of this paragraph. Now, to see that property $(i)$ in Theorem \ref{thm:ext-lch-nil} holds, note that the map $\iota:\mathcal{T}^{\db{n}}\rightarrow \mathrm{X}^{\db{n+i}}$, $(\mathrm{c}_0,\mathrm{c}_1)\mapsto \langle \mathrm{c}_0,\mathrm{c}_1\rangle_i$ is continuous (see \cite[\S 3.1.4]{Cand:Notes1} for the definition of arrows $\langle \mathrm{c}_0,\mathrm{c}_1\rangle_i$), and $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathcal{T})=\iota^{-1}(\mathrm{C}^{n+i}(\mathrm{X}))$. Thus, those sets are all closed and $(i)$ follows. To see that $(ii)$ holds, note that for any corner $(\mathrm{c}_0',\mathrm{c}_1')\in \mathrm{Cor}^{k+1}(\mathcal{T})$, its completion is just $(\mathcal{K}_{k+1}(\mathrm{c}_0'),\mathcal{K}_{k+1}(\mathrm{c}_1'))$, where $\mathcal{K}_{k+1}$ is the completion function on $\mathrm{Cor}^{k+1}(\mathrm{X})$. Finally, to show that $(iii)$ holds, we need to prove the continuity of the map $\mathcal{K}_{(q)}$ defined on $\Delta_{q:\mathcal{T}\rightarrow \mathrm{X}}$. For every element $(\mathrm{c}_0'\times \mathrm{c}_1',\mathrm{c})\in \Delta_{q:\mathcal{T}\rightarrow \mathrm{X}}$ we have $\mathcal{K}_{(q)}(\mathrm{c}_0'\times \mathrm{c}_1',\mathrm{c}) = \mathcal{K}_{k+1}(\langle \mathrm{c},\mathrm{c}_1'\rangle_i)$, where the ``corner arrow'' $\langle \mathrm{c},\mathrm{c}_1'\rangle_i$ here is defined as in \cite[\S 3.1.4]{Cand:Notes1}.\footnote{Specifically $\langle \mathrm{c},\mathrm{c}_1'\rangle_i$ is a map $\db{k+1}\setminus\{1^{k+1}\}\rightarrow \mathrm{X}$ defined as follows: for every vertex in $\db{k+1}\setminus\{1^{k+1}\}$, written as $(v,w)\in \db{(k+1-i)+i}\setminus\{1^{k+1}\}$, we have $\langle \mathrm{c},\mathrm{c}_1'\rangle_i(v,w)=\mathrm{c}(v)$ if $w\not=1^i$ and $\langle \mathrm{c},\mathrm{c}_1'\rangle_i(v,1^i)=\mathrm{c}_1'(v)$ for $v\not=1^{k+1-i}$.} (Note that $\mathrm{c}|_{\db{k+1}\setminus\{1^{k+1}\}} = \mathrm{c}_0'$.) Since the map $(\mathrm{c}_0'\times \mathrm{c}_1',\mathrm{c})\mapsto \langle \mathrm{c},\mathrm{c}_1'\rangle_i$ is continuous, and so is $\mathcal{K}_{k+1}$, the result follows.

nodes.name: Compact-open topology
nodes.statement: Recall (e.g.\ from \cite[\S 46]{Mu}) that  for arbitrary topological spaces $X,Y$, the compact-open topology on $C(X,Y)$ is the smallest topology containing all sets of the form $\{f\in C(X,Y): f(K)\subset U\}$, for all choices of a compact set $K\subset X$ and an open set $U\subset Y$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.39
nodes.statement: We argue by induction on $k$. Since a 0-step nilspace is a singleton, the case $k=0$ is trivial. For $k>0$, as the structure group $\mathrm{Z}_k$ is an abelian Lie group, it is locally connected (being a manifold), and then, from Theorem \ref{thm:local-triviality-bundle} and the inductive assumption that $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ is locally-connected, it follows that every point of $\mathrm{X}$ has a basis of connected neighborhoods.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.40
nodes.statement: We have already proved that the topology induced on $\Theta_i(\mathrm{X})$ by the compact-open topology is Polish, so it suffices to prove that the group operation and inversion are both continuous. For the group operation (composition of translations), this follows directly from \cite[\S 46, Ex. 7]{Mu}. For the inversion, first note that $\Theta_i(\mathrm{X})$ is a subset of the set of homeomorphisms of $\mathrm{X}$. This is because the inverse of a continuous translation is continuous by Corollary \ref{cor:inv-cont-lcfr}. Moreover, by \cite[Theorem 4]{Ar46} the set of homeomorphisms with the compact-open topology is a topological group under composition, provided that the space is \textsc{lch} and locally connected.\footnote{Since Lie-fibered nilspaces are manifolds, one could also use \cite{Ka}, where a uniqueness property of the compact-open topology is also proved.} Thus, the set $\Theta_i(\mathrm{X})$ inherits the continuity of the inversion from that of the set of homeomorphisms.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.42
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{prop:cont-LCH-polish} we have that $C(\mathrm{X},\mathrm{Z})$ is a Polish space. We claim that $\hom(\mathrm{X},\mathcal{D}_t(\mathrm{Z}))$ is a closed subset of $C(\mathrm{X},\mathrm{Z})$. To prove this, let $(f_n)$ be a sequence in $\hom(\mathrm{X},\mathcal{D}_t(\mathrm{Z}))$ converging to $f\in C(\mathrm{X},\mathrm{Z})$. We need to prove that for every $\mathrm{c}\in \mathrm{C}^m(\mathrm{X})$ we have $f\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}\in \mathrm{C}^m(\mathcal{D}_t(\mathrm{Z}))$. Since $f_n\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}\in \mathrm{C}^m(\mathcal{D}_t(\mathrm{Z}))$ and $\mathrm{C}^m(\mathcal{D}_t(\mathrm{Z}))$ is closed, our claim follows. Now we need to prove that the group operations are also continuous. We will just do it for addition, as the argument is almost identical for the inverse. Fix any sequence of elements $(f_n,g_n)\in \hom(\mathrm{X},\mathcal{D}_t(\mathrm{Z}))^2$ converging to some $(f,g)\in \hom(\mathrm{X},\mathcal{D}_t(\mathrm{Z}))^2$. We need to prove that $f_n+g_n\rightarrow f+g$. Suppose for a contradiction that this fails. Let $d$ be a metric on $\mathrm{Z}$ compatible with the topology. By \cite[Theorems 46.8 and 46.2]{Mu}, there is then some compact set $K\subset \mathrm{X}$ and some $\epsilon_0>0$ such that $\sup_{x\in K} d((f_n+g_n)(x),(f+g)(x))>\epsilon_0$ for infinitely many $n$. Passing to a subsequence if necessary, we may assume that the previous lower bound holds for all $n$. Passing to a further subsequence, we obtain a sequence $(x_n)$ in $K$ such that $x_n\rightarrow x$ and $ d((f_n+g_n)(x_n),(f+g)(x_n))>\epsilon_0$ for all $n$. This yields a contradiction, as by \cite[Theorem 46.10]{Mu} the evaluation map is continuous and thus $f_n(x_n)+g_n(x_n)\rightarrow f(x)+g(x)$.

Passing to a subsequence if necessary, we may assume that the previous lower bound holds for all $n$. Passing to a further subsequence, we obtain a sequence $(x_n)$ in $K$ such that $x_n\rightarrow x$ and $ d((f_n+g_n)(x_n),(f+g)(x_n))>\epsilon_0$ for all $n$.

nodes.name: Discrete and continuous parts of a free nilspace
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be a $k$-step free nilspace $\prod_{i=1}^k \mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{Z}^{a_i}\times \mathbb{R}^{b_i})$, where $a_i,b_i\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$ for each $i\in [k]$. Thus an element $g$ of $F$ is a sequence of pairs $\left((x_i,y_i)\in \mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{Z}^{a_i}\times \mathbb{R}^{b_i})\right)_{i\in[k]}$ where $x_i\in \mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{Z}^{a_i})$, $y_i\in \mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{R}^{b_i})$. By a permutation of coordinates (which will often be used tacitly), we can write any $g\in F$ as a pair $g=(x,y)$ where $x:=(x_i=(x_{i,j})_{j\in [a_i]})_{i\in[k]}$ lies in the product nilspace $\prod_{i=1}^k \mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{Z}^{a_i})$, nilspace which we call the \emph{discrete part} of $F$, and $y:=(y_i=(y_{i,j})_{j\in [b_i]})_{i\in[k]}$ lies in the product nilspace $\prod_{i=1}^k \mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{R}^{b_i})$, the \emph{continuous part} of $F$. We shall often refer to $x,y$ as the \emph{discrete and continuous parts} of $g$ respectively.

nodes.name: Filtered degree $|(m,n)|$ and binomial monomials
nodes.statement: Let $k\in \mathbb{N}$, and for each $i\in [k]$ let $a_i,b_i\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$. Then, for any element $(m,n)= \big(((m_{i,j})_{j\in [a_i]})_{i\in[k]},((n_{i,\ell})_{\ell\in [b_i]})_{i\in[k]}\big) \in (\prod_{i=1}^k \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^{a_i})\times (\prod_{i=1}^k \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^{b_i})$, we define \[ |(m,n)|_{k,(a_i)_i,(b_i)_i}:=\sum_{i=1}^k i\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{a_i} m_{i,j}+\sum_{\ell=1}^{b_i} n_{i,\ell}\Big). \] If there is no risk of confusion, we abbreviate this to $|(m,n)|$. Given variables $x_{i,j},y_{i,\ell}$ for $i\in[k], j\in [a_i],\ell\in[b_i]$, we write $\binom{(x,y)}{(m,n)}$ for the monomial\footnote{Here $\binom{x}{n}$ denotes the standard binomial coefficient. It turns out to be technically convenient here to consider monomials as products of binomial coefficients rather than the more usual products of variables.} $\prod_{i=1}^k\prod_{j=1}^{a_i} \binom{x_{i,j}}{m_{i,j}}\prod_{\ell=1}^{b_i} \binom{y_{i,\ell}}{n_{i,\ell}}$.

Thus we shall refer to $|(m,n)|$ as the \emph{filtered degree} of the monomial $\binom{(x,y)}{(m,n)}$.

nodes.name: Taylor expansion of morphisms into discrete groups
nodes.statement: Let $k\in \mathbb{N}$. For each $i\in [k]$ let $a_i,b_i\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$, and let $F$ be the free nilspace $\big[\prod_{i=1}^k \mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{Z}^{a_i})\big] \times \big[\prod_{i=1}^k \mathcal{D}_i( \mathbb{R}^{b_i})\big]$. Let $A$ be a discrete finitely generated abelian group, and let $\phi:F\rightarrow \mathcal{D}_k(A)$ be a continuous nilspace morphism. Then for each $m\in \prod_{i=1}^k \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^{a_i}$ with $|(m,0)|_{k,(a_i),(0)}\le k$ there exists a coefficient $g_m\in A$, such that for every $x\in \prod_{i=1}^k \mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{Z}^{a_i})$ and $y\in \prod_{i=1}^k \mathcal{D}_i( \mathbb{R}^{b_i})$ we have \begin{equation} \phi(x,y)=\sum_{m:|(m,0)|_{k,(a_i),(0)}\le k} g_m \binom{(x,y)}{(m,0)}. \end{equation} Conversely, every map $\phi$ of the form \eqref{eq:Taylor-discrete} is a continuous morphism $F\rightarrow\mathcal{D}_k(A)$.

nodes.statement: As mentioned in Remark \ref{rem:monomial-degree}, the number $|(m,n)|$ gives a notion of filtered degree of a monomial $\binom{(x,y)}{(m,n)}$. Lemmas \ref{lem:Taylor-discrete} and \ref{lem:poly-free-to-R} together tell us that a morphism $\phi$ from a free nilspace $F$ to $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{Z}$ is a multivariate polynomial, more precisely a linear combination of monomials of the form $\binom{(x,y)}{(m,n)}$. Therefore we can now define the \emph{filtered degree} of such a polynomial to be the maximum of $|(m,n)|$ over all the monomials forming the polynomial. We can then summarize the results so far in this section as follows.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.11
nodes.statement: First we address the discrete part, in which $A$ is just a finite abelian group. In this case, letting $r$ be the rank of $A$, the conclusion is the following: \begin{equation} \textrm{there exists a morphism $\psi:F\rightarrow \mathcal{D}_k(\mathbb{Z}^r)$ such that $\phi=\pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\psi$.} \end{equation} Indeed, it suffices to take the expansion \eqref{eq:Taylor-discrete} for $\phi$, and lift it to a Taylor expansion of a morphism $\psi:F\rightarrow \mathcal{D}_k(B=\mathbb{Z}^r)$ by replacing each coefficient $g_m\in A$ by some $g_m'\in B$ such that $\pi(g_m')=g_m$. Next we treat the continuous part of the problem, where the image group $A$ is a torus $\mathbb{T}^s$. Letting $\pi:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{T}$ be the canonical quotient homomorphism, the main claim here is that \begin{equation} \textrm{there exists a morphism $\psi:F\rightarrow \mathcal{D}_k(\mathbb{R}^s)$ such that $\phi=\pi^s\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\psi$.} \end{equation} This follows readily by applying Lemma \ref{lem:Taylor-cont} to each of the $s$ coordinate maps of $\phi$ and taking the product of the resulting maps. The theorem now follows. Indeed, we can first lift separately the morphisms $\pi_d\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\phi$ and $\pi_c\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\phi$, using \eqref{prop:lift-disc} and \eqref{prop:lift-cont} respectively, where $\pi_d$ is the coordinate projection from $A$ to its discrete (finite) part $Z$ and $\pi_c$ is the coordinate projection from $A$ to its continuous part $\mathbb{T}^s$. Then we put together the two lifts to obtain $\psi$ (taking the product of the two maps).

nodes.name: Convention $\mathcal{D}_t(\mathrm{Z})$ for $t\le 0$
nodes.statement: In the following result, we use the basic degree-$t$ nilspace structure on an abelian group $\mathrm{Z}$, denoted by $\mathcal{D}_t(\mathrm{Z})$; see \cite[equation $(2.9)$]{Cand:Notes1}. However, we shall use this even for $t\leq 0$. Note that for $t=0$ the resulting nilspace is non-ergodic, and the $n$-cubes on this nilspace are the constant maps $\db{n}\rightarrow\mathrm{Z}$. It follows that for any (ergodic) nilspace $\mathrm{X}$, the set of morphisms $\hom(\mathrm{X},\mathcal{D}_0(\mathrm{Z}))$ is the set of constant maps $\mathrm{X} \rightarrow \mathrm{Z}$. For $t<0$ we take $\mathcal{D}_t(\mathrm{Z})$ to be $\{0_{\mathrm{Z}}\}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.15
nodes.statement: First we prove that any such function $\alpha$ is in $\Theta_s(\mathrm{X})$. We argue by induction on $k$. For $k=1$, since $\alpha$ then just adds a constant, it is indeed a translation on $\mathcal{D}_1(A_1)$. For $k\geq 2$ and $s\in [k]$, by induction the map $(x_1,\ldots,x_{k-1})+(0,\ldots,0,T_s,T_{s+1}(x_1),\ldots,T_{k-1}(x_1,\ldots,x_{k-1-s}))$ is in $\Theta_s(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$. Hence it suffices to prove that the map $\alpha': x=(x_1,,\ldots,x_k)\mapsto x+\big(0,\ldots,0,T_k(x_1,\ldots,x_{k-s})\big)$ is in $\Theta_s(\mathrm{X})$. By \cite[Lemma 3.2.32]{Cand:Notes1} it suffices to prove that for every $\mathrm{c}=(\mathrm{c}_1,\ldots,\mathrm{c}_k)\in \mathrm{C}^n\big(\prod_{i=1}^{k}\mathcal{D}_i(A_i)\big)$ the $s$-arrow $\langle \mathrm{c},\alpha'\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}\rangle_s$ is in $\mathrm{C}^{n+s}(\mathrm{X})$. Now $\langle \mathrm{c},\alpha'\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}\rangle_s=\langle \mathrm{c},\mathrm{c}\rangle_s + g$, for $g:\db{n+s}\rightarrow \prod_{i=1}^k A_i$, $v\mapsto (0,\ldots,0,\langle 0,T_k\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} (\mathrm{c}_1,\ldots,\mathrm{c}_{k-s})\rangle_s(v))$. Thus it suffices to prove that $\langle 0,T_k\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} (\mathrm{c}_1,\ldots,\mathrm{c}_{k-s})\rangle_s\in \mathrm{C}^n(\mathcal{D}_{k-s}(A_k))$. By \cite[Lemma 2.2.19]{Cand:Notes1}, this follows if $T_k\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} (\mathrm{c}_1,\ldots,\mathrm{c}_{k-s})\in \mathrm{C}^n(\mathcal{D}_{k-s}(A_k))$, which holds by our assumption on $T_k$. Now we prove that every translation $\alpha\in \Theta_s(\mathrm{X})$ has the form claimed in the theorem. Note that by the previous paragraph, adding a constant $x_i$ in the $i$-th component of $\mathrm{X}$ is a translation in $\Theta_i(\mathrm{X})$. Moreover, for $i\geq k-s+1$ such translations are central in $\Theta_s(\mathrm{X})$. Hence for every $x\in \mathrm{X}$ we have $\alpha(x)=\alpha(x_1,\ldots,x_{k-s},0^s)+(0^{k-s},x_{k-s+1},\ldots,x_k)$. By induction, the first summand here equals $(x_1,\ldots,x_{k-s},0^s)+(0^{k-s},T_s,T_{s+1}(x_1),\ldots,T_{k-1}(x_1,\ldots,x_{k-1-s}),g(x))$ for some map $g:\mathrm{X}\rightarrow A_k$ which factors through $\pi_{k-s}$, i.e.\ $g(x)=g'(x_1,\ldots,x_{k-s})$ for some map $g':\mathrm{X}_{k-s}\rightarrow A_k$. It now suffices to prove that $g'\in \hom(\prod_{i=1}^{k-s}\mathcal{D}_i(A_i),\mathcal{D}_{k-s}(A_k))$. Fix any $\mathrm{c}\in \mathrm{C}^n(\prod_{i=1}^{k-s}\mathcal{D}_i(A_i))$. Let $\mathrm{c}^*\in \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$ be defined by $\mathrm{c}^*(v)=(\mathrm{c}(v),0^s)$ for $v\in\db{n}$, and consider the map $\langle\mathrm{c}^*,\alpha\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}^*\rangle_s$. On one hand, by \cite[Lemma 3.2.32]{Cand:Notes1} this map is a cube. On the other hand, by the above expression of $\alpha$, this map equals $\langle\mathrm{c}^*,\mathrm{c}^*\rangle_s+\langle0,\mathrm{c}'\rangle_s+\langle 0,\mathrm{c}''\rangle_s$ for some $\mathrm{c}'=(\mathrm{c}'_1,\ldots,\mathrm{c}'_{k-s},0^s)\in \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$, and with $\mathrm{c}''(v)=(0^{k-s},g'\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}(v))$. Then $\langle 0,\mathrm{c}''\rangle_s\in \mathrm{C}^{n+s}(\mathrm{X})$, since it is the combination of cubes $\langle\mathrm{c}^*,\alpha\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}^*\rangle_s-\langle\mathrm{c}^*, \mathrm{c}^*\rangle_s - \langle0,\mathrm{c}'\rangle_s$. Hence $\langle 0,g'\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}\rangle_s\in \mathrm{C}^{n+s}(\mathcal{D}_k(A_k))$, so $g'\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}\in \mathrm{C}^n(\mathcal{D}_{k-s}(A_k))$ by \cite[Lemma 2.2.19]{Cand:Notes1}, as required.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.18
nodes.statement: Recall that we equip $\Theta(\mathrm{X})$ with the compact-open topology, which in this case equals the topology of convergence in compact sets (see \S \ref{sec:trans-group}). Let $(\alpha_n)_n$ be a sequence in $\Theta(\mathrm{X})$ converging to some $\alpha\in \Theta(\mathrm{X})$. We want to prove that $\eta_{k-1}(\alpha_n)\rightarrow \eta_{k-1}(\alpha)$. Let $K\subset \mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ be any compact set. By Corollary \ref{cor:cpct-sets-are-im-of-cpct-sets} there is a compact set $K'\subset \mathrm{X}$ such that $\pi_{k-1}(K')=K$. Fix any metric $d$ metrizing the topology on $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$. We claim that $\sup_{y\in K}d\big(\eta_{k-1}(\alpha_n)(y),\eta_{k-1}(\alpha)(y)\big)\rightarrow 0$ as $n\rightarrow \infty$. Since $\pi_{k-1}$ is surjective from $K'$ onto $K$, this last supremum is at most $\sup_{x\in K'}d(\pi_{k-1}(\alpha_n(x)),\pi_{k-1}(\alpha(x)))$ for every $n$. Suppose this supremum does not converge to 0 as $n\rightarrow \infty$. Then there exists $\epsilon>0$ and a sequence $(x_n)$ in $K'$ such that for every $n$ we have $d(\pi_{k-1}(\alpha_n(x_n)),\pi_{k-1}(\alpha(x_n)))>\epsilon$. As $K'$ is compact, passing to a subsequence we can assume that $x_n$ converges to some $x'\in K'$. This yields a contradiction because $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\alpha_n(x_n)=\alpha(x')=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \alpha(x_n)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.17
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lem:h-is-cont} and Theorem \ref{thm:trans-group-polish}, the map $\eta_{k-1}$ is a continuous homomorphism between the Polish groups $\Theta(\mathrm{X})$ and $\Theta(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$. Moreover, the map $\eta_{k-1}$ is seen to be surjective using the description of $\Theta(\mathrm{X})$ and $\Theta(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$ given in \eqref{eq:str-trans-ab-nil}. Indeed, since $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ is isomorphic as an Lie-fibered nilspace to $\prod_{i=1}^{k-1}\mathcal{D}_i(A_i)$, by \eqref{eq:str-trans-ab-nil} applied to $\Theta(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$ any $\alpha'\in \Theta(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$ corresponds uniquely to a tuple $(T_1,\ldots,T_{k-1})$, and then by \eqref{eq:str-trans-ab-nil} applied to $\Theta(\mathrm{X})$ the tuple $(T_1,\ldots,T_{k-1},0)$ corresponds to a translation $\alpha\in \Theta(\mathrm{X})$ such that $\eta_{k-1}(\alpha)=\alpha'$. Finally, letting $\iota$ denote the inclusion homomorphism $\ker(\eta_{k-1}) \xrightarrow{\iota} \Theta(\mathrm{X})$, note that $\iota$ and $\eta_{k-1}$ are open maps onto their images, by the open mapping theorem for Polish groups (see \cite[Chapter 1]{BeKe}). We have thus confirmed that we have the short exact sequence of topological groups $0\rightarrow \ker(\eta_{k-1}) \xrightarrow{\iota} \Theta(\mathrm{X}) \xrightarrow{\eta_{k-1}}\Theta(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})\rightarrow 0$.
nodes.section: 3.3 On the translation groups and structure groups of free nilspaces
nodes.statement_short: $\eta_{k-1}$ is a continuous surjective homomorphism of Polish groups, hence open, giving the exact sequence.

nodes.name: Continuous homomorphism of Polish groups
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lem:h-is-cont} and Theorem \ref{thm:trans-group-polish}, the map $\eta_{k-1}$ is a continuous homomorphism between the Polish groups $\Theta(\mathrm{X})$ and $\Theta(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$.
nodes.section: 3.3 On the translation groups and structure groups of free nilspaces

nodes.name: Surjectivity
nodes.statement: Moreover, the map $\eta_{k-1}$ is seen to be surjective using the description of $\Theta(\mathrm{X})$ and $\Theta(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$ given in \eqref{eq:str-trans-ab-nil}. Indeed, since $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ is isomorphic as an Lie-fibered nilspace to $\prod_{i=1}^{k-1}\mathcal{D}_i(A_i)$, by \eqref{eq:str-trans-ab-nil} applied to $\Theta(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$ any $\alpha'\in \Theta(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$ corresponds uniquely to a tuple $(T_1,\ldots,T_{k-1})$, and then by \eqref{eq:str-trans-ab-nil} applied to $\Theta(\mathrm{X})$ the tuple $(T_1,\ldots,T_{k-1},0)$ corresponds to a translation $\alpha\in \Theta(\mathrm{X})$ such that $\eta_{k-1}(\alpha)=\alpha'$.
nodes.section: 3.3 On the translation groups and structure groups of free nilspaces

nodes.name: Open maps and exact sequence
nodes.statement: Finally, letting $\iota$ denote the inclusion homomorphism $\ker(\eta_{k-1}) \xrightarrow{\iota} \Theta(\mathrm{X})$, note that $\iota$ and $\eta_{k-1}$ are open maps onto their images, by the open mapping theorem for Polish groups (see \cite[Chapter 1]{BeKe}). We have thus confirmed that we have the short exact sequence of topological groups $0\rightarrow \ker(\eta_{k-1}) \xrightarrow{\iota} \Theta(\mathrm{X}) \xrightarrow{\eta_{k-1}}\Theta(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})\rightarrow 0$.
nodes.section: 3.3 On the translation groups and structure groups of free nilspaces
nodes.statement_short: Open mapping theorem for Polish groups.

nodes.name: Morphisms from a free nilspace into $\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z})$ form a Lie group
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be a free nilspace, let $\mathrm{Z}$ be an abelian \textup{(}compactly generated\textup{)} Lie group, and let $k$ be any positive integer. Then $\hom(F,\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}))$ is an abelian Lie group.
nodes.section: 3.3 On the translation groups and structure groups of free nilspaces
assumptions: Let $F$ be a free nilspace, let $\mathrm{Z}$ be an abelian \textup{(}compactly generated\textup{)} Lie group, and let $k$ be any positive integer.
conclusions: Then $\hom(F,\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}))$ is an abelian Lie group.
nodes.label: lem:hom-Lie

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.19
nodes.statement: Let $B$ be the covering group of $\mathrm{Z}$ as in \S \ref{subsec:lift-inv-free-nil}, thus $B=\mathbb{Z}^r\times \mathbb{R}^s$ with a continuous surjective homomorphism $\pi:B\rightarrow \mathrm{Z}$. It is readily seen from Lemmas \ref{lem:Taylor-discrete} and \ref{lem:poly-free-to-R} that $\hom(F,\mathcal{D}_k(B))\cong \mathbb{Z}^m\times \mathbb{R}^n$ for some $m,n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$, so this is a Lie group. Let $\phi:\hom(F,\mathcal{D}_k(B))\rightarrow \hom(F,\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}))$ be the homomorphism $f\mapsto \pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} f$. Arguing as in the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:h-is-cont}, we see that $\phi$ is continuous. Hence $\ker(\phi)$ is a closed subgroup of $\hom(F,\mathcal{D}_k(B))$, hence a Lie group. By Theorem \ref{thm:lift-mor-cfr-ab-gr} the map $\phi$ is also surjective. It follows as in the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:freetransLie} that $\hom(F,\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}))\cong \hom(F,\mathcal{D}_k(B))/\ker(\phi)$, whence $\hom(F,\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}))$ is a Lie group by \cite[Theorem 2.6]{Mosk}.
nodes.section: 3.3 On the translation groups and structure groups of free nilspaces
nodes.statement_short: Morphisms into the covering group form $\mathbb{Z}^m\times\mathbb{R}^n$; the induced map onto $\hom(F,\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}))$ is a continuous surjection with closed kernel.

nodes.name: Morphisms into the covering group
nodes.statement: Let $B$ be the covering group of $\mathrm{Z}$ as in \S \ref{subsec:lift-inv-free-nil}, thus $B=\mathbb{Z}^r\times \mathbb{R}^s$ with a continuous surjective homomorphism $\pi:B\rightarrow \mathrm{Z}$. It is readily seen from Lemmas  \ref{lem:Taylor-discrete} and \ref{lem:poly-free-to-R} that $\hom(F,\mathcal{D}_k(B))\cong \mathbb{Z}^m\times \mathbb{R}^n$ for some $m,n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$, so this is a Lie group.
nodes.section: 3.3 On the translation groups and structure groups of free nilspaces

nodes.name: Continuous projection with Lie kernel
nodes.statement: Let $\phi:\hom(F,\mathcal{D}_k(B))\rightarrow \hom(F,\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}))$ be the homomorphism $f\mapsto \pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} f$. Arguing as in the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:h-is-cont}, we see that $\phi$ is continuous. Hence $\ker(\phi)$ is a closed subgroup of $\hom(F,\mathcal{D}_k(B))$, hence a Lie group.
nodes.section: 3.3 On the translation groups and structure groups of free nilspaces

nodes.name: Quotient is Lie
nodes.statement: By Theorem \ref{thm:lift-mor-cfr-ab-gr} the map $\phi$ is also surjective. It follows as in the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:freetransLie} that $\hom(F,\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}))\cong \hom(F,\mathcal{D}_k(B))/\ker(\phi)$, whence $\hom(F,\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}))$ is a Lie group by \cite[Theorem 2.6]{Mosk}.
nodes.section: 3.3 On the translation groups and structure groups of free nilspaces

nodes.name: The kernel of $\eta_{k-1}$ on a free nilspace is Lie
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be a $k$-step free nilspace, and let $\eta_{k-1}:\Theta(F)\rightarrow\Theta(F_{k-1})$ be the surjective continuous homomorphism from \eqref{eq:etaj}. Then $\ker(\eta_{k-1})$ is a Lie group.
nodes.section: 3.3 On the translation groups and structure groups of free nilspaces
assumptions: Let $F$ be a $k$-step free nilspace, and let $\eta_{k-1}:\Theta(F)\rightarrow\Theta(F_{k-1})$ be the surjective continuous homomorphism from \eqref{eq:etaj}.
conclusions: Then $\ker(\eta_{k-1})$ is a Lie group.
nodes.label: lem:ker-h-Lie

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.20
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lem:hom-Lie} it suffices to prove that the group $\ker(\eta_{k-1})$ is topologically isomorphic to $\hom(F_{k-1},\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}_k))$. The algebraic part is given by \cite[Lemma 2.9.5]{Cand:Notes2}, which gives us an (purely algebraic so far) isomorphism $\varphi:\ker(\eta_{k-1})\rightarrow \hom(F_{k-1},\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}_k))$. Hence, it suffices to check that $\varphi$ is continuous, as then it is open (by the open mapping theorem for Polish groups) and therefore a topological-group isomorphism. To check this continuity, recall that we are using the compact-open topology on both $\ker(\eta_{k-1})$ and $\hom(F_{k-1},\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}_k))$. Suppose that $\varphi$ is not continuous. Then there is a convergent sequence $(\alpha_n)$ in $\ker(\eta_{k-1})$ with limit $\alpha\in \ker(\eta_{k-1})$ such that, for some compact $K\subset F_{k-1}$ and $\epsilon>0$, for infinitely many $n$ we have $\sup_{f\in K}d_{\mathrm{Z}_k}(\varphi(\alpha_n)(f),\varphi(\alpha)(f))>\epsilon$. Passing to a subsequence we can assume that for every $n\in \mathbb{N}$ there exists $f_n\in K$ such that $d_{\mathrm{Z}}(\varphi(\alpha_n)(f_n),\varphi(\alpha)(f_n))>\epsilon$. By Corollary \ref{cor:cpct-sets-are-im-of-cpct-sets} we know that there exists a compact set $K'\subset F$ such that $\pi_{k-1}(K')=K$. For each $n$ let $x_n\in K'$ be such that $\pi(x_n)=f_n$. By compactness, passing to a subsequence we can assume that $x_n\rightarrow x$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$. Hence $d_{\mathrm{Z}_k}(\alpha_n(x_n)-x_n,\alpha(x_n)-x_n)>\epsilon$ for all $n$. Now letting $n\rightarrow \infty$, we know that $\alpha_n(x_n)\rightarrow \alpha(x)$, and by continuity of subtraction in an \textsc{lch} nilspace we deduce $0=d_{\mathrm{Z}_k}(\alpha(x)-x,\alpha(x)-x)>\epsilon$, a contradiction.
nodes.section: 3.3 On the translation groups and structure groups of free nilspaces
nodes.statement_short: Identify $\ker(\eta_{k-1})$ with $\hom(F_{k-1},\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}_k))$; continuity of the isomorphism by contradiction with compact lifts.

nodes.name: Reduce to continuity of $\varphi$
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lem:hom-Lie} it suffices to prove that the group $\ker(\eta_{k-1})$ is topologically isomorphic to $\hom(F_{k-1},\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}_k))$. The algebraic part is given by \cite[Lemma 2.9.5]{Cand:Notes2}, which gives us an (purely algebraic so far) isomorphism $\varphi:\ker(\eta_{k-1})\rightarrow \hom(F_{k-1},\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}_k))$. Hence, it suffices to check that $\varphi$ is continuous, as then it is open (by the open mapping theorem for Polish groups) and therefore a topological-group isomorphism.

nodes.statement_short: Algebraic isomorphism from Notes 2; open mapping theorem.

nodes.name: Continuity by contradiction
nodes.statement: To check this continuity, recall that we are using the compact-open topology on both $\ker(\eta_{k-1})$ and $\hom(F_{k-1},\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}_k))$. Suppose that $\varphi$ is not continuous. Then there is a convergent sequence $(\alpha_n)$ in $\ker(\eta_{k-1})$ with limit $\alpha\in \ker(\eta_{k-1})$ such that, for some compact $K\subset F_{k-1}$ and $\epsilon>0$, for infinitely many $n$ we have $\sup_{f\in K}d_{\mathrm{Z}_k}(\varphi(\alpha_n)(f),\varphi(\alpha)(f))>\epsilon$. Passing to a subsequence we can assume that for every $n\in \mathbb{N}$ there exists $f_n\in K$ such that $d_{\mathrm{Z}}(\varphi(\alpha_n)(f_n),\varphi(\alpha)(f_n))>\epsilon$. By Corollary \ref{cor:cpct-sets-are-im-of-cpct-sets} we know that there exists a compact set $K'\subset F$ such that $\pi_{k-1}(K')=K$. For each $n$ let $x_n\in K'$ be such that $\pi(x_n)=f_n$. By compactness, passing to a subsequence we can assume that $x_n\rightarrow x$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$. Hence $d_{\mathrm{Z}_k}(\alpha_n(x_n)-x_n,\alpha(x_n)-x_n)>\epsilon$ for all $n$. Now letting $n\rightarrow \infty$, we know that $\alpha_n(x_n)\rightarrow \alpha(x)$, and by continuity of subtraction in an \textsc{lch} nilspace we deduce $0=d_{\mathrm{Z}_k}(\alpha(x)-x,\alpha(x)-x)>\epsilon$, a contradiction.

nodes.statement_short: Compact lifts and continuity of subtraction.

nodes.name: Assume discontinuity
nodes.statement: To check this continuity, recall that we are using the compact-open topology on both $\ker(\eta_{k-1})$ and $\hom(F_{k-1},\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}_k))$. Suppose that $\varphi$ is not continuous. Then there is a convergent sequence $(\alpha_n)$ in $\ker(\eta_{k-1})$ with limit $\alpha\in \ker(\eta_{k-1})$ such that, for some compact $K\subset F_{k-1}$ and $\epsilon>0$, for infinitely many $n$ we have $\sup_{f\in K}d_{\mathrm{Z}_k}(\varphi(\alpha_n)(f),\varphi(\alpha)(f))>\epsilon$. Passing to a subsequence we can assume that for every $n\in \mathbb{N}$ there exists $f_n\in K$ such that $d_{\mathrm{Z}}(\varphi(\alpha_n)(f_n),\varphi(\alpha)(f_n))>\epsilon$.
nodes.section: 3.3 On the translation groups and structure groups of free nilspaces
nodes.statement_short: Get a uniform gap on a compact set.

nodes.name: Lift to a compact set in $F$
nodes.statement: By Corollary \ref{cor:cpct-sets-are-im-of-cpct-sets} we know that there exists a compact set $K'\subset F$ such that $\pi_{k-1}(K')=K$. For each $n$ let $x_n\in K'$ be such that $\pi(x_n)=f_n$. By compactness, passing to a subsequence we can assume that $x_n\rightarrow x$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$.

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: Hence $d_{\mathrm{Z}_k}(\alpha_n(x_n)-x_n,\alpha(x_n)-x_n)>\epsilon$ for all $n$. Now letting $n\rightarrow \infty$, we know that $\alpha_n(x_n)\rightarrow \alpha(x)$, and by continuity of subtraction in an \textsc{lch} nilspace we deduce $0=d_{\mathrm{Z}_k}(\alpha(x)-x,\alpha(x)-x)>\epsilon$, a contradiction.
nodes.section: 3.3 On the translation groups and structure groups of free nilspaces

nodes.name: Translation and structure groups of free nilspaces are Lie
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be a $k$-step free nilspace. Then $\Theta(F)$ and all structure groups of $F$ are Lie groups.
nodes.section: 3.3 On the translation groups and structure groups of free nilspaces
assumptions: Let $F$ be a $k$-step free nilspace.
conclusions: Then $\Theta(F)$ and all structure groups of $F$ are Lie groups.
nodes.label: cor:trans&structFree

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 3.21
nodes.statement: We argue by induction on $k$. For $k=1$ the translation group is isomorphic to the abelian group underlying $F$, which is Lie. For $k>1$, by induction $\Theta(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$ is Lie, and $\ker(h\eta_{k-1})$ is Lie by Lemma \ref{lem:ker-h-Lie}. Hence $\Theta(\mathrm{X})$ is Lie by Theorem \ref{thm:freetransLie} and \cite[Theorem 2.6]{Mosk}.
nodes.section: 3.3 On the translation groups and structure groups of free nilspaces
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $k$ via the extension of Theorem 3.17 and Lemma 3.20.

nodes.name: Base case $k=1$
nodes.statement: We argue by induction on $k$. For $k=1$ the translation group is isomorphic to the abelian group underlying $F$, which is Lie.
nodes.section: 3.3 On the translation groups and structure groups of free nilspaces
nodes.statement_short: The translation group is the underlying abelian Lie group.

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement: For $k>1$, by induction $\Theta(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$ is  Lie, and $\ker(h\eta_{k-1})$ is Lie by Lemma \ref{lem:ker-h-Lie}. Hence $\Theta(\mathrm{X})$ is Lie by Theorem \ref{thm:freetransLie} and \cite[Theorem 2.6]{Mosk}.
nodes.section: 3.3 On the translation groups and structure groups of free nilspaces
nodes.statement_short: Extension of Lie groups is Lie.

nodes.name: Lie-fibered extensions of free nilspaces split
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be a $k$-step free nilspace and let $\mathrm{Y}$ be a degree-$k$ extension of $F$ by an abelian Lie group $\mathrm{Z}$, with corresponding fibration $q:\mathrm{Y}\rightarrow F$. Then this extension splits, i.e., there exists a continuous morphism $s:F\rightarrow\mathrm{Y}$ such that $q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} s=\mathrm{id}$. In particular $\mathrm{Y}$ is isomorphic as an \textsc{lch} nilspace to the product-nilspace $F\times \mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z})$.
nodes.section: 4 Lie-fibered extensions of free nilspaces are split extensions
assumptions: Let $F$ be a $k$-step free nilspace and let $\mathrm{Y}$ be a degree-$k$ extension of $F$ by an abelian Lie group $\mathrm{Z}$, with corresponding fibration $q:\mathrm{Y}\rightarrow F$.
conclusions: Then this  extension splits, i.e., there exists a continuous morphism $s:F\rightarrow\mathrm{Y}$ such that $q\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} s=\mathrm{id}$.
In particular $\mathrm{Y}$ is isomorphic as an \textsc{lch} nilspace to the product-nilspace $F\times \mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z})$.
nodes.statement_short: Every degree-$k$ extension of a $k$-step free nilspace by an abelian Lie group has a continuous cross-section, so it is $F\times\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z})$.
nodes.label: thm:splitext

nodes.name: Topological extensions of torsion-free abelian Lie groups split
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be a torsion-free abelian Lie group, let $\mathrm{Z}$, $G$ be locally-compact abelian groups, and suppose that $G$ is a topological-group extension of $F$ by $\mathrm{Z}$, i.e.\ there is a proper exact sequence of topological groups $0\rightarrow \mathrm{Z} \rightarrow G \rightarrow F\rightarrow 0$. Then this extension splits.
nodes.section: 4 Lie-fibered extensions of free nilspaces are split extensions
assumptions: Let $F$ be a torsion-free abelian Lie group, let $\mathrm{Z}$, $G$ be locally-compact abelian groups, and suppose that $G$ is a topological-group extension of $F$ by $\mathrm{Z}$, i.e.\ there is a proper exact sequence of topological groups $0\rightarrow \mathrm{Z} \rightarrow G \rightarrow F\rightarrow 0$.
conclusions: Then this extension splits.
nodes.label: lem:abcasesplit

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.2
nodes.statement: We have that $F$ is a direct product $\mathbb{R}^n \oplus \mathbb{Z}^m$, so by \cite[Theorem 3.3]{Mosk} the group $F$ is projective for \textsc{lch} groups, and then the result follows from \cite[Theorem 3.5]{Mosk}.
nodes.section: 4 Lie-fibered extensions of free nilspaces are split extensions
nodes.statement_short: Torsion-free abelian Lie groups are projective for LCH groups (Moskowitz).

nodes.name: Cross-section
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{X},\mathrm{Y}$ be nilspaces and let $\varphi:\mathrm{Y}\rightarrow \mathrm{X}$ be a fibration. A \emph{cross-section} for $\varphi$ is a nilspace morphism $s:\mathrm{X}\rightarrow \mathrm{Y}$ such that $\varphi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} s =\mathrm{id}_{\mathrm{X}}$.
nodes.section: 4 Lie-fibered extensions of free nilspaces are split extensions

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.1
nodes.section: 4 Lie-fibered extensions of free nilspaces are split extensions
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $k$: build a cross-section by lifting the generating translations and one-parameter subgroups of $F$ through the continuous surjective homomorphism $\widehat{q}:\Theta(\mathrm{Y})\to\Theta(F)$. Surjectivity of $\widehat{q}$ uses translation-lifting and the inductive splitting; lifting one-parameter subgroups needs $\Theta(\mathrm{Y})$ to be Lie.

nodes.name: Base case $k=1$
nodes.statement: We argue by induction on $k$. The case $k=1$ is given by Lemma \ref{lem:abcasesplit}.
nodes.section: 4 Lie-fibered extensions of free nilspaces are split extensions

nodes.name: Strategy
nodes.statement: For $k>1$, we assume that the result holds for step at most $k-1$. The crux of the proof consists in specifying a continuous cross-section $\mathrm{s}:F\rightarrow \mathrm{Y}$. Fixing some $y\in q^{-1}(0)$, we will obtain from each element $f\in F$ a translation on $\mathrm{Y}$ in a consistent way, defining then $\mathrm{s}(f)$ as the image of $y$ under this translation.
nodes.section: 4 Lie-fibered extensions of free nilspaces are split extensions
nodes.statement_short: Define the cross-section by applying lifted translations to a base point.

nodes.name: Lower-degree extensions of free nilspaces split
nodes.section: 4 Lie-fibered extensions of free nilspaces are split extensions
conclusions: for any $t\le k-1$, and any free nilspace $F'$ (of arbitrary finite step), any degree-$t$ extension $\psi:\mathrm{Y}'\rightarrow F'$ splits.
nodes.statement_short: By the induction hypothesis, every degree-$t$ extension ($t\le k-1$) of a free nilspace splits.

nodes.name: Factor diagram
nodes.section: 4 Lie-fibered extensions of free nilspaces are split extensions

nodes.name: Factor diagram of a degree-$t$ extension of a free nilspace
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned}[c] \begin{tikzpicture} \matrix (m) [matrix of math nodes,row sep=2em,column sep=4em,minimum width=2em] {\mathrm{Y}' & F' \\ \mathrm{Y}'_{t} & F'_{t}. \\}; \path[-stealth] (m-1-1) edge node [above] {$\psi$} (m-1-2) (m-1-1) edge node [right] {$\pi_t$} (m-2-1) (m-1-2) edge node [right] {$\pi_t$} (m-2-2) (m-2-1) edge node [above] {$\psi_t$} (m-2-2); \end{tikzpicture} \end{aligned}
nodes.section: 4 Lie-fibered extensions of free nilspaces are split extensions
nodes.label: diag:splt-1

nodes.name: Fiber product homeomorphism
nodes.statement: By \cite[Proposition A.19]{CGSS-p-hom} we already know that $\mathrm{Y}'$ is isomorphic (algebraically) to the nilspace $\mathrm{Y}'_t\times_{F'_t} F'$, the isomorphism being the map $y\mapsto (\pi_t(y),\psi(y))$. As this map is a continuous fibration between Lie-fibered nilspaces, it is an open map by Theorem \ref{thm:open-mapping-thm}. Hence it is a homeomorphism.
nodes.section: 4 Lie-fibered extensions of free nilspaces are split extensions
nodes.statement_short: Algebraic isomorphism is open by Theorem 2.21.

nodes.name: Cross-section from the factor
nodes.statement: By the induction hypothesis, the extension $\psi_t:\mathrm{Y}'_t\rightarrow F'_t$ splits, so there exists a continuous cross-section $s_t:F'_t\rightarrow \mathrm{Y}'_t$ such that $\psi_t\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} s_t=\mathrm{id}$. Then, the map $F'\rightarrow \mathrm{Y}'_t\times_{F'_t} F'$, $x\mapsto(s_t(\pi_t(x)),x)$ is a continuous cross-section from $F'$ to $\mathrm{Y}'$.
nodes.section: 4 Lie-fibered extensions of free nilspaces are split extensions

nodes.name: The homomorphism $\widehat{q}$
nodes.statement: Now let $q:\mathrm{Y}\rightarrow F$ be the continuous fibration given in the theorem. Note that $q_{k-1}$ is then an isomorphism $\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}\rightarrow F_{k-1}$ (by similar arguments as in the proof of Proposition \ref{prop:ext-lie-is-lie-1}). This implies that for every translation $\alpha\in\Theta(\mathrm{Y})$ the map $q$ is \emph{$\alpha$-consistent}, meaning that  $q(y)=q(y')\Rightarrow q(\alpha y)=q(\alpha y')$. Indeed, if $q(y)=q(y')$, then from $q_{k-1}$ being an isomorphism it follows that $y,y'$ are in the same fiber of $\pi_{k-1,\mathrm{Y}}$, so $y'=y+z$ for some $z\in\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})$, and then $q(y)=q(y')$ also implies that $z$ is in the kernel of the $k$-th structure homomorphism $\phi_{k,q}$ of $q$ (see \cite[Definition 3.3.1]{Cand:Notes1}). Then $\alpha (y')=\alpha(y)+ z$, so $q(\alpha y')=q(\alpha(y))+ \phi_{k,q}(z)=q(\alpha(y))$ as claimed. We can then define (as in \cite[Lemma 1.5]{CGSS}) a homomorphism $\widehat{q}:\Theta(\mathrm{Y}) \rightarrow \Theta(F)$, which is a \emph{filtered} group homomorphism, i.e.\ such that for each $i\in [k]$, $\widehat{q}$ sends $\alpha\in \Theta_i(\mathrm{Y})$ to the translation $\widehat{q}(\alpha): x\in F\mapsto q(\alpha(y))$ in $\Theta_i(F)$ (for any $y\in \mathrm{Y}$ with $q(y)=x$).
nodes.section: 4 Lie-fibered extensions of free nilspaces are split extensions
nodes.statement_short: $q$ is consistent with translations, giving a filtered homomorphism $\widehat{q}$.

nodes.name: $\widehat{q}$ is continuous
nodes.statement:
To obtain the desired cross-section $\mathrm{s}$ below, we shall use the following properties of $\widehat{q}$. 

First note that $\widehat{q}$ is continuous (relative to the compact-open topology on $\Theta_i(\mathrm{Y})$ and $\Theta_i(F)$; recall \S \ref{sec:trans-group}). Indeed, suppose for a contradiction that there was a sequence $(\alpha_n)_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ converging to $\alpha$ in $\Theta_i(\mathrm{Y})$ such that $\widehat{q}(\alpha_n)\not\rightarrow \widehat{q}(\alpha)$. Then there would be a compact set $K\subset F$ and some $\epsilon>0$ such that $\sup_{x\in K}d_F(\widehat{q}(\alpha_n)(x),\widehat{q}(\alpha)(x))>\epsilon$ for all $n$. Thus there would exist a sequence $(x_n)_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ in $K$ such that $d_F(\widehat{q}(\alpha_n)(x_n),\widehat{q}(\alpha)(x_n))>\epsilon$ for all $n$. By compactness of $K$ we can assume that $x_n$ converges to some $x^*\in K$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$. Letting $y_n,y\in\mathrm{Y}$ be such that $x_n=q(y_n)$ for all $n$ and $x^*=q(y)$, by Lemma \ref{lem:conv-quot} there would exist a sequence $z_n\in \mathrm{Z}$ such that $y_n+z_n\rightarrow y$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$. Renaming this sequence, we could assume that $y_n\rightarrow y$. By \cite[Theorem 46.10]{Mu} we would then have  $\alpha_n(y_n)\rightarrow \alpha(y)$ as $n\rightarrow \infty$. Since $\widehat{q}(\alpha_n)(x_n)=q(\alpha_n(y_n))$ and $\widehat{q}(\alpha)(x^*)=q(\alpha(y))$, by continuity of $q$ we would have $\widehat{q}(\alpha_n)(x_n)\rightarrow \widehat{q}(\alpha)(x^*)$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$, contradicting $d_F(\widehat{q}(\alpha_n)(x_n),\widehat{q}(\alpha)(x_n))>\epsilon$ for $n$ large enough.
nodes.section: 4 Lie-fibered extensions of free nilspaces are split extensions

nodes.name: Assume discontinuity
nodes.statement:
To obtain the desired cross-section $\mathrm{s}$ below, we shall use the following properties of $\widehat{q}$. 

First note that $\widehat{q}$ is continuous (relative to the compact-open topology on $\Theta_i(\mathrm{Y})$ and $\Theta_i(F)$; recall \S \ref{sec:trans-group}). Indeed, suppose for a contradiction that there was a sequence $(\alpha_n)_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ converging to $\alpha$ in $\Theta_i(\mathrm{Y})$ such that $\widehat{q}(\alpha_n)\not\rightarrow \widehat{q}(\alpha)$. Then there would be a compact set $K\subset F$ and some $\epsilon>0$ such that $\sup_{x\in K}d_F(\widehat{q}(\alpha_n)(x),\widehat{q}(\alpha)(x))>\epsilon$ for all $n$. Thus there would exist a sequence $(x_n)_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ in $K$ such that $d_F(\widehat{q}(\alpha_n)(x_n),\widehat{q}(\alpha)(x_n))>\epsilon$ for all $n$. By compactness of $K$ we can assume that $x_n$ converges to some $x^*\in K$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$.
nodes.section: 4 Lie-fibered extensions of free nilspaces are split extensions
nodes.statement_short: Get a uniform gap on a compact set.

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: Letting $y_n,y\in\mathrm{Y}$ be such that $x_n=q(y_n)$ for all $n$ and $x^*=q(y)$, by Lemma \ref{lem:conv-quot} there would exist a sequence $z_n\in \mathrm{Z}$ such that $y_n+z_n\rightarrow y$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$. Renaming this sequence, we could assume that $y_n\rightarrow y$. By \cite[Theorem 46.10]{Mu} we would then have  $\alpha_n(y_n)\rightarrow \alpha(y)$ as $n\rightarrow \infty$. Since $\widehat{q}(\alpha_n)(x_n)=q(\alpha_n(y_n))$ and $\widehat{q}(\alpha)(x^*)=q(\alpha(y))$, by continuity of $q$ we would have $\widehat{q}(\alpha_n)(x_n)\rightarrow \widehat{q}(\alpha)(x^*)$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$, contradicting $d_F(\widehat{q}(\alpha_n)(x_n),\widehat{q}(\alpha)(x_n))>\epsilon$ for $n$ large enough.
nodes.section: 4 Lie-fibered extensions of free nilspaces are split extensions
nodes.statement_short: Lift sequences and use continuity of evaluation.

nodes.name: $\widehat{q}$ is surjective
nodes.statement: Next we prove the key fact that $\widehat{q}$ is surjective from $\Theta_i(\mathrm{Y})$ onto $\Theta_i(F)$, for each $i\in [k]$. Note that for $i=k$ this is clear by virtue of $q$ being a fibration (its $k$-th structure homomorphism is then surjective), so we may assume that $i<k$. Let $\eta_{k-1}:\Theta_i(F)\rightarrow\Theta_i(F_{k-1})$ be the homomorphism from \eqref{eq:etaj}. Since $q_{k-1}:\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}\rightarrow F_{k-1}$ is an \textsc{lch}-nilspace isomorphism, for every $\gamma\in \Theta_i(F)$ we can treat $\eta_{k-1}(\gamma)$ as a translation on $\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}$. By Corollary \ref{cor:ext-of-lcfr-is-lcfr}, $\mathrm{Y}$ is also a Lie-fibered $k$-step nilspace. Now, we want to apply Proposition \ref{prop:cont-lift-of-trans} to prove the existence of a (continuous) translation in $\Theta_i(\mathrm{Y})$ which is a lift of $\eta_{k-1}(\gamma)$ (viewing the latter as a translation in $\Theta_i(\mathrm{Y}_{k-1})$). To be able to apply Proposition \ref{prop:cont-lift-of-trans}, we need the associated translation bundle to be a \emph{split} extension of $\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}$. But since $\mathrm{Y}_{k-1}$ is isomorphic to $F_{k-1}$, this translation bundle is thus a degree-$(k-i)$ extension of $F_{k-1}$, so by the above observation related to \eqref{diag:splt-1}, this extension does split. Hence we can indeed apply Proposition \ref{prop:cont-lift-of-trans} and thus we obtain a continuous translation $\beta\in \Theta_i(\mathrm{Y})$ that lifts $\eta_{k-1}(\gamma)$ through $\pi_{k-1}$. Now a remaining issue is that a priori $\widehat{q}(\beta)$ may not equal $\gamma$. However, the images of these translations through $\eta_{k-1}$ are both equal to $\eta_{k-1}(\gamma)$. Hence $\widehat{q}(\beta)-\gamma:F\rightarrow \mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}_k(F))$ is a well-defined continuous morphism. Let $\phi_k$ be the $k$-th structure morphism of $q$, thus $\phi_k$ is a surjective continuous group homomorphism $\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})\rightarrow \mathrm{Z}_k(F)$. These last two groups are Lie groups (by assumption for $\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})$, and by Corollary \ref{cor:trans&structFree} for $\mathrm{Z}_k(F)$). By Lemma \ref{lem:abcasesplit} we have that $\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})$ is a \emph{split} topological-group extension of $\mathrm{Z}_k(F)$, so there is a continuous homomorphism $s_k:\mathrm{Z}_k(F)\rightarrow  \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})$ such that $\phi_k\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} s_k$ is the identity map on $\mathrm{Z}_k(F)$. We can now define the map $\alpha:=\beta+s_k\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}(\gamma-\widehat{q}(\beta))\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} q:\mathrm{Y}\rightarrow\mathrm{Y}$. This is a continuous translation on $\mathrm{Y}$, and a simple calculation shows that  $\widehat{q}(\alpha)=\gamma$, as required.
nodes.section: 4 Lie-fibered extensions of free nilspaces are split extensions
nodes.statement_short: Lift via Proposition 2.32 using split translation bundles, then correct with a split of $\phi_k$.

nodes.name: Reduce to $i<k$
nodes.statement: Next we prove the key fact that $\widehat{q}$ is surjective from $\Theta_i(\mathrm{Y})$ onto $\Theta_i(F)$, for each $i\in [k]$. Note that for $i=k$ this is clear by virtue of $q$ being a fibration (its $k$-th structure homomorphism is then surjective), so we may assume that $i<k$. Let $\eta_{k-1}:\Theta_i(F)\rightarrow\Theta_i(F_{k-1})$ be the homomorphism from \eqref{eq:etaj}. By Corollary \ref{cor:ext-of-lcfr-is-lcfr}, $\mathrm{Y}$ is also a Lie-fibered $k$-step nilspace.

nodes.name: Lift the factor translation
nodes.statement: Now, we want to apply Proposition \ref{prop:cont-lift-of-trans} to prove the existence of a (continuous) translation in $\Theta_i(\mathrm{Y})$ which is a lift of $\eta_{k-1}(\gamma)$ (viewing the latter as a translation in $\Theta_i(\mathrm{Y}_{k-1})$). nodes.name: Correction term
nodes.statement: Now a remaining issue is that a priori $\widehat{q}(\beta)$ may not equal $\gamma$. However, the images of these translations through $\eta_{k-1}$ are both equal to $\eta_{k-1}(\gamma)$. Hence $\widehat{q}(\beta)-\gamma:F\rightarrow \mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}_k(F))$ is a well-defined continuous morphism. Let $\phi_k$ be the $k$-th structure morphism of $q$, thus $\phi_k$ is a surjective continuous group homomorphism $\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})\rightarrow \mathrm{Z}_k(F)$. nodes.name: Corrected translation

nodes.name: Need the Lie property
nodes.statement: Having proved that $\widehat{q}$ is a continuous surjective homomorphism, we are nearly ready to define the desired cross-section, by lifting from $\Theta_i(F)$ to $\Theta_i(\mathrm{Y})$ using the surjectivity. But to do so consistently on the continuous part of $F$, we shall use that $\Theta(\mathrm{Y})$ is a Lie group (which enables us to lift 1-parameter subgroups), so let us now establish this Lie property.
nodes.section: 4 Lie-fibered extensions of free nilspaces are split extensions

nodes.name: $\ker(\widehat{q})$ is Lie
nodes.statement:
First we claim that $\ker(\widehat{q})$ is a Lie group. For each $\alpha\in \ker(\widehat{q})=\ker(\widehat{q})\cap\Theta_1(\mathrm{Y})$  we have a well-defined map $\xi_\alpha:F\rightarrow \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})$, $x\mapsto y-\alpha(y)$ for any $y\in q^{-1}(x)$, and by \cite[Lemma 2.9.5]{Cand:Notes2} this map $\xi_\alpha$ is a nilspace morphism $F\rightarrow \mathcal{D}_{k-1}(\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y}))$. Let $\varphi:\ker(\widehat{q})\rightarrow \hom(F,\mathcal{D}_{k-1}(\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})))$ be the map $\alpha\mapsto \xi_\alpha$. We claim that $\varphi$ is a continuous group homomorphism (where, as usual, $\hom\big(F,\mathcal{D}_{k-1}(\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y}))\big)$ is equipped with pointwise addition and the compact-open topology). Let $\alpha,\beta\in \ker(\widehat{q})$. The value of  $\varphi(\alpha)+\varphi(\beta)$ at $x\in F$ can be calculated as follows. Let $y\in q^{-1}(x)$ and note that by the assumption $\alpha\in \ker(\widehat{q})$ we have $\alpha(y)\in q^{-1}(x)$. Hence $\varphi(\alpha)+\varphi(\beta)=(y-\alpha(y))+(\alpha(y)-\beta(\alpha(y)) = y-\beta(\alpha(y)) = \varphi(\beta\alpha)$. The calculation for the inverse follows similarly. Continuity of $\varphi$ follows by a similar argument as in previous proofs: let $K\subset F$ be compact and $(\alpha_n)$ be a convergent sequence in $\ker(\widehat{q})$ with limit $\alpha$. Suppose for a contradiction that there is $\epsilon >0$ such that $\sup_{x\in K} d(\varphi(\alpha_n)(x),\varphi(\alpha)(x))>\epsilon$ for all $n$. Then passing to a subsequence we may assume that there exists $x_n\rightarrow x\in K$ such that $d(\varphi(\alpha_n)(x_n),\varphi(\alpha)(x_n))>\epsilon$ for all $n$. By Lemma \ref{lem:conv-quot} we can further assume that there exists $y_n\in \mathrm{Y}$ with $y_n\rightarrow y$ as $n\rightarrow \infty$ such that $q(y_n)=x_n$ for all $n$. We thus obtain a contradiction, as then $\epsilon<d(y_n-\alpha_n(y_n),y_n,\alpha(y_n))\rightarrow 0$ as $n\rightarrow \infty$. 
Now to deduce that $\ker(\widehat{q})$ is a Lie group, note that the continuous homomorphism $\varphi:\ker(\widehat{q})\rightarrow \hom(F,\mathcal{D}_{k-1}(\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})))$ is easily checked to be an isomorphism, with its inverse $\varphi^{-1}:\hom(F,\mathcal{D}_{k-1}(\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})))\rightarrow \ker(\widehat{q})$ being $\varphi^{-1}(f)(x)=x+f(q(x))$. Indeed, for any $f\in \hom(F,\mathcal{D}_{k-1}(\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})))$ the map $x\mapsto x+f(q(x))$ is continuous (since $f$, $q$, and the $\mathrm{Z}_k$-action are all continuous), so this map is indeed a \emph{continuous} translation in $\ker(\widehat{q})$. Hence $\varphi$ is a bijective continuous homomorphism, hence an isomorphism (by the open mapping theorem). By Lemma \ref{lem:hom-Lie} the group $\hom(F,\mathcal{D}_{k-1}(\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})))$ is Lie, and our claim follows.

nodes.statement_short: Identify it with a morphism group via $\xi_\alpha$.

nodes.name: The map $\varphi:\alpha\mapsto\xi_\alpha$
nodes.statement: For each $\alpha\in \ker(\widehat{q})=\ker(\widehat{q})\cap\Theta_1(\mathrm{Y})$  we have a well-defined map $\xi_\alpha:F\rightarrow \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})$, $x\mapsto y-\alpha(y)$ for any $y\in q^{-1}(x)$, and by \cite[Lemma 2.9.5]{Cand:Notes2} this map $\xi_\alpha$ is a nilspace morphism $F\rightarrow \mathcal{D}_{k-1}(\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y}))$. nodes.name: $\varphi$ is a homomorphism
nodes.statement: We claim that $\varphi$ is a continuous group homomorphism (where, as usual, $\hom\big(F,\mathcal{D}_{k-1}(\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y}))\big)$ is equipped with pointwise addition and the compact-open topology). Hence $\varphi(\alpha)+\varphi(\beta)=(y-\alpha(y))+(\alpha(y)-\beta(\alpha(y)) = y-\beta(\alpha(y)) = \varphi(\beta\alpha)$. The calculation for the inverse follows similarly.

nodes.name: $\varphi$ is continuous
nodes.statement: Continuity of $\varphi$ follows by a similar argument as in previous proofs: let $K\subset F$ be compact and $(\alpha_n)$ be a convergent sequence in $\ker(\widehat{q})$ with limit $\alpha$. nodes.name: $\varphi$ is an isomorphism onto a Lie group
nodes.statement: Now to deduce that $\ker(\widehat{q})$ is a Lie group, note that the continuous homomorphism $\varphi:\ker(\widehat{q})\rightarrow \hom(F,\mathcal{D}_{k-1}(\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})))$ is easily checked to be an isomorphism, with its inverse $\varphi^{-1}:\hom(F,\mathcal{D}_{k-1}(\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})))\rightarrow \ker(\widehat{q})$ being $\varphi^{-1}(f)(x)=x+f(q(x))$. Hence $\varphi$ is a bijective continuous homomorphism, hence an isomorphism (by the open mapping theorem). By Lemma \ref{lem:hom-Lie} the group $\hom(F,\mathcal{D}_{k-1}(\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{Y})))$ is Lie, and our claim follows.

nodes.name: $\Theta_i(\mathrm{Y})$ is Lie
nodes.statement:
To see that $\Theta_i(\mathrm{Y})$ is a Lie group for each $i$, note first for $i=1$ that by the continuity and surjectivity of $\widehat{q}$ we have the short exact sequence 
$0\rightarrow \ker(\widehat{q})\rightarrow \Theta_1(\mathrm{Y})\rightarrow \Theta_1(F)\rightarrow 0$. 
We know that $\Theta_1(\mathrm{Y})$ is a Polish group (by Theorem \ref{thm:trans-group-polish}), that its closed normal subgroup $\ker(\widehat{q})$ is a Lie group, and that $\Theta_1(F)$ is also a Lie group (by Corollary \ref{cor:trans&structFree}). Therefore by \cite[Corollary A.2]{HK-non-conv} we have that $\Theta_1(\mathrm{Y})$ is also locally compact, and then it is a Lie group by \cite[Lemma A.3]{HK-non-conv}. The Lie property of the closed subgroups $\Theta_i(\mathrm{Y})$, $i>1$, now follows by Cartan's theorem.
nodes.section: 4 Lie-fibered extensions of free nilspaces are split extensions
nodes.statement_short: Extension of Lie by Lie (Host-Kra) and Cartan's theorem.

nodes.name: Construct the cross-section
nodes.statement:
We can now complete the proof by specifying the cross-section $F\rightarrow \mathrm{Y}$. Recall that $F=\prod_{i=1}^k \mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{Z}^{a_i}\times \mathbb{R}^{b_i})$. For $i\in[k]$ and $j\in[a_i]$ we denote by $\gamma_{i,j}\in \Theta_i(F)$ the translation that adds 1 to the $j$-th coordinate of elements of $F$ in the discrete part of $\mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{Z}^{a_i}\times \mathbb{R}^{b_i})$. Similarly, for every $i\in[k]$ and every $s\in [b_i]$ we denote by $\delta_{i,s}:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow \Theta_i(F)$ the one-parameter subgroup defined by mapping $t\in \mathbb{R}$ to the translation in $\Theta_i(F)$ that adds $t$ to the $s$-th coordinate of elements of $F$ in the continuous part of  $\mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{Z}^{a_i}\times \mathbb{R}^{b_i})$. Since $\widehat{q}$ is surjective, for every $i\in[k]$ and $j\in[a_i]$ there exists  $\alpha_{i,j}\in \Theta_i(\mathrm{Y})$ such that $\widehat{q}(\alpha_{i,j})= \gamma_{i,j}$. Similarly, for each $i\in[k]$ and $s\in [b_i]$, the surjectivity of $\widehat{q}$ makes it a quotient morphism in the sense of \cite[p.\ 169]{H&M-ProLie} (by the open mapping theorem), so by the one-parameter subgroup lifting lemma \cite[Lemma 4.19]{H&M-ProLie} there exists a homomorphism $\beta_{i,s}:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow \Theta_i(\mathrm{Y})$ such that for all $t\in \mathbb{R}$ we have $\widehat{q}(\beta_{i,s}(t))=\delta_{i,s}(t)$. Now, writing the elements of $F$ as tuples $((x_{i,j})_{j\in[a_i]},(x'_{i,\ell})_{\ell\in[b_i]})_{i\in [k]}$, and fixing any $y\in q^{-1}(0)$, let
\begin{eqnarray} \mathrm{s}:\hspace{2cm}  F & \rightarrow & \mathrm{Y} \nonumber\\
 ((x_{i,j}),(x'_{i,\ell})) & \mapsto & \Big[\prod_{i=1}^k\Big(\prod_{j=1}^{a_i} \alpha_{i,j}^{x_{i,j}}\Big)\Big(\prod_{\ell=1}^{b_i} \beta_{i,\ell}(x'_{i,\ell})\Big)\Big] (y).
\end{eqnarray}
This is clearly a continuous morphism, and by construction  it is a cross-section for $q$.
nodes.section: 4 Lie-fibered extensions of free nilspaces are split extensions
nodes.statement_short: Lift generators and one-parameter subgroups and act on a base point.

nodes.statement_short: Product of lifted translations applied to $y$.

nodes.statement: \mathrm{s}:\hspace{2cm} F & \rightarrow & \mathrm{Y} \nonumber\\ ((x_{i,j}),(x'_{i,\ell})) & \mapsto & \Big[\prod_{i=1}^k\Big(\prod_{j=1}^{a_i} \alpha_{i,j}^{x_{i,j}}\Big)\Big(\prod_{\ell=1}^{b_i} \beta_{i,\ell}(x'_{i,\ell})\Big)\Big] (y).

nodes.label: eq:maincrosssec

nodes.name: Lie-fibered nilspaces are fibration images of free nilspaces
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step Lie-fibered nilspace. Then there exists a $k$-step free nilspace $F$ and a continuous fibration $\varphi:F\rightarrow\mathrm{X}$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Lie-fibered nilspaces as fibration images of free nilspaces
assumptions: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step Lie-fibered nilspace.
conclusions: Then there exists a $k$-step free nilspace $F$ and a continuous fibration $\varphi:F\rightarrow\mathrm{X}$.
nodes.label: thm:lcfr-factor-of-free

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.4
nodes.statement: We argue by induction on the step $k$. For $k=1$, the nilspace $\mathrm{X}$ is topologically isomorphic to $\mathcal{D}_1(\mathrm{Z})$ where $\mathrm{Z}$ is an abelian Lie group. By known results (see e.g.\ \cite[Theorem 2.4]{Mosk}) we have $\mathrm{Z}\cong \mathbb{R}^m\times \mathbb{T}^n\times D$ for some discrete abelian group $D$. By \cite[Corollary 12]{Fu&Shak}, if $\mathrm{Z}$ is compactly generated then $D$ is finitely generated, hence of the form $\mathbb{Z}^r\times G$ for some finite abelian group $G$. The conclusion of the theorem then clearly holds in this case. Let $k>1$ and suppose by induction that $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ satisfies the desired conclusion, so there is a $(k-1)$-step free nilspace $F_{k-1}$, and a fibration $\varphi_{k-1}: F_{k-1}\rightarrow \mathrm{X}_{k-1}$. We then define the fiber-product $\mathrm{Y}:=F_{k-1}\times_{\mathrm{X}_{k-1}}\mathrm{X} = \{(f,x)\in F_{k-1}\times \mathrm{X}: \varphi_{k-1}(f)=\pi_{k-1}(x)\}$. Algebraically this is a $k$-step nilspace that is a degree-$k$ extension of $F$ by the structure group $\mathrm{Z}_k=\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})$ (see \cite[Proposition A.17]{CGSS-p-hom}). In particular (using for instance \cite[Proposition A.21]{CGSS-p-hom}) for each $i\in [k-1]$ the $i$-th nilspace factor $\pi_i(\mathrm{Y})$ is isomorphic to the $i$-th nilspace factor $F_i$ of $F_{k-1}$. Recall also that $\pi_{k-1,\mathrm{Y}}$ is just projection to the $F_{k-1}$ component. By Lemma \ref{lem:fib-prod-top-nil} we also know that $\mathrm{Y}$ is a Lie-fibered nilspace. It is straightforwardly seen that the component projections $p_1:\mathrm{Y}\rightarrow F_{k-1}$, $(f,x)\mapsto f$ and $p_2:\mathrm{Y}\rightarrow \mathrm{X}$, $(f,x)\mapsto x$ are continuous fibrations. By Theorem \ref{thm:splitext}, the nilspace $\mathrm{Y}$ is a split extension, so $\mathrm{Y}\cong F_{k-1}\times \mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}_k)$. Let $\mathrm{Z}_k'$ be a covering group of $\mathrm{Z}_k$ as per Theorem \ref{thm:lift-mor-cfr-ab-gr}. In particular $\mathrm{Z}_k'= \mathbb{Z}^b\times\mathbb{R}^c$ for some integers $b,c\ge 0$. Let $\phi$ be the natural continuous surjective homomorphism $\mathrm{Z}_k'\rightarrow \mathrm{Z}_k$. We now define the free nilspace $F:= F_{k-1}\times \mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}_k')$. The map $\pi_\phi:F\rightarrow\mathrm{Y}$, $(f,f_k)\rightarrow (f,\phi(f_k))$ is easily checked to be a fibration, and then the composition $p_2\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \pi_{\phi}$ is a fibration $\varphi:F\rightarrow \mathrm{X}$ as required.
nodes.section: 4.1 Lie-fibered nilspaces as fibration images of free nilspaces
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $k$: the fiber product of $F_{k-1}$ with $\mathrm{X}$ splits by Theorem 4.1; cover its top structure group by $\mathbb{Z}^b\times\mathbb{R}^c$.

nodes.name: Base case $k=1$
nodes.statement: We argue by induction on the step $k$. For $k=1$, the nilspace $\mathrm{X}$ is topologically isomorphic to $\mathcal{D}_1(\mathrm{Z})$ where $\mathrm{Z}$ is an abelian Lie group. By known results (see e.g.\ \cite[Theorem 2.4]{Mosk}) we have $\mathrm{Z}\cong \mathbb{R}^m\times \mathbb{T}^n\times D$ for some discrete abelian group $D$. By \cite[Corollary 12]{Fu&Shak}, if $\mathrm{Z}$ is compactly generated then $D$ is finitely generated, hence of the form $\mathbb{Z}^r\times G$ for some finite abelian group $G$. The conclusion of the theorem then clearly holds in this case.

nodes.statement_short: Structure of compactly generated abelian Lie groups.

nodes.name: Reduce to an abelian Lie group
nodes.statement: We argue by induction on the step $k$. For $k=1$, the nilspace $\mathrm{X}$ is topologically isomorphic to $\mathcal{D}_1(\mathrm{Z})$ where $\mathrm{Z}$ is an abelian Lie group.

nodes.name: Covering by $\mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{Z}^r$
nodes.statement: By known results (see e.g.\ \cite[Theorem 2.4]{Mosk}) we have $\mathrm{Z}\cong \mathbb{R}^m\times \mathbb{T}^n\times D$ for some discrete abelian group $D$. By \cite[Corollary 12]{Fu&Shak}, if $\mathrm{Z}$ is compactly generated then $D$ is finitely generated, hence of the form $\mathbb{Z}^r\times G$ for some finite abelian group $G$. nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement:
Let $k>1$ and suppose by induction that $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ satisfies the desired conclusion, so there is a $(k-1)$-step free nilspace $F_{k-1}$, and a fibration $\varphi_{k-1}: F_{k-1}\rightarrow \mathrm{X}_{k-1}$. We then define the fiber-product
$\mathrm{Y}:=F_{k-1}\times_{\mathrm{X}_{k-1}}\mathrm{X} = \{(f,x)\in F_{k-1}\times \mathrm{X}: \varphi_{k-1}(f)=\pi_{k-1}(x)\}$. Algebraically this is a $k$-step nilspace that is a degree-$k$ extension of $F$ by the structure group $\mathrm{Z}_k=\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})$ (see \cite[Proposition A.17]{CGSS-p-hom}). In particular (using for instance \cite[Proposition A.21]{CGSS-p-hom}) for each $i\in [k-1]$ the $i$-th nilspace factor $\pi_i(\mathrm{Y})$ is isomorphic to the $i$-th nilspace factor $F_i$ of $F_{k-1}$. Recall also that $\pi_{k-1,\mathrm{Y}}$ is just projection to the $F_{k-1}$ component. By Lemma \ref{lem:fib-prod-top-nil} we also know that $\mathrm{Y}$ is a Lie-fibered nilspace. It is straightforwardly seen that the component projections $p_1:\mathrm{Y}\rightarrow F_{k-1}$, $(f,x)\mapsto f$ and $p_2:\mathrm{Y}\rightarrow \mathrm{X}$, $(f,x)\mapsto x$ are continuous fibrations. By Theorem \ref{thm:splitext}, the nilspace $\mathrm{Y}$ is a  split extension, so $\mathrm{Y}\cong F_{k-1}\times \mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}_k)$. Let $\mathrm{Z}_k'$ be a covering group of $\mathrm{Z}_k$ as per Theorem \ref{thm:lift-mor-cfr-ab-gr}. In particular $\mathrm{Z}_k'= \mathbb{Z}^b\times\mathbb{R}^c$ for some integers $b,c\ge 0$.  Let $\phi$ be the natural continuous surjective homomorphism $\mathrm{Z}_k'\rightarrow \mathrm{Z}_k$.  We now define the free nilspace $F:= F_{k-1}\times \mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}_k')$. The map $\pi_\phi:F\rightarrow\mathrm{Y}$, $(f,f_k)\rightarrow (f,\phi(f_k))$ is easily checked to be a fibration, and then the composition $p_2\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \pi_{\phi}$ is a fibration $\varphi:F\rightarrow \mathrm{X}$ as required.
nodes.section: 4.1 Lie-fibered nilspaces as fibration images of free nilspaces
nodes.statement_short: Split fiber product and covering group give the free nilspace.

nodes.name: Morphism groups from Lie-fibered nilspaces are Lie
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step Lie-fibered nilspace, let $\mathrm{Z}$ be an abelian Lie group and let $t\in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$. Then the set $\hom(\mathrm{X},\mathcal{D}_t(\mathrm{Z}))$ equipped with pointwise addition and the compact-open topology is a Lie group.
nodes.section: 4.1 Lie-fibered nilspaces as fibration images of free nilspaces
assumptions: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step Lie-fibered nilspace, let $\mathrm{Z}$ be an abelian Lie group and let $t\in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$.
conclusions: Then the set $\hom(\mathrm{X},\mathcal{D}_t(\mathrm{Z}))$ equipped with pointwise addition and the compact-open topology is a Lie group.
nodes.label: cor:hom-is-lie

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 4.5
nodes.statement: By Theorem \ref{thm:lcfr-factor-of-free} there is a $k$-step free nilspace $F$ and a continuous fibration $\varphi:F\rightarrow\mathrm{X}$. By Lemma \ref{lem:hom-Lie} the group $\hom(F,\mathcal{D}_t(\mathrm{Z}))$ is Lie. Let \[ C:=\{g\in \hom(F,\mathcal{D}_t(\mathrm{Z})): \forall x,y\in F, \text{ if } \varphi(x)=\varphi(y) \text{ then } g(x)=g(y)\}. \] Note that this is a closed subset of $\hom(F,\mathcal{D}_t(\mathrm{Z}))$ (as can be seen straightforwardly, considering converging sequences in $C$). Hence, as a closed subgroup of $\hom(F,\mathcal{D}_t(\mathrm{Z}))$, in particular $C$ is a Lie group. By Proposition \ref{prop:hom-ns-z-polish}, $\hom(\mathrm{X},\mathcal{D}_t(\mathrm{Z}))$ is a Polish group. Consider the map $\iota:\hom(\mathrm{X},\mathcal{D}_t(\mathrm{Z}))\rightarrow C\subset \hom(F,\mathcal{D}_t(\mathrm{Z}))$, $\gamma\mapsto \gamma\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \varphi$. This map is readily seen to be continuous and injective. Moreover, given any $g\in C$, defining $\gamma^*\in \hom(\mathrm{X},\mathcal{D}_t(\mathrm{Z}))$ by the formula $\gamma^*(s):=g(x)$ for any $x\in \varphi^{-1}(s)$, using that $\varphi$ is open by Theorem \ref{thm:open-mapping-thm} we get that $\gamma^*$ is in fact continuous (using that $\varphi$ is 1-sequence covering as in \cite[\S 4]{Li}). Hence, $C$ is topologically isomorphic to $\hom(\mathrm{X},\mathcal{D}_t(\mathrm{Z}))$ and so the latter is a Lie group.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 4.6
nodes.statement: As in the previous proof, let $F$ be a $k$-step free nilspace such that there exists a fibration $\varphi:F\rightarrow\mathrm{X}$. Arguing similarly, we have that $\hom(\mathrm{X},\mathcal{D}_t(\mathrm{Z}))$ is topologically isomorphic to a subgroup of $\hom(F,\mathcal{D}_t(\mathrm{Z}))$. nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.7
nodes.statement: We argue by induction on $k$, with the case $k=0$ being trivial. For $k>0$, we use the notation in diagram \eqref{diag:lift-1}. Thus $\varphi := p_2\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \pi_\phi$. Let $\alpha\in \Theta_i(\mathrm{X})$, and let $\alpha_{k-1}\in\Theta_i(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$ be such that $\pi_{k-1}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\alpha = \alpha_{k-1}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \pi_{k-1}$. By induction there exists $\beta_{k-1}'\in\Theta_i(F_{k-1})$ such that $\varphi_{k-1}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \beta'_{k-1} = \alpha_{k-1}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \varphi_{k-1}$. Note that $(\beta_{k-1}',\alpha)$ is an element of $\Theta_i( F_{k-1}\times_{\mathrm{X}_{k-1}} \mathrm{X})$ acting coordinate-wise. By Theorem \ref{thm:lift-trans} we can lift this to some $\beta\in \Theta_i(F)$, and the result follows.
