nodes.section: 4.1 Lie-fibered nilspaces as fibration images of free nilspaces
assumptions: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step Lie-fibered nilspace.
conclusions: For each $i\in [k]$, $\Theta_i(\mathrm{X})$ is a Lie group.
also_stated_at: The last consequence of Theorem \ref{thm:lcfr-factor-of-free} in this subsection is that if $\mathrm{X}$ is a $k$-step, Lie-fibered nilspace then $\Theta(\mathrm{X})$ is a Lie group.
nodes.label: thm:LFnstransLie

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.8
nodes.statement: We know that $\Theta_i(\mathrm{X})$ is a closed subgroup of $\Theta(\mathrm{X})$ by Lemma \ref{lem:tran-i-closed-subset}, so by Cartan's theorem it suffices to prove that $\Theta(\mathrm{X})$ is a Lie group. Let $\varphi:F\rightarrow \mathrm{X}$ be the fibration in Theorem \ref{thm:lcfr-factor-of-free}, and let $C:=\{\alpha\in \Theta(F):\forall x,y\in \mathrm{X}, \text{ if } \varphi(x)=\varphi(y) \text{ then } \varphi(\alpha(x))=\varphi(\alpha(y))\}$. Note that $C$ is a closed subgroup of $\Theta(F)$. Hence $C$ is a Lie group (by Theorem \ref{thm:freetransLie} and Cartan's theorem). Let $\widehat{\varphi}:C\rightarrow \Theta(\mathrm{X})$ be the homomorphism induced by $\varphi$ as in \cite[Lemma 1.5]{CGSS}. To see that $\widehat{\varphi}$ is continuous, let $\alpha_n\rightarrow\alpha$ in $\Theta(F)$, that is, for any compact set $K\subset F$ we have $\sup_{s\in K}d_{F}(\alpha_n(s),\alpha(s))\rightarrow 0$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$. We need to check that for every compact set $K'\subset \mathrm{X}$ we have $\sup_{x\in K'}d_{\mathrm{X}}(\widehat{\varphi}(\alpha_n)(x),\widehat{\varphi}(\alpha)(x))\rightarrow 0$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$. By Corollary \ref{cor:cpct-sets-are-im-of-cpct-sets}, there exists a compact set $K\subset F$ such that $\varphi(K)=K'$. Suppose for a contradiction that $\sup_{x\in K'}d_{\mathrm{X}}(\widehat{\varphi}(\alpha_n)(x),\widehat{\varphi}(\alpha)(x))\not\rightarrow 0$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$. Then, passing to a subsequence if necessary, we can assume that for some $\epsilon>0$ we have $\sup_{x\in K'}d_{\mathrm{X}}(\widehat{\varphi}(\alpha_n)(x),\widehat{\varphi}(\alpha)(x))>\epsilon$ for all $n$. In particular, there exists a sequence $x_n\in K'$ such that $d_{\mathrm{X}}(\widehat{\varphi}(\alpha_n)(x_n),\widehat{\varphi}(\alpha)(x_n))>\epsilon$ for all $n$. For each $n$ let $s_n\in K$ be any element such that $\varphi(s_n)=x_n$. By compactness of $K'$ we can assume that $s_n\rightarrow s\in K$ as $n\rightarrow \infty$. This yields a contradiction, because $d_{\mathrm{X}}(\varphi(\alpha_n(s_n)),\varphi(\alpha(s_n)))=d_{\mathrm{X}}(\widehat{\varphi}(\alpha_n)(x_n),\widehat{\varphi}(\alpha)(x_n))>\epsilon$, whereas $\alpha_n(s_n))\rightarrow \alpha(s)$ and $\alpha(s_n))\rightarrow\alpha(s)$ as $n\rightarrow \infty$. Thus we have a continuous homomorphism $\widehat{\varphi}:C\rightarrow \Theta(\mathrm{X})$, which is also surjective by Lemma \ref{lem:lift-tran-to-free}. As $C$ and $\Theta(\mathrm{X})$ are Polish, the map $\widehat{\varphi}$ is also open (by the open mapping theorem) and $\Theta(\mathrm{X})$ is topologically isomorphic to $C/\ker(\widehat{\varphi})$. But $\ker(\widehat{\varphi})$ is Lie (being a closed subgroup of a Lie group). Hence $\Theta(\mathrm{X})$ is Lie by \cite[Theorem 2.6]{Mosk}.

nodes.statement: Suppose for a contradiction that $\sup_{x\in K'}d_{\mathrm{X}}(\widehat{\varphi}(\alpha_n)(x),\widehat{\varphi}(\alpha)(x))\not\rightarrow 0$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$. Then, passing to a subsequence if necessary, we can assume that for some $\epsilon>0$ we have  $\sup_{x\in K'}d_{\mathrm{X}}(\widehat{\varphi}(\alpha_n)(x),\widehat{\varphi}(\alpha)(x))>\epsilon$ for all $n$. In particular, there exists a sequence $x_n\in K'$ such that $d_{\mathrm{X}}(\widehat{\varphi}(\alpha_n)(x_n),\widehat{\varphi}(\alpha)(x_n))>\epsilon$ for all $n$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Lie-fibered nilspaces as fibration images of free nilspaces

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: For each $n$ let $s_n\in K$ be any element such that $\varphi(s_n)=x_n$. By compactness of $K'$ we can assume that $s_n\rightarrow s\in K$ as $n\rightarrow \infty$. This yields a contradiction, because $d_{\mathrm{X}}(\varphi(\alpha_n(s_n)),\varphi(\alpha(s_n)))=d_{\mathrm{X}}(\widehat{\varphi}(\alpha_n)(x_n),\widehat{\varphi}(\alpha)(x_n))>\epsilon$, whereas $\alpha_n(s_n))\rightarrow \alpha(s)$ and $\alpha(s_n))\rightarrow\alpha(s)$ as $n\rightarrow \infty$.

nodes.name: Quotient of a Lie group
nodes.statement: Thus we have a continuous homomorphism $\widehat{\varphi}:C\rightarrow \Theta(\mathrm{X})$, which is also surjective by Lemma \ref{lem:lift-tran-to-free}. As $C$ and $\Theta(\mathrm{X})$ are Polish, the map $\widehat{\varphi}$ is also open (by the open mapping theorem) and $\Theta(\mathrm{X})$ is topologically isomorphic to $C/\ker(\widehat{\varphi})$. But $\ker(\widehat{\varphi})$ is Lie (being a closed subgroup of a Lie group). Hence $\Theta(\mathrm{X})$ is Lie by \cite[Theorem  2.6]{Mosk}.

nodes.name: Quotient map $\pi_\sim$
nodes.statement: Given an equivalence relation $\sim$ on a set $X$, let us denote by $\pi_\sim$ the natural map sending $x\in X$ to the equivalence class $\{y\in X: y\sim x\}$.

nodes.name: Congruence on a nilspace
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a nilspace. A \emph{congruence} on $\mathrm{X}$ is an equivalence relation $\sim$ on $\mathrm{X}$ such that $\pi_{\sim}(\mathrm{X})$ equipped with the image cube sets $\pi_{\sim}^{\db{n}}\big(\! \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})\big)$, $n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$, is a nilspace.

nodes.name: Cube-surjective morphism
nodes.statement: Recall that a nilspace morphism $\varphi:\mathrm{X}\rightarrow\mathrm{Y}$ is \emph{cube-surjective} if $\varphi^{\db{n}}$ maps $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$ onto $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{Y})$ for every $n\geq 0$.

nodes.name: Congruences correspond to cube-surjective morphisms

Conversely, if $\mathrm{Y}$ is a nilspace and $\varphi:\mathrm{X}\rightarrow\mathrm{Y}$ is a cube-surjective morphism, then the relation $x\sim y \Leftrightarrow \varphi(x)=\varphi(y)$ is a congruence on $\mathrm{X}$.

nodes.name: $\sim$-vertical and $\sim$-consistent maps
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a set and let $\sim$ be an equivalence relation on $X$. We say that a map $g:X\rightarrow X$ is \emph{$\sim$-vertical} (or \emph{$\sim$-fiber-preserving over the identity map}) if we have $x\sim g(x)$ for every $x\in \mathrm{X}$. We say that $g$ is \emph{$\sim$-consistent} (or that $\sim$ is \emph{$g$-consistent}) if for every $x,y\in \mathrm{X}$ we have $x\sim y \Rightarrow g(x)\sim g(y)$.

nodes.name: Vertical maps are consistent
nodes.statement: If $g$ is $\sim$-vertical then it is $\sim$-consistent; the converse  fails (e.g.\ congruences on abelian groups).

nodes.name: Action finer than an equivalence relation
nodes.statement: Let us say that a group $H$ acting on $X$ is \emph{finer} (or that its action is finer) than an equivalence relation $\sim$ on $X$ if the orbit relation of $H$ (i.e.\ the equivalence relation whose classes are the orbits of $H$) is finer than $\sim$ (i.e.\ every orbit of $H$ is a subset of some equivalence class of $\sim$).

nodes.name: Groupable congruence
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a nilspace. A \emph{groupable congruence} on $\mathrm{X}$ is an equivalence relation $\sim$ on $\mathrm{X}$ that satisfies the following property: \begin{eqnarray} &\textrm{for every $i\geq 0$, for all $x,y\in \mathrm{X}$ such that $x\sim y$ and $\pi_i(x)=\pi_i(y)$,}&\nonumber \\ &\textrm{there exists $g\in \Theta(\mathrm{X})^{(\sim)}\cap \Theta_{i+1}(\mathrm{X})$ such that $g\,x=y$.}& \end{eqnarray}

nodes.name: Orbit relations of translation subgroups need not be congruences
nodes.statement: An orbit relation of a subgroup of $\Theta(\mathrm{X})$ is not necessarily a congruence. For instance, let $\mathrm{X}:=\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{Z}_2)\times \mathcal{D}_2(\mathbb{Z}_2)$ and $\alpha\in \Theta(\mathrm{X})$ be the map $(x,y)\mapsto (x,x+y)$ (this is a translation by Theorem \ref{thm:decrip-trans-group}). Then letting $G=\langle \alpha \rangle$, it turns out that the relation $\sim$ induced by $G$ (i.e., $x\sim y$ iff there exists $\beta\in G$ such that $\beta(x)=y$) is not a congruence. To prove this, consider the cubes $\mathrm{c}_1,\mathrm{c}_2\in \mathrm{C}^3(\mathrm{X})$ defined as $\mathrm{c}_1(v_1,v_2,v_3)=(1-v_3,0)$ and $\mathrm{c}_2(v_1,v_2,v_3)= (v_3,v_1v_2)$. Note that the cubes $\pi_\sim \circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}_1 $ and $\pi_\sim \circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}_2$ are adjacent (see \cite[Definition 3.1.6]{Cand:Notes1}) in the sense that $\pi_\sim \circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}_1(v_1,v_2,0)= \pi_\sim \circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}_2(v_1,v_2,1)$. Thus, by \cite[Lemma 3.1.7]{Cand:Notes1} we have that the function $\mathrm{c}_3\in (\pi_\sim(\mathrm{X}))^{\db{3}}$ defined as $\mathrm{c}_3(v_1,v_2,v_3):=\pi_\sim(0,0)$ for $(v_1,v_2,v_3)\not=(1,1,0)$ and $\mathrm{c}_3(1,1,0)=\pi_\sim(0,1)$ should be in $\mathrm{C}^3(\pi_\sim(\mathrm{X})):=\{\pi_\sim \circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}:\mathrm{c}\in \mathrm{C}^3(\mathrm{X})\}$. It can be checked that $\mathrm{c}_3$ does not equal $\pi_\sim\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}$ for any $\mathrm{c}\in \mathrm{C}^3(\mathrm{X})$. Moreover, it is easy to check that $\Theta(\mathrm{X})^{(\sim)} = G$. This shows that some condition on a subgroup $G$ of $\Theta(\mathrm{X})$ (or the congruence that it generates) is needed to ensure that $\sim_G$ is a congruence.

nodes.statement_short: For $\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{Z}_2)\times\mathcal{D}_2(\mathbb{Z}_2)$, the orbit relation of $\langle(x,y)\mapsto(x,x+y)\rangle$ is not a congruence.

nodes.name: Groupable congruences are congruences with fibration quotient maps
nodes.statement: Let $\sim$ be a groupable congruence on a nilspace $\mathrm{X}$. Then $\sim$ is a congruence and $\pi_{\sim}$ is a fibration from $\mathrm{X}$ to the nilspace $\pi_{\sim}(\mathrm{X})$.

assumptions: Let $\sim$ be a groupable congruence on a nilspace $\mathrm{X}$.
conclusions: Then $\sim$ is a congruence and $\pi_{\sim}$ is a fibration from $\mathrm{X}$ to the nilspace $\pi_{\sim}(\mathrm{X})$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.7
nodes.statement: To prove that $\pi_{\sim}$ is a congruence, we need to show that $\pi_{\sim}(\mathrm{X})$, equipped with the cube sets $\{\pi_{\sim}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c} : \mathrm{c}\in \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})\}$, $n\in\mathbb{N}$, is a nilspace. The ergodicity and composition axioms are clear. To prove the completion axiom, let $\mathrm{c}'$ be an $n$-corner on $\pi_{\sim}(\mathrm{X})$, and for each $i\in [n]$ let $F_i$ denote the lower face $\{v\in \db{n}:v\sbr{i}=0\}$. Then for each $i$, by definition there is a cube $\mathrm{c}_{F_i}\in \mathrm{C}^{n-1}(\mathrm{X})$ such that $\pi_{\sim}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}_{F_i} = \mathrm{c}'|_{F_i}$ (where by an abuse of notation we identify $F_i$ and $\db{n-1}$). We now argue by induction on the height $|v|$ of $v\in \db{n}$ to show that the cubes $\mathrm{c}_{F_i}$ can be modified, by applying $\sim$-vertical maps to their vertices, in order to obtain cubes $\mathrm{c}_i$ that agree at every $w\leq v$ (where by ``agree at $w$" we mean that for any $i,j\in [n]$ such that $w\in F_i\cap F_j$, we have $\mathrm{c}_i(w)=\mathrm{c}_j(w)$). For $v=0^n$, by \eqref{eq:groupable}, for each $i\in [2,n]$ there is $g_i\in \Theta(\mathrm{X})$ such that the $(n-1)$-cube $g_i^{F_i}\mathrm{c}_{F_i}:= v\mapsto g\cdot \mathrm{c}_{F_i}(v)$ satisfies $g^{F_i}\mathrm{c}_{F_i}(0^n)=\mathrm{c}_{F_1}(0^n)$. Thus, relabeling these cubes $g_i^{F_i}\mathrm{c}_{F_i}$ as our new $\mathrm{c}_i$ for $i\in [2,n]$, and relabeling $\mathrm{c}_{F_1}$ as $\mathrm{c}_1$, we now have that all $\mathrm{c}_i$ agree at $0^n$. Now let $v\in \db{n}$ with $|v|>0$ and suppose by induction that the $\mathrm{c}_i$ all agree at any $w < v$, i.e.\ at any $w\in \db{n}$ with $w\sbr{j}\leq v\sbr{j}$ for all $j\in [n]$ and $w\neq v$ (i.e.\ for any such $w$, for all $i\in [n]$ such that $w\in F_i$ the value $\mathrm{c}_i(w)$ is the same). Let $I_v\subset [n]$ be the set of all $i$ such that $v\in F_i$ (note that $I_v=\{i\in [n]: v\sbr{i}=0\}$). Let $i_0=\min I_v$. Then for every $i>i_0$ in $I_v$, since $\mathrm{c}_i(w)=\mathrm{c}_{i_0}(w)$ for every $w<v$, we have $\pi_{|v|-1}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}_i(v)=\pi_{|v|-1}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}_{i_0}(v)$, so by \eqref{eq:groupable} there exists a $\sim$-vertical $g_{i,v}\in \Theta_{|v|}(\mathrm{X})$ such that $g_{i,v} \mathrm{c}_i(v) = \mathrm{c}_{i_0}(v)$. Also, since $g_{i,v}\in \Theta_{|v|}(\mathrm{X})$, we can multiply every value $\mathrm{c}_i(u)$ at any vertex $u\in F_i$ with $v\leq u$, and still thus get an $(n-1)$-cube (because we are multiplying on an upper face of codimension $|v|$ by an element of $\Theta_{|v|}(\mathrm{X})$). Doing this for each $i\in I_v$ greater than $i_0$, we upgrade our set of cubes $\mathrm{c}_i$ to agree now also at $v$, with value $\mathrm{c}_{i_0}(v)$ at this vertex, and note that this upgrade preserves the agreement of the $\mathrm{c}_i$ at every other vertex $w$ with $|w|\leq |v|$ previously upgraded. This completes the inductive step. The above induction eventually ``glues" adequately all the initial cubes $\mathrm{c}_{F_i}$ to yield an $n$-corner $\mathrm{c}''$ on $\mathrm{X}$ with $\pi_{\sim}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}'' = \mathrm{c}'$. Then, by completing $\mathrm{c}''$ in $\mathrm{X}$ and projecting this completion to $\pi_\sim(\mathrm{X})$, the completion axiom follows. To complete the proof we establish that $\pi_\sim$ is a fibration. Let $\mathrm{c}'$ be an $n$-corner on $\mathrm{X}$ and let $\mathrm{c}\in \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}/\!\sim)$ be a completion of $\pi_\sim\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}'$. We know by definition of the cube structure on $\mathrm{X}/\!\sim$ that there is a cube $\mathrm{c}_0\in\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$ such that $\pi_\sim\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}_0=\mathrm{c}$. We now want to move progressively the values $\mathrm{c}_0(v)$, $v\neq 1^n$, by $\sim$-vertical transformations, to get a cube $\tilde {\mathrm{c}}\in \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$ completing $\mathrm{c}'$; then $\pi_\sim \circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \tilde {\mathrm{c}}$ will still be equal to $\mathrm{c}$, and this will complete the proof that $\pi_{\sim}$ is a fibration. To get $\tilde {\mathrm{c}}$ we can argue as we did above. First, since $\mathrm{c}_0(0^n)\sim \mathrm{c}'(0^n)$, there is a translation $g$ such that if we multiply every value of $\mathrm{c}_0$ by $g$ then we obtain a new cube $\mathrm{c}_1$ that is pointwise $\sim$equivalent to $\mathrm{c}_0$ and such that $\mathrm{c}_1(0^n)=\mathrm{c}'(0^n)$. Relabel $\mathrm{c}_1$ as $\mathrm{c}_0$. Now let $|v|>0$ and suppose by induction that $\mathrm{c}_0(w)=\mathrm{c}'(w)$ for all $w$ with $|w|<|v|$, thus in particular for all $w<v$. Then we deduce again that $\pi_{|v|-1}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}_0(v)=\pi_{|v|-1}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}'(v)$ and so by \eqref{eq:groupable} there is a $\sim$-vertical $g\in \Theta_{|v|}(\mathrm{X})$ such that $g\mathrm{c}_0(v)= \mathrm{c}'(v)$. Applying $g$ to $\mathrm{c}_0(u)$ for every $u\in\db{n}$ with $v\leq u$, we upgrade $\mathrm{c}_0$ to a new cube $\mathrm{c}_1$ that now also agrees with $\mathrm{c}'$ at $v$ (and still agrees at any other $w$ with $|w|\leq |v|$ previously upgraded). The result follows.

Let $I_v\subset [n]$ be the set of all $i$ such that $v\in F_i$ (note that $I_v=\{i\in [n]: v\sbr{i}=0\}$). Let $i_0=\min I_v$. Then for every $i>i_0$ in $I_v$, since $\mathrm{c}_i(w)=\mathrm{c}_{i_0}(w)$ for every $w<v$, we have $\pi_{|v|-1}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}_i(v)=\pi_{|v|-1}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}_{i_0}(v)$, so by \eqref{eq:groupable} there exists a $\sim$-vertical $g_{i,v}\in \Theta_{|v|}(\mathrm{X})$ such that $g_{i,v} \mathrm{c}_i(v) = \mathrm{c}_{i_0}(v)$. Also, since $g_{i,v}\in \Theta_{|v|}(\mathrm{X})$, we can multiply every value $\mathrm{c}_i(u)$ at any vertex $u\in F_i$ with $v\leq u$, and still thus get an $(n-1)$-cube (because we are multiplying on an upper face of codimension $|v|$ by an element of $\Theta_{|v|}(\mathrm{X})$). Doing this for each $i\in I_v$ greater than $i_0$, we upgrade our set of cubes $\mathrm{c}_i$ to agree now also at $v$, with value $\mathrm{c}_{i_0}(v)$ at this vertex, and note that this upgrade preserves the agreement of the $\mathrm{c}_i$ at every other vertex $w$ with $|w|\leq |v|$ previously upgraded. This completes the inductive step.
nodes.section: 5 Groupable congruences and fiber-transitive filtrations
nodes.statement_short: Correct at $v$ with a vertical translation in $\Theta_{|v|}$.

nodes.name: Completion axiom
nodes.statement: The above induction eventually ``glues" adequately all the initial cubes $\mathrm{c}_{F_i}$ to yield an $n$-corner $\mathrm{c}''$ on $\mathrm{X}$ with $\pi_{\sim}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}'' = \mathrm{c}'$. Then, by completing $\mathrm{c}''$ in $\mathrm{X}$ and projecting this completion to $\pi_\sim(\mathrm{X})$, the completion axiom follows.
nodes.section: 5 Groupable congruences and fiber-transitive filtrations

nodes.name: Fibration property
nodes.statement: To complete the proof we establish that $\pi_\sim$ is a fibration. Let $\mathrm{c}'$ be an $n$-corner on $\mathrm{X}$ and let $\mathrm{c}\in \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}/\!\sim)$ be a completion of $\pi_\sim\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}'$. We know by definition of the cube structure on $\mathrm{X}/\!\sim$ that there is a cube $\mathrm{c}_0\in\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$ such that $\pi_\sim\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}_0=\mathrm{c}$. We now want to move progressively the values $\mathrm{c}_0(v)$, $v\neq 1^n$, by $\sim$-vertical transformations, to get a cube $\tilde {\mathrm{c}}\in \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$ completing $\mathrm{c}'$; then $\pi_\sim \circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \tilde {\mathrm{c}}$ will still be equal to $\mathrm{c}$, and this will complete the proof that $\pi_{\sim}$ is a fibration.
nodes.section: 5 Groupable congruences and fiber-transitive filtrations
nodes.statement_short: Move values of a lifted cube by vertical maps.

nodes.name: Construct the completing cube
nodes.statement: To get $\tilde {\mathrm{c}}$ we can argue as we did above. First, since $\mathrm{c}_0(0^n)\sim \mathrm{c}'(0^n)$, there is a translation $g$ such that if we multiply every value of $\mathrm{c}_0$ by $g$ then we obtain a new cube $\mathrm{c}_1$ that is pointwise $\sim$equivalent to $\mathrm{c}_0$ and such that  $\mathrm{c}_1(0^n)=\mathrm{c}'(0^n)$. Relabel $\mathrm{c}_1$ as $\mathrm{c}_0$. Now let $|v|>0$ and suppose by induction that $\mathrm{c}_0(w)=\mathrm{c}'(w)$ for all $w$ with $|w|<|v|$, thus in particular for all $w<v$. Then we deduce again that $\pi_{|v|-1}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}_0(v)=\pi_{|v|-1}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}'(v)$ and so by \eqref{eq:groupable} there is a $\sim$-vertical $g\in \Theta_{|v|}(\mathrm{X})$ such that $g\mathrm{c}_0(v)= \mathrm{c}'(v)$. Applying $g$ to $\mathrm{c}_0(u)$ for every $u\in\db{n}$ with $v\leq u$, we upgrade $\mathrm{c}_0$ to a new cube $\mathrm{c}_1$ that now also agrees with $\mathrm{c}'$ at $v$ (and still agrees at any other $w$ with $|w|\leq |v|$ previously upgraded). The result follows.
nodes.section: 5 Groupable congruences and fiber-transitive filtrations

nodes.name: Correct at $0^n$
nodes.statement: To get $\tilde {\mathrm{c}}$ we can argue as we did above. First, since $\mathrm{c}_0(0^n)\sim \mathrm{c}'(0^n)$, there is a translation $g$ such that if we multiply every value of $\mathrm{c}_0$ by $g$ then we obtain a new cube $\mathrm{c}_1$ that is pointwise $\sim$equivalent to $\mathrm{c}_0$ and such that  $\mathrm{c}_1(0^n)=\mathrm{c}'(0^n)$. Relabel $\mathrm{c}_1$ as $\mathrm{c}_0$.
nodes.section: 5 Groupable congruences and fiber-transitive filtrations

nodes.name: Correct at higher vertices
nodes.statement: Now let $|v|>0$ and suppose by induction that $\mathrm{c}_0(w)=\mathrm{c}'(w)$ for all $w$ with $|w|<|v|$, thus in particular for all $w<v$. Then we deduce again that $\pi_{|v|-1}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}_0(v)=\pi_{|v|-1}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}'(v)$ and so by \eqref{eq:groupable} there is a $\sim$-vertical $g\in \Theta_{|v|}(\mathrm{X})$ such that $g\mathrm{c}_0(v)= \mathrm{c}'(v)$. Applying $g$ to $\mathrm{c}_0(u)$ for every $u\in\db{n}$ with $v\leq u$, we upgrade $\mathrm{c}_0$ to a new cube $\mathrm{c}_1$ that now also agrees with $\mathrm{c}'$ at $v$ (and still agrees at any other $w$ with $|w|\leq |v|$ previously upgraded). The result follows.
nodes.section: 5 Groupable congruences and fiber-transitive filtrations

nodes.name: Filtration $\Theta_\bullet(\mathrm{X})$ of the translation group
nodes.statement: Recall from \cite[Definition 3.2.27]{Cand:Notes1} that given a nilspace $\mathrm{X}$, the group of translations $\Theta(\mathrm{X})$ is naturally endowed with a filtration $\Theta_\bullet(\mathrm{X})=(\Theta_i(\mathrm{X}))_{i\ge 0}$, which is of degree $k$ if $\mathrm{X}$ is $k$-step.
nodes.section: 5 Groupable congruences and fiber-transitive filtrations

nodes.name: Filtered subgroup
nodes.statement: Let us also say that a filtered group $(G,G_\bullet)$ is a \emph{filtered subgroup} of another filtered group $(H,H_\bullet)$ if $G_i\leq H_i$ for all $i\geq 0$.
nodes.section: 5 Groupable congruences and fiber-transitive filtrations

nodes.name: Subfiltration
nodes.statement: We shall also say that $G_\bullet$ is a \emph{subfiltration} of $H_\bullet$.
nodes.section: 5 Groupable congruences and fiber-transitive filtrations

nodes.name: Convention on $G_\bullet$
nodes.statement: When we only write ``$G_\bullet$",  the associated filtered group $(G,G_\bullet)$ is always meant to be the one with $G$ being the first term of this filtration $G_\bullet$, i.e.\ $G=G_0=G_1$.
nodes.section: 5 Groupable congruences and fiber-transitive filtrations

nodes.name: Orbit relation $\sim_G$
nodes.statement: Finally, whenever we have an action of a group $G$ on a set $X$, we denote the orbit relation of $G$ on $X$ by $\sim_G$.
nodes.section: 5 Groupable congruences and fiber-transitive filtrations

nodes.name: Groupable congruences give filtrations with the fiber-transitivity property
nodes.section: 5 Groupable congruences and fiber-transitive filtrations

nodes.name: Fiber-transitivity property of a filtration
nodes.statement: \textrm{if $x,y\in \mathrm{X}$ satisfy $x \sim_G y$ and $\pi_i(x)=\pi_i(y)$ for some $i\geq 0$, then $x\sim_{G_{i+1}} y$.}
nodes.section: 5 Groupable congruences and fiber-transitive filtrations
nodes.label: eq:ft-fil

nodes.name: Fiber-transitive filtrations and groups
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a nilspace and let $G_\bullet$ be a subfiltration of $\Theta_\bullet(\mathrm{X})$. We say that $G_\bullet$ is a \emph{fiber-transitive filtration on} $\mathrm{X}$ (or that $(G,G_\bullet)$ is a \emph{fiber-transitive} filtered group on $\mathrm{X}$) if it satisfies property \eqref{eq:ft-fil}. A subgroup $\Gamma$ of $\Theta(\mathrm{X})$ will be said to be \emph{fiber-transitive on} $\mathrm{X}$ if the filtration $(\Gamma\cap \Theta_i(\mathrm{X}))_{i\geq 0}$ is fiber-transitive on $\mathrm{X}$.
nodes.section: 5 Groupable congruences and fiber-transitive filtrations
nodes.label: def:ft-fil

nodes.name: Fiber-transitive filtrations correspond to groupable congruences
nodes.statement: Clearly, if $G_\bullet$ is fiber-transitive on $\mathrm{X}$ then $\sim_G$ is a groupable congruence on $\mathrm{X}$ (where, as mentioned earlier, we always take $G=G_0$). Conversely, given a groupable congruence $\sim$ on $\mathrm{X}$, the group $G:=\Theta(\mathrm{X})^{(\sim)}$ equipped with the filtration induced by $\Theta_\bullet(\mathrm{X})$ is fiber-transitive.
nodes.section: 5 Groupable congruences and fiber-transitive filtrations
conclusions: Clearly, if $G_\bullet$ is fiber-transitive on $\mathrm{X}$ then $\sim_G$ is a groupable congruence on $\mathrm{X}$ (where, as mentioned earlier, we always take $G=G_0$).
Conversely, given a groupable congruence $\sim$ on $\mathrm{X}$, the group $G:=\Theta(\mathrm{X})^{(\sim)}$ equipped with the filtration induced by $\Theta_\bullet(\mathrm{X})$ is fiber-transitive.

nodes.name: A non-fiber-transitive group inducing a groupable congruence
nodes.statement: However, it may be the case that $\Gamma$ induces a groupable congruence $\sim_\Gamma$ but $\Gamma$ (with filtration $\Gamma_\bullet:=(\Gamma\cap \Theta_i(\mathrm{X}))_{i\in[k]}$) is not fiber-transitive. For example let $F:=\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{R})\times \mathcal{D}_3(\mathbb{R})$ and $\Gamma:=\{ \alpha_r \}_{r\in \mathbb{R}}$ where $\alpha_r(x,y)=(x,y+r(x^2+1))$. This group is not fiber-transitive. Indeed we have $(0,0)\sim_\Gamma (0,1)$ (using $\alpha_1$) and $\pi_2(0,0)=\pi_2(0,1)$, but the only translation of height 3 that could take $(0,0)$ to $(0,1)$, namely the translation $(x,y)\mapsto (x,y+1)$, is not in $\Gamma$. On the other hand, the relation $\sim_\Gamma$ is simply given by $(x,y)\sim_\Gamma (x',y')$ if and only if $x=x'$ (to see this, fix any $(x_0,y_0)\in F$ and note that $\alpha_r(x_0,y_0)=(x_0,y_0+r(x_0^2+1))$ and thus, as $r\in \mathbb{R}$ the class of $(x_0,y_0)$ is $(x_0,\mathbb{R})$). But this relation is a groupable congruence. Indeed, the group $\Gamma':=\{(x,y)\mapsto (x,y+r):r\in \mathbb{R}\}$ is fiber-transitive and $\sim_\Gamma = \sim_{\Gamma'}$.
nodes.section: 5 Groupable congruences and fiber-transitive filtrations
nodes.statement_short: On $\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{R})\times\mathcal{D}_3(\mathbb{R})$, translations $(x,y)\mapsto(x,y+r(x^2+1))$ are not fiber-transitive yet induce a groupable congruence.

nodes.name: Coset nilspaces as quotients by groupable congruences
nodes.statement: Important (and particularly simple) examples of nilspaces that arise as quotients by groupable congruences are \emph{coset nilspaces}. Recall (e.g.\ from \cite[Proposition 2.3.1]{Cand:Notes1}) that a $k$-step coset nilspace $\mathrm{X}$ is constructed starting with a filtered group $(G,G_\bullet)$ of degree $k$ and a subgroup $\Gamma\subset G$, and letting $\mathrm{X}$ be the set $G/\Gamma = \pi_\Gamma(G)$ of left cosets of $\Gamma$ in $G$ equipped with the cube sets $\pi_\Gamma^{\db{n}}(\mathrm{C}^n(G_\bullet))$, $n\geq 0$. Then the orbit relation $\sim_\Gamma$ (where elements of $\Gamma$ act by right-multiplication on $G$) is a groupable congruence on the \emph{group nilspace} $\widetilde{\mathrm{X}}$ associated with $(G,G_\bullet)$. Indeed if $g,g'\in G$ satisfy $g'= g\gamma$ for some $\gamma\in \Gamma$ and $g G_{i+1} = g' G_{i+1}$ (i.e.\ $\pi_i(g)=\pi_i(g')$ in the group nilspace), then clearly $\gamma\in G_{i+1}$, so the translation on $\widetilde{\mathrm{X}}$ consisting in right-multiplication by $\gamma$ is already in $\Theta_{i+1}(\widetilde{\mathrm{X}})$, and therefore \eqref{eq:groupable} holds. In Section \ref{sec:DC} we shall see a more general example of groupable congruences, involving \emph{double}-coset spaces.
nodes.section: 5 Groupable congruences and fiber-transitive filtrations
nodes.label: rem:cosnilex

nodes.name: Coset nilspace
nodes.statement: Recall (e.g.\ from  \cite[Proposition 2.3.1]{Cand:Notes1}) that a $k$-step coset nilspace $\mathrm{X}$ is constructed starting with a filtered group $(G,G_\bullet)$ of degree $k$ and a subgroup $\Gamma\subset G$, and letting $\mathrm{X}$ be the set $G/\Gamma = \pi_\Gamma(G)$ of left cosets of $\Gamma$ in $G$ equipped with the cube sets $\pi_\Gamma^{\db{n}}(\mathrm{C}^n(G_\bullet))$, $n\geq 0$.
nodes.section: 5 Groupable congruences and fiber-transitive filtrations

nodes.name: Cube-surjective morphisms need not be fibrations
nodes.statement: The following example shows that not all cube-surjective morphisms are fibrations, thus confirming the fact mentioned earlier, that not every congruence induces a fibration. Let $\mathrm{X}=\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{Z}_2)\times \mathcal{D}_2(\mathbb{Z}_2)$, and let $\mathbb{F}_2^\omega=\bigoplus_{n=1}^\infty \mathbb{F}_2$. It can be proved that there exists a map $f:\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{F}_2^\omega)\rightarrow \mathrm{X}$ that is arbitrarily well-balanced, meaning that for every $b>0$ there exists $N_b>0$ such that for any $n\ge N_b$ the map $f_n:\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{F}_2^n)\rightarrow \mathrm{X}$, $v\mapsto f(v\times 0^{\mathbb{N}\setminus [n]})$ is $b$-balanced in the sense of \cite[Definition 5.1]{CSinverse} (this is a non-trivial fact about nilspaces, but we omit the details in this paper as we will avoid such examples). Let $\sim$ be the equivalence induced by $f$, i.e.\ for $x,y\in \mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{F}_2^\omega)$ we have $x\sim y$ $\Leftrightarrow$ $f(x)=f(y)$. Then $\sim$ is a nilspace congruence and $\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{F}_2^\omega)/\!\!\sim$ is isomorphic to the nilspace $\mathrm{X}$. Indeed, first note that the map $f_\sim:\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{F}_2^\omega)/\!\!\sim\, \rightarrow \mathrm{X}$, $\pi_\sim(x) \mapsto f(x)$ is well-defined and injective. We claim that for all $n\ge 0$ the map $f^{\db{n}}:\mathrm{C}^n(\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{F}_2^\omega))\rightarrow \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$ is surjective (hence in particular $f_\sim$ is surjective, hence bijective). Let us denote by $i_n:\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{F}_2^n)\rightarrow \mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{F}_2^\omega)$ the usual inclusion. As $\mathrm{X}$ is finite, so is $\mathrm{C}^m(\mathrm{X})$ for any $m\ge 0$. The Haar probability measure $\mu_{\mathrm{C}^m(\mathrm{X})}$ is then the normalized counting measure. Fixing any $\mathrm{c}\in\mathrm{C}^m(\mathrm{X})$, we therefore have $\mu_{\mathrm{C}^m(\mathrm{X})}(\{\mathrm{c}\})\gg_{m} 1$. Then, by definition of balance, there is $N_{\mathrm{c}}>0$ such that for $n\geq N_{\mathrm{c}}$ the pushforward measure $\nu:=\mu_{\mathrm{C}^n(\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{F}_2^n))}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} (f\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} i_n)^{-1}$ is sufficiently close to $\mu_{\mathrm{C}^m(\mathrm{X})}$ in the vague topology to be able to conclude that $\nu(\{\mathrm{c}\})>0$, which implies the claimed surjectivity of $f^{\db{n}}$. Hence $f$ is a cube-surjective morphism. Now note that $f_\sim:\pi_\sim(x)\mapsto f(x)$ is a nilspace a morphism, and its inverse is a morphism as well, because for any $\mathrm{c}\in \mathrm{C}^m(\mathrm{X})$, by the cube-surjectivity we know that there exists $\mathrm{c}^*\in \mathrm{C}^m(\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{F}_2^\omega))$ such that $f\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}^*=\mathrm{c}$. But $f$ factors through $\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{F}_2^\omega)/\sim$, $f=f_\sim \circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \pi_\sim$ and as $f_\sim$ is a bijection we have that $f_\sim^{-1}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c} = \pi_\sim \circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}^*\in \mathrm{C}^m(\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{F}_2^\omega)/\sim)$. We have thus proved that $f$ is a cube-surjective morphism. However $f$ cannot be a fibration, because the image nilspace of a fibration is always of step at most as large as the step of its domain nilspace, and here $\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{F}_2^\omega)$ is 1-step whereas $\mathrm{X}$ is 2-step.
nodes.section: 5 Groupable congruences and fiber-transitive filtrations
nodes.statement_short: A well-balanced map $\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{F}_2^\omega)\to\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{Z}_2)\times\mathcal{D}_2(\mathbb{Z}_2)$ is cube-surjective but cannot be a fibration.
nodes.label: rem:congfibr

nodes.name: Equivalence classes of groupable congruences are coset nilspaces
nodes.statement: There are several additional pleasant features of groupable congruences, though we shall not directly use them in this paper. For example, it can be shown that if $\sim$ is a groupable congruence on a nilspace $\mathrm{X}$, then every equivalence class of $\sim$ is a coset nilspace. More precisely, since $\pi_{\sim}$ is a fibration, it already follows from basic results (e.g. \cite[Lemma 3.2]{CGSS}) that every fiber of $\pi_{\sim}$ is a sub-nilspace $\mathrm{Y}$ of $\mathrm{X}$, and it can then be shown using \eqref{eq:groupable} that $G:=\Theta(\mathrm{X})^{(\sim)}$ has $\mathrm{C}^n(G_\bullet)$ acting transitively on every cube set $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{Y})$ (where $G_\bullet$ is the filtration on $G$ induced by $\Theta_\bullet(\mathrm{X})$).
nodes.section: 5 Groupable congruences and fiber-transitive filtrations
nodes.label: rem:addgpcongprops

nodes.name: Fiber-transitive filtrations descend to factors
nodes.statement: If $H_\bullet$ is a fiber-transitive filtration on a $k$-step nilspace $\mathrm{X}$, then for every $j\ge 0$ the filtration $\eta_j(H_\bullet):=(\eta_j(H_i))_{i\ge 0}$ is fiber-transitive on $\mathrm{X}_j$. Equivalently, every groupable congruence $\sim$ on $\mathrm{X}$ induces a groupable congruence $\sim_{(j)}$ on $\mathrm{X}_j$ defined by $\pi_j(x)\sim_{(j)}\pi_j(y) \Leftrightarrow \exists x'\sim x$, $\pi_j(x')=\pi_j(y)$.
nodes.section: 5.1 Algebraic aspects of groupable congruences and fiber-transitive filtrations
assumptions: If $H_\bullet$ is a fiber-transitive filtration on a $k$-step nilspace $\mathrm{X}$
conclusions: then for every $j\ge 0$ the filtration $\eta_j(H_\bullet):=(\eta_j(H_i))_{i\ge 0}$ is fiber-transitive on $\mathrm{X}_j$

Equivalently, every groupable congruence $\sim$ on $\mathrm{X}$ induces a groupable congruence $\sim_{(j)}$ on $\mathrm{X}_j$ defined by $\pi_j(x)\sim_{(j)}\pi_j(y) \Leftrightarrow \exists x'\sim x$, $\pi_j(x')=\pi_j(y)$.
nodes.label: lem:group-cong-to-factors

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.12
nodes.statement: By induction it suffices to prove this for $j=k-1$. If $\pi_i(x)=\pi_i(y)$ and $g_{k-1}\pi_{k-1}(x)=\pi_{k-1}(y)$ we have $gx+z=y$ for some $z$ in the $k$-th structure group $\mathrm{Z}_k$ of $\mathrm{X}$. The translation $g$ commutes with the action of $\mathrm{Z}_k$ (by \cite[Lemma 3.2.37]{Cand:Notes1}). Hence, $g(x+z)=y$. Applying the hypothesis, we get that there exists $g'\in H_{i+1}$ such that $g'(x+z)=y$ and thus $g'_{k-1}\pi_{k-1}(x)=\pi_{k-1}(y)$ where $g'_{k-1}\in \eta_{k-1}(H_{i+1})$.

nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $j=k-1$; translations commute with the top structure group, so apply fiber-transitivity upstairs.

nodes.name: Reduce to $j=k-1$
nodes.statement: By induction it suffices to prove this for $j=k-1$. If $\pi_i(x)=\pi_i(y)$ and $g_{k-1}\pi_{k-1}(x)=\pi_{k-1}(y)$ we have $gx+z=y$ for some $z$ in the $k$-th structure group $\mathrm{Z}_k$ of $\mathrm{X}$.

nodes.statement_short: Lift the relation up to a structure-group element.

nodes.name: Commute with $\mathrm{Z}_k$
nodes.statement: The translation $g$ commutes with the action of $\mathrm{Z}_k$ (by \cite[Lemma 3.2.37]{Cand:Notes1}). Hence, $g(x+z)=y$.

nodes.statement_short: Translations commute with the top structure group.

nodes.name: Apply fiber-transitivity
nodes.statement: Applying the hypothesis,  we get that there exists $g'\in H_{i+1}$ such that $g'(x+z)=y$ and thus $g'_{k-1}\pi_{k-1}(x)=\pi_{k-1}(y)$ where $g'_{k-1}\in \eta_{k-1}(H_{i+1})$.
nodes.section: 5.1 Algebraic aspects of groupable congruences and fiber-transitive filtrations

nodes.name: Quotient map $\pi_H$
nodes.statement: Given a fiber-transitive filtration $H_\bullet$ on $\mathrm{X}$, we denote by $\pi_H$ the quotient map for the groupable congruence $\sim_H$ induced by $H=H_0$.
nodes.section: 5.1 Algebraic aspects of groupable congruences and fiber-transitive filtrations

nodes.name: Structure groups of quotients by fiber-transitive filtrations
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step nilspace, with structure groups $\mathrm{Z}_i$, $i\in [k]$, and let $H_\bullet$ be a fiber-transitive filtration on $\mathrm{X}$. Then for each $i\in[k]$ the $i$-th structure group of $\pi_H(\mathrm{X})$ is $\mathrm{Z}_i/\eta_i(H_i)$. Moreover, for every $n\geq 0$, for each $\mathrm{c}\in\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$ the group $\mathrm{C}^n(H_\bullet)$ acts transitively on $\{\mathrm{c}'\in\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}): \pi_H \circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}' = \pi_H \circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}\}$.
nodes.section: 5.1 Algebraic aspects of groupable congruences and fiber-transitive filtrations
assumptions: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step nilspace, with structure groups $\mathrm{Z}_i$, $i\in [k]$, and let $H_\bullet$ be a fiber-transitive filtration on $\mathrm{X}$.
conclusions: Then for each $i\in[k]$ the $i$-th structure group of $\pi_H(\mathrm{X})$ is $\mathrm{Z}_i/\eta_i(H_i)$.

Moreover, for every $n\geq 0$, for each $\mathrm{c}\in\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$ the group $\mathrm{C}^n(H_\bullet)$ acts transitively on $\{\mathrm{c}'\in\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}): \pi_H \circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}' = \pi_H \circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}\}$.
nodes.label: lem:cong-equi

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.13
nodes.statement: We already know by Lemma \ref{lem:gpequivcong} that $\pi_H$ is a fibration. For the claim about the structure groups, note that by induction on $k$ it suffices to prove it for $i=k$. Indeed, for $i<k$, by the previous lemma $\eta_{k-1}(H_\bullet)$ is fiber-transitive on $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$, so by induction the $i$-th structure group of $\pi_{\eta_{k-1}(H)}(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$ is $\mathrm{Z}_i(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})/\eta_i(\eta_{k-1}(H_i))=\mathrm{Z}_i(\mathrm{X})/\eta_i(H_i)$ as required. Now for $i=k$, the defining property \eqref{eq:ft-fil} clearly implies that when we quotient by $\sim_H$, in each $\pi_{k-1}$-fiber (which is an orbit of $\mathrm{Z}_k$) we quotient by the action of $H_k=\eta_k(H_k)$ (note that $\eta_k$ is the identity). Therefore the $k$-th structure group of $\mathrm{X}$ is $\mathrm{Z}_k / H_k$ as required. For the last claim in the lemma it suffices to prove that if two cubes $\mathrm{c},\mathrm{c}'\in \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$ satisfy $\pi_H\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}'=\pi_H\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}$ then there exists $\tilde{\mathrm{c}}\in \mathrm{C}^n(H_\bullet)$ such that $\mathrm{c}'=\tilde{\mathrm{c}}\cdot \mathrm{c}$ (i.e.\ for every $v\in \db{n}$, the value $\mathrm{c}'(v)$ is the image of $\mathrm{c}(v)$ under the action of $\tilde{\mathrm{c}}(v)$). This can again be proved by induction on $k$: the $\pi_{k-1}$-images of $\mathrm{c},\mathrm{c}'$ are pointwise equivalent under $\pi_{\eta_{jk-1}(H)}$, so by induction there is a cube $\mathrm{c}_0\in \mathrm{C}^n(H_\bullet/H_k)$ such that $\pi_{k-1}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}' = \mathrm{c}_0\cdot \pi_{k-1}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}$. Then any lift $\tilde {\mathrm{c}}_0$ of $\mathrm{c}_0$ in $ \mathrm{C}^n(H_\bullet)$ satisfies $\pi_{k-1}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}' = \pi_{k-1}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} (\tilde {\mathrm{c}}_0\cdot \mathrm{c})$, and then the difference $ \mathrm{c}' -\tilde {\mathrm{c}}_0\cdot \mathrm{c}$ is a cube $\mathrm{c}''\in \mathrm{C}^n(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}_k))$ which, by the assumption of point-wise $\pi_H$-equivalence of $\mathrm{c},\mathrm{c}'$, must in fact be in $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathcal{D}_k(H_k))$, by \eqref{eq:ft-fil}. Setting $\tilde {\mathrm{c}}=\mathrm{c}''\cdot\tilde{\mathrm{c}}_0$, the result follows.
nodes.section: 5.1 Algebraic aspects of groupable congruences and fiber-transitive filtrations
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $k$ via factors: the top fibers are quotiented by $H_k$; cube transitivity by lifting and correcting with a top-degree cube.

nodes.name: $\pi_H$ is a fibration
nodes.statement: We already know by Lemma \ref{lem:gpequivcong} that $\pi_H$ is a fibration.
nodes.section: 5.1 Algebraic aspects of groupable congruences and fiber-transitive filtrations

nodes.name: Structure groups
nodes.statement: For the claim about the structure groups, note that by induction on $k$ it suffices to prove it for $i=k$. Indeed, for $i<k$, by the previous lemma $\eta_{k-1}(H_\bullet)$ is fiber-transitive on $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$, so by induction the $i$-th structure group of $\pi_{\eta_{k-1}(H)}(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$ is $\mathrm{Z}_i(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})/\eta_i(\eta_{k-1}(H_i))=\mathrm{Z}_i(\mathrm{X})/\eta_i(H_i)$ as required. Now for $i=k$, the defining property \eqref{eq:ft-fil} clearly implies that when we quotient by $\sim_H$, in each $\pi_{k-1}$-fiber (which is an orbit of $\mathrm{Z}_k$) we quotient by the action of $H_k=\eta_k(H_k)$ (note that $\eta_k$ is the identity). Therefore the $k$-th structure group of $\mathrm{X}$ is $\mathrm{Z}_k / H_k$ as required.
nodes.section: 5.1 Algebraic aspects of groupable congruences and fiber-transitive filtrations
nodes.statement_short: Induction for $i<k$; for $i=k$ quotient each fiber by $H_k$.

nodes.name: Lower structure groups
nodes.statement: For the claim about the structure groups, note that by induction on $k$ it suffices to prove it for $i=k$. Indeed, for $i<k$, by the previous lemma $\eta_{k-1}(H_\bullet)$ is fiber-transitive on $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$, so by induction the $i$-th structure group of $\pi_{\eta_{k-1}(H)}(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$ is $\mathrm{Z}_i(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})/\eta_i(\eta_{k-1}(H_i))=\mathrm{Z}_i(\mathrm{X})/\eta_i(H_i)$ as required.

nodes.name: Top structure group
nodes.statement: Now for $i=k$, the defining property \eqref{eq:ft-fil} clearly implies that when we quotient by $\sim_H$, in each $\pi_{k-1}$-fiber (which is an orbit of $\mathrm{Z}_k$) we quotient by the action of $H_k=\eta_k(H_k)$ (note that $\eta_k$ is the identity). Therefore the $k$-th structure group of $\mathrm{X}$ is $\mathrm{Z}_k / H_k$ as required.
nodes.section: 5.1 Algebraic aspects of groupable congruences and fiber-transitive filtrations

nodes.name: Transitive action on lifts of cubes
nodes.statement: For the last claim in the lemma it suffices to prove that if two cubes $\mathrm{c},\mathrm{c}'\in \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$ satisfy $\pi_H\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}'=\pi_H\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}$ then there exists $\tilde{\mathrm{c}}\in \mathrm{C}^n(H_\bullet)$ such that $\mathrm{c}'=\tilde{\mathrm{c}}\cdot \mathrm{c}$ (i.e.\ for every $v\in \db{n}$, the value $\mathrm{c}'(v)$ is the image of $\mathrm{c}(v)$ under the action of $\tilde{\mathrm{c}}(v)$). This can again be proved by induction on $k$: the $\pi_{k-1}$-images of $\mathrm{c},\mathrm{c}'$ are pointwise equivalent under $\pi_{\eta_{jk-1}(H)}$, so by induction there is a cube $\mathrm{c}_0\in \mathrm{C}^n(H_\bullet/H_k)$ such that $\pi_{k-1}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}' = \mathrm{c}_0\cdot \pi_{k-1}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}$. Then any lift $\tilde {\mathrm{c}}_0$ of $\mathrm{c}_0$ in $ \mathrm{C}^n(H_\bullet)$ satisfies $\pi_{k-1}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}' = \pi_{k-1}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} (\tilde {\mathrm{c}}_0\cdot \mathrm{c})$, and then the difference $ \mathrm{c}' -\tilde {\mathrm{c}}_0\cdot \mathrm{c}$ is a cube $\mathrm{c}''\in \mathrm{C}^n(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}_k))$ which, by the assumption of point-wise $\pi_H$-equivalence of $\mathrm{c},\mathrm{c}'$, must in fact be in $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathcal{D}_k(H_k))$,  by \eqref{eq:ft-fil}. Setting $\tilde {\mathrm{c}}=\mathrm{c}''\cdot\tilde{\mathrm{c}}_0$, the result follows.
nodes.section: 5.1 Algebraic aspects of groupable congruences and fiber-transitive filtrations
nodes.statement_short: Induction and a correction cube in $\mathcal{D}_k(H_k)$.

nodes.name: Fiber-transitive closure
nodes.statement: Given a fiber-transitive filtration $H_\bullet$ on a nilspace $\mathrm{X}$, we denote by $\compl{H}$ the group $\Theta(\mathrm{X})^{(\sim_H)}$ of all translations that are $\sim_H$-vertical, and call this the \emph{fiber-transitive closure} of $H$. We shall always take the filtration $\compl{H}_\bullet$ on this group to be the filtration induced by $\Theta_\bullet(\mathrm{X})$ (i.e.\ with $i$-term ${\compl{H}}\cap \Theta_i(\mathrm{X})$ for $i\ge 0$). Note that $H\subset {\compl{H}}$ and that $\compl{H}_\bullet$ is fiber-transitive on $\mathrm{X}$.
nodes.section: 5.1 Algebraic aspects of groupable congruences and fiber-transitive filtrations
nodes.label: def:closure-of-fib-tran-group

nodes.name: Fiber-transitive closure larger than $H$
nodes.statement: The group $\compl{H}$ may be larger than $H$. For example, let $\mathrm{X}=\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{Z})\times \mathcal{D}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ and $H=\langle \alpha,\beta\rangle$ where $\alpha(x,y)=(x+2,y)$ and $\beta(x,y)=(x,y+2)$. The filtration $\langle \alpha,\beta\rangle= \langle \alpha,\beta\rangle \ge \langle \beta\rangle \ge \langle \mathrm{id}\rangle$ is a fiber-transitive filtration. Indeed, it is easy to check that $\pi_H(\mathrm{X})$ is isomorphic as a nilspace to $\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{Z}_2)\times \mathcal{D}_2(\mathbb{Z}_2)$. However, note that for example $\gamma(x,y):=(x,y+2x)$ is $\sim_H$-vertical but it is not in $H$, i.e.\ $\gamma\in \compl{H}\setminus H$.
nodes.section: 5.1 Algebraic aspects of groupable congruences and fiber-transitive filtrations
nodes.statement_short: For $H=\langle(x+2,y),(x,y+2)\rangle$ on $\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{Z})\times\mathcal{D}_2(\mathbb{Z})$, the map $(x,y+2x)$ lies in $\overline{H}\setminus H$.

nodes.name: Equivalent filtrations on a nilspace
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step nilspace. We say that two subfiltrations $H^0_\bullet, H^1_\bullet$ of $\Theta_\bullet(\mathrm{X})$ are \emph{equivalent} if for each $i\in\{0,1\}$, for every $\mathrm{c}\in \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$ and every $d\in \mathrm{C}^n(H^i_\bullet)$, there exists $d^*=d^*_{\mathrm{c},d}\in \mathrm{C}^n(H^{1-i}_\bullet)$ such that $d\cdot \mathrm{c} = d^*\cdot \mathrm{c}$.
nodes.section: 5.1 Algebraic aspects of groupable congruences and fiber-transitive filtrations

nodes.name: Fiber-transitivity is invariant under equivalence of filtrations
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step nilspace and let $H^1_\bullet, H^2_\bullet$ be equivalent subfiltrations on $\mathrm{X}$. Then $H^1_\bullet$ is fiber-transitive if and only if $H^2_\bullet$ is fiber-transitive.
nodes.section: 5.1 Algebraic aspects of groupable congruences and fiber-transitive filtrations
assumptions: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step nilspace and let $H^1_\bullet, H^2_\bullet$ be equivalent subfiltrations on $\mathrm{X}$.
conclusions: Then $H^1_\bullet$ is fiber-transitive if and only if $H^2_\bullet$ is fiber-transitive.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.16
nodes.statement: Without loss of generality assume that $H^2_\bullet$ is fiber-transitive. We have to prove that if $\alpha(x)=y$ for some $\alpha\in H^1$ and $\pi_i(x)=\pi_i(y)$ then there exists $\gamma\in H^1_{i+1}$ such that $\gamma(x)=y$. Let us see first that by induction on $k$ we can assume that $i=k-1$. Note that $\eta_{k-1}(H_\bullet^1)$ is equivalent to $\eta_{k-1}(H_\bullet^2)$, so by induction $\eta_{k-1}(H_\bullet^1)$ is fiber-transitive on $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$. Since $\eta_{k-1}(\alpha)(\pi_{k-1}(x)) = \pi_{k-1}(y)$ and $\pi_i(\pi_{k-1}(x))=\pi_i(\pi_{k-1}(y))$, it follows that there exists $\beta_{k-1}\in \eta_{k-1}(H^1_{i+1})$ such that $\beta_{k-1}(\pi_{k-1}(x)) = \pi_{k-1}(y)$. If $\beta_{k-1}=\eta_{k-1}(\beta)$ we have that for some $t\in \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})$, $\beta(x)=y+t=\alpha(x)+t$. Since $\mathrm{Z}_k$ is central in $\Theta(\mathrm{X})$, we have $x-t=\beta^{-1}\alpha(x)$. If now we define $y':=x-t$ note that $\pi_{k-1}(y')=\pi_{k-1}(x)$ and that $y'=\beta^{-1}\alpha(x)$ where $\beta^{-1}\alpha\in H^1$. Hence, if we knew that the result was true for $i=k-1$ we could conclude from here that there exists $h\in H^1_k$ such that $x+h=y'$. But this would imply that $x+h = \beta^{-1}\alpha(x)$ and so $\beta(x+h)=\alpha(x)=y$. As the function $\beta(\cdot+t)\in H^1_{i+1}$, this would complete the proof. Thus assume that $x,y\in\mathrm{X}$ satisfy $\alpha(x)=y$ for some $\alpha\in H^1$ and $\pi_{k-1}(x)=\pi_{k-1}(y)$. We need to prove that $y-x\in H^1_k$. By the equivalence of $H^1_\bullet$ and $H^2_\bullet$, there exists $\beta\in H^2$ such that $\beta(x)=y$. As $H^2_\bullet$ satisfies \eqref{eq:ft-fil} we have $z:=y-x\in H^2_k$. Let $\mathrm{c}_x\in\mathrm{C}^k(\mathrm{X})$ be the constant cube with value $x\in \mathrm{X}$ and let $d\in\mathrm{C}^k(H^2_\bullet)$ be the cube such that $d(v)=0$ for all $v\not=1^k$ and $d(1^k)=z$. By the assumed equivalence, there exists $s\in\mathrm{C}^k(H^1_\bullet)$ such that $s\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}_x = d+\mathrm{c}_x$. By \cite[Lemma 2.2.5]{Cand:Notes1} we can write $s$ as $g_{2^k-1}^{F_{2^k-1}}\cdots g_1^{F_1}g_0^{F_0}$ where $g_i\in H^1_{\mathrm{codim}(F_i)}$ (here the order is the inverse as the one in \cite[Lemma 2.2.5]{Cand:Notes1}, but as $\mathrm{C}^k(H^1_\bullet)$ is a group, we can just take the inverse). From this expression it is readily seen that $g_0$ stabilizes $x$. In fact, evaluating at $v=0^k$ we see that $s(\mathrm{c}_x(0^k))=g_0(x)=x=(d+\mathrm{c}_x)(0^k)$. Then we repeat evaluating at points $v\in \db{k}$ which are all $0$s and just one element equal to $1$. This shows that $g_1,\ldots,g_k$ also stabilizes $x$. We repeat this process for $v\in \db{k}$ with two non-zero elements, then three, etc.. In the last step of this process we have the fact that $g_{2^k-1}(x)=x+z$ (where $F_{2^k-1}=\{1^k\}$). Since $H^1$ is of degree $k$, we have that $g_{2^k-1}$ is just addition by an element of the last structure group, so it has to be the element $z$. Hence $z\in H^1_k$.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 5.17
nodes.statement: Note that it is enough to assume that $\mathrm{X}$ is $k$-step and prove that $H^0_k=H^1_k$. Let $z\in H^0_k$ and any $x\in \mathrm{X}$. Let $\mathrm{c}\in \mathrm{C}^k(\mathrm{X})$ be the constant map equal to $x$, and let $d\in \mathrm{C}^k(H^0_k)$ be the map whose values equal $\mathrm{id}$ in every point except in $v=1^k$, where it equals $z$ (recall that $\Theta_k(\mathrm{X})$ equals the $k$th structure group of $\mathrm{X}$). By definition of equivalence, there exists $d^*\in \mathrm{C}^k(H^1_\bullet)$ such that $d\cdot \mathrm{c}=d^*\cdot \mathrm{c}$. Thus $d^*(1^k)(x)=d(1^k)(x)=x+z$ and $\pi_{k-1}(x)=\pi_{k-1}(x+z)$. As $H^1_\bullet$ is fiber-transitive, there exists $z'\in H_k^1$ such that $x+z'=x+z$. Hence $z=z'$ and we have that $H_k^0\subset H_k^1$. The opposite inclusion is proved similarly and the result follows.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.18
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lem:ft-iff} we have that if either $H^1_\bullet$ or $H^2_\bullet$ is fiber-transitive so is the other. Thus both quotients $\pi_{H^1}(\mathrm{X})$ and $\pi_{H^2}(\mathrm{X})$ define nilspaces. We prove that the map $\pi_{H^1}(\mathrm{X}) \rightarrow \pi_{H^2}(\mathrm{X})$, $\pi_{H^1}(x)\mapsto \pi_{H^2}(x)$ is a well-defined nilspace isomorphism. To see that it is well-defined, note that if $\pi_{H^1}(x)=\pi_{H^1}(y)$ then there exists $\alpha\in H^1$ such that $\alpha(x)=y$. By hypothesis, there exists $\beta\in H^2$ such that $y=\alpha(x)=\beta(x)$. Hence $\pi_{H^2}(x)=\pi_{H^2}(y)$. This map is a morphism because given a cube $\pi_{H^1}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}$ for some $\mathrm{c}\in\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$ we have that its image is $\pi_{H^2}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}\in\mathrm{C}^n(\pi_{H^2}(\mathrm{X}))$. Taking inverses it follows that this map is a nilspace isomorphism.
nodes.section: 5.1 Algebraic aspects of groupable congruences and fiber-transitive filtrations
nodes.statement_short: The identity on representatives is a well-defined cube-preserving bijection between the quotients.

nodes.name: Both quotients are nilspaces
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lem:ft-iff} we have that if either $H^1_\bullet$ or $H^2_\bullet$ is fiber-transitive so is the other. Thus both quotients $\pi_{H^1}(\mathrm{X})$ and $\pi_{H^2}(\mathrm{X})$ define nilspaces.
nodes.section: 5.1 Algebraic aspects of groupable congruences and fiber-transitive filtrations

nodes.name: The natural map is well defined
nodes.statement: We prove that the map $\pi_{H^1}(\mathrm{X}) \rightarrow \pi_{H^2}(\mathrm{X})$, $\pi_{H^1}(x)\mapsto \pi_{H^2}(x)$ is a well-defined nilspace isomorphism. To see that it is well-defined, note that if $\pi_{H^1}(x)=\pi_{H^1}(y)$ then there exists $\alpha\in H^1$ such that $\alpha(x)=y$. By hypothesis, there exists $\beta\in H^2$ such that $y=\alpha(x)=\beta(x)$. Hence $\pi_{H^2}(x)=\pi_{H^2}(y)$.

nodes.name: Nilspace isomorphism
nodes.statement: This map is a morphism because given a cube $\pi_{H^1}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}$ for some $\mathrm{c}\in\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$ we have that its image is $\pi_{H^2}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}\in\mathrm{C}^n(\pi_{H^2}(\mathrm{X}))$. Taking inverses it follows that this map is a nilspace isomorphism.

nodes.statement_short: Cubes map to cubes, and symmetrically.

nodes.name: Quotient by the fiber-transitive closure
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step nilspace, let $H_\bullet$ be a fiber-transitive filtration on $\mathrm{X}$, and let ${\compl{H}}$ be the fiber-transitive closure of $H$. Then $\pi_H(\mathrm{X}) \cong \pi_{{\compl{H}}}(\mathrm{X})$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.19
nodes.statement: By Lemmas \ref{lem:ft-iff} and \ref{lem:eq-sub-implies-eq-nil} it suffices to see that the filtrations are equivalent. The only non-trivial part is to prove that if $\mathrm{c}\in\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$ and $d\in\mathrm{C}^n({\compl{H}})$ then there exists $d^*\in \mathrm{C}^n(H)$ such that $d\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c} = d^*\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}$. We prove this by induction on $k$, with the case $k=0$ being trivial. Note that $\pi_{k-1}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}\in \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$ and $\eta_{k-1}(d)\in\mathrm{C}^n(\eta_{k-1}({\compl{H}}))$. It is easy to see that $\eta_{k-1}({\compl{H}})\subset \compl{\eta_{k-1}(H)}$. Hence, by induction we have that there exists $d_{k-1}^*\in \mathrm{C}^n(\eta_{k-1}(H))$ such that $\eta_{k-1}(d) \circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} (\pi_{k-1}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}) = d_{k-1}^*\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \pi_{k-1}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}$. Therefore, if $d_{k-1}^* = \eta_{k-1}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} d^*$ for some $d^*\in \mathrm{C}^n(H)$ we get that $\pi_{k-1}(d\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c})=\pi_{k-1}(d^*\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c})$. But by definition of ${\compl{H}}$ we have that for every $v\in \db{n}$, $d(\mathrm{c}(v))\sim_H d^*(\mathrm{c}(v))$. Since $H_\bullet$ is fiber-transitive, this implies that $d(\mathrm{c}(v))-d^*(\mathrm{c}(v))\in H_k$ for all $v\in \db{n}$ and so $d\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}-d^*\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}\in \mathrm{C}^n(\mathcal{D}_k(H_k))$. Therefore $d\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c} = d^*\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}+(d\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}-d^*\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c})$ which is the composition of $\mathrm{c}$ with the cube $d^*\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} (\cdot)+(d\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}-d^*\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c})\in \mathrm{C}^n(H_\bullet)$.

nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step Lie-fibered nilspace. Then for every $i\in [k]$ the homomorphism $\eta_i:\Theta(\mathrm{X})\rightarrow \Theta(\mathrm{X}_i)$ from \eqref{eq:etaj} is continuous.\footnote{Here it is convenient to assume that $\mathrm{X}$ is Lie-fibered, so that by Theorem \ref{thm:trans-group-polish} we know that $\Theta(\mathrm{X})$ is a topological (Polish) group. nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.21
nodes.statement: It suffices to prove this for $i=k-1$, because for $i<k-1$ the homomorphism $\eta_i$ is the composition of $\eta_{k-1}$ on $\Theta(\mathrm{X})$ with the map $\eta_i$ on $\Theta(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$, and the latter map can be assumed to be continuous by induction on $k$. Let $(\alpha_n)_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ be a convergent sequence in $\Theta(\mathrm{X})$ with limit $\alpha$ (which is in $\Theta(\mathrm{X})$, since $\Theta(\mathrm{X})$ is closed by Lemma \ref{lem:tran-i-closed-subset}). Suppose for a contradiction that $\eta_{k-1}(\alpha_n)\not\rightarrow\eta_{k-1}(\alpha)$, so there exists a compact set $K\subset \mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ and $\epsilon_0>0$ such that $\sup_{\pi_{k-1}(x)\in K}d_{\mathrm{X}_{k-1}}(\eta_{k-1}(\alpha_n)(\pi_{k-1}(x)),\eta_{k-1}(\alpha)(\pi_{k-1}(x))) > \epsilon$ for infinitely many $n$. Passing to a subsequence if necessary, we can assume that this inequality holds for all $n$. In particular, for each $n$ there exists $\pi_{k-1}(x_n)\in K$ such that \begin{equation} d_{\mathrm{X}_{k-1}}(\eta_{k-1}(\alpha_n)(\pi_{k-1}(x_n)),\eta_{k-1}(\alpha)(\pi_{k-1}(x_n))) > \epsilon. \end{equation} By compactness of $K$, and passing to a subsequence if necessary, we can assume that there exists $x\in \mathrm{X}$ such that $\pi_{k-1}(x_n)\rightarrow \pi_{k-1}(x)$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$. By Lemma \ref{lem:conv-quot} there exists a sequence $z_n\in \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})$ such that $x_n+z_n\rightarrow x$ in $\mathrm{X}$. Since $\mathrm{X}$ is \textsc{lch}, the evaluation map is continuous (see e.g.\ \cite[Theorem 46.10]{Mu}), so $\alpha_n(x_n+z_n)\rightarrow \alpha(x)$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$. By continuity of $\pi_{k-1}$, it follows that $\eta_{k-1}(\alpha_n)(\pi_{k-1}(x_n)) = \eta_{k-1}(\alpha_n)(\pi_{k-1}(x_n+z_n)) = \pi_{k-1} (\alpha_n (x_n+z_n)) \rightarrow \pi_{k-1} (\alpha x) = \eta_{k-1}(\alpha)(\pi_{k-1}(x))$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$. Similarly, by continuity of $\alpha$ and $\pi_{k-1}$ we have $\eta_{k-1}(\alpha)(\pi_{k-1}(x_n))\rightarrow \eta_{k-1}(\alpha)(\pi_{k-1}(x))$. This implies that $d_{\mathrm{X}_{k-1}}(\eta_{k-1}(\alpha_n)(\pi_{k-1}(x_n)),\eta_{k-1}(\alpha)(\pi_{k-1}(x_n)))\rightarrow 0$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$, contradicting \eqref{eq:convfail}.

nodes.name: Closed groupable congruences and fiber-transitive filtrations
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step \textsc{lch} nilspace, and let $H_\bullet$ be a fiber-transitive filtration on $\mathrm{X}$. We say that $H_\bullet$ is \emph{closed} if for all $j\in [k]$ and $i\in[j]$, the subgroup $\eta_j(H_i)$ of $\Theta_i(\mathrm{X}_j)$ is a closed subset of $\Theta_i(\mathrm{X}_j)$. We say that a groupable congruence $\sim$ on $\mathrm{X}$ is \emph{closed} if the associated fiber-transitive filtration $\big(\Theta(\mathrm{X})^{(\sim)}\cap \Theta_i(\mathrm{X})\big)_{i\geq 0}$ is closed.

nodes.name: Topology on the top translation group
nodes.statement: Recall that for a $k$-step \textsc{lch} nilspace $\mathrm{X}$, its $k$-th structure group $\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})$ is homeomorphic to any fiber $\pi_{k-1}^{-1}(\pi_{k-1}(x_0))$ (for any $x_0\in \mathrm{X}$) equipped with the subspace topology as a subset of $\mathrm{X}$. Also, it is known (\cite[Lemma 3.2.37]{Cand:Notes1}) that $\Theta_k(\mathrm{X})$ is (algebraically) isomorphic as a group to $\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})$ where the isomorphism is given by $\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})\rightarrow \Theta_k(\mathrm{X})$, $z\mapsto g_z$ where $g_z(x):=x+z$. In particular, $\Theta_k(\mathrm{X})$ is naturally endowed with the subspace topology as a subset of $\Theta(\mathrm{X})$ (which is endowed with the compact-open topology by \S \ref{sec:trans-group}). We leave it as an exercise for the reader to check that the map $\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})\rightarrow \Theta_k(\mathrm{X})$ is a topological group isomorphism with respect to the aforementioned topologies.
nodes.section: 5.2 Topological aspects of groupable congruences and fiber-transitive filtrations

nodes.name: Discreteness of top groups implies closedness of the filtration
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step Lie-fibered nilspace and let $H_\bullet$ be a fiber-transitive filtration on $\mathrm{X}$ such that for every $i\in [k]$ the group $\eta_i(H_i)$ is a discrete subgroup of $\mathrm{Z}_i(\mathrm{X})$. Then for all $i,j\in [k]$ the group $\eta_j(H_i)$ is a discrete subgroup of $\Theta_i(\mathrm{X}_j)$, whence closed. In particular $H_\bullet$ is then a closed fiber-transitive filtration on $\mathrm{X}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.24
nodes.statement: We argue by induction on $k$, with the case $k=1$ being trivial. By induction it suffices to prove that $H_i$ is a discrete subgroup of $\Theta(\mathrm{X})$ for every $i\in[k]$. Note that the case $i=k$ holds by assumption ($\eta_k$ is the identity map). For every $i\in [k-1]$ consider the continuous map $\eta^{(i)}:\Theta_i(\mathrm{X})\rightarrow \Theta_i(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$, $\alpha\mapsto \eta_{k-1}(\alpha)$. This homomorphism factors through $\Theta_i(\mathrm{X})/\ker(\eta^{(i)})$. Thus, there is a continuous homomorphism $\overline{\eta^{(i)}}:\Theta_i(\mathrm{X})/\ker(\eta^{(i)})\rightarrow \Theta_i(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$ such that, letting $\pi:\Theta_i(\mathrm{X})\rightarrow\Theta_i(\mathrm{X})/\ker(\eta^{(i)})$ be the canonical quotient map, we have $\eta^{(i)} = \overline{\eta^{(i)}}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \pi$ (here, as usual $\Theta_i(\mathrm{X})/\ker(\eta^{(i)})$ is endowed with the quotient topology). Let $(\alpha_n)$ be a sequence in $H_i$ converging to some $\alpha\in \Theta_i(\mathrm{X})$. We want to prove that $\alpha_n=\alpha$ for $n$ large enough. By continuity the sequence $(\eta^{(i)}(\alpha_n))$ is convergent in $\Theta_i(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$. By induction, this sequence is constant for $n$ large enough, so by continuity of $\eta^{(i)}$ we have $\eta^{(i)}(\alpha_n) = \eta^{(i)}(\alpha)$ for $n\ge N$. In particular, for $n,m\ge N$ we have $\alpha_n^{-1}\alpha_m\in \ker(\eta^{(i)})$. By \cite[Lemma 2.9.5]{Cand:Notes2} we know that $\ker(\eta^{(i)})=\hom\big(\mathrm{X}_{k-1},\mathcal{D}_{k-i}(\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X}))\big)$. That is, the elements $f\in \ker(\eta^{(i)})$ are precisely the maps of the form $f(x)=x+\tilde{f}(\pi_{k-1}(x))$ for some $\tilde{f}\in \hom\big(\mathrm{X}_{k-1},\mathcal{D}_{k-i}(\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X}))\big)$. Moreover, for any $x\in \mathrm{X}$ we have $\alpha_n^{-1}\alpha_m(x)=x+z$ for some unique $z\in \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})$, and since $H_\bullet$ is fiber-transitive, by \eqref{eq:ft-fil} we must have $z\in H_k$. Hence $\alpha_n^{-1}\alpha_m \in \hom\big(\mathrm{X}_{k-1},\mathcal{D}_{k-i}(H_k)\big) $ for $n,m\ge N$. In particular, note that $(\alpha_n^{-1}\alpha_N)_n$ is a convergent sequence in $\hom(\mathrm{X}_{k-1},\mathcal{D}_{k-i}(H_k))$, the latter being discrete by Corollary \ref{cor:hom-is-discrete}, so $\alpha_n^{-1}\alpha_N = \alpha_M^{-1}\alpha_N$ for $n\ge \max(N,M)$. Thus $\alpha_n=\alpha_N (\alpha_M^{-1}\alpha_N)^{-1} $ for $n$ large enough.

nodes.statement: By \cite[Lemma 2.9.5]{Cand:Notes2} we know that $\ker(\eta^{(i)})=\hom\big(\mathrm{X}_{k-1},\mathcal{D}_{k-i}(\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X}))\big)$. That is, the elements $f\in \ker(\eta^{(i)})$ are precisely the maps of the form $f(x)=x+\tilde{f}(\pi_{k-1}(x))$ for some $\tilde{f}\in \hom\big(\mathrm{X}_{k-1},\mathcal{D}_{k-i}(\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X}))\big)$. Moreover, for any $x\in \mathrm{X}$ we have  $\alpha_n^{-1}\alpha_m(x)=x+z$ for some unique $z\in \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})$, and since $H_\bullet$ is fiber-transitive, by \eqref{eq:ft-fil} we must have $z\in H_k$. Hence $\alpha_n^{-1}\alpha_m \in \hom\big(\mathrm{X}_{k-1},\mathcal{D}_{k-i}(H_k)\big) $ for $n,m\ge N$. In particular, note that $(\alpha_n^{-1}\alpha_N)_n$ is a convergent sequence in $\hom(\mathrm{X}_{k-1},\mathcal{D}_{k-i}(H_k))$, the latter being discrete by Corollary \ref{cor:hom-is-discrete}, so $\alpha_n^{-1}\alpha_N = \alpha_M^{-1}\alpha_N$ for $n\ge \max(N,M)$. Thus $\alpha_n=\alpha_N (\alpha_M^{-1}\alpha_N)^{-1} $ for $n$ large enough.

nodes.name: Reparametrizing convergent sequences in a closed fiber-transitive filtration
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step Lie-fibered nilspace and let $H_\bullet$ be a closed fiber-transitive filtration on $\mathrm{X}$. Let $i\in [k]$, let $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence in $\mathrm{X}$ and $(h_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence in $H_i$ such that for some $x,x'\in\mathrm{X}$ we have $x_n\rightarrow x$ and $h_n(x_n)\rightarrow x'$ as $n\rightarrow \infty$. Then there is a sequence $(h_n')_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ in $H_i$ and $h\in H_i$ with $h_n'\rightarrow h$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$ and $h_n'(x_n)=h_n(x_n)$ for all $n$.

Let $i\in [k]$, let $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence in $\mathrm{X}$ and $(h_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence in $H_i$ such that for some $x,x'\in\mathrm{X}$ we have $x_n\rightarrow x$ and $h_n(x_n)\rightarrow x'$ as $n\rightarrow \infty$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.25
nodes.statement: We argue by induction on $k$, with the case $k=0$ being trivial. Let us denote by $\pi$ the map $\pi_{k-1}:\mathrm{X}\rightarrow\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$ and by $\eta$ the map $\eta_{k-1}:H_i\rightarrow \eta_{k-1}(H_i)$. By continuity of $\pi$ we have $\pi(x_n)\rightarrow \pi(x)$ and $\eta(h_n)(\pi(x_n))=\pi(h_nx_n)\rightarrow \pi(x')$. By Lemma \ref{lem:group-cong-to-factors} and the hypothesis we have that $\eta(H_\bullet)$ is a closed fiber-transitive filtration on $\mathrm{X}_{k-1}$, so by induction there exist $h_n', h'\in H_i$ such that $\eta(h_n)\rightarrow \eta(h')$ and $\eta(h_n)(\pi(x_n))=\eta(h_n')(\pi(x_n))$ for all $n$, that is, we have $\pi(h_n(x_n))=\pi(h_n'(x_n))$ for all $n$. Since $H_\bullet$ is fiber-transitive, for each $n$ there exists $\gamma_n\in H_k$ such that $h_n'(x_n)+\gamma_n=h_n(x_n)$. Since $\Theta(\mathrm{X})$ and $\Theta(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$ are Polish groups (by Theorem \ref{thm:trans-group-polish}) and by assumption $H_i$ and $\eta(H_i)$ are closed subgroups of these respectively, it follows from \cite[Proposition 1.2.1]{BeKe} that $H_i$ and $\eta(H_i)$ are Polish groups. By Lemma \ref{lem:conv-polish-group} applied to $\eta:H_i\rightarrow \eta(H_i)$ we can assume that $h_n'\rightarrow h'$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$. Then, since by assumption $h_n(x_n)\rightarrow x'$, and $h_n'(x_n)\rightarrow h'(x)$ (by \cite[Theorem 46.10]{Mu}), it follows that $\gamma_n=h_n(x_n)-h_n'(x_n)\rightarrow x'-h'(x)$. The element $\gamma:=x'-h'(x)$ is in $H_k$, by closure of $H_k$. Hence $(h_n'+\gamma_n)_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ is a sequence in $H_i$ satisfying the desired conclusion with $h=h'+\gamma\in H_i$.

nodes.name: Closed factor groups do not imply a closed filtration
nodes.statement: It may be tempting to try to strengthen Lemma \ref{lem:closedconseq} by weakening the \emph{discreteness} assumption to just a \emph{closure} assumption on the subgroups $\eta_i(H_i)$. However, the following example shows that even if $\eta_i(H_i)$ is closed for each $i\in [k]$, it may happen that $H$ is not closed, even assuming that $H_\bullet$ is fiber-transitive. Let $F:=\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{R})\times \mathcal{D}_2(\mathbb{R})$, and let $f:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be a linear map that is not continuous (it is known that such maps can be defined using a Hamel basis for $\mathbb{R}$ as a vector space over $\mathbb{Q}$). For each $\lambda\in \mathbb{R}$ let $\alpha_\lambda$ be the translation $(x,y)\mapsto (x+\lambda,y+f(\lambda))$ on $F$, and let $H$ denote the group $\{\alpha_\lambda:\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\}$. The filtration $H=H_0=H_1\ge \{\mathrm{id}\}$ is fiber-transitive on $F$. Indeed, if $\alpha_\lambda$ fixes the $\pi_1$ factor then clearly $\lambda=0$ so there is nothing to prove in this case. Also, $\eta_1(H_1)=\mathbb{R}$ and $\eta_2(H_2)=\{\mathrm{id}\}$, so both of these groups are closed. But clearly $H$ is not a closed subgroup of $\Theta(F)$, by discontinuity of $f$.

nodes.statement_short: A discontinuous additive $f$ gives translations $(x+\lambda,y+f(\lambda))$ with closed $\eta_i(H_i)$ but $H$ not closed.

nodes.name: Closed subgroups $H_i$ do not suffice
nodes.statement: Another seemingly natural condition on $H_\bullet$ that one could have tried to use instead of Definition \ref{def:oldclosed} is to require just that each subgroup $H_i$ is closed in $\Theta(\mathrm{X})$. However, this leaves open the possibility that at the level of some lower-step factor of $\mathrm{X}$ a failure of closure occurs, making the quotient of $\mathrm{X}$ by $\sim_H$ non-viable topologically because some of its factors are not Hausdorff. Indeed, for example, let $\mathrm{X}$ be the group nilspace $\mathbb{R}$ with the 2-step filtration $\mathbb{R}=\mathbb{R}\ge \mathbb{Z}\ge \{0\}$. Let $H\subset \Theta(\mathrm{X})$ be the subgroup of translations $\{ x\mapsto x+\sqrt{2}n: n\in\mathbb{Z}\}$. Clearly $H$ is a discrete subgroup, hence closed. Moreover, no translation in $H$ is in $\Theta_2(\mathrm{X})\cong\mathbb{Z}$, so $H_2=\{\mathrm{id}\}$ and is therefore also closed. However, the 1-step factor of $\mathrm{X}$ is $\mathrm{X}_1 = \mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$, and $\eta_1(H)$ acts on $\mathrm{X}_1$ as the group $\{\sqrt{2}n\!\!\mod 1:n\in \mathbb{Z}\}$, a non-closed subgroup of $\Theta_1(\mathrm{X}_1) = \mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$. Thus, the quotient $\mathrm{X}/H$ (which algebraically is a perfectly valid quotient nilspace) has 1-step factor the group $\sqrt{2}\mathbb{Z}\backslash (\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z})\cong \mathbb{R}/(\mathbb{Z}+\sqrt{2}\mathbb{Z})$, which is not Hausdorff.

nodes.name: Quotients by closed fiber-transitive filtrations are LCH spaces
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step Lie-fibered nilspace and let $H_\bullet$ be a closed fiber-transitive filtration on $\mathrm{X}$. Then $\pi_H(\mathrm{X})$ equipped with the quotient topology is an \textsc{lch} space.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.28
nodes.statement: Since $\pi_H(\mathrm{X})$ is the quotient of an \textsc{lch} space by the action of a group of homeomorphisms, the map $\pi_H$ is continuous and open. Hence $\pi_H(\mathrm{X})$ is second-countable, and it is also locally compact \cite[Ex.\ 29.3]{Mu}. To prove that $\pi_H(\mathrm{X})$ is Hausdorff it suffices to show that the set $C=\{(x,y)\in\mathrm{X}^2:x\sim_H y\}$ is closed in the product topology \cite[p.\ 79, Prop.\ 8]{BourbakiGT1}. Since $\mathrm{X}$ is \textsc{lch}, it is metrizable \cite[Ex.\ 32.3 and Thm.\ 34.1]{Mu}, so closure in $\mathrm{X}$ is equivalent to sequential closure. Let $((x_n,h_n x_n))_n$ be a sequence in $C$ convergent to $(x,y)\in \mathrm{X}^2$. By Lemma \ref{lem:re-param-conv-seq} there is a convergent sequence $(h_n')_n$ in $H$ with limit $h\in H$ such that $h_nx_n=h_n'x_n$ for all $n$. Since $x_n\rightarrow x$, the continuity of the action implies $h_n' x_n\rightarrow hx$, so $y=hx$ and $C$ is closed.

nodes.name: Closedness of sums of cubes with a closed subgroup
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{Z}$ be a Polish abelian group and let $H$ be a closed subgroup of $\mathrm{Z}$. Then for all integers $n\ge 0$ and $k\ge 1$ the following holds: for every convergent sequence $(g_m)_{m\in \mathbb{N}}$ in $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}))+H^{\db{n}}$ (in the product topology on $\mathrm{Z}^{\db{n}}$), there exist convergent sequences $(\mathrm{c}_m)_m$ in $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}))$ and $(d_m)_m$ in $H^{\db{n}}$ such that $\mathrm{c}_m+d_m=g_m$ for all $m$. In particular, the group $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}))+H^{\db{n}}$ is a closed subgroup of $\mathrm{Z}^{\db{n}}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.29
nodes.statement: Note first that the result is trivial if $k\le n$, as then $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}))=\mathrm{Z}^{\db{n}}$. Hence, we assume that $n\ge k+1$. We prove the result for $n=k+1$, as the idea of the proof is clearer in this case and other cases are similar. Let $(g_m)_m$ be a convergent sequence in $\mathrm{C}^{k+1}(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}))+H^{\db{k+1}}$. Let us define $\mathrm{c}_m'\in \mathrm{Cor}^{k+1}(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}))$ as $\mathrm{c}_m':=g_m|_{\db{k+1}\setminus\{1^{k+1}\}}$ (note that $\mathrm{c}_m'$ is indeed in $\mathrm{Cor}^{k+1}(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}))$ since any map $\db{k}\rightarrow \mathrm{Z}$ is in $\mathrm{C}^k(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}))$). As $(g_m)$ is convergent, so is $(\mathrm{c}_m')$. For every $m$ let $\mathrm{c}_m^*\in \mathrm{C}^{k+1}(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}))$ be the unique completion of $\mathrm{c}_m'$. By continuity of the completion function, the sequence $(\mathrm{c}_m^*)$ converges to a limit in $\mathrm{C}^{k+1}(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}))$ (equal to the completion of the limit of $(\mathrm{c}_m')$). Finally, let us define $f_m:=g_m-\mathrm{c}_m^*\in \mathrm{Z}^{\db{k+1}}$. As a pointwise difference of two convergent sequences, the sequence $(f_m)$ converges. We now prove that $f_m\in H^{\db{k+1}}$ for every $m$, which will complete the proof in this case (since $H$ is closed). First note that clearly $f_m\sbr{v}=0$ for all $v\not=1^{k+1}$ so it suffices to prove that $f_m(1^{k+1})\in H$. Recall from \cite[Definition 2.2.22]{Cand:Notes1} the Gray-code map $\sigma_{k+1}:\mathrm{Z}^{\db{k+1}}\rightarrow\mathrm{Z}$, $r\mapsto \sum_{v\in \db{k+1}} (-1)^{|v|}r\sbr{v}$, where $|v|:=v\sbr{1}+\cdots+v\sbr{k+1}$. We have $(-1)^{k+1}f_m(1^{k+1}) = \sigma_{k+1}(f_m) = \sigma_{k+1}(g_m-\mathrm{c}_m^*)=\sigma_{k+1}(g_m)-\sigma_{k+1}(\mathrm{c}_m^*)$, and this lies in $H$ because both of $\sigma_{k+1}(g_m), \sigma_{k+1}(\mathrm{c}_m^*)$ do (the former term does because by assumption $g_m\in \mathrm{C}^{k+1}(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}))+H^{\db{k+1}}$ and $\sigma_{k+1}(\mathrm{c})=0$ for any $\mathrm{c}\in \mathrm{C}^{k+1}(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}))$). This completes the proof in this case $n=k+1$. For $n\ge k+2$ let us sketch the argument. First, given any such converging sequence $(g_m)_m$ in $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}))+H^{\db{n}}$ we define\footnote{Recall that given $v\in \db{n}$ we define $|v|:=v\sbr{1}+\cdots+v\sbr{n}$.} $\mathrm{c}_m':=g_m|_{\{v\in \db{n}:|v|\le k\}}\in \mathrm{Z}^{\{v\in \db{n}:|v|\le k\}}$. Note that there exists a unique cube $\mathrm{c}_m^*\in \mathrm{C}^n(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}))$ such that $\mathrm{c}_m^*|_{\{v\in \db{n}:|v|\le k\}} = \mathrm{c}_m'$. We then let $f_m:=g_m-\mathrm{c}_m^*$. Applying the map $\sigma_{k+1}$ on faces of dimension $k+1$ on the function $f_m\in \mathrm{Z}^{\db{n}}$ it follows similarly as before that $f_m\in H^{\db{n}}$. The result follows.

nodes.name: Cube sets of quotients by closed fiber-transitive filtrations are closed
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step Lie-fibered nilspace and let $H_\bullet$ be a closed fiber-transitive filtration on $\mathrm{X}$. Then for every $n\ge 0$ the cube set $\mathrm{C}^n(\pi_H(\mathrm{X}))$ is a closed subset of $\pi_H(\mathrm{X})^{\db{n}}$.
nodes.section: 5.2 Topological aspects of groupable congruences and fiber-transitive filtrations
assumptions: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step Lie-fibered nilspace and let $H_\bullet$ be a closed fiber-transitive filtration on $\mathrm{X}$.
conclusions: Then for every $n\ge 0$ the cube set $\mathrm{C}^n(\pi_H(\mathrm{X}))$ is a closed subset of $\pi_H(\mathrm{X})^{\db{n}}$.
nodes.label: prop:closure-cubes-coset

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.30
nodes.statement: It suffices to prove that $\mathrm{C}^n(\pi_H(\mathrm{X}))$ is closed for $n\leq k+1$ (arguing as for \cite[Lemma 2.1.1]{Cand:Notes2}). The map $\pi_H^{\db{n}}:\mathrm{X}^{\db{n}}\rightarrow (\pi_H(\mathrm{X}))^{\db{n}}$ is open, so to prove the closure of $\mathrm{C}^n(\pi_H(\mathrm{X}))$ it suffices to prove that $(\pi_H^{\db{n}})^{-1}\mathrm{C}^n(\pi_H(\mathrm{X}))=H^{\db{n}} \cdot \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$ is closed. Note that it suffices to prove that if $(g_m)$ is a convergent sequence in $H^{\db{n}}\cdot \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$ then there exist convergent sequences $(d_m')$ in $H^{\db{n}}$ and $(\mathrm{c}_m')$ in $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$ such that $d_m'\cdot \mathrm{c}_m' = g_m$ for all $m$. We prove this by induction on $k$, the case $k=0$ being trivial. For $k>0$, we first prove that $H^{\db{n}} \cdot \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$ is (algebraically) an abelian bundle over $\eta_{k-1}(H)^{\db{n}} \cdot \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$ with structure group $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}_k))+H_k^{\db{n}}$, where $\mathrm{Z}_k=\mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})$. For $n\le k$ note that the claimed structure group $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}_k))+H_k^{\db{n}}$ is simply $\mathrm{Z}_k^{\db{n}}$. But if $d\cdot \mathrm{c}, d'\cdot \mathrm{c}'\in H^{\db{n}} \cdot\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$ have the same image under $\pi_{k-1}^{\db{n}}$ then they indeed differ in an element $f\in \mathrm{Z}_k^{\db{n}}$ by definition, so our claim holds. For $n= k+1$, suppose again that $d\cdot \mathrm{c}, d'\cdot \mathrm{c}'\in H^{\db{n}}\cdot \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$ are equal modulo $\pi_{k-1}^{\db{n}}$. For each $v\in \db{k+1}\setminus\{1^{k+1}\}$, let $f(v)\in \mathrm{Z}_k$ be the unique element such that $(d\cdot \mathrm{c})(v)+f(v)=(d'\cdot\mathrm{c}')(v)$. By uniqueness of $(k+1)$-corner completion on $\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}_k)$, the map $f$ extends uniquely to an element $f\in \mathrm{C}^n(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}_k))$. Since the action of $\mathrm{Z}_k$ commutes with translations, we can assume (renaming $\mathrm{c}+f$ as $\mathrm{c}$) that $d\cdot \mathrm{c}(v)=d' \cdot \mathrm{c}'(v)$ for every $v\neq 1^{k+1}$, and $\pi_{k-1}(d\cdot \mathrm{c}(1^{k+1}))=\pi_{k-1}(d' \cdot \mathrm{c}'(1^{k+1}))$. Hence there is $z\in \mathrm{Z}_k$ such that $(d\cdot \mathrm{c})(1^{k+1})=(d'\cdot \mathrm{c}')(1^{k+1})+z$. We claim that $z\in H_k$. Let us denote by $\mathrm{c}_z\in \mathrm{Z}_k^{\db{k+1}}$ the map that equals $z$ at $1^{k+1}$ and 0 elsewhere. Then $\mathrm{c}+\mathrm{c}_z=d^{-1}d'\cdot \mathrm{c}'$, and we want to deduce that $z\in H_k$. Note that $(d^{-1}d'\cdot \mathrm{c}')|_{\db{k+1}\setminus\{1^{k+1}\}} = \mathrm{c}|_{\db{k+1}\setminus\{1^{k+1}\}}$, so this is in $\mathrm{Cor}^{k+1}(\mathrm{X})$. By the last sentence of Lemma \ref{lem:cong-equi}, there exists $d^*\in \mathrm{C}^{k+1}(H_\bullet)$ such that $(d^{-1}d'\cdot \mathrm{c}')|_{\db{k+1}\setminus\{1^{k+1}\}} = (d^*\cdot \mathrm{c}')|_{\db{k+1}\setminus\{1^{k+1}\}}$. Let $\gamma:=(d^{-1}d'(d^*)^{-1})(1^{k+1})\in H$, and let $d_\gamma\in H^{\db{k+1}}$ be the map with $d_\gamma(1^{k+1})=\gamma$ and $d_\gamma(v)=\mathrm{id}_H$ otherwise. Then $d^{-1}d'\cdot \mathrm{c}' = d_\gamma d^*\cdot \mathrm{c}'$. Hence $\mathrm{c}+\mathrm{c}_z = d_\gamma d^*\cdot \mathrm{c}'$. But $\mathrm{c}$ and $d^*\cdot \mathrm{c}'$ are elements of $\mathrm{C}^{k+1}(\mathrm{X})$ that are equal when restricted to $\db{k+1}\setminus\{1^{k+1}\}$. By uniqueness of completion we then have $\mathrm{c}(1^{k+1})+z= \gamma(d^*\cdot\mathrm{c}'(1^{k+1})) = \gamma(\mathrm{c}(1^{k+1}))$. By property \eqref{eq:ft-fil}, this implies that $z\in H_k$. Now let $(d_m\cdot \mathrm{c}_m)$ be a convergent sequence in $H^{\db{n}}\cdot \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$. This implies that the sequence $(\eta_{k-1}(d_m)\cdot \pi_{k-1}(\mathrm{c}_m))$ converges in $\eta_{k-1}(H)^{\db{n}}\cdot \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$. By induction, there exist $d_m'\in H^{\db{n}}$ and $\mathrm{c}_m'\in \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$ such that the sequence $\eta_{k-1}(d_m')$ converges in $\eta_{k-1}(H)^{\db{n}}$, $(\pi_{k-1}(\mathrm{c}_m'))$ converges in $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X}_{k-1})$, and $\eta_{k-1}(d_m')\pi_{k-1}(\mathrm{c}_m')=\eta_{k-1}(d_m)\cdot \pi_{k-1}(\mathrm{c}_m)$. By Lemma \ref{lem:conv-polish-group} we can assume that $d_m'$ converges in $H^{\db{n}}$ and by Lemma \ref{lem:open-projection-of-cubes} we can assume that $\mathrm{c}_m'$ converges in $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$ as well. Since $d_m'\cdot \mathrm{c}_m'$ is an element of $H^{\db{n}}\cdot \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$ equal to $d_m\cdot \mathrm{c}_m$ modulo $\pi_{k-1}$, by the previous paragraph we have $d_m'\cdot \mathrm{c}_m'-d_m\cdot \mathrm{c}_m\in \mathrm{C}^n(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}_k))+H_k^{\db{n}}$. As both $(d_m'\cdot \mathrm{c}_m')$ and $(d_m\cdot \mathrm{c}_m)$ converge, so does $(d_m'\cdot \mathrm{c}_m'-d_m\cdot \mathrm{c}_m)$. Moreover, by Lemma \ref{lem:closure-sum-of-cu-and-h} there exist convergent sequences $(f_m)$ in $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}_k))$ and $(\gamma_m)$ in $H_k^{\db{n}}$ such that $d_m'\cdot \mathrm{c}_m'-d_m\cdot \mathrm{c}_m=f_m+\gamma_m$. In particular $d_m\cdot \mathrm{c}_m = d_m'\cdot\mathrm{c}_m'-f_m-d_m = (d_m'-\gamma_m)\cdot (\mathrm{c}_m'-f_m)$. But $(\mathrm{c}_m'-f_m)$ is a convergent sequence in the closed set $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$, with limit $\mathrm{c}$ say, and so is $(d_m'-\gamma_m)$ in $H^{\db{n}}$, with limit $d$, so $d_m\cdot \mathrm{c}_m$ converges to $d\cdot \mathrm{c}\in H^{\db{n}}\cdot \mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$, which proves the claimed closure.

nodes.name: Bundle structure over the factor
