nodes.name: Left and right groupable congruences coincide
nodes.statement: Thus, the left-action of $K$ on $G/{\Gamma}$ induces a groupable congruence if and only if the right-action of ${\Gamma}$ on $K\backslash G$ yields a groupable congruence.
nodes.section: 7 Double-coset nilspaces
conclusions: Thus, the left-action of $K$ on $G/{\Gamma}$ induces a groupable congruence if and only if the right-action of ${\Gamma}$ on $K\backslash G$ yields a groupable congruence.

nodes.name: Groupable nilpairs give double-coset nilspaces with fibration quotient maps
nodes.statement: Thus, by Lemmas \ref{lem:nil-pair-good-fil} and \ref{lem:cong-equi}, if $(K,\Gamma)$ is a groupable nilpair in $(G,G_\bullet)$ then $K\backslash G/{\Gamma}$ is indeed a double-coset nilspace as per Definition \ref{def:dcn}, and the quotient map $G\rightarrow K\backslash G/\Gamma$ is a fibration (to see this, note that we can write it as a composition $G\rightarrow G/{\Gamma}\rightarrow K\backslash G/{\Gamma}$ where both maps are fibrations by Lemma \ref{lem:cong-equi}).
nodes.section: 7 Double-coset nilspaces
conclusions: Thus, by Lemmas \ref{lem:nil-pair-good-fil} and \ref{lem:cong-equi}, if $(K,\Gamma)$ is a groupable nilpair in $(G,G_\bullet)$ then $K\backslash G/{\Gamma}$ is indeed a double-coset nilspace as per Definition \ref{def:dcn}, and the quotient map $G\rightarrow K\backslash G/\Gamma$ is a fibration (to see this, note that we can write it as a composition $G\rightarrow G/{\Gamma}\rightarrow K\backslash G/{\Gamma}$ where both maps are fibrations by Lemma \ref{lem:cong-equi}).

nodes.name: Right-closed groupable nilpair
nodes.statement: Let $(G,G_\bullet)$ be a degree-$k$ filtered Lie group such that for every $i\in [k]$ the subgroup $G_i$ is closed, and let $(K,\Gamma)$ be a groupable nilpair in $G$. We say that $(K,\Gamma)$ is a \emph{right-closed} nilpair if for all $i\in[k]$, $KG_{i+1}/G_{i+1}$ is a closed subgroup of $G/G_{i+1}$ and the filtration $(\Gamma_j:=\Gamma\cap G_j)_{j\in[k]}$ is closed as a fiber-transitive filtration (acting by right multiplication) on the coset nilspace $K \backslash G$.
nodes.section: 7.1 Topological aspects of double-coset nilspaces
nodes.label: def:rcc

nodes.name: Right-closed nilpairs give Lie-fibered double-coset nilspaces
nodes.statement: Let $(G,G_\bullet)$ be a degree-$k$ filtered Lie group such that for every $i\in [k]$ the subgroup $G_i$ is closed, and let $(K,{\Gamma})$ be a groupable right-closed nilpair. Then $K\backslash G/{\Gamma}$ is a $k$-step Lie-fibered nilspace, and for each $i\in [k]$ the $i$-th structure group of $K\backslash G/ \Gamma$ is $G_i/(K_i \Gamma_i G_{i+1})$.
nodes.section: 7.1 Topological aspects of double-coset nilspaces
assumptions: Let $(G,G_\bullet)$ be a degree-$k$ filtered Lie group such that for every $i\in [k]$ the subgroup $G_i$ is closed, and let $(K,{\Gamma})$ be a groupable right-closed nilpair.
conclusions: Then  $K\backslash G/{\Gamma}$ is a $k$-step Lie-fibered nilspace, and for each $i\in [k]$ the $i$-th structure group of $K\backslash G/ \Gamma$ is $G_i/(K_i \Gamma_i G_{i+1})$.
nodes.label: thm:top-double-coset

nodes.name: Subgroups $K_iG_{i+1}$ and $K_i\Gamma_iG_{i+1}$
nodes.statement: The normality of each $G_i$ in $G$ implies that $KG_i$ is a subgroup of $G$. Similarly $K_iG_{i+1}$ is a subgroup of $G_i$ ($\forall\, k_1,k_2\in K_i, g_1,g_2\in G_{i+1}$ we have $k_1g_1k_2g_2=k_1k_2(k_2^{-1}g_1k_2)g_2\in K_i G_{i+1}$). Moreover $K_iG_{i+1}$ is a normal subgroup of $G_i$, indeed for any $g\in G_{i+1}$, $h\in G_i$, $k\in K_i$, we have $hkgh^{-1} = kh[h,k]gh^{-1}$, and as $[h,k]g\in G_{i+1}$ (which is normal in $G_i$), we have $h([h,k]g)h^{-1}\in G_{i+1}$, so $hkgh^{-1} \in K_iG_{i+1}$ as required. It is seen similarly that $K_i \Gamma_i G_{i+1}$ is a subgroup of $G$. Moreover $G_i/(K_iG_{i+1})$ is an abelian group (as a quotient of $G_i/G_{i+1}$).

nodes.name: Closed subgroups act as closed groups of translations
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a group nilspace associated with a filtered Lie group of finite degree $(G,G_\bullet)$. Let $\tau:G\rightarrow \Theta(\mathrm{X})$ be the injective homomorphism $g\mapsto \tau_g$ where $\tau_g(s):=gs$. Then for any closed subgroup $H$ of $G$, we have that $\tau(H)$ is a closed subgroup of $\Theta(\mathrm{X})$.
nodes.section: 7.1 Topological aspects of double-coset nilspaces
assumptions: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a group nilspace associated with a filtered Lie group of finite degree $(G,G_\bullet)$.
Let $\tau:G\rightarrow \Theta(\mathrm{X})$ be the injective homomorphism $g\mapsto \tau_g$ where $\tau_g(s):=gs$.
conclusions: Then for any closed subgroup $H$ of $G$, we have that $\tau(H)$ is a closed subgroup of $\Theta(\mathrm{X})$.
nodes.label: lem:closed-group-as-trans

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 7.9
nodes.statement: Let $(g_n)_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence in $H$ such that $(\tau_{g_n})_n$ is Cauchy in $\Theta(\mathrm{X})$. Then for any compact set $C\subset G$ we have $\lim_{n,m\rightarrow\infty} \sup_{x\in C}d_G(\tau_{g_n}x,\tau_{g_m}x)=0$ (where $d_G$ is any compatible metric on $G$). The special case of this for $C=\{\mathrm{id}_G\}$ implies that $\lim_{n,m\rightarrow\infty} d_G(g_n,g_m)=0$, so $(g_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ is Cauchy in $G$. Thus $(g_n)$ has a limit $g\in H$ and a simple argument then shows that $\tau_{g_n}\rightarrow \tau_g$, so $\tau(H)$ is complete and therefore closed.
nodes.section: 7.1 Topological aspects of double-coset nilspaces
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy sequences of translations restrict to Cauchy sequences in $G$ at the identity; completeness gives closedness.

nodes.name: Cauchy in $G$
nodes.statement: Let $(g_n)_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence in $H$ such that $(\tau_{g_n})_n$ is Cauchy in $\Theta(\mathrm{X})$. Then for any compact set $C\subset G$ we have $\lim_{n,m\rightarrow\infty} \sup_{x\in C}d_G(\tau_{g_n}x,\tau_{g_m}x)=0$ (where $d_G$ is any compatible metric on $G$). The special case of this for $C=\{\mathrm{id}_G\}$ implies that $\lim_{n,m\rightarrow\infty} d_G(g_n,g_m)=0$, so $(g_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ is Cauchy in $G$.

nodes.name: Completeness
nodes.statement: Thus $(g_n)$ has a limit $g\in H$ and a simple argument then shows that $\tau_{g_n}\rightarrow \tau_g$, so $\tau(H)$ is complete and therefore closed.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 7.7
nodes.statement: That $K\backslash G/{\Gamma}$ is algebraically a (double-coset) nilspace follows from the assumption that $(K,\Gamma)$ is a groupable nilpair. We claim that the fiber-transitive filtration $(K_i:=K\cap G_i)_{i\geq 0}$ is closed on $ G$. Indeed, by Lemma \ref{lem:closed-group-as-trans}, for each $i$ the group $KG_{i+1}/G_{i+1}$ acting by left-multiplication on $G/G_{i+1}$ is a closed subgroup of $\Theta(G/G_{i+1})$ (since $KG_{i+1}/G_{i+1}$ is closed in $G/G_{i+1}$). Moreover, using the identity $\eta_i(K_j)=(K\cap G_j)G_{i+1}/G_{i+1}= (KG_{i+1}/G_{i+1}) \cap (G_j G_{i+1}/G_{i+1})$, we have that for all $i\in[k]$, the closure of $KG_{i+1}/G_{i+1}$ implies that for all $i,j\in[k]$ the subgroup $\eta_i(K\cap G_j)$ is closed. This proves our claim. Applying Theorem \ref{thm:coset-quot-closed} to the group nilspace $(G,G_\bullet)$ and the closed fiber-transitive filtration $(K_i)_{i\geq 0}$ we get that $K\backslash G$ is a $k$-step Lie-fibered nilspace. Applying Theorem \ref{thm:coset-quot-closed} again but now to the action of $\Gamma$ by right multiplication on $K\backslash G$ (noting that the assumptions imply that this defines a closed groupable congruence), the result follows.
nodes.section: 7.1 Topological aspects of double-coset nilspaces
nodes.statement_short: Show the left filtration by $K$ is closed, then apply Theorem 5.35 twice (left by $K$, right by $\Gamma$).

nodes.name: Algebraic part

We claim that the fiber-transitive filtration $(K_i:=K\cap G_i)_{i\geq 0}$ is closed on $ G$. Indeed, by Lemma \ref{lem:closed-group-as-trans}, for each $i$ the group 
$KG_{i+1}/G_{i+1}$ acting by left-multiplication on $G/G_{i+1}$ is a closed subgroup of $\Theta(G/G_{i+1})$ (since $KG_{i+1}/G_{i+1}$ is closed in $G/G_{i+1}$). nodes.name: Right-closed but not left-closed nilpair
nodes.statement: Let $G=\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{R})$ and consider the subgroups $K:=\mathbb{R}$ and $\Gamma:=\mathbb{Q}$. It is trivial that $(K,\Gamma)$ is a right-closed nilpair, since the quotienting by $K$ yields a 1-point nilspace. However $(K,\Gamma)$ is not ``left-closed" (in the obvious sense) since $\Gamma= \mathbb{Q}$ is not closed in $\mathbb{R}$.
nodes.section: 7.1 Topological aspects of double-coset nilspaces

nodes.name: Non-Hausdorff double-coset space
nodes.statement: Let $G:=\mathcal{D}_1(\mathbb{R})$, $K:=\mathbb{Z}$ and ${\Gamma}:=\sqrt{2}\mathbb{Z}$. Clearly the latter two subgroups are closed (even discrete), but $\Gamma+K$ is dense (and not closed) in $G$. Thus the double-coset space $K\backslash G/ \Gamma$ is not even a Hausdorff space. This does not satisfy Definition \ref{def:rcc} and indeed with that definition we avoid such examples.

nodes.name: Closed right-discrete implies right-closed
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lem:closedconseq} any closed right-discrete nilpair is in particular right-closed.
nodes.section: 7.1 Topological aspects of double-coset nilspaces
nodes.label: rem:closed-right-discrete-implies-right-closed

nodes.name: Double-coset representation theorem
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step \textsc{cfr} nilspace. Then there exists a degree-$k$ filtered Lie group $(G,G_\bullet)$ and two closed subgroups $K,\Gamma\subset G$ such that $(K,\Gamma)$ is a closed right-discrete groupable nilpair in $(G,G_\bullet)$, and $\mathrm{X}$ and $K\backslash G/ \Gamma$ are isomorphic \textsc{cfr} nilspaces.
nodes.section: 7.2 The double-coset representation theorem
assumptions: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step \textsc{cfr} nilspace.
conclusions: Then there exists a degree-$k$ filtered Lie group $(G,G_\bullet)$ and two closed subgroups $K,\Gamma\subset G$ such that $(K,\Gamma)$ is a closed right-discrete groupable nilpair in $(G,G_\bullet)$, and $\mathrm{X}$ and $K\backslash G/ \Gamma$ are isomorphic \textsc{cfr} nilspaces.
nodes.label: thm:cfr=double-coset

nodes.name: Free nilspaces as right-coset nilspaces of their translation groups
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be a free nilspace, let $G=\Theta(F)$ and fix any point $f_0\in F$. Let $K=\mathrm{Stab}_G(f_0):=\{g\in G:g(f_0)=f_0\}$. Then the following properties hold: \begin{enumerate} \item The right-coset nilspace $K\backslash G$ is a Lie-fibered nilspace. \item The map $\psi:K\backslash G\rightarrow F$, $Kg\mapsto g^{-1}(f_0)$ is an isomorphism of \textsc{lch} nilspaces. \item The map $\psi$ is equivariant relative to the action of $G$ on $F$ by translations and the action of $G$ on $K\backslash G$ defined by $(Kg,h)\mapsto Kgh^{-1}$ for any $g,h\in G$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 7.2 The double-coset representation theorem
assumptions: Let $F$ be a free nilspace, let $G=\Theta(F)$ and fix any point $f_0\in F$.
Let $K=\mathrm{Stab}_G(f_0):=\{g\in G:g(f_0)=f_0\}$.
conclusions:
Then the following properties hold:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item The right-coset nilspace $K\backslash G$ is a Lie-fibered nilspace.
    \item The map $\psi:K\backslash G\rightarrow F$, $Kg\mapsto g^{-1}(f_0)$ is an isomorphism of \textsc{lch} nilspaces.
    \item The map $\psi$ is  equivariant relative to the action of $G$ on $F$ by translations and the action of $G$ on $K\backslash G$ defined by $(Kg,h)\mapsto Kgh^{-1}$ for any $g,h\in G$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 7.15
nodes.statement: First let us prove $(i)$. By Theorem \ref{thm:coset-quot-closed} it suffices to show that the fiber-transitive filtration induced by $K$ on the group nilspace associated with $(G,G_\bullet)$ is closed. Arguing as in the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:top-double-coset}, the only non-trivial thing to check is that for all $i\in[k]$, the subgroup $KG_{i+1}/G_{i+1}$ of $G/G_{i+1}$ is closed. Consider the continuous homomorphism $\eta_i:G=\Theta(F)\rightarrow \Theta(F_i)$ (Lemma \ref{lem:h-is-cont}). We claim that $\eta_i^{-1}(\mathrm{Stab}_{\Theta(F_i)}(\pi_i(f_0))) = KG_{i+1}$. The latter group is clearly included in the former. To prove the other inclusion, note that for any $g\in \eta_i^{-1}(\mathrm{Stab}_{\Theta(F_i)}(\pi_i(f_0)))$ we have $\pi_i(g(f_0))=\pi_i(f_0)$ and thus, since $f_0, g(f_0)$ are elements of the free nilspace $F$ (which is an abelian group nilspace in particular) we have that $f_0-g(f_0)$ is an element of the $(i+1)$-th term in the filtration of $F=\prod_{j=1}^k \mathcal{D}_j(\mathbb{Z}^{a_j}\times \mathbb{R}^{b_j})$, that is, we have $f_0-g(f_0) \in \prod_{j=1}^i \{0\}\times \prod_{j=i+1}^k \mathcal{D}_j(\mathbb{Z}^{a_j}\times \mathbb{R}^{b_j})$. In particular, by Theorem \ref{thm:decrip-trans-group} the map $h:F\rightarrow F$, $f\mapsto f+f_0-g(f_0)$ is in $\Theta_{i+1}(F)=G_{i+1}$. Hence $hg\in K$ (as $hg(f_0)=g(f_0)+f_0-g(f_0)=f_0$) and thus $g = h^{-1}hg\in KG_{i+1}$. Since $\mathrm{Stab}_{\Theta(F_i)}(\pi_i(f_0))$ is clearly closed, so is $KG_{i+1}$. Next let us prove $(ii)$. We claim that the map $\psi:K\backslash G\rightarrow F$, $Kg \mapsto g^{-1}(f_0)$ is a nilspace isomorphism. First note that $\psi$ is well-defined, since $Kg=Kg'$ means that there exists $k\in K$ such that $kg=g'$, and then ${g'}^{-1}(f_0)=(kg)^{-1}(f_0)=g^{-1}k^{-1}(f_0)=g^{-1}(f_0)$ by definition of $K$. The map $\psi$ is injective, since $g^{-1}(f_0)={g'}^{-1}(f_0)$ implies $g{g'}^{-1}\in K$. Moreover $\psi$ is surjective, since for every $f\in F$ the map $g_f:F\rightarrow F$, $x\mapsto x-f$ (using addition on the abelian group $F$) is a translation in $G$ and $\psi(Kg_{f_0-f})=g^{-1}_{f-f_0}(f_0)=f$. Next let us prove that both $\psi$ and $\psi^{-1}$ are nilspace morphisms. Any element of $\mathrm{C}^n(K\backslash G)$ is of the form $K\mathrm{c}$ for some $\mathrm{c}\in \mathrm{C}^n(G)$. Thus $\psi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} (K\mathrm{c}) = \mathrm{c}^{-1} \circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} f_0^{\db{n}}$ where $f_0^{\db{n}}\in \mathrm{C}^n(F)$ is the constant cube equal to $f_0$. As $\mathrm{C}^n(G)$ is a group we have that $\mathrm{c}^{-1}\in \mathrm{C}^n(G)$ and hence $\mathrm{c}^{-1}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} f_0^{\db{n}}\in\mathrm{C}^n(F)$. To prove that $\psi^{-1}$ is a morphism, note that given any cube in $\mathrm{C}^n(F)$ we can write it as $\mathrm{c}^*\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} f_0^{\db{n}}$ for some $\mathrm{c}^*\in \mathrm{C}^n(G)$ where $\mathrm{c}^*$ is just a product of maps of the form $g_f:F\rightarrow F$ defined as $x\mapsto x-f$.\footnote{ If $f\in \prod_{i=1}^j\{0\}\times \prod_{i=j+1}^k \mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{Z}^{a_i}\times \mathbb{R}^{b_i})\subset \prod_{i=1}^k \mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{Z}^{a_i}\times \mathbb{R}^{b_i})$ then it is easy to check that $g_f\in \Theta_{j+1}(F)$. By definition, letting $0^{\db{n}}\in \mathrm{C}^n(F)$ be the constant 0 function, any element of $\mathrm{C}^n(F)$ is of the form $(\prod_{d=1}^\ell g_{f_d}^{C_d} )\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} 0^{\db{n}}$ where for any $d\in[\ell]$, $C_d\subset \db{n}$ is a face of $\db{n}$ and $f_d\in \prod_{i=1}^{\mathrm{codim}(C_d)-1}\{0\}\times \prod_{i=\mathrm{codim}(C_d)}^k \mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{Z}^{a_i}\times \mathbb{R}^{b_i})$ and $g_{f_d}^{C_d}$ means that we apply the function $g_{f_d}$ only of the face $C_d$.} Therefore, $\psi^{-1} \circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} (\mathrm{c}^*\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} f_0^{\db{n}}) = K(\mathrm{c}^*)^{-1}\in \mathrm{C}^n(K\backslash G)$ and the result follows. This shows that $K\backslash G$ and $F$ are isomorphic algebraically as nilspaces. Finally, note that the map $\psi$ is continuous. Indeed, if $Kg_n\rightarrow Kg$ in $K\backslash G$ then (using that the quotient map $G\rightarrow K\backslash G$ is open) there exists $k_n\in K$ such that $k_ng_n\rightarrow g$ in $G$. Thus $g_n^{-1}(f_0) = (k_ng_n)^{-1}(f_0)\rightarrow g^{-1}(f_0)$, so $\psi$ is indeed continuous. The map $\psi^{-1}$ can be defined as $f\mapsto Kg_{f_0-f}$, which is clearly continuous as well. This completes the proof of $(ii)$. Property $(iii)$ follows from the definitions: for any $h,g\in G$ we have $\psi(Kgh^{-1})=hg^{-1}(f_0) = h(\psi(Kg))$.

nodes.name: Part (ii)
nodes.statement: Next let us prove $(ii)$.  We claim that the map $\psi:K\backslash G\rightarrow F$, $Kg \mapsto g^{-1}(f_0)$ is a nilspace isomorphism. First note that $\psi$ is well-defined, since $Kg=Kg'$ means that there exists $k\in K$ such that $kg=g'$, and then ${g'}^{-1}(f_0)=(kg)^{-1}(f_0)=g^{-1}k^{-1}(f_0)=g^{-1}(f_0)$ by definition of $K$. The map $\psi$ is injective, since $g^{-1}(f_0)={g'}^{-1}(f_0)$ implies $g{g'}^{-1}\in K$. Moreover $\psi$ is surjective, since for every $f\in F$ the map $g_f:F\rightarrow F$, $x\mapsto x-f$ (using addition on the abelian group $F$) is a translation in $G$ and $\psi(Kg_{f_0-f})=g^{-1}_{f-f_0}(f_0)=f$. Next let us prove that both $\psi$ and $\psi^{-1}$ are nilspace morphisms. Any element of $\mathrm{C}^n(K\backslash G)$ is of the form $K\mathrm{c}$ for some $\mathrm{c}\in \mathrm{C}^n(G)$. Thus $\psi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} (K\mathrm{c}) = \mathrm{c}^{-1} \circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} f_0^{\db{n}}$ where $f_0^{\db{n}}\in \mathrm{C}^n(F)$ is the constant cube equal to $f_0$. As $\mathrm{C}^n(G)$ is a group we have that $\mathrm{c}^{-1}\in \mathrm{C}^n(G)$ and hence $\mathrm{c}^{-1}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} f_0^{\db{n}}\in\mathrm{C}^n(F)$. To prove that $\psi^{-1}$ is a morphism, note that given any cube in $\mathrm{C}^n(F)$ we can write it as $\mathrm{c}^*\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} f_0^{\db{n}}$ for some $\mathrm{c}^*\in \mathrm{C}^n(G)$ where $\mathrm{c}^*$ is just a product of maps of the form $g_f:F\rightarrow F$ defined as $x\mapsto x-f$.\footnote{ If $f\in \prod_{i=1}^j\{0\}\times \prod_{i=j+1}^k \mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{Z}^{a_i}\times \mathbb{R}^{b_i})\subset \prod_{i=1}^k \mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{Z}^{a_i}\times \mathbb{R}^{b_i})$ then it is easy to check that $g_f\in \Theta_{j+1}(F)$. By definition, letting $0^{\db{n}}\in \mathrm{C}^n(F)$ be the constant 0 function, any element of $\mathrm{C}^n(F)$ is of the form $(\prod_{d=1}^\ell g_{f_d}^{C_d} )\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} 0^{\db{n}}$ where for any $d\in[\ell]$, $C_d\subset \db{n}$ is a face of $\db{n}$ and $f_d\in \prod_{i=1}^{\mathrm{codim}(C_d)-1}\{0\}\times \prod_{i=\mathrm{codim}(C_d)}^k \mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{Z}^{a_i}\times \mathbb{R}^{b_i})$ and $g_{f_d}^{C_d}$ means that we apply the function $g_{f_d}$ only of the face $C_d$.} Therefore, $\psi^{-1} \circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} (\mathrm{c}^*\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} f_0^{\db{n}}) = K(\mathrm{c}^*)^{-1}\in \mathrm{C}^n(K\backslash G)$ and the result follows. This shows that $K\backslash G$ and $F$ are isomorphic algebraically as nilspaces. Finally, note that the map $\psi$ is continuous. Indeed, if $Kg_n\rightarrow Kg$ in $K\backslash G$ then  (using that the quotient map $G\rightarrow K\backslash G$ is open) there exists $k_n\in K$ such that $k_ng_n\rightarrow g$ in $G$. Thus $g_n^{-1}(f_0) = (k_ng_n)^{-1}(f_0)\rightarrow g^{-1}(f_0)$, so $\psi$ is indeed continuous. The map $\psi^{-1}$ can be defined as $f\mapsto Kg_{f_0-f}$, which is clearly continuous as well. This completes the proof of $(ii)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 7.14
nodes.statement: By Theorem \ref{thm:groupequivrep} there is a free nilspace $F$ and a fiber-transitive group $\Gamma\subset \Theta(F)$ which is fiber-discrete and fiber-cocompact, such that $\pi_\Gamma(F)\cong \mathrm{X}$. Let $G=\Theta(F)$, which is a Lie group by Corollary \ref{cor:trans&structFree}, and let $G_\bullet$ be the filtration $(G_i:=\Theta_i(F))_{i\geq 0}$. Let $\Gamma_\bullet$ be the filtration $(\Gamma_i:=\Gamma\cap G_i)_{i\geq 0}$. Fix any point $f_0\in F$ and let $K:=\mathrm{Stab}_G(f_0)=\{g\in G:g(f_0)=f_0\}$, a closed subgroup of $G$. Similarly, for each $i\ge 0$ let $K_i:=K\cap G_i$. By Lemma \ref{lem_aux-for-dou-coset} we already know that $\psi:K\backslash G\rightarrow F$, $Kg\mapsto g^{-1}(f_0)$ is an equivariant nilspace isomorphism. In particular, it induces an isomorphism $\widehat{\psi}:\Theta(K\backslash G)\rightarrow G$ between the translation groups of $K\backslash G$ and $F$. We now claim that $(K,\Gamma)$ is a closed right-discrete groupable nilpair in $(G,G_\bullet)$. Via the equivariance of $\psi$, the action of $\Gamma$ on $F$ by translations corresponds to the right-action of $\Gamma$ on $K\backslash G$ defined by $(Kg,\gamma)\mapsto Kg\gamma^{-1}$. As $\Gamma$ is a fiber-transitive group on $K\backslash G$ (by right-multiplication), by Lemma \ref{lem:nil-pair-good-fil} we have that $(K,\Gamma)$ is a groupable nilpair. To complete the proof of our claim, we now show that the groupable nilpair $(K,\Gamma)$ is closed right-discrete. To prove this, we note that the proof of Lemma \ref{lem_aux-for-dou-coset} already gives us that for every $i\in [k]$ the subgroup $KG_{i+1}/G_{i+1}$ of $G/G_{i+1}$ is closed. Thus it only remains to prove that for every $i\in [k]$ the subgroup $K_i\Gamma_i G_{i+1}/(K_i G_{i+1})$ of $G_i/(K_iG_{i+1})$ is discrete. To prove this we shall use again that $\psi$ is equivariant. Indeed, note that the $i$-th structure group of the $i$-step nilspace factor of $K\backslash G$ is isomorphic as a topological group to $(G_i/G_{i+1})\,/\, \big((KG_{i+1}/G_{i+1})\cap (G_i/G_{i+1})\big)$ by (the proof of) Theorem \ref{thm:coset-quot-closed}. This latter group in turn equals $(G_i/G_{i+1})\,/\, (K_iG_{i+1}/G_{i+1})$. Finally, using the third isomorphism theorem for topological groups we conclude that the $i$-th structure group of the $i$-step factor of $K\backslash G$ is isomorphic to $G_i/(K_iG_{i+1})$. Using the equivariance of $\psi$ (which implies straightforwardly that the maps $\psi_i:(K\backslash G)_i\rightarrow F_i$ between factors are similarly equivariant) we see that the action of $\eta_i(\widehat{\psi^{-1}}(\Gamma_i))$ on the $i$-step factor of $K\backslash G$ is given by addition of the group $\Gamma_iK_iG_{i+1}/(K_iG_{i+1})$ (which is a subgroup of $G_i/(K_iG_{i+1})$, the $i$-th structure group of the $i$-step factor of $K\backslash G$). Therefore, if $\eta_i(\Gamma_i)$, seen as a subgroup of the $i$-th structure group of $F_i$, is discrete, then so is $\Gamma_iK_iG_{i+1}/(K_iG_{i+1})$ as a subgroup of $G_i/(K_iG_{i+1})$ (simply because $\psi$ is an isomorphism of \textsc{lch} nilspaces and hence it induces isomorphisms between all the structure groups of $F$ and $K\backslash G$). This proves our claim. Thus $(K,\Gamma)$ is a closed right-discrete groupable nilpair in $(G,G_\bullet)$, so by Theorem \ref{thm:top-double-coset} and Remark \ref{rem:closed-right-discrete-implies-right-closed}, $K\backslash G / \Gamma$ is a Lie-fibered nilspace. Moreover, the map $\psi$ induces a nilspace isomorphism $\psi_\Gamma:K\backslash G/\Gamma \rightarrow \pi_\Gamma(F)$ defined as $\psi_\Gamma(Kg\Gamma):=\pi_H(\psi(Kg))$. Using the equivariance of $\psi$, it is straightforwardly checked that $\psi_\Gamma$ is an isomorphism of \textsc{lch} nilspaces. As $\mathrm{X}\cong \pi_\Gamma(F)$ we conclude that $\mathrm{X}\cong K\backslash G /\Gamma$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 7.16
nodes.statement: First we apply Theorem \ref{thm:groupequivrep} to any 2-step \textsc{cfr} nilspace. Recall that in the case $k=2$ of Theorem \ref{thm:groupequivrep}, on the resulting free nilspace $F'$, the fiber-transitive filtration $K_\bullet$ that we obtain is also free, by Corollary \ref{cor:k=2-str-good}. Hence, by Proposition \ref{prop:embeb-strong-good} there is an injective morphism $\iota:\pi_K(F')\hookrightarrow H/\Gamma$ for some compact nilmanifold $H/\Gamma$. Indeed, by Remark \ref{rem:isometric-embedding}, given any metric $d$ on $H/\Gamma$ we can choose an appropriate metric on $\pi_K(F')$ in such a way that $\iota$ is an isometry. Thus, without loss of generality we apply Theorem \ref{thm:inv-high-ord-latti-intro} with a metrization $D$ such that each $2$-step \textsc{cfr} nilspace is endowed with such an appropriate metric.\footnote{Recall that in Theorem \ref{thm:inv-high-ord-latti-intro} we can choose an arbitrary metrization. The chosen metric for each 2-step \textsc{cfr} nilspace $\pi_K(F')$ is the one that makes $\iota:\pi_K(F')\rightarrow H/\Gamma$ an isometry.} Hence, the Lipschitz map $F:\pi_K(F')\rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ can be interpreted as a map $\tilde{F}:\iota(\pi_K(F'))\rightarrow \mathbb{C}$, $\iota(x)\mapsto F(x)$. Moreover, as $\iota$ is an isometry, relative to the (restriction of the) metric $d$ on the subset $\iota(\pi_K(F'))\subset H/\Gamma$ we have that $\tilde{F}$ is also Lipschitz with the same Lipschitz constant as $F$. We can extend $\tilde{F}$ to the whole space $H/\Gamma$ in such a way that its Lipschitz constant is at most twice as large as the Lipschitz constant of $F$. A standard way of doing so (essentially using Kirszbraun's theorem) consists in separating the real ($\Re$) and imaginary ($\Im$) parts and defining $\tilde{F}^*:H/\Gamma\rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ as \[ \tilde{F}^*(x):=\inf_{y\in \iota(\pi_k(F'))}(\Re(\tilde{F}(y))+\mathrm{Lip}(\Re(\tilde{F}))d(x,y))+i\inf_{y\in \iota(\pi_K(F'))}(\Im(\tilde{F}(y))+\mathrm{Lip}(\Im(\tilde{F}))d(x,y)) \] where $\mathrm{Lip}(\cdot)$ is the Lipschitz constant of a function. This function extends $\tilde{F}$ to $H/\Gamma$ and has a Lipschitz constant $\mathrm{Lip}(\tilde{F}^*)\le \sqrt{2}\mathrm{Lip}(\tilde{F})=\sqrt{2}\mathrm{Lip}(F)$. Thus, if $F\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \phi$ was the correlating function given by Theorem \ref{thm:inv-high-ord-latti-intro} we have that $F\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \phi = \tilde{F}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\iota\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\phi$. Now note that $\iota\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \phi$ is a morphism and as the Lipschitz constant of $\tilde{F}$ is bounded in terms of the Lipschitz constant of $F$ the result follows.
nodes.section: 7.4 On a result of Jamneshan and Tao
nodes.statement_short: Embed 2-step CFR nilspaces isometrically into nilmanifolds (Corollary 6.4, Proposition 5.46), apply Theorem 1.19, and extend the Lipschitz function (Kirszbraun-type extension).

nodes.name: Embed into a nilmanifold
nodes.statement: First we apply Theorem \ref{thm:groupequivrep} to any 2-step \textsc{cfr} nilspace. Recall that in the case $k=2$ of Theorem \ref{thm:groupequivrep}, on the resulting free nilspace $F'$, the fiber-transitive filtration $K_\bullet$ that we obtain is also free, by Corollary \ref{cor:k=2-str-good}. Hence, by Proposition \ref{prop:embeb-strong-good} there is an injective morphism $\iota:\pi_K(F')\hookrightarrow H/\Gamma$ for some compact nilmanifold $H/\Gamma$.
nodes.section: 7.4 On a result of Jamneshan and Tao

nodes.name: Isometric metrization
nodes.statement: Indeed, by Remark \ref{rem:isometric-embedding}, given any metric $d$ on $H/\Gamma$ we can choose an appropriate metric on $\pi_K(F')$ in such a way that $\iota$ is an isometry. Thus, without loss of generality we apply Theorem \ref{thm:inv-high-ord-latti-intro} with a metrization $D$ such that each $2$-step \textsc{cfr} nilspace is endowed with such an appropriate metric.\footnote{Recall that in Theorem \ref{thm:inv-high-ord-latti-intro} we can choose an arbitrary metrization. The chosen metric for each 2-step \textsc{cfr} nilspace $\pi_K(F')$ is the one that makes $\iota:\pi_K(F')\rightarrow H/\Gamma$ an isometry.} Hence, the Lipschitz map $F:\pi_K(F')\rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ can be interpreted as a map $\tilde{F}:\iota(\pi_K(F'))\rightarrow \mathbb{C}$, $\iota(x)\mapsto F(x)$. Moreover, as $\iota$ is an isometry, relative to the (restriction of the) metric $d$ on the subset $\iota(\pi_K(F'))\subset H/\Gamma$ we have that $\tilde{F}$ is also Lipschitz with the same Lipschitz constant as $F$.
nodes.section: 7.4 On a result of Jamneshan and Tao

nodes.name: Lipschitz extension
nodes.statement:
We can extend $\tilde{F}$ to the whole space $H/\Gamma$ in such a way that its Lipschitz constant is at most twice as large as the Lipschitz constant of $F$. A standard way of doing so (essentially using Kirszbraun's theorem) consists in separating the real ($\Re$) and imaginary ($\Im$) parts and defining $\tilde{F}^*:H/\Gamma\rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ as
\[
\tilde{F}^*(x):=\inf_{y\in \iota(\pi_k(F'))}(\Re(\tilde{F}(y))+\mathrm{Lip}(\Re(\tilde{F}))d(x,y))+i\inf_{y\in \iota(\pi_K(F'))}(\Im(\tilde{F}(y))+\mathrm{Lip}(\Im(\tilde{F}))d(x,y))
\]
where $\mathrm{Lip}(\cdot)$ is the Lipschitz constant of a function. This function extends $\tilde{F}$ to $H/\Gamma$ and has a Lipschitz constant $\mathrm{Lip}(\tilde{F}^*)\le \sqrt{2}\mathrm{Lip}(\tilde{F})=\sqrt{2}\mathrm{Lip}(F)$.
nodes.section: 7.4 On a result of Jamneshan and Tao
nodes.statement_short: Inf-convolution of real and imaginary parts.

nodes.name: Correlation with a nilsequence
nodes.statement: Thus, if $F\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \phi$ was the correlating function given by Theorem \ref{thm:inv-high-ord-latti-intro} we have that $F\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \phi = \tilde{F}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\iota\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\phi$. Now note that $\iota\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \phi$ is a morphism and as the Lipschitz constant of $\tilde{F}$ is bounded in terms of the Lipschitz constant of $F$ the result follows.
nodes.section: 7.4 On a result of Jamneshan and Tao

nodes.name: Extension to compact abelian groups and nilmanifolds
nodes.statement: The regularity and inverse theorems from \cite{CSinverse} used to obtain Theorems \ref{thm:cfr=double-coset-intro} and \ref{thm:gpcongrep-intro} hold with domains more general than finite abelian groups, in particular compact abelian groups and nilmanifolds; specifically \cite[Theorem 1.5 and Theorem 5.2]{CSinverse}. This enables an extension of Theorem \ref{thm:jam-tao} to such domains. We omit the details.
nodes.section: 7.4 On a result of Jamneshan and Tao
nodes.label: rem:invthmextension

nodes.name: Pro-free nilspaces need not be LCH
nodes.statement: Note that pro-free nilspaces, unlike all previous topological nilspaces in this paper, may fail to be \textsc{lch} (indeed an infinite product of copies of $\mathbb{R}$ is not locally-compact). However they are still \emph{Polish} spaces. In this section we will not generalize the concept of \textsc{lch} nilspaces to more general \emph{Polish} nilspaces, as we will not need to do so for our main results. Indeed, this topology on a pro-free nilspace will not be used in the results below until Theorem \ref{thm:cpct-as-quotient-of-infinite-free}. In the latter theorem and subsequent two results we will carefully indicate how this topology is used.
nodes.section: 8 Compact nilspaces as quotients of pro-free nilspaces and as double-coset nilspaces
nodes.label: rem:not-gen-theory

nodes.name: Graded translation group
nodes.statement: Let $d\in \mathbb{N}\cup\{\omega\}$. For every $i< d$ let $F_i$ be a free nilspace and let $F=\prod_{i<d}F_i$ be the associated graded pro-free nilspace. The \emph{graded translation group} $\Theta(F,(F_i)_{i< d})$ consists of maps $\alpha: F\rightarrow F$ such that, for every projection $\pi_j:F\rightarrow \prod_{i=1}^j F_i$, $j\in \mathbb{N}$, there is a translation $\alpha_j\in \Theta(\prod_{i=1}^j F_i)$ satisfying $\alpha_j\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \pi_j = \pi_j\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \alpha$.
nodes.section: 8 Compact nilspaces as quotients of pro-free nilspaces and as double-coset nilspaces
nodes.label: def:gr-tran

nodes.name: Graded translations are continuous translations forming a group
nodes.statement: Note that it follows from this definition that such a map $\alpha$ is continuous (by the last equality and definition of the product topology on $F$), and also that it is a translation on $F$ (by checking the translation property in each component $F_i$). Moreover, it is not hard to deduce from the definition that  these maps do form a group (under composition).
nodes.section: 8 Compact nilspaces as quotients of pro-free nilspaces and as double-coset nilspaces
conclusions: Note that it follows from this definition that such a map $\alpha$ is continuous (by the last equality and definition of the product topology on $F$), and also that it is a translation on $F$ (by checking the translation property in each component $F_i$).
Moreover, it is not hard to deduce from the definition that  these maps do form a group (under composition).

nodes.name: Graded translation groups are pro-Lie groups
nodes.statement: For any graded pro-free nilspace $F=\prod_{i<\omega} F_i$, the group $\Theta(F,(F_i)_{i\in \mathbb{N}})$ equipped with the compact-open topology is a $k$-step nilpotent pro-Lie group. Moreover, this topology on $\Theta(F,(F_i)_{i\in \mathbb{N}})$ is equivalent to the topology as an inverse limit of the graded groups of translations $\Theta(\prod_{i=1}^jF_i,(F_i)_{i\in [j]})$ for $j\in \mathbb{N}$.
nodes.section: 8 Compact nilspaces as quotients of pro-free nilspaces and as double-coset nilspaces
conclusions: For any graded pro-free nilspace $F=\prod_{i<\omega} F_i$, the group $\Theta(F,(F_i)_{i\in \mathbb{N}})$ equipped with the compact-open topology is a $k$-step nilpotent pro-Lie group.

Moreover, this topology on $\Theta(F,(F_i)_{i\in \mathbb{N}})$ is equivalent to the  topology as an inverse limit of the graded groups of translations $\Theta(\prod_{i=1}^jF_i,(F_i)_{i\in [j]})$ for $j\in \mathbb{N}$.
nodes.label: lem:top-graded-trans-gr

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 8.3
nodes.statement: For any positive integers $j\le \ell$ consider the projection $p_{j,\ell}:\prod_{i=1}^\ell F_i \rightarrow \prod_{i=1}^j F_i$. By the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:LFnstransLie}, the group $C_{j,\ell}:=\{\alpha\in \Theta(\prod_{i=1}^\ell F_i): \forall x,y\in \mathrm{X}, \text{ if } p_{j,\ell}(x)=p_{j,\ell}(y) \text{ then } p_{j,\ell}(\alpha(x))=p_{j,\ell}(\alpha(y))\}$ is a closed subgroup of $\Theta(\prod_{i=1}^\ell F_i)$. Therefore, the group $C_\ell:=\cap_{j=1}^\ell C_{j,\ell}$ is also a closed subgroup of $\Theta(\prod_{i=1}^\ell F_i)$ and hence a Lie group, by Cartan's theorem. Note that $C_\ell = \Theta(\prod_{i=1}^\ell F_i,(F_i)_{i\in [\ell]})$. Let $\widehat{p_{j,\ell}}:\Theta(\prod_{i=1}^\ell F_i,(F_i)_{i\in [\ell]})\rightarrow \Theta(\prod_{i=1}^j F_i)$ be the group homomorphism induced by $p_{j,\ell}$. Then $\widehat{p_{\ell-1,\ell}}:\Theta(\prod_{i=1}^\ell F_i,(F_i)_{i\in [\ell]})\rightarrow \Theta(\prod_{i=1}^{\ell-1} F_i,(F_i)_{i\in [\ell-1]})$ is a well-defined continuous surjective homomorphism.\footnote{The surjectivity follows easily from the fact that given $\alpha\in \Theta(\prod_{i=1}^{\ell-1} F_i,(F_i)_{i\in [\ell-1]})$ the map $(\alpha,\mathrm{id}): (\prod_{i=1}^{\ell-1} F_i)\times F_\ell\rightarrow ( \prod_{i=1}^{\ell-1} F_i)\times F_\ell$ is in $\Theta(\prod_{i=1}^{\ell} F_i,(F_i)_{i\in [\ell]})$.} This defines an inverse system of $k$-step nilpotent Lie groups, whence $\Theta(F,(F_i)_{i\in \mathbb{N}})=\varprojlim \Theta(\prod_{i=1}^\ell F_i,(F_i)_{i\in [\ell]})$ is a pro-Lie group. Finally, we have to show that the topology on $\Theta(F,(F_i)_{i\in \mathbb{N}})$ as a subset of the set of continuous functions from $F$ to $F$ with the compact-open topology is equal to the topology generated by the limit maps for the inverse system defined by $\widehat{p_{\ell-1,\ell}}$ for $\ell\in \mathbb{N}$. By \cite[Theorem 46.8]{Mu} the compact-open topology in both $C(F,F)$ and $C(\Theta(\prod_{i=1}^\ell F_i,(F_i)_{i\in [\ell]}),\Theta(\prod_{i=1}^\ell F_i,(F_i)_{i\in [\ell]}))$ for $\ell\in \mathbb{N}$ coincides with the topology of compact convergence. Note that given any metric $d_\ell$ in $\prod_{i=1}^\ell F_i$ for $\ell\in \mathbb{N}$, we can define a bounded equivalent metric just by taking $\max(1,d_\ell(\cdot,\cdot))$. Furthermore, if $d_\ell$ is 1-bounded for all $\ell\in \mathbb{N}$ on $F=\prod_{i<\omega} F_i$ we can define the metric $d_F(x,x'):=\sum_{\ell=1}^\infty \frac{d_\ell(\pi_\ell(x),\pi_\ell(x'))}{2^\ell}$ where $\pi_\ell:F\rightarrow \prod_{i=1}^\ell F_i$ is the projection map. Also note that by construction of the maps $\pi_\ell$ we have the following property: for any compact $D_\ell\subset \prod_{i=1}^\ell F_i$ there exists a compact $D\subset F$ such that $\pi_\ell(D)=D_\ell$. Using this it follows that the topology of $\Theta(F,(F_i)_{i\in \mathbb{N}})$ as an inverse limit and as a subset of $C(F,F)$ coincide. We omit the details.

nodes.name: Topologies coincide
nodes.statement: Finally, we have to show that the topology on $\Theta(F,(F_i)_{i\in \mathbb{N}})$ as a subset of the set of continuous functions from $F$ to $F$ with the compact-open topology is equal to the topology generated by the limit maps for the inverse system defined by  $\widehat{p_{\ell-1,\ell}}$ for $\ell\in \mathbb{N}$. Note that given any metric $d_\ell$ in $\prod_{i=1}^\ell F_i$ for $\ell\in \mathbb{N}$, we can define a bounded equivalent metric just by taking $\max(1,d_\ell(\cdot,\cdot))$. Furthermore, if $d_\ell$ is 1-bounded for all $\ell\in \mathbb{N}$ on $F=\prod_{i<\omega} F_i$ we can define the metric $d_F(x,x'):=\sum_{\ell=1}^\infty \frac{d_\ell(\pi_\ell(x),\pi_\ell(x'))}{2^\ell}$ where $\pi_\ell:F\rightarrow \prod_{i=1}^\ell F_i$ is the projection map. Also note that by construction of the maps $\pi_\ell$ we have the following property: for any compact $D_\ell\subset \prod_{i=1}^\ell F_i$ there exists a compact $D\subset F$ such that $\pi_\ell(D)=D_\ell$. Using this it follows that the topology of $\Theta(F,(F_i)_{i\in \mathbb{N}})$ as an inverse limit and as a subset of $C(F,F)$ coincide. We omit the details.

nodes.name: Fiber products of free covers
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{X}$, $\mathrm{X}'$ be $k$-step \textsc{cfr} nilspaces, and let $\varphi:\mathrm{X}'\rightarrow\mathrm{X}$ be a fibration. Let $F,F'$ be free $k$-step nilspaces and $G,G'$ be fiber-transitive, fiber-cocompact and fiber-discrete subgroups of $\Theta(F),\Theta(F')$ respectively, such that $\mathrm{X}\cong F/G$ and $\mathrm{X}'\cong F'/G'$. Let $\tilde{F}$ be the fiber-product nilspace $\tilde{F}=\{(f,f')\in F\times F': \varphi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\pi_{G'}(f')= \pi_{G}(f)\}$, where $\pi_G$, $\pi_{G'}$ are the quotient fibrations $F\rightarrow F/G$, $F'\rightarrow F'/G'$ respectively. Then $\tilde{F}$ is a sub-nilspace of $F\times F'$ which is itself a free nilspace. Moreover, letting the group $G\times G'$ act the natural way on $\tilde{F}$ \textup{(}namely $(g,g')(f,f')=(gf,g'f')$\textup{)}, we embed $G\times G'$ as a subgroup of $\Theta(\tilde{F})$ which is fiber-transitive on $\tilde{F}$ with $\mathrm{X}'\cong \tilde{F}/H$, and we have the following commutative diagram: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned}[c] \begin{tikzpicture} \matrix (m) [matrix of math nodes,row sep=2em,column sep=4em,minimum width=2em] { \tilde{F} & F' & \mathrm{X}' \\ & F & \mathrm{X}, \\}; \path[-stealth] (m-1-1) edge node [above] {$ p_2$} (m-1-2) (m-1-2) edge node [above] {$ \pi_{G'}$} (m-1-3) (m-1-1) edge node [right] {$p_1$} (m-2-2) (m-1-3) edge node [right] {$\varphi$} (m-2-3) (m-2-2) edge node [above] {$\pi_G$} (m-2-3); \end{tikzpicture} \end{aligned} \end{equation} \vspace{-0.3cm} \noindent where $p_1,p_2$ are the restrictions to $\tilde{F}$ of the 1-st and 2-nd coordinate projections on $F\times F'$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 8.5
nodes.statement: We argue by induction on the step $k$. For $k=1$, it follows from classical results on torsion-free abelian groups that a 1-step sub-nilspace of a free 1-step nilspace is again a free nilspace. Indeed, note that up to the addition of a constant, we can consider $\varphi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \pi_{G'}$ and $\pi_G$ as surjective homomorphisms where we identify $F$ and $F'$ with two abelian groups of the form $\mathbb{Z}^a\times \mathbb{R}^b$ and $\mathbb{Z}^{a'}\times \mathbb{R}^{b'}$ respectively. Thus, the 1-step nilspace $\tilde{F}$ is identified with the following abelian group: $\mathrm{Z}:=\{(f,f')\in (\mathbb{Z}^a\times \mathbb{R}^b)\times (\mathbb{Z}^{a'}\times \mathbb{R}^{b'}):\varphi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \pi_{G'}(f')=\pi_G(f)\}$. But now we have a short exact sequence $0\rightarrow \ker(\pi_G)\rightarrow \mathrm{Z}\rightarrow \mathbb{Z}^{a'}\times \mathbb{R}^{b'}\rightarrow 0$ where $f\in \ker(\pi_G)\mapsto (f,0)\in \mathrm{Z}$ and $(f,f')\in \mathrm{Z}\mapsto f'\in \mathbb{Z}^{a'}\times \mathbb{R}^{b'}$. By \cite[Theorem 3.3]{Mosk} the group $\mathbb{Z}^{a'}\times \mathbb{R}^{b'}$ is projective and thus $\mathrm{Z}$ is isomorphic (as a topological group) to $\mathbb{Z}^{a'}\times \mathbb{R}^{b'}\times \ker(\pi_G)$ by \cite[Theorem 3.5]{Mosk}. The closed subgroup $\ker(\pi_G)\leq \mathbb{Z}^{a}\times \mathbb{R}^b$ is also of the form $\mathbb{Z}^{a''}\times \mathbb{R}^{b''}$. The case $k=1$ follows. For $k>1$, we begin by observing that by Lemma \ref{lem:diff-cont} (see also \cite[Proposition A.20]{CGSS-p-hom}) the $(k-1)$-th factor $\tilde{F}_{k-1}$ of $\tilde{F}$ is isomorphic to the fiber-product $F_{k-1}\times_{\mathrm{X}_{k-1}} F'_{k-1}$. Note that we have again a commutative diagram exactly as \eqref{eq:k-stepdiag}, but at step $k-1$ and with $\tilde{F}_{k-1}$. By induction, we can thus assume that $\tilde{F}_{k-1}$ is a free nilspace. Since $\tilde{F}$ is a degree-$k$ extension of this \emph{free} nilspace $\tilde{F}_{k-1}$, by Theorem \ref{thm:splitext} we have $\tilde{F}\cong \tilde{F}_{k-1}\times \mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z})$ where $\mathrm{Z}=\mathrm{Z}_k(\tilde{F})$, the $k$-th structure group of $\tilde{F}$. Moreover $\mathrm{Z}_k(\tilde{F})=\{(z,z')\in \mathrm{Z}_k(F)\times \mathrm{Z}_k(F'): \phi_k(z)=\phi_k'(z')\}$, by Lemma \ref{lem:diff-cont} (where $\mathrm{Z}_k(F)$ and $\mathrm{Z}_k(F')$ are the $k$-th structure groups of $F$ and $F'$ respectively, and $\phi_k:\mathrm{Z}_k(F)\rightarrow \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})$, $\phi_k':\mathrm{Z}_k(F')\rightarrow \mathrm{Z}_k(\mathrm{X})$ are the $k$-th structure homomorphisms of $\pi_G$ and $\varphi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \pi_{G'}$ respectively). By the facts for torsion-free abelian groups used in the case $k=1$ above, we have that $\mathrm{Z}_k(\tilde{F})\cong \mathbb{Z}^a\times \mathbb{R}^b$, for some $a,b\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$.

nodes.name: Short exact sequence
nodes.statement: Thus, the 1-step nilspace $\tilde{F}$ is identified with the following abelian group: $\mathrm{Z}:=\{(f,f')\in (\mathbb{Z}^a\times \mathbb{R}^b)\times (\mathbb{Z}^{a'}\times \mathbb{R}^{b'}):\varphi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \pi_{G'}(f')=\pi_G(f)\}$. nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement: For $k>1$, we begin by observing that by Lemma \ref{lem:diff-cont} (see also \cite[Proposition A.20]{CGSS-p-hom}) the $(k-1)$-th factor $\tilde{F}_{k-1}$ of $\tilde{F}$ is isomorphic to the fiber-product $F_{k-1}\times_{\mathrm{X}_{k-1}} F'_{k-1}$. Note that we have again a commutative diagram exactly as \eqref{eq:k-stepdiag}, but at step $k-1$ and with $\tilde{F}_{k-1}$. By induction, we can thus assume that $\tilde{F}_{k-1}$ is a free nilspace. nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 8.6
nodes.statement: Let $(f,f')\in \tilde{F}$ and $(g,g')\in G\times G'$. Now $(f,f')\in \tilde{F}$ means by definition that $\varphi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\pi_{G'}(f')=\pi_G(f)$, and then clearly $\varphi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\pi_{G'}(g'f')=\pi_G(gf)$, so $G\times G'$ indeed leaves $\tilde{F}$ globally invariant. In particular we have $p_2(gf,g'f')=g'f'=g'p_2(f,f')$, and similarly with $p_1$ instead of $p_2$. Hence $G\times G'$ is consistent with both $p_1,p_2$ in the sense of \cite[Definition 1.2]{CGSS}. We want to prove that $G\times G'$ is a fiber-transitive group on $\tilde{F}$ and that the quotient nilspace $\tilde{F}/(G\times G')$ is a compact nilspace isomorphic (as a compact nilspace) to $\mathrm{X}'$. Let us check the fiber-transitivity property. We have by assumption that $G$ is fiber-transitive on $F$ and so is $G'$ on $F'$. Suppose that $(f,f'), (h,h')$ in $\tilde{F}$ satisfy $\pi_{i,\tilde{F}} (f,f') = \pi_{i,\tilde{F}}(h,h')$ for some $i\in[k]$ and there is $(g,g')\in G\times G'$ such that $(g,g')(f,f')=(h,h')$. Letting $(p_1)_i:\pi_i(\tilde{F})\rightarrow \pi_i(F)$ be the morphism such that $(p_1)_i\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \pi_{i,\tilde{F}} = \pi_{i,F}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} p_1$, we deduce that $\pi_{i,F}(f)=\pi_{i,F}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} p_1(f,f') = (p_1)_i\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \pi_{i,\tilde{F}}(f,f') = (p_1)_i\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \pi_{i,\tilde{F}}(h,h') = \pi_{i,F}(h)$. Applying $p_1$ to both sides of $(g,g')(f,f')=(h,h')$ we also deduce that $gf = h$. Similarly, we have $\pi_{i,F'}(f')=\pi_{i,F'}(h')$ and $g' f'= h'$. By the fiber-transitivity of $G,G'$, we deduce that there exist $g_{i+1}\in G_{i+1}:=G\cap \Theta_{i+1}(F)$, $g_{i+1}'\in G_{i+1}'$, such that $g_{i+1}f=h$ and $g_{i+1}'f'=h'$, whence $(g_{i+1},g_{i+1}')\in G_{i+1}\times G_{i+1}'$ satisfies $(g_{i+1},g_{i+1}')(f,f')=(h,h')$. Next, we need to check that if $G,G'$ are fiber-discrete on $F,F'$ respectively then so is $G\times G'$ on $\tilde{F}$. Note that it suffices to check this for the last structure group, as then the result for lower factors follows by induction. Clearly $G_{k}\times G'_k$ is discrete (as a product of two discrete groups). To see that $G\times G'$ is fiber-cocompact, recall that by Lemma \ref{lem:diff-cont} we have $\mathrm{Z}_k(\tilde{F})=\{(z,z')\in \mathrm{Z}_k(F)\times \mathrm{Z}_k(F'):\phi_k(z)=\phi'_k(z')\}$ where $\phi_k,\phi_k'$ are the $k$-th structure homomorphisms of $\pi_G$ and $\varphi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \pi_{G'}$ respectively. Then consider the map $\psi_k:\mathrm{Z}_k(\tilde{F})\rightarrow \mathrm{Z}_k(F')/G_k'$ defined by $(z,z')\mapsto z'\mod G_k'$. The map $\psi_k$ is clearly a continuous surjective homomorphism. We claim that its kernel equals precisely $G_k\times G_k'$. The inclusion $G_k\times G_k'\subset \ker(\psi_k)$ is clear. Now let $(z,z')\in \mathrm{Z}_k(\tilde{F})$ and suppose that $0=\psi_k(z,z')=z'\mod G_k'$. Hence $z'\in G_k'$. Fix any $(f,f')\in \tilde{F}$ and note that $\varphi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \pi_{G'}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} p_2(f+z,f'+z') = \varphi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \pi_{G'}(f'+z') = \varphi(\pi_{G'}(f')) = \pi_G(f)$ (by definition of $(f,f')$ being in $\tilde{F}$). On the other hand, using the commutativity of \eqref{eq:k-stepdiag} we have $\varphi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \pi_{G'}\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} p_2(f+z,f'+z') = \pi_G(p_1(f+z,f'+z')) = \pi_G(f+z) = \pi_G(f)+(z\mod G_k)$. Combining this with the previous formula we conclude that $z\mod G_k=0$ and thus $z\in G_k$, which proves our claim. Hence, since $\mathrm{Z}_k(F')/G_k'$ is compact and isomorphic to $\mathrm{Z}_k(\tilde F)/(G_k\times G_k')$, we obtain that $G_k\times G_k'$ is cocompact as desired.\footnote{Note that we have not used the hypothesis that $G$ is fiber-cocompact. This is not strictly necessary because if we are in a situation as in Proposition \ref{prop:fiber-prod-of-free}, the fact that $\mathrm{X}'$ is compact forces $\mathrm{X}$ to be compact. Since $\mathrm{X}\cong F/G$, this implies directly that $G$ is fiber-cocompact.} Combining the above facts we obtain that $G\times G'$ is a subgroup of $\Theta(\tilde{F})$ which is fiber-transitive, fiber-discrete and fiber-cocompact group on $\tilde{F}$. Moreover, the morphism $p_2:\tilde{F}\rightarrow F'$ is equivariant relative to the actions of $G\times G'$ and $G'$. This induces a well-defined morphism $\overline{p_2}:\tilde{F}/(G\times G')\rightarrow F'/G'$. By the previous paragraphs all structure groups are isomorphic, so $\overline{p_2}$ is an isomorphism.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 8.9
nodes.statement: We argue by induction on $k:=\max(k_1,k_2)$ where for $i\in[2]$, $F_i$ is $k_i$-step. For $k=1$ the result follows by an argument similar to the start of the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:fiber-prod-of-free-is-free}. For $k>1$, for $i=1,2$ let us write $F_i=\pi_{k-1}(F_i)\times \mathcal{D}_k(A_i)$ where $\pi_{k-1}(F_i)$ is $(k-1)$-step and $A_i$ is some abelian group. By Lemmas \ref{lem:Taylor-discrete} and \ref{lem:poly-free-to-R} we can write the map $\phi:\pi_{k-1}(F_2)\times H_2\rightarrow \pi_{k-1}(F_1)\times H_1$ as $(x,y)\mapsto (f(x),g(x,y))$. By induction on $k$, there exists a free nilspace $F_3'$ and a nilspace isomorphism $\tau':\pi_{k-1}(F_1)\times F_3' \rightarrow \pi_{k-1}(F_2)$ such that $f\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \tau':\pi_{k-1}(F_1)\times F_3'\rightarrow \pi_{k-1}(F_1)$ is just the projection to the first coordinate. Letting $(\tau',\mathrm{id}):\pi_{k-1}(F_1)\times F_3'\times \mathcal{D}_k(A_2)\rightarrow \pi_{k-1}(F_2)\times \mathcal{D}_k(A_2)$ denote the map $ (a,b,c)\mapsto (\tau'(a,b),c)$ then $(\tau',\mathrm{id})$ is an isomorphism and $\phi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} (\tau',\mathrm{id})(s,r,y)=(s,g'(s,r,y))$ for some morphism $g':\pi_{k-1}(F_1)\times F_3' \times \mathcal{D}_k(A_2)\rightarrow \mathcal{D}_k(A_1)$. Let us define $\phi':=\phi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} (\tau',\mathrm{id})$. As both $F_3'$ and $\pi_{k-1}(F_1)$ are at most $(k-1)$-step, the map $g'(s,r,y)$ equals $g'(s,r,0)+\alpha(y)$ for some homomorphism $\alpha:A_2\rightarrow A_1$ (see \cite[Definition 3.3.1]{Cand:Notes1}). As $\phi$ is a fibration, so is $\phi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} (\tau',\mathrm{id})$ and hence $\alpha$ is a surjective homomorphism. Since $\alpha$ is a surjective homomorphism between abelian Lie groups of the form $\mathbb{Z}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m$, by the case $k=1$ of the lemma we have that $A_2$ is isomorphic as an abelian Lie group to $A_1\times B$. In particular there exists a homomorphism $c:A_1\rightarrow A_2$ such that $\alpha\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} c =\mathrm{id}_{A_1}$. Let us now consider the map $\tau'':\pi_{k-1}(F_1)\times F_3'\times \mathcal{D}_k(A_2)\rightarrow \pi_{k-1}(F_1)\times F_3' \times \mathcal{D}_k(A_2)$ defined as $(s,r,y)\mapsto(s,r,y-c\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} g'(s,r,0))$. This is clearly a nilspace isomorphism and, letting $\phi'':=\phi'\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \tau''$, we have $\phi''(s,r,y)=(s,\alpha(y))$. Finally, again by the case $k=1$ of the lemma, there exists an isomorphism $\tau''':A_1\times B\rightarrow A_2$ such that $\alpha \circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \tau'''(y',y'')=y'$. If we define $(\mathrm{id},\tau'''):\pi_{k-1}(F_1)\times F_3' \times \mathcal{D}_k(A_1\times B)\rightarrow \pi_{k-1}(F_1)\times F_3' \times \mathcal{D}_k(A_2)$ as $(s,r,y',y'')\mapsto (s,r,\tau'''(y,y'))$ we get that $\phi''\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} (\mathrm{id},\tau''')$ is just the map $(s,r,y',y'')\mapsto (s,y')$ which completes the proof (just let $\tau:=(\tau',\mathrm{id})\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \tau''\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}(\mathrm{id},\tau''')$).

nodes.statement:
For $k>1$, for $i=1,2$ let us write $F_i=\pi_{k-1}(F_i)\times \mathcal{D}_k(A_i)$ where $\pi_{k-1}(F_i)$ is $(k-1)$-step and $A_i$ is some abelian group.

By Lemmas \ref{lem:Taylor-discrete} and \ref{lem:poly-free-to-R} we can write the map $\phi:\pi_{k-1}(F_2)\times H_2\rightarrow \pi_{k-1}(F_1)\times H_1$ as $(x,y)\mapsto (f(x),g(x,y))$. By induction on $k$, there exists a free nilspace $F_3'$ and a nilspace isomorphism $\tau':\pi_{k-1}(F_1)\times F_3' \rightarrow \pi_{k-1}(F_2)$ such that $f\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \tau':\pi_{k-1}(F_1)\times F_3'\rightarrow \pi_{k-1}(F_1)$ is just the projection to the first coordinate.  Letting $(\tau',\mathrm{id}):\pi_{k-1}(F_1)\times  F_3'\times \mathcal{D}_k(A_2)\rightarrow \pi_{k-1}(F_2)\times \mathcal{D}_k(A_2)$ denote the map $ (a,b,c)\mapsto (\tau'(a,b),c)$  then $(\tau',\mathrm{id})$ is an isomorphism and $\phi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} (\tau',\mathrm{id})(s,r,y)=(s,g'(s,r,y))$ for some morphism $g':\pi_{k-1}(F_1)\times F_3' \times \mathcal{D}_k(A_2)\rightarrow \mathcal{D}_k(A_1)$. Let us define $\phi':=\phi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} (\tau',\mathrm{id})$.

nodes.name: Remove the dependence on lower coordinates
nodes.statement: As both $F_3'$ and $\pi_{k-1}(F_1)$ are at most $(k-1)$-step, the map $g'(s,r,y)$ equals $g'(s,r,0)+\alpha(y)$ for some homomorphism $\alpha:A_2\rightarrow A_1$ (see \cite[Definition 3.3.1]{Cand:Notes1}). As $\phi$ is a fibration, so is $\phi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} (\tau',\mathrm{id})$ and hence $\alpha$ is a surjective homomorphism. Since $\alpha$ is a surjective homomorphism between abelian Lie groups of the form $\mathbb{Z}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m$, by the case $k=1$ of the lemma we have that $A_2$ is isomorphic as an abelian Lie group to $A_1\times B$. In particular there exists a homomorphism $c:A_1\rightarrow A_2$ such that $\alpha\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} c =\mathrm{id}_{A_1}$. Let us now consider the map $\tau'':\pi_{k-1}(F_1)\times  F_3'\times \mathcal{D}_k(A_2)\rightarrow \pi_{k-1}(F_1)\times  F_3' \times \mathcal{D}_k(A_2)$ defined as $(s,r,y)\mapsto(s,r,y-c\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} g'(s,r,0))$. This is clearly a nilspace isomorphism and, letting $\phi'':=\phi'\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \tau''$,  we have $\phi''(s,r,y)=(s,\alpha(y))$.

nodes.name: Split the top group

If we define $(\mathrm{id},\tau'''):\pi_{k-1}(F_1)\times  F_3' \times \mathcal{D}_k(A_1\times B)\rightarrow \pi_{k-1}(F_1)\times  F_3' \times \mathcal{D}_k(A_2)$ as $(s,r,y',y'')\mapsto (s,r,\tau'''(y,y'))$ we get that $\phi''\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} (\mathrm{id},\tau''')$ is just the map $(s,r,y',y'')\mapsto (s,y')$ which completes the proof (just let $\tau:=(\tau',\mathrm{id})\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \tau''\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}(\mathrm{id},\tau''')$).

nodes.name: Consistent groups become graded translations
nodes.statement: Under the assumptions of Lemma \ref{lem:strong-splitting}, suppose that we have a subgroup $G\le \Theta(F_2)$ consistent with $\phi$ and such that $\widehat{\phi}(G)=G'\le \Theta(F_1)$. Then, under the isomorphism $\widehat{\tau}^{-1}:\Theta(F_2)\rightarrow\Theta(F_1\times F_3) $ the elements of $G$ are of the form $(x,y)\in F_1\times F_3\mapsto (\alpha(x),\beta(x,y))$ where $\alpha\in G'$ and $(\alpha,\beta)\in \Theta(F_1\times F_3)$. In other words, $\widehat{\tau}^{-1}(G)$ is a subgroup of $\Theta(F_1\times F_3,(F_1,F_3))$ the graded translation group of $F$ with grading $(F_1,F_3)$.

nodes.name: Graded free covers of inverse systems of CFR nilspaces
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a compact $k$-step nilspace, and let $(\mathrm{X}_j)_{j\in\mathbb{N}}$ be any inverse system of $k$-step \textsc{cfr} nilspaces such that $\mathrm{X}=\varprojlim \mathrm{X}_j$. Then there is a graded pro-free nilspace $(F',(F_i')_{i\in\mathbb{N}})$ such that for every $j\in \mathbb{N}$ there is a fiber-discrete, fiber-cocompact subgroup $G_j$ of the graded translation group of $(\prod_{i=1}^j F_i',(F_i')_{i\le j})$ such that $(\mathrm{X}_j\cong \prod_{i=1}^j F_i')/G_j$. Moreover the groups $G_j$ together with the homomorphisms $\widehat{p_{\ell,j}}:\Theta(\prod_{i\le j} F_i',(F_i')_{i\le j})\rightarrow \Theta(\prod_{i\le \ell} F_i',(F_i')_{i\le \ell})$, $j,\ell\in \mathbb{N}$, form an inverse system of topological groups with $\widehat{p_{\ell,j}}(G_j)=G_\ell$ for all $j\ge \ell$.

nodes.name: Lifting points through the inverse limit
nodes.statement: The case $n=0$ of Lemma \ref{lem:strong-surjectivity} implies that in diagram \eqref{eq:inv-lim-2}, if $(x_i)_{i\in \mathbb{N}}\in \varprojlim \mathrm{X}_i$ and for some $j\in \mathbb{N}$ we fix any preimage $y_j\in \tilde F_j$ of $x_j\in \mathrm{X}_j$, then there exists $(y_i')_{i\in \mathbb{N}}\in \varprojlim \tilde F_i$ such that $y_j'=y_j$ and $y_i'\mapsto x_i$ for all $i\in \mathbb{N}$. The proof consists in constructing inductively the sequence $y_i'$. Given $y'_j$, note that by taking its image through the maps $\tilde{F}_j\rightarrow \tilde{F}_{j-1}\rightarrow \cdots$ we can form $y'_i$ for $i\le j$ satisfying the requirements of the lemma. nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 8.13
nodes.statement: Let $(\mathrm{X}_i)_{i\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of $k$-step \textsc{cfr} nilspaces such that $\mathrm{X}=\varprojlim \mathrm{X}_i$ (with limit maps $\zeta_i:\mathrm{X}\rightarrow \mathrm{X}_i$), let $F'$ and $G_i$ ($i\in\mathbb{N}$) be the objects resulting from applying Theorem \ref{thm:covering-of-inverse limit}, and let $G:=\varprojlim G_i$. For any $j\in \mathbb{N}$ we have the following commutative diagram: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned}[c] \begin{tikzpicture} \matrix (m) [matrix of math nodes,row sep=2em,column sep=4em,minimum width=2em] {F' & F'/G & \mathrm{X} \\ \prod_{i=1}^jF_i'& & \mathrm{X}_j. \\}; \path[-stealth] (m-1-1) edge node [above] {$\pi_G$} (m-1-2) (m-1-2) edge node [above] {$\varphi$} (m-1-3) (m-1-1) edge node [right] {$p_j$} (m-2-1) (m-2-1) edge node [above] {$\psi_j$} (m-2-3) (m-1-3) edge node [right] {$\zeta_j$} (m-2-3); \end{tikzpicture} \end{aligned} \end{equation} \vspace{-0.3cm} We have to prove that $\varphi$ is a well-defined map and an isomorphism of compact nilspaces. We first define a map $\tilde\varphi:F'\rightarrow \mathrm{X}$ using the inverse limit expression of $\mathrm{X}$, namely $\tilde\varphi: (f_i)_{i\in \mathbb{N}}\in F'=\prod_{i=1}^\infty F_i' \mapsto (\psi_j(p_j((f_i)_{i\in \mathbb{N}}))))_{j\in \mathbb{N}}$ where $p_j$ is just the projection to the first $j$ coordinates. We claim that $\tilde \varphi$ factors through $\pi_G$, thus yielding a well-defined map $\varphi:F'/G\rightarrow \mathrm{X}$ such that $\tilde\varphi=\varphi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\pi_G$. To prove this, suppose that $\pi_G((f_i)_{i\in \mathbb{N}})=\pi_G((h_i)_{i\in \mathbb{N}})$. Then there exists $g = (g_j)_{j\in \mathbb{N}}\in G$ where $g_j\in G_j\subset \Theta(\prod_{i=1}^j F_i',(F_i')_{i\in[j]})$ such that for all $j\in \mathbb{N}$, $g_j(f_1,\ldots,f_j)=(h_1,\ldots,h_j)$. As $\psi_j$ is invariant under the action of $G_j$ the claim follows. Let us now prove that the well-defined map $\varphi$ is bijective. For injectivity, suppose that $\varphi(\pi_G((f_i)_{i\in \mathbb{N}}))=\varphi(\pi_G((h_i)_{i\in \mathbb{N}}))$. Then $\psi_j(f_1,\ldots,f_j)= \psi_j(h_1,\ldots,h_j)$ for every $j\in \mathbb{N}$. Starting with $\psi_1(f_1)= \psi_1(h_1)$, by definition of $\psi_1$ there is $g_1\in G_1$ such that $g_1(f_1)=h_1$. Then, by Remark \ref{rem:lifting-of-consistent-trans} there is $g_2\in G_2$ such that $g_2\mapsto g_1$ and $g_2(f_1,f_2)=(h_1,h_2)$. Continuing this process, we deduce that there exists $g=(g_j)\in \varprojlim G_j$ with $g(f_i)_{i\in \mathbb{N}}=(h_i)_{i\in \mathbb{N}}$, whence $\pi_G((f_i)_{i\in \mathbb{N}})=\pi_G((h_i)_{i\in \mathbb{N}})$, which proves injectivity. Surjectivity follows from Lemma \ref{lem:strong-surjectivity}. By the second part of Remark \ref{rem:lifting-of-consistent-trans} we have that $G=\varprojlim G_i$ is fiber-transitive on $F'$. Lemma \ref{lem:strong-surjectivity} implies that $\varphi$ is an isomorphism of nilspaces (in the sense that $\varphi$ and $\varphi^{-1}$ send cubes to cubes). To see that $\varphi$ is a homeomorphism, it suffices prove that it is continuous and open. To prove that $\varphi$ is continuous note that by definition of inverse limit and the quotient topology on $F'/G$ it suffices to prove that $\zeta_j\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \varphi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \pi_G$ is continuous for every $j\in \mathbb{N}$. However this map equals $\psi_j\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} p_j$ which is continuous. To prove that $\varphi$ is open note first that the sets of the form $p_j^{-1}(U)$ for any $j\in \mathbb{N}$ and any $U\subset \prod_{i=1}^j F_i'$ form a basis of the topology of $F'$. Thus it is enough to prove that for any such $p_j^{-1}(U)$, $\varphi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \pi_G(p_j^{-1}(U))$ is open. By Lemma \ref{lem:strong-surjectivity} (for $n=0$) we have that $\varphi(\pi_G(p_j^{-1}(U))) = \zeta_j^{-1}(\psi_j(U))$. As $\psi_j$ is an open map the result follows. Finally, we need to prove that for every $n\in \mathbb{N}$, the cube set $\mathrm{C}^n(F'/G)$ is a closed subset of $(F'/G)^{\db{n}}$. However, as $\varphi^{\db{n}}:(F'/G)^{\db{n}}\rightarrow \mathrm{X}^{\db{n}}$ is a homeomorphism and $\varphi^{\db{n}}(\mathrm{C}^n(F'/G))=\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$, the closure of $\mathrm{C}^n(F'/G)$ follows from that of $\mathrm{C}^n(\mathrm{X})$.

nodes.name: Graded pro-free nilspaces as coset spaces of graded translation groups
nodes.statement: Let $(F',(F_i')_{i=1}^\infty)$ be a graded pro-free nilspace, and let $G=\Theta(F',(F_i')_{i=1}^\infty)$. Fix any $f_0\in F'$ and let $K:=\mathrm{Stab}_G(f_0)=\{\alpha\in G: \alpha(f_0)=f_0\}$. The following properties hold: \setlength{\leftmargini}{0.7cm} \begin{enumerate} \item The map $\psi:K\backslash G\rightarrow F'$ defined as $Kg\mapsto g^{-1}(f_0)$ is a homeomorphism and a nilspace isomorphism.\footnote{Note that as we have not defined a category of \emph{Polish} nilspaces (as we highlighted in Remark \ref{rem:not-gen-theory}), here we simply show that $\psi$ is an isomorphism as an algebraic nilspace morphism and also that it is a homeomorphism when $F'$ and $K\backslash G$ are endowed with the product and the compact-open topology respectively, see Lemma \ref{lem:top-graded-trans-gr}.} \item The map $\psi$ is equivariant with respect to the action of $G$ on $K\backslash G$ defined as $(Kg,g')\in (K\backslash G)\times G\mapsto Kg{g'}^{-1}$ and on $F'$ defined as $(f,g)\in F'\times \Theta(F',(F_i')_{i=1}^\infty)\mapsto g(f)$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 8.14
nodes.statement: Many parts of this result follow by the same arguments as in Lemma \ref{lem_aux-for-dou-coset}. In particular, all algebraic statements ($\psi$ being a nilspace isomorphism and its claimed equivariance) follow by the same arguments. Hence, it only remains to check that $\psi$ is a homeomorphism. To do so, note that for any $j\in \mathbb{N}$, letting $F_j:=\prod_{i=1}^j F_i'$, the following diagram commutes: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned}[c] \begin{tikzpicture} \matrix (m) [matrix of math nodes,row sep=1.5em,column sep=4em,minimum width=2em] {\Theta(F',(F_i')_{i\in \mathbb{N}}) & F' \\ \Theta(F_j,(F_i')_{i=1}^j) & F_j. \\}; \path[-stealth] (m-1-1) edge node [above] {$\psi'$} (m-1-2) (m-1-1) edge node [right] {$p_j'$} (m-2-1) (m-2-1) edge node [above] {$\psi_j'$} (m-2-2) (m-1-2) edge node [right] {$p_j$} (m-2-2); \end{tikzpicture} \end{aligned} \end{equation} \vspace{-0.3cm} \noindent Here $p_j'$ is just the restriction to the $F_j$ coordinates, $p_j$ is the usual projection to $F_j$, $\psi'(g):=g^{-1}(f_0)$, and $\psi_j'(p_j'(g)):=p_j'(g^{-1})(p_j(f_0))$. In order to analyze this diagram, it is useful to analyze first what happens between the different factors of the inverse limits of $F'$ and $\Theta(F',(F_i')_{i\in \mathbb{N}})$. In fact, for any $j\in \mathbb{N}$ we have the following diagram: \begin{equation} \begin{tikzpicture} \matrix (m) [matrix of math nodes,row sep=1.5em,column sep=4em,minimum width=2em] {\Theta(F',(F_i')_{i\in \mathbb{N}}) & \Theta(F_j,(F_i')_{i=1}^j) & \Theta(F_{j-1},(F_i')_{i=1}^{j-1}) & \Theta(F_1,(F_1')) \\ F' & F_j & F_{j-1} & F_1. \\}; \path[dotted,->] (m-1-1) edge node [above] {} (m-1-2) (m-2-1) edge node [above] {} (m-2-2) (m-1-3) edge node [above] {} (m-1-4) (m-2-3) edge node [above] {} (m-2-4); \path[-stealth] (m-1-2) edge node [above] {$p_{j-1,j}'$} (m-1-3) (m-1-2) edge node [right] {$\psi_j'$} (m-2-2) (m-2-2) edge node [above] {$p_{j-1,j}$} (m-2-3) (m-1-3) edge node [right] {$\psi_{j-1}'$} (m-2-3) (m-1-4) edge node [right] {$\psi_1'$} (m-2-4) (m-1-1) edge node [right] {$\psi'$} (m-2-1); \end{tikzpicture} \end{equation} Now let $f\in F'$ and for any $j\in \mathbb{N}$ let $g^{(j-1)}\in \Theta(F_{j-1},(F_i')_{i=1}^{j-1})$ be such that $\psi'_{j-1}(g)=p_j(f)$. We claim that there exists $g\in \Theta(F',(F_i')_{i\in \mathbb{N}})$ such that $\psi'(g)=f$ and $p_j'(g)=g^{(j-1)}$. To see this, note that by induction it suffices to lift $g^{(j-1)}$ to an element in $\Theta(F_{j},(F_i')_{i=1}^{j})$ with the desired properties. In fact, since we are considering the graded translations, it is clear that we can find such an element. That is, any element of $F_{j}=(F_i')_{i=1}^{j}$ is of the form $(f',f^{(j-1)})\in F_j'\times F_{j-1}$ and we know that $(g^{(j-1)})^{-1}(f_0)=f^{(j-1)}$. The translation $g^{(j)}\in \Theta(F_j,(F_i')_{i=1}^j)$ defined as $(a,b)\in F_j'\times F_{j-1}\mapsto(a+f_0-f',g^{(j-1)}(b))$ works. The map $\psi'$ factorizes as $\psi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \pi_K$, where $\pi_K:G\rightarrow K\backslash G$ is the quotient map to the space of right cosets (recall that $G=\Theta(F',(F_i')_{i\in \mathbb{N}})$). To prove that $\psi$ is a homeomorphism it suffices to check that $\psi'$ is open and continuous. Continuity follows from the fact that by definition of $F'$ it suffices to prove that $p_j\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \psi'$ is continuous for every $j\in \mathbb{N}$. Since this equals $\psi_j'\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} p_j'$, which is clearly continuous, the continuity of $\psi'$ follows. To prove openness, note that it is enough to prove it for the basis of the topology on $G$ consisting of sets of the form ${p_j'}^{-1}(U)$ where $U\subset \Theta(F_j,(F_i')_{i=1}^j)$ is open and $j\in \mathbb{N}$. Arguing just as in the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:cpct-as-quotient-of-infinite-free}, by the previous paragraph we have that $\psi'({p_j'}^{-1}(U)) = p_j^{-1}(\psi_j(U))$, and the openness follows.

nodes.name: $\psi$ is a homeomorphism
nodes.statement: The map $\psi'$ factorizes as $\psi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \pi_K$, where $\pi_K:G\rightarrow K\backslash G$ is the quotient map to the space of right cosets (recall that $G=\Theta(F',(F_i')_{i\in \mathbb{N}})$). To prove that $\psi$ is a homeomorphism it suffices to check that $\psi'$ is open and continuous. Continuity follows from the fact that by definition of $F'$ it suffices to prove that $p_j\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \psi'$ is continuous for every $j\in \mathbb{N}$. Since this equals $\psi_j'\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} p_j'$, which is clearly continuous, the continuity of $\psi'$ follows. To prove openness, note that it is enough to prove it for the basis of the topology on $G$ consisting of sets of the form ${p_j'}^{-1}(U)$ where $U\subset \Theta(F_j,(F_i')_{i=1}^j)$ is open and $j\in \mathbb{N}$. Arguing just as in the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:cpct-as-quotient-of-infinite-free}, by the previous paragraph we have that $\psi'({p_j'}^{-1}(U)) = p_j^{-1}(\psi_j(U))$, and the openness follows.

nodes.name: Compact nilspaces as double-coset nilspaces of pro-Lie groups
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step compact nilspace. Then there exists a $k$-step graded pro-free nilspace $(F',(F_i')_{i\in \mathbb{N}})$ such that, letting $G$ be the degree-$k$ filtered pro-Lie group $\Theta(F',(F_i')_{i\in \mathbb{N}})$, and letting $K$ be the closed pro-Lie subgroup\footnote{Here we took the stabilizer of the constant $\underline{0}$ element, but this can be replaced by any element of $F'=(F_i')_{i\in \mathbb{N}}$.} $\mathrm{Stab}_G(\underline{0})$, there is a fiber-transitive pro-discrete subgroup $\Gamma$ of $G$ such that the following properties hold: \setlength{\leftmargini}{0.7cm} \begin{enumerate} \item For $j\in \mathbb{N}$ let $p_j':\Theta(F',(F_i')_{i\in \mathbb{N}})\rightarrow \Theta(\prod_{i=1}^jF_i',(F_i')_{i\le j})$ be the projection to the $j$-th factor. Then $p_j'(\Gamma)$ acting on $\prod_{i=1}^jF_i'$ is fiber-transitive, fiber-discrete and fiber-cocompact. \item The double-coset nilspace $K\backslash G/\Gamma$ endowed with the quotient topology is isomorphic as a compact nilspace to $\mathrm{X}$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 8 Compact nilspaces as quotients of pro-free nilspaces and as double-coset nilspaces
assumptions: Let $\mathrm{X}$ be a $k$-step compact nilspace.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 8.15
nodes.statement: This follows from combining Lemma \ref{lem:inf-free-as-quo-of-trans-by-k} with Theorem \ref{thm:cpct-as-quotient-of-infinite-free}.

nodes.name: Morphisms into discrete groups ignore continuous coordinates
nodes.statement: Let $F=\prod_{i=1}^k \mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{Z}^{a_i}\times \mathbb{R}^{b_i})$ be a free nilspace where $a_i,b_i\ge 0$ for $i\in[k]$. Let $A$ be a discrete finitely generated abelian group. Let $\phi:F\rightarrow \mathcal{D}_k(A)$ be a continuous morphism. Then $\phi(x,y)=\phi(x,0)$ for every $x\in \prod_{i=1}^k \mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{Z}^{a_i})$ and $y\in \prod_{i=1}^k \mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{R}^{b_i})$. \footnote{Here we wrote $0$ for the element of $\prod_{i=1}^k \mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{R}^{b_i})$ with all coordinates equal to zero.}
nodes.section: A Polynomials between free nilspaces
assumptions: Let $F=\prod_{i=1}^k \mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{Z}^{a_i}\times \mathbb{R}^{b_i})$ be a free nilspace where $a_i,b_i\ge 0$ for $i\in[k]$.
Let $A$ be a discrete finitely generated abelian group.
Let $\phi:F\rightarrow \mathcal{D}_k(A)$ be a continuous morphism.
conclusions:
Then  $\phi(x,y)=\phi(x,0)$
for every $x\in \prod_{i=1}^k \mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{Z}^{a_i})$ and $y\in \prod_{i=1}^k \mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{R}^{b_i})$.
nodes.label: lem:non-dep-cont-coord

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma A.1
nodes.statement: The morphism property of $\phi$ plays no role, this is purely a topological result. For any $x\in \prod_{i=1}^k\mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{Z}^{a_i})$ let $\phi_x:\prod_{i=1}^k\mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{R}^{b_i})\rightarrow \mathcal{D}_k(A)$ be the map $\phi_x(y):=\phi(x,y)$. Clearly, $\phi_x$ is also continuous, and as $\prod_{i=1}^k\mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{R}^{b_i})$ is connected and $\mathcal{D}_k(A)$ is discrete we have that $\phi_x$ must be constant. Thus $\phi_x(y)=\phi_x(0)$ for any $y\in \prod_{i=1}^k\mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{R}^{b_i})$, as claimed.
nodes.section: A Polynomials between free nilspaces
nodes.statement_short: Continuous maps from a connected space to a discrete one are constant.

nodes.name: Restriction to a fiber
nodes.statement: The morphism property of $\phi$ plays no role, this is purely a topological result. For any $x\in \prod_{i=1}^k\mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{Z}^{a_i})$ let $\phi_x:\prod_{i=1}^k\mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{R}^{b_i})\rightarrow \mathcal{D}_k(A)$ be the map $\phi_x(y):=\phi(x,y)$.

nodes.name: Connectedness

nodes.statement_short: Constant on the connected continuous part.

nodes.name: Morphisms between higher-degree abelian groups
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{Z}$, $\mathrm{Z}'$ be abelian groups and let $k,\ell\in\mathbb{N}$. Then \begin{equation} \hom(\mathcal{D}_{\ell}(\mathrm{Z}),\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}'))= \hom(\mathcal{D}_1(\mathrm{Z}),\mathcal{D}_{\lfloor k/\ell\rfloor}(\mathrm{Z}')). \end{equation}
nodes.section: A Polynomials between free nilspaces
assumptions: Let $\mathrm{Z}$, $\mathrm{Z}'$ be abelian groups and let $k,\ell\in\mathbb{N}$.
nodes.label: lem:higher-ab-hom-set

nodes.name: $\hom(\mathcal{D}_\ell(\mathrm{Z}),\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}'))=\hom(\mathcal{D}_1(\mathrm{Z}),\mathcal{D}_{\lfloor k/\ell\rfloor}(\mathrm{Z}'))$
nodes.statement: \hom(\mathcal{D}_{\ell}(\mathrm{Z}),\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}'))= \hom(\mathcal{D}_1(\mathrm{Z}),\mathcal{D}_{\lfloor k/\ell\rfloor}(\mathrm{Z}')).
nodes.section: A Polynomials between free nilspaces

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma A.2
nodes.statement: Assume first that $\ell\le k$. To see that $\hom(\mathcal{D}_{\ell}(\mathrm{Z}),\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}'))\subset \hom(\mathcal{D}_1(\mathrm{Z}),\mathcal{D}_{\lfloor k/\ell\rfloor}(\mathrm{Z}'))$, fix any $f\in \hom(\mathcal{D}_\ell(\mathrm{Z}),\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}'))$ and note that by \cite[Theorem 2.2.14]{Cand:Notes1} it suffices to check that for every $z_1,\ldots,z_t\in \mathrm{Z}$ the derivative $\partial_{z_1}\cdots \partial_{z_t}f$ takes values in the $t$-th term of the filtration defining $\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}')$. Note that this holds trivially if any of the $z_i$ is 0 (as then the derivative vanishes). Note that it is also clear if $t\le \lfloor k/\ell\rfloor$, since then we have to check that the derivative is $\mathrm{Z}'$-valued, which holds trivially. Thus, the only non-trivial case is when $t\ge \lfloor k/\ell\rfloor+1$, in which case we have to check that $\partial_{z_1}\cdots \partial_{z_t}f$ is the 0 function. Since $f\in \hom(\mathcal{D}_\ell(\mathrm{Z}),\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}'))$, viewing the elements $z_i$ as elements of the $\ell$-th term of the filtration defining $\mathcal{D}_\ell(\mathrm{Z})$ (this term being $\mathrm{Z}$), we see that $\partial_{z_1}\cdots \partial_{z_t}f$ takes values in the $t\ell$-th term of the filtration $\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}')$. By assumption $t\ell\ge \ell(\lfloor k/\ell\rfloor+1)\ge k+1$, so the derivative takes values in the $(k+1)$-th term of the filtration associated with $\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}')$, which is $\{0\}$ as required. This proves the desired inclusion. To see the opposite inclusion, let $f\in \hom(\mathcal{D}_1(\mathrm{Z}),\mathcal{D}_{\lfloor k/\ell\rfloor}(\mathrm{Z}'))$ and note that, again, the only non-trivial case consists in checking that for every $z_1,\ldots,z_t\in \mathrm{Z}$ with $\ell t\ge k+1$ we have $\partial_{z_1}\cdots \partial_{z_t}f=0$. Note that the last inequality implies that $t\ge \lceil (k+1)/\ell\rceil$, and it is easily shown that we always have $\lceil (k+1)/\ell\rceil=\lfloor k/\ell\rfloor+1$, so $t\ge \lfloor k/\ell\rfloor+1$ and therefore, since $f\in \hom(\mathcal{D}_1(\mathrm{Z}),\mathcal{D}_{\lfloor k/\ell\rfloor}(\mathrm{Z}'))$, the derivative in question is indeed 0. This proves the case $\ell\leq k$. To complete the proof, suppose that $\ell>k$, and fix any $f\in \hom(\mathcal{D}_l(\mathrm{Z}),\mathcal{D}_k(\mathrm{Z}'))$. To see that $f$ must be constant, fix any $z\in \mathrm{Z}$ and consider $\mathrm{c}_z\in \mathrm{C}^{k+1}(\mathrm{Z})$ the cube such that $\mathrm{c}_z(1^{k+1})=z$ and $\mathrm{c}_z(v)=0$ for any $v\neq 1^{k+1}$. Then $f\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}_z\in \mathrm{C}^{k+1}(\mathrm{Z}')$. By unique corner-completion in the latter nilspace, we have that $f\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\mathrm{c}_z$ is the constant cube with value $f(0)$, so in particular $f\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \mathrm{c}_z(1^{k+1})=f(z)=f(0)$. Since $z$ was arbitrary, we deduce that $f$ is indeed constant.
nodes.section: A Polynomials between free nilspaces
nodes.statement_short: Compare vanishing of iterated derivatives in both filtrations; for $\ell>k$ morphisms are constant by unique completion.

nodes.name: Binomial coefficients are morphisms
nodes.statement: Let $n$ be a non-negative integer, and let $\binom{\cdot}{n}$ denote the map $\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ sending $x$ to the binomial coefficient $\binom{x}{n}$. Then for every $i\ge 1$ the map $\binom{\cdot}{n}$ is a morphism $\mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{Z})\rightarrow \mathcal{D}_{ni}(\mathbb{Z})$.
nodes.section: A Polynomials between free nilspaces
assumptions: Let $n$ be a non-negative integer, and let  $\binom{\cdot}{n}$ denote the map $\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ sending $x$ to the binomial coefficient $\binom{x}{n}$.
conclusions: Then for every $i\ge 1$ the map $\binom{\cdot}{n}$ is a morphism $\mathcal{D}_i(\mathbb{Z})\rightarrow \mathcal{D}_{ni}(\mathbb{Z})$.
nodes.label: lem:binompoly

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma A.3
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lem:higher-ab-hom-set}, it suffices to prove the case $i=1$, namely, that $\binom{\cdot}{n}$ is a polynomial map of degree $n$. This is clear (note that $\partial_1 \binom{x}{n}=\binom{x}{n-1}$ for any $x\in \mathbb{Z}$).
nodes.section: A Polynomials between free nilspaces
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $i=1$ by Lemma A.2; binomial coefficients are polynomials of degree $n$.

nodes.name: Products of morphisms into $\mathcal{D}_q(\mathbb{Z})$
nodes.statement: For $i\in\{0,1\}$, let $(G^{(i)},G^{(i)}_\bullet)$ be a filtered abelian group and for some $q_i\in \mathbb{N}$ let $\phi^{(i)}:G^{(i)}\rightarrow \mathcal{D}_{q_i}(\mathbb{Z})$ be a morphism. Let $\mathrm{X}$ be the nilspace associated with the group $G^{(0)}\times G^{(1)}$ equipped with the product filtration $G^{(0)}_\bullet\times G^{(1)}_\bullet$. Then the map $\psi:\mathrm{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{D}_{q_0+q_1}(\mathbb{Z})$, $(x_0,x_1)\mapsto\phi^{(0)}(x_0)\,\phi^{(1)}(x_1)$ is a morphism.
nodes.section: A Polynomials between free nilspaces
assumptions: For $i\in\{0,1\}$, let $(G^{(i)},G^{(i)}_\bullet)$ be  a filtered abelian group and for some $q_i\in \mathbb{N}$ let $\phi^{(i)}:G^{(i)}\rightarrow \mathcal{D}_{q_i}(\mathbb{Z})$ be a morphism.
Let $\mathrm{X}$ be the nilspace associated with the group $G^{(0)}\times G^{(1)}$ equipped with the product filtration $G^{(0)}_\bullet\times G^{(1)}_\bullet$.
conclusions: Then the map $\psi:\mathrm{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{D}_{q_0+q_1}(\mathbb{Z})$, $(x_0,x_1)\mapsto\phi^{(0)}(x_0)\,\phi^{(1)}(x_1)$ is a morphism.
nodes.label: lem:prodpolys

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma A.4
nodes.statement: By \cite[Theorem 2.2.14]{Cand:Notes1} it suffices to show that $\psi$ is a polynomial map between the corresponding filtered groups. Note that if $g_i\in G^{(i)}$ for $i\in\{0,1\}$ we have that $\partial_{(g_0,g_1)}\psi(x_0,x_1)=\partial_{(0,g_1)}\psi(x_0+g_0,x_1)+\partial_{(g_0,0)}\psi(x_0,x_1)$. Thus it suffices to prove that the derivatives lie in the correct term in the filtration when we derivate only with respect to elements that are 0 in either the first or the second coordinate. By construction of $\psi$, if we take the derivative with respect to the elements $(g_0^1,0),\ldots,(g_0^t,0),(0,g_1^1),\ldots,(0,g_1^s)\in G^{(0)}\times G^{(1)}$ for some integers $t,s\ge 0$ we have that \[ \partial_{(g_0^1,0)}\cdots \partial_{(g_0^t,0)}\partial_{(0,g_1^1)}\cdots \partial_{(0,g_1^s)}\psi(x_0,x_1)= \partial_{(g_0^1,0)}\cdots \partial_{(g_0^t,0)}\phi^{(0)}(x_0) \partial_{(0,g_1^1)}\cdots \partial_{(0,g_1^s)}\phi^{(1)}(x_1). \] Thus, if the elements $g_0^i\in G^{(0)}_{u_i}$ for all $i\in [t]$ for some integers $u_i\ge 1$ and $g_1^j\in G^{(1)}_{v_j}$ for all $j\in [t]$ for some integers $v_j\ge 0$ we have $ \begin{cases} \partial_{(g_0^1,0)}\cdots \partial_{(g_0^t,0)}\phi^{(0)}(x_0)\in G^{(0)}_{u_1+\cdots+u_t} \\ \partial_{(0,g_1^1)}\cdots \partial_{(0,g_1^s)}\phi^{(1)}(x_1) \in G^{(1)}_{v_1+\cdots+v_s}. \end{cases}$. Hence, if $(u_1+\cdots+u_t)+(v_1+\cdots+v_s)>q_0+q_1$ it must happen that either $(u_1+\cdots+u_t)>q_0$ or $(v_1+\cdots+v_s)>q_1$. In either case we conclude that the corresponding derivative of $\psi$ is $0$.
nodes.section: A Polynomials between free nilspaces
nodes.statement_short: Leibniz-type expansion of derivatives of a product of morphisms.

nodes.name: Reduce to separated derivatives
nodes.statement: By \cite[Theorem 2.2.14]{Cand:Notes1} it suffices to show that $\psi$ is a polynomial map between the corresponding filtered groups. Note that if $g_i\in G^{(i)}$ for $i\in\{0,1\}$ we have that $\partial_{(g_0,g_1)}\psi(x_0,x_1)=\partial_{(0,g_1)}\psi(x_0+g_0,x_1)+\partial_{(g_0,0)}\psi(x_0,x_1)$. Thus it suffices to prove that the derivatives lie in the correct term in the filtration when we derivate only with respect to elements that are 0 in either the first or the second coordinate.

nodes.name: Product rule
nodes.statement:
By construction of $\psi$, if we take the derivative with respect to the elements $(g_0^1,0),\ldots,(g_0^t,0),(0,g_1^1),\ldots,(0,g_1^s)\in G^{(0)}\times G^{(1)}$ for some integers $t,s\ge 0$ we have that
\[
\partial_{(g_0^1,0)}\cdots \partial_{(g_0^t,0)}\partial_{(0,g_1^1)}\cdots \partial_{(0,g_1^s)}\psi(x_0,x_1)= \partial_{(g_0^1,0)}\cdots \partial_{(g_0^t,0)}\phi^{(0)}(x_0) \partial_{(0,g_1^1)}\cdots \partial_{(0,g_1^s)}\phi^{(1)}(x_1).
\]
Thus, if the elements $g_0^i\in G^{(0)}_{u_i}$ for all $i\in [t]$ for some integers $u_i\ge 1$ and $g_1^j\in G^{(1)}_{v_j}$ for all $j\in [t]$ for some integers $v_j\ge 0$ we have $
\begin{cases}
 \partial_{(g_0^1,0)}\cdots \partial_{(g_0^t,0)}\phi^{(0)}(x_0)\in G^{(0)}_{u_1+\cdots+u_t} \\
 \partial_{(0,g_1^1)}\cdots \partial_{(0,g_1^s)}\phi^{(1)}(x_1) \in G^{(1)}_{v_1+\cdots+v_s}.
\end{cases}$.
nodes.section: A Polynomials between free nilspaces

nodes.name: Degree count
nodes.statement: Hence, if $(u_1+\cdots+u_t)+(v_1+\cdots+v_s)>q_0+q_1$ it must happen that either $(u_1+\cdots+u_t)>q_0$ or $(v_1+\cdots+v_s)>q_1$. In either case we conclude that the corresponding derivative of $\psi$ is $0$.

nodes.name: Filtered degree $|m|$ on discrete free nilspaces
