nodes.name: Proof of Theorem A.6
nodes.statement: First note that the set $T:=\{m\in \prod_{i=1}^k \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^{a_i}: |m|\le k\}$ is a finite set. Let us define $e_{i_0,j_0}\in \prod_{i=1}^k \mathbb{Z}^{a_i}$ as the element that equals 1 only at the coordinate indexed by $i_0\in[k]$ and $j_0\in[a_{i_0}]$ and 0 otherwise. Note that if $m\notin T$, by \cite[Theorem 2.2.14]{Cand:Notes1} we have $\partial_{e_{1,1}}^{m_{1,1}}\cdots \partial_{e_{k,a_k}}^{m_{k,a_k}}\phi(x)=0$. Given two elements $m,m'\in \prod_{i=1}^k \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^{a_i}$, we write $m\le m'$ if $m_{i,j}\le m'_{i,j}$ for all $i\in[k]$ and $j\in[a_i]$. We write $m<m'$ if $m\not=m'$ and $m\le m'$. Let $S\subset \prod_{i=1}^k \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^{a_i}$ be any finite subset. We say that $S$ is \emph{simplicial} if for every $m\in S$ and every $m'\le m$ we have $m'\in S$. For any function $\psi:\prod_{i=1}^k \mathbb{Z}^{a_i}\rightarrow A$, let us define the \emph{support} of $\psi$ as follows: \[ {\rm supp}(\psi):=\prod_{i=1}^k \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^{a_i}\setminus\left\{m \in \prod_{i=1}^k \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^{a_i}: \partial_{e_{1,1}}^{m_{1,1}}\cdots \partial_{e_{k,a_k}}^{m_{k,a_k}}\phi(x)=0 \text{ for all }x\in \prod_{i=1}^k \mathbb{Z}^{a_i}\right\}. \] Note that if $\phi:F\rightarrow \mathcal{D}_k(A)$ is a morphism then its support is finite, since ${\rm supp}(\phi)\subset \{m \in \prod_{i=1}^k \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^{a_i}:|m|\le k\}$. Note also that ${\rm supp}(\psi)$ is always a simplicial set. We shall now prove that if $\psi:\prod_{i=1}^k \mathbb{Z}^{a_i}\rightarrow A$ has finite support then $\psi(x)=\sum_{m\in {\rm supp}(\psi)}a_m \binom{x}{m}$ for some coefficients $a_m\in A$. In particular this will imply the result for morphisms on discrete free nilspaces. The proof will argue by induction on the size of ${\rm supp}(\psi)$. Clearly, if $|{\rm supp}(\psi)|=0$ then the result holds trivially. Suppose then that $k:=|{\rm supp}(\psi)|>0$, and let $m\in {\rm supp}(\psi)$ be any element such that there is no other $m'\in {\rm supp}(\psi)$ with $m<m'$. We claim that $\psi'(x):=\partial_{e_{1,1}}^{m_{1,1}}\cdots \partial_{e_{k,a_k}}^{m_{k,a_k}}\psi(x)$ is a constant function of $x\in \prod_{i=1}^k \mathbb{Z}^{a_i}$. Indeed, note that for any $a\in \prod_{i=1}^k \mathbb{Z}^{a_i}$ we have $\partial_a \psi'(x)=\psi'(x+a)-\psi'(x)=0$ for all $x\in \prod_{i=1}^k \mathbb{Z}^{a_i}$, since we can decompose this derivative as a sum of derivatives with respect to the elements $e_{i,j}$. As those are all 0, so is $\partial_a\psi'(x)$, and therefore $\psi'(x)$ is indeed constant. Let us denote this constant by $\lambda$. We then claim that $\psi^*(x):=\psi(x)-\lambda\binom{x}{m} $ is a map from $\prod_{i=1}^k \mathbb{Z}^{a_i}$ to $A$ such that ${\rm supp}(\psi^*)\subset {\rm supp}(\psi)\setminus \{m\}$. The fact that $n$ is not included in the support of $\psi^*$ follows by definition and noting that $\partial_{e_{i,j}} \binom{x_{i,j}}{t} = \binom{x_{i,j}}{t-1}$ for any integer $t\ge 0$. Furthermore, using the latter formula it is easy to check that the term \[ \partial_{e_{1,1}}^{m'_{1,1}}\cdots \partial_{e_{k,a_k}}^{m'_{k,a_k}}\binom{x}{m}=\partial_{e_{1,1}}^{m'_{1,1}}\cdots \partial_{e_{k,a_k}}^{m'_{k,a_k}}\left(\lambda\prod_{i=1}^k\prod_{j=1}^{a_i} \binom{x_{i,j}}{n_{i,j}}\right) = \lambda\prod_{i=1}^k\prod_{j=1}^{a_i}\partial_{e_{i,j}}^{n'_{i,j}}\binom{x_{i,j}}{m_{i,j}} \] vanishes as soon as there exists some $(i,j)\in [k]\times [a_i]$ such that $m'_{i,j}>m_{i,j}$. This confirms that ${\rm supp}(\psi^*)\subset {\rm supp}(\psi)\setminus \{m\}$. By induction we have $\psi^*(x)=\sum_{m'\in {\rm supp}(\psi^*)}a_{m'} \binom{x}{m'}$, and then $\psi(x) =\lambda\binom{x}{m}+ \sum_{m'\in {\rm supp}(\psi^*)}a_{m'} \binom{x}{m'}$. The result follows.

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement:
Suppose then that $k:=|{\rm supp}(\psi)|>0$, and let $m\in {\rm supp}(\psi)$ be any element such that there is no other $m'\in {\rm supp}(\psi)$ with $m<m'$. We claim that $\psi'(x):=\partial_{e_{1,1}}^{m_{1,1}}\cdots \partial_{e_{k,a_k}}^{m_{k,a_k}}\psi(x)$ is a constant  function of $x\in \prod_{i=1}^k \mathbb{Z}^{a_i}$. Indeed, note that for any $a\in \prod_{i=1}^k \mathbb{Z}^{a_i}$ we have $\partial_a \psi'(x)=\psi'(x+a)-\psi'(x)=0$ for all $x\in \prod_{i=1}^k \mathbb{Z}^{a_i}$, since we can decompose this derivative as a sum of derivatives with respect to the elements $e_{i,j}$. As those are all 0,  so is $\partial_a\psi'(x)$, and therefore $\psi'(x)$ is indeed constant. Let us denote this constant by $\lambda$. 
We then claim that $\psi^*(x):=\psi(x)-\lambda\binom{x}{m}
$ is a map from $\prod_{i=1}^k \mathbb{Z}^{a_i}$ to $A$ such that ${\rm supp}(\psi^*)\subset {\rm supp}(\psi)\setminus \{m\}$.

The fact that $n$ is not included in the support of $\psi^*$ follows by definition and noting that $\partial_{e_{i,j}} \binom{x_{i,j}}{t} = \binom{x_{i,j}}{t-1}$ for any integer $t\ge 0$. Furthermore, using the latter formula it is easy to check that the term
\[
\partial_{e_{1,1}}^{m'_{1,1}}\cdots \partial_{e_{k,a_k}}^{m'_{k,a_k}}\binom{x}{m}=\partial_{e_{1,1}}^{m'_{1,1}}\cdots \partial_{e_{k,a_k}}^{m'_{k,a_k}}\left(\lambda\prod_{i=1}^k\prod_{j=1}^{a_i} \binom{x_{i,j}}{n_{i,j}}\right) = \lambda\prod_{i=1}^k\prod_{j=1}^{a_i}\partial_{e_{i,j}}^{n'_{i,j}}\binom{x_{i,j}}{m_{i,j}}
\]
vanishes as soon as there exists some $(i,j)\in [k]\times [a_i]$ such that $m'_{i,j}>m_{i,j}$. This confirms that ${\rm supp}(\psi^*)\subset {\rm supp}(\psi)\setminus \{m\}$. By induction we have $\psi^*(x)=\sum_{m'\in {\rm supp}(\psi^*)}a_{m'} \binom{x}{m'}$, and then $\psi(x) =\lambda\binom{x}{m}+ \sum_{m'\in {\rm supp}(\psi^*)}a_{m'} \binom{x}{m'}$. The result follows.

nodes.name: Lifting continuous homomorphisms to the circle
nodes.statement: Let $a,b\ge 0$ be two integers and let $\phi:\mathbb{Z}^a\times \mathbb{R}^b\rightarrow \mathbb{T}$ be a continuous homomorphism. Then there exists a continuous homomorphism $\psi:\mathbb{Z}^a\times \mathbb{R}^b\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ of the form $(x,y)\mapsto \alpha\cdot x+\beta\cdot y$ for some $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}^a$ and $\beta\in \mathbb{R}^b$ such that $\phi = \pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm} \psi$ where $\pi:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow \mathbb{T}$ is the quotient map.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma A.8
nodes.statement: Splitting the problem between the different coordinates it is enough to prove the result for $\phi:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow \mathbb{T}$ (a homomorphism from $\mathbb{Z}$ to $\mathbb{T}$ is trivially of the desired form). As $\mathbb{R}$ is the universal covering of $\mathbb{T}$, we have that $\phi$ factorizes though $\mathbb{R}$. That is, there exists a continuous homomorphism $\psi:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that $\pi\circ\hspace{-0.02 cm}\psi = \phi$, which completes the proof.

nodes.name: Induction on support size
nodes.statement:
We want to prove that if $\psi$ has finite support then $\psi(x,y)=\pi\left(\sum_{(m,n)\in {\rm supp}(\psi)}\lambda_{m,n} \binom{(x,y)}{(m,n)}\right)$ for some coefficients $\lambda_{m,n}\in \mathbb{R}$ (provided that $\psi$ is continuous).

We prove this by induction on the size of ${\rm supp}(\psi)$. Note that if the support of $\psi$ is 0 then this automatically means that the function equals 0, so there is nothing to prove. For the general case, let $(m,n)\in {\rm supp}(\psi)$ be an element such that if $(m',n')\in L$ satisfies $(m,n)<(m',n')$ then $(m',n')\notin {\rm supp}(\psi)$. Assume without loss of generality that $n_{i_0,\ell_0}>0$ for some $(i_0,\ell_0)\in[k]\times [b_i]$. We leave as an exercise to the reader to check the easier case when for some $(i_0,j_0)\in[k]\times[a_i]$ we have $m_{i_0,j_0}>0$. Note that if none of these exists (neither in the continuous part nor in the discrete part), then $\partial_{(u,v)}\psi(x,y)=0$ for all $(u,v)\in D$. Thus $\psi$ in this case is constant and the result follows.

nodes.name: Quotients of LCH spaces by actions with closed orbit relation
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be an \textsc{lch} space and let $G$ be a topological group acting continuously on $X$ and such that $\{(x,x')\in X\times X:\exists g\in G \text{ such that }x=gx'\}$ is a closed subset of $X\times X$. Then $X/G$ with the quotient topology is also an \textsc{lch} space.

assumptions: Let $X$ be an \textsc{lch} space and let $G$ be a topological group acting continuously on $X$ and such that $\{(x,x')\in X\times X:\exists g\in G \text{ such that }x=gx'\}$ is a closed subset of $X\times X$.
conclusions: Then $X/G$ with the quotient topology is also an \textsc{lch} space.
nodes.label: lem:quo-by-cont-gr-act

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma B.1
nodes.statement: The fact that $G$ acts continuously on $X$ implies that the quotient map $\pi:X\rightarrow X/G$ is open. Hence it is $X/G$ is second-countable and the fact that it is \textsc{lch} follows from \cite[\S 8.3, Proposition 8 and \S 10.4 Proposition 10]{BourbakiGT1}.
nodes.section: B Some results in topology
nodes.statement_short: Open quotient map and Bourbaki's criteria.

nodes.name: Convergence in quotients by group actions
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be an \textsc{lch} space and let $G$ be a group acting continuously on $X$ and such that $\{(x,x')\in X\times X:\exists g\in G \text{ such that }x=gx'\}$ is a closed subset of $X\times X$. Then $\pi(x_n)\rightarrow \pi(x)$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$ in $X/G$ if and only if there exists a sequence $g_n\in G$ such that $g_nx_n\rightarrow x$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$ in $X$.

nodes.name: Lifting convergent sequences through Polish group quotients
nodes.statement: Let $H,G$ be Polish groups and let $\varphi:G\rightarrow H$ be a surjective continuous homomorphism. Then for every sequence $(\varphi(g_n))_{n\ge 0}\subset H$ such that $\varphi(g_n)\rightarrow \varphi(g)$ for some $g\in G$ there exists a sequence $r_n\in \ker(\varphi)$ such that $g_n r_n\rightarrow g$ in $G$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma B.3

nodes.name: Polish groups onto Lie groups

nodes.section: B Some results in topology
assumptions: Let $X,Y$ be \textsc{lch} spaces.
conclusions: Then the space $C(X,Y)$ is Polish.
nodes.label: prop:cont-LCH-polish

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition B.5
nodes.statement: As $X$ is \textsc{lch}, by \cite[\S 46 Ex. 10. (b)]{Mu} there exists a sequence of nested compact subsets $K_n\subset X$ such that $X=\cup_{n=1}^\infty K_n^\circ$ where $A^\circ$ is the interior of the set $A$. Then consider the map $\iota:C(X,Y)\rightarrow \prod_{n=1}^\infty C(K_n,Y)$ that sends $f\mapsto \prod_{n=1}^{\infty} f|_{K_n}$. Then, if $\phi_{n,n+1}:C(K_{n+1},Y)\rightarrow C(K_n,Y)$ is the map $g\mapsto g|_{K_n}$ it is easy to see that this map is continuous. Furthermore, we have $\iota(C(X,Y))= \{(f_n)_{n\ge 1}\in \prod_{n=1}^\infty C(K_n,Y): \phi_{n,n+1}(f_{n+1})=f_n\}$. As the maps $\phi_{n,n+1}$ are continuous we get that $\iota(C(X,Y))$ is a closed subset of $\prod_{n=1}^\infty C(K_n,Y)$. Moreover, the map $\iota$ is injective so there exists a well-defined map $\iota^{-1}:\iota(C(X,Y))\rightarrow C(X,Y)$. Using that $X=\cup_{n=1}^\infty K_n^\circ$ it follows that this map is indeed continuous. Hence $C(X,Y)$ is homeomorphic to a closed subset of $\prod_{n=1}^\infty C(K_n,Y)$. By \cite[Theorem 4.19]{Kechris} each $C(K_n,Y)$ is Polish. Hence so is $\prod_{n=1}^\infty C(K_n,Y)$ and also $\iota(C(X,Y))$, being a closed subset of a Polish space.
nodes.section: B Some results in topology
nodes.statement_short: Embed $C(X,Y)$ as a closed subset of $\prod_n C(K_n,Y)$ for a compact exhaustion; each factor is Polish.
